  52. Notes

The Author’s Introduction

In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. May God bless our master Muḥammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Qutayba said: This is a book in which I have gathered knowledge that it is fitting for anyone who has been granted the honor of a high station, raised through cultivation above the rank of the common crowd, and distinguished from the public by learning and eloquence, to undertake to learn and train himself to retain. For it is indispensable in the courts of kings, if one sits with them; in the gatherings of nobles, if one keeps their company; and in the circles of scholars, if one converses with them. There is scarcely a gathering convened for inquiry, founded on sound judgment, or conducted according to the way of gentlemanly conduct in which some occasion for knowledge does not arise: whether mention is made of a prophet, a king, or a scholar; a lineage, an ancestor, or a period; or one of the days of the Arabs. Then those present need to know the precise story, the tribe’s place, the king’s period, the circumstances of the man mentioned, and the origin of the well-known proverb.

For I have seen many nobles who do not know their lineage, and people of distinguished ancestry who do not know their forebears; and among Quraysh, people who do not know how they are related to the Messenger of God ﷺ—and [his family], or their kinship with the eminent figures among his Companions. I have seen sons of the kings of the non-Arabs who do not know their fathers’ circumstances or times. I have seen people who claim descent from a clan without knowing which of the great tribal divisions it belongs to, and people who claim descent from a sub-clan without knowing which tribe it belongs to. I have seen people who disdained their own fine lineage and claimed descent from a man who left no descendants, like a man I saw claiming descent from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, although Abū Dharr had no descendants; and another claiming descent from Ḥassān ibn Thābit, although the line of Ḥassān’s descendants had died out; and like another who entered before al-Maʾmūn and spoke words that pleased him. Al-Maʾmūn asked him about his lineage, and he said:

“From Ṭayyiʾ, descended from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.”

Al-Maʾmūn said to him, “Are you descended from him in the direct male line?”

“Yes.”

He said:

“Far from it! You are mistaken! Abū Ṭarīf left no descendants.” So his embarrassment at not knowing the circumstances of the man he had chosen as his claimed ancestor was worse than his embarrassment over the lineage he had disdained.

A man may be a leader in belles-lettres, having excelled in it and gained the greatest share of it, yet have neglected some matter of the lawful that he had greater reason to know than some of what he memorized. Then a deficiency attaches to him in that respect, and reproach for it returns upon him—like one who seeks out abstruse points of jurisprudence but neglects the chapters on prayer and the obligatory duties; one who seeks the chains of transmission of hadith but neglects their texts and meanings; or one who seeks the technicalities of grammar and its inflections, yet makes grammatical mistakes in a note he writes or a verse of poetry he recites.

This book of mine comprises many branches of knowledge.

The first is the beginning of creation, the stories of the prophets [may blessings and peace be upon them], their eras, descriptions, lifespans, descendants, and the dispersal of their offspring, and their settlement in the eastern and western regions of the earth, and along the shores of the seas, in the wildernesses, and in the sands, up to the time of the Messiah, Jesus ﵇, and the interval after him.

I connected this with a concise account of the genealogies of the Arabs, limiting it to the great tribal divisions and well-known sub-clans.

Then I followed it with reports about the Messenger of God ﷺ—concerning his lineage; his paternal uncles and aunts, maternal aunts, and grandmothers on his father’s and mother’s sides; his relatives who nursed him; his wives, children, and freedmen; and his circumstances during his call and military expeditions, up to the time he died ﷺ.

[Then come] reports about the Ten among the Emigrants—may God have mercy on them—then the famous Companions; then the caliphs, from Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān to Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Muʿtaṣim, al-Mustaʿīn bi-llāh; the notable Companions of the Sultan and those who rebelled against them among the Khārijites; then the Successors and those after them among the transmitters of hadith and adherents of personal opinion; those among them known for Rāfiḍism, Shiʿism, irjāʾ, and Qadarism; reciters from the people of the Ḥijāz, Mecca, the two Iraqs, and Syria; genealogists and purveyors of historical reports; transmitters of poetry and rare vocabulary; grammarians; those who shunned one another among the Companions and Successors; and the first person to introduce something that endured over the passage of time.

I mentioned the famous mosques, such as the Kaʿba, the Sacred Mosque in Jerusalem, the Mosque of Medina, the Mosque of Basra, the Mosque of Kufa, and the Mosque of Damascus; when they were built, and by whose hands they were founded.

I identified the Arabian Peninsula, the boundaries of al-Sawād and the Jazīra between the Tigris and Euphrates, and the boundaries of Najd, the Ḥijāz, and Tihāma.

I reported on the conquests: which were taken by force and which by treaty, and who held both Iraqs.

And on the difference between the earliest and later Emigrants.

And on the mukhāḍramūn, those who lived through both the Jāhiliyya and Islam.

And on the reason for reducing the alms levied on the Christians of Banū Taghlib.

And on the religions of the Arabs in the Jāhiliyya.

And on the professions of the nobles in the Jāhiliyya.

And on those afflicted by ailments prevalent among them, such as leprosy, lameness, deafness, mutilation, elephantiasis, urinary retention, blue eyes, prognathism, hairlessness, baldness, bad breath, blindness, and loss of both hands.

And on things that occurred successively in a single sequence and had no counterpart.

And on those excessively tall, and those excessively short.

[And on those whose mothers carried them beyond the usual term of pregnancy, and those whose mothers carried them for less than the usual term]; and on those attributed to clans and fathers other than their own.

And on those known by their teknonyms.

And on the plagues and the times when they occurred.

And on the famous days, such as the Day of Dhū Qār, the two Fijār battles, the Alliance of al-Fuḍūl, the Alliance of the Perfumed Ones, the war between Bakr and Taghlib, and the War of Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ.

And on the tales of people whose names became proverbial, such as Ḥājib’s bow, [and the stupidity] of Bāqil, Māriya’s earrings, Khuraym the Delicate, the barber of Sābāṭ, the anemones of al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir, the tale of Khurāfa, Barjān the Thief, Saḥbān Wāʾil, Ṭufayl, after whom the ṭufayliyyūn are named, the treasure of al-Nuṭf, al-Kasʿī’s regret, ʿArqūb’s promises, Ḥunayn’s sandals, the perfume of Minsham, and the like.

I reported on the kings of al-Ḥīra, the rīdāfa, the kings of Yemen, and the kings of Persia and others, king by king, their number and the lengths of their reigns, and a selection of their histories.

In all that I have recounted, my aim was brevity and concision, and to focus on the well-known reports rather than the obscure, and on what is commonly spoken of rather than what is not. Had I aimed at exhaustive coverage, the book would have grown so long that people would be unable to copy it, let alone memorize it; the obscure and the clear would have become intermixed, so that ears would reject it and people would grow weary of it. A person is more curious about what they already know something about, and more eager to learn it; it is closer to them and more firmly fixed in their minds.

I have stipulated that you learn and familiarize yourself with what is in this book. Had I made it longer and included what would have kept you occupied for most of your life, I would have wearied and exhausted you and left you needing to pick out some things from it for knowledge and memorization and leave others. I spared you that and took the greatest care on your behalf, and compared my own judgment with that of the traditionists among our brethren and the genealogists.

I hope that I have fulfilled your heart’s desire, brought comfort to your heart, and achieved for myself what I hoped for in enlightening and guiding you: God’s success and a good reward.

The Beginning of Creation

Abū Muḥammad said: I read in the Torah, in the first of its books, that the first of God’s creation that He, exalted is He, created was heaven and earth. The earth was desolate and empty, darkness was over the deep, and the wind of God [blessed and exalted is He] moved over the face of the water. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. God saw that it was good; He separated it from the darkness and called it Day, and He called the darkness Night. There was evening and there was morning: Sunday.

God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let there be a vault in the midst of the water, to separate water from water.”

And there was a vault. He separated the water that was below from the water that was above, and God called that upper vault Heaven. There was evening and there was morning: Monday. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb Ziyād ibn Yaḥyā related to us; he said: Mālik ibn Suʿayr related to us; he said: Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid related to us, from Abū Ṣāliḥ:

Concerning God’s saying, “By the sea, filled,” 52:6, he said: ʿAlī ﵁ used to say: “It is a sea beneath the Throne.”

This resembles what is mentioned in the Torah, that heaven lies between two waters.

The account returns to the Torah:

God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let all the water beneath heaven gather in one place, and let the dry land appear.” And so it was. God called the dry land Earth, and He called the gathered waters Seas.

Then God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let the earth bring forth the green growth of plants and trees bearing fruit, each according to its kind, with its seed in it.” The earth brought this forth, and God saw that it was good. There was evening and there was morning: Tuesday.

God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let there be two lights in the vault of heaven, to separate night from day, and let them be signs for days and years.” And there were two lights: the greater, to rule the day, and the lesser, to rule the night. God saw that it was good. There was evening and there was morning: Wednesday.

God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let every living creature move in the water, and let birds fly over the earth in the expanse of the vault.” And God, mighty and glorious, created great sea monsters, and made every living creature in the water move according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind. God saw that it was good, blessed them, and said, “Be fruitful and multiply.”

There was evening and there was dawn: Thursday.

Then God, mighty and glorious, said, “Let Us create a human being in Our image.” He created Adam from the earth’s soil and breathed into his face the breath of life. He said, “It is not right for Adam to be alone; I shall make for him a helper like himself.” He cast a deep sleep upon him, took one of his ribs, and closed the place with flesh. He named the rib he had taken:

“Woman,” because she was taken from man. He brought her to Adam. Adam said, “Bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh! For this reason a man leaves his father and mother and follows his wife, and the two of them become one body.” God, mighty and glorious, left them and said, “Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth, and have dominion over the kinds of the sea, the birds of heaven, the livestock, the beasts, the plants of the earth, its trees, and its fruit.” He saw all that He had created, and it was very good. There was evening and there was morning: Friday.

All the works of God, mighty and glorious, which He had made, were completed. Then He rested on the seventh day from His creation, blessed it, purified it, and sanctified it.

[Abū Muḥammad said]:

“Rest” means completing and finishing a matter. This is the meaning of His saying, “We shall attend to you, O two weighty ones,” 55:31: that is, “We shall turn our attention to you,” for He, mighty and glorious, is not distracted by one affair from another.

Our Lord planted Paradise in Eden, and in it was a river watering Paradise. It divided into four branches: Pishon, which encircles all the land of Havilah, where the finest gold, crystal stones, and turquoise are found. The name of the second river is Gihon, which encircles the land of Cush and the Abyssinians. The name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Asshur. He said:

“This is al-Mawṣil.” The fourth river is the Euphrates.

He planted the Tree of Life in the midst of Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and said to Adam:

“Eat whatever you wish from the trees of Paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for on the day you eat from it, you will die.”

[Abū Muḥammad said]: He means that you will pass into the condition of one who dies.

The serpent was the most cunning of the beasts of the earth. It said to the woman, “You will not die if you eat from it. Rather, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” The woman took some of its fruit, ate, and gave it to her husband. Their eyes were opened, and they realized that they were naked. They joined fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths. Then they heard the voice of God, mighty and glorious, in the Garden at the light of day. Adam and his wife hid among the trees of the Garden. God, exalted is He, called to them. Adam said, “I heard Your voice in Paradise and saw that I was naked, so I hid from You.” He said:

“Who showed you that you were naked? Ah, have you eaten from the tree I forbade you?” He said, “The woman gave it to me.” The woman said, “The serpent gave it to me.” God, mighty and glorious, said to the serpent:

“Because you have done this, you are accursed. You shall crawl on your belly and eat dust. I shall set enmity between you and the woman and her child: he shall tread on your head, and you shall bite his heel.” He said to the woman, “As for you, I shall greatly increase your pains and pregnancies. You shall bear children in pain, and you shall turn to your husband, and he shall rule over you.” He said to Adam, “The earth is accursed because of you. It will bring forth thistles and thorns, and you shall eat from it in hardship, with the sweat of your face and brow, until you return to the dust, for you are dust.”

God, mighty and glorious, named his wife Eve, because she is the mother of every living thing, and clothed her and him in garments of skins.

He said, “Adam has come to know good and evil; perhaps he will put forth his hand and take from the Tree of Life and eat from it, and live forever.” God, mighty and glorious, expelled him from the east of the Garden of Eden to the earth from which he had been taken.

This is what is in the Torah. As for Wahb ibn Munabbih, he related:

“The jinn were the inhabitants of the earth before Adam. A group among them disbelieved and shed blood, so God, mighty and glorious, commanded a host of angels from the lowest heaven—among them Iblīs, who was their leader—to descend to earth and drive the jinn from it. He cited as evidence His saying, exalted is He:

‘And the jinn We created before, from the scorching fire,’ 15:27; that is, before We created Adam. They drove them to the farthest borders and the islands of the seas. Iblīs and the host with him inhabited the settled lands and countryside of the earth. Iblīs’s name was ʿAzāzīl.” Then he mentioned God’s creation, exalted is He, of Adam, and said: “Then He clothed him in a garment of nail.” The garment became newer and more beautiful each day. But when they ate from the tree, the garment peeled away from them, and it was like the sun’s rays, until it reached the tips of their fingers, on their hands and feet.

He said: God, mighty and glorious, created him on Friday, and they remained in Paradise for six days. The first thing they ate in Paradise was grapes. The tree from which they were forbidden to eat was the tree of grain. God, mighty and glorious, made the serpent Adam’s servant in Paradise. It was the most beautiful of God’s creatures, exalted is He, and had legs like a camel’s. Iblīs offered himself to all the beasts of the earth, saying that they should let him into Paradise. All refused, except the serpent. It carried him between two of its fangs and then brought him into Paradise.

He said: When God, mighty and glorious, accepted Adam’s repentance, He commanded him to travel to Mecca. He folded the earth for him and drew the wastelands close, so that wherever he set foot on earth, it became cultivated, until he reached Mecca. His descent from the Garden of Eden was in the east of the land of India. God, mighty and glorious, sent Eve down at Jeddah, the serpent in the wilderness, and Iblīs on the shore of the Sea of al-Ubulla. Ibn Isḥāq said:

“The learned say that Adam and Eve descended upon a mountain called Wāsim, in the land of India. It is a mountain between villages in India today, between al-Dahnaj and al-Mandal.”

[Abū Muḥammad said]: The Arabs attribute perfume and al-yalanjūj to al-Mandal. The poet said of a woman:

When she appears, what is in her garments calls out: fragrant in scent, and scented with al-Mandal.

Al-mandalī is al-ʿūd; al-muṭayyar means split.

The Appearance of Adam—Peace Be Upon Him

He said: Adam was beardless; beards grew only for his descendants after him. He was tall, very hairy, curly-haired, dark-complexioned, and the most handsome of all creatures.

When he descended to earth, he ploughed, while Eve separated the hair and wove it with her hands.

Abū Muḥammad said:

I read in the Torah that Adam lay with his wife Eve, and she bore him Cain. She said, “I have acquired a man for God.” Then she bore Abel, his brother. Cain was a ploughman, and Abel a shepherd. They each brought an offering. Abel’s offering was accepted, but Cain’s was not, so he killed his brother Abel.

Wahb said:

Adam used to have a boy and a girl born to him in each pregnancy. The men among them would marry whichever of their sisters they wished, except their twin sister. Cain refused to marry his sister—his twin—to his brother Abel, and said, “I have a greater claim to my sister, who is my twin.” Adam grew angry and said, “Go and submit your case to God by means of an offering. Whichever of you has his offering accepted has the greater claim to her.” They brought their offerings at Minā, and this is why the place where people sacrifice has been there ever since. A fire descended and accepted Abel’s offering. Cain killed his brother Abel, smashing his head with a stone, and carried away his sister until he came to a valley among the valleys of Yemen in the east of Eden, and hid there. Adam learned what he had done and found Abel slain. The earth had dried up his blood, so Adam cursed the earth. Because of Adam’s curse, the earth no longer dries blood and it brings forth thorns.

Abū Muḥammad said:

In the Torah: Adam lay with his wife Eve, and she bore him a boy. He named him Seth, because he was a substitute from God in place of Abel.

Adam had forty children, born in twenty pregnancies. The prohibition of carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine was revealed to them, along with the letters of the alphabet on twenty-one sheets. This was the first book in the world, by which God set a boundary for all tongues.

Abū Muḥammad said: Zayd ibn Akhzam related to me; he said: Yaḥyā ibn Kathīr related to me; he said: ʿUthmān ibn Saʿd the scribe related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from ʿUtayy, from Ubayy:

When Adam ﵇ was near death, he desired a cluster from among the clusters of Paradise. His sons went to seek one for him, and the angels met them. They said, “Where are you going, children of Adam?” They replied, “Our father desires a cluster from among the clusters of Paradise.” They said, “Go back; we will take care of him.” They returned to him, and the angels took his soul, washed him, embalmed him, and shrouded him. Gabriel prayed over him, with the angels behind Gabriel and his sons behind the angels, and they buried him. They said, “This is your practice for your dead, children of Adam.”

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

A grave was dug for him on Mount Abū Qubays (1), in a place called the Cave of the Treasure. Adam remained in that cave until the time of the Flood. Noah took him out and placed him with him in a coffin aboard the Ark. When the water had receded and the people aboard the Ark saw the land, Noah returned him to his place.

Abū Muḥammad said:

I found in the Torah (2) that Adam lived for a total of nine hundred and thirty years.

Wahb said:

Adam lived for one thousand years.

Seth ibn Adam

Wahb said:

Seth ibn Adam was the most handsome of Adam’s children, the best of them, the most like him, and the dearest to him.

He was his father’s legatee and heir-designate. He was the one from whom all humankind descended, and the genealogies of people ended with him. He was the one who built the Kaʿba of clay and stones. There was a tent there for Adam, which God had placed there for him from Paradise. God sent down fifty scrolls to Seth ibn Adam. Seth lived nine hundred and twelve years.

Seth had sons and daughters, among them Enosh. Enosh had Qīnāṇ.

Qīnāṇ had Mahlāʾīl. Mahlāʾīl had Yārid. Yārid had Akhnūkh, who was Idrīs ﵇.

Idrīs ﷺ

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

The Prophet Idrīs ﷺ was tall, with a large belly and broad chest, little body hair, and abundant hair on his head. One of his ears was larger than the other. There was a white spot on his body, though it was not leprosy. He had a soft voice and spoke gently; when he walked, his steps were short. He was named Idrīs because he studied the Book of God Most High and the practices of Islam so much. God Most High sent down to him thirty scrolls. He was the first to write with a pen and the first to weave clothes and wear them. Before him, people wore animal skins. One thousand people whom he called to the faith responded to him. When God raised him up, they differed after him and introduced innovations until the time of Noah. He was Noah’s great-grandfather. He was raised up when he was three hundred and sixty-five years old.

In the Torah:

“Akhnūkh was one of God’s finest servants,” and God raised him up to Himself.

The Prophet Idrīs ﷺ had Methuselah when he was three hundred years old. Methuselah had Lamech. Lamech had a son and named him Noah.

Noah ﵇

Wahb said:

Noah was the first prophet whom God commissioned after Idrīs. He was a carpenter, tending toward a dark complexion, with a narrow face and an elongated head, large eyes, thick upper arms, thin shins, fleshy thighs, thin forearms, a prominent navel, and a long, broad beard. He was tall and imposing. He was severe in his anger and rebukes. God sent him to his people when he was fifty years old. He remained among them for a thousand years less fifty: three centuries among his people, living with them and growing old among them, but they did not respond to him, and only a few followed him, as God—mighty and sublime is He—said. (2)

In the Torah: (1) God—mighty and sublime is He—inspired him: “Build the Ark, and let its length be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. Let its door be in its side. Enter the Ark, you, your wife, your sons, and your sons’ wives; and of every kind of flesh, two of each, male and female. For I will send rain upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and destroy everything I have created on the earth. Make a coffin in which to place the body of Adam, and make the coffin from cypress wood (2); and take provisions for a year with you.”

Noah did so.

God sent the Flood upon the earth in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month. The Ark remained on the water for one hundred and fifty days. Then God sent a wind that swept over the earth, and the earth dried up the water. The springs of the earth and the sluices of the heavens were closed, and the Ark came to rest in the sixth month on Mount Qardā (3). In the tenth month, the mountain peaks appeared. When it was the six-hundred-and-first year, on the first day of the first month, the water receded from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the Ark and saw the surface of the earth.

On the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth had dried.

This is what is in the Torah.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

It was related to us that the Ark set sail on the tenth day of Rajab. It remained on the water for one hundred and fifty days, then came to rest on al-Jūdī—a mountain in the land of al-Jazīra—for a month.

Noah went out onto the earth on the tenth day of Muḥarram.

In the Torah: (1) God commanded Noah to leave the Ark, he and those with him. They went out, and Noah built an altar to God. He offered a sacrifice on the altar. God made the sacrifice a pleasing fragrance, blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: “Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth. Let the fear of you fall upon the beasts of the earth, every bird of the heavens, and the fish of the seas. But you shall not eat flesh with its life-blood in it. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood will be shed by humans, for God—mighty and sublime is He—created Adam in His image.” And God said to Noah: “The sign of My covenant, which I establish with you, that I will not destroy the earth by a flood, is the bow that I have placed in the clouds. When you see it, remember My covenant.”

Wahb ibn Munabbih related:

Noah entered the Ark with his three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—their wives, and forty men and forty women among the Muslims. When they came out, they built a village and named it:

“Eighty” (1), because there were eighty houses in it, one house for each person who had believed with him. It is today called Sūq Thamānīn. He offered a sacrifice and fasted the month of Ramaḍān; he was the first to fast it.

He said: Water was called a flood because it rose over everything.

He said: From the death of Adam ﵇ until the earth was inundated, two thousand two hundred and forty-two years passed.

In the Torah:

Noah lived for three hundred and fifty years after the Flood, so Noah’s lifespan was nine hundred and fifty years.

Wahb said:

Noah’s lifespan was one thousand years: he was commissioned to his people when he was fifty years old, and remained among them, calling them, until he died after nine hundred and fifty years.

Noah’s Children ﵇

Abū Muḥammad said:

In the Torah (2): Noah had Shem, Ham, and Japheth after he had lived five hundred years.

As for the one who differed from him—the one who said to him, “O my son, embark with us”—he was Yām. He was the one to whom Noah said:

“O my son, embark with us, and do not be with the unbelievers.” I have found no mention of him in the Torah. All people descend from these three.

He said: Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Maslama ibn ʿAlqama al-Māzinī:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said to Kaʿb: (1) “From which of Adam’s two sons did humankind descend?” He replied: “Neither of them had descendants. The murdered one passed away (2), while the murderer’s descendants perished in the Flood. People are from the sons of Noah, Noah is from the sons of Seth, and Seth is the son of Adam.”

In the Torah: (3) When Noah came out of the Ark, he planted a vineyard, then pressed wine from its fruit, drank, became drunk, and lay uncovered inside his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers about it. Shem and Japheth took a cloak, laid it across their shoulders, and walked backward, covering their father’s nakedness while facing away. Noah awoke from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him. He said: “Cursed be the father of Canaan; he shall be a slave of slaves to his brothers.” And he said: “Blessed be Shem. May God multiply Japheth’s descendants, and may he dwell in the dwelling of Shem. The father of Canaan shall be a slave to them both.”

Ham ibn Noah

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

Ham ibn Noah was a white man, handsome in face and form. God—mighty and sublime is He—changed his complexion and the complexions of his descendants because of his father’s curse. He went away, followed by his children, and they settled on the seacoast. God increased their numbers and caused them to multiply; they are the Sudan. Their food was fish, so they sharpened their teeth until they made them like needles, because fish would stick to them. Some of his children settled in the Maghrib. Ham’s sons were Kūsh ibn Ham, Canaan ibn Ham, and Qūṭ ibn Ham.

As for Qūṭ ibn Ham, he traveled and settled in the land of India and Sind; their people are his descendants.

As for Kūsh and Canaan, the peoples of the Sudan, Nubia, the Zanj, the Qazzān, the Zaghāwa, the Abyssinians, the Copts, and the Berbers are descended from their sons.

Japheth ibn Noah

As for Japheth, his descendants include the Ṣaqāliba, Burjān, and Ashbān. Their dwelling places were in the land of the Romans before the Romans. Among his descendants are the Turks, the Khazars, Gog, and Magog.

Shem ibn Noah

As for Shem ibn Noah, he settled in the middle of the earth: the Ḥaram and its environs, Yemen as far as Ḥaḍramawt, then ʿUmān, Baḥrayn, ʿĀlij (1), Yabrīn, Wabār, al-Daww, and al-Dahnāʾ.

Among Shem’s descendants are Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah and Arpachshad ibn Shem ibn Noah.

Among the descendants of Arpachshad ibn Shem are Qaḥṭān ibn ʿĀbir ibn Shālakh ibn Arpachshad ibn Shem ibn Noah, and his son Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān, the first to speak Arabic. He settled in the land of Yemen and is the forefather of all the Yemenis. He was the first to be greeted by his children with the greeting of kings: “May you greet the morning in prosperity,” and “May you be spared the curse.”

Among the descendants of Arpachshad is Yaqṭan ibn ʿĀbir ibn Shālakh ibn Arpachshad ibn Shem ibn Noah.

Yaqṭan is the forefather of Jurhum, and Jurhum is Yaʿrub’s cousin. Jurhum were among those who lived in Yemen and spoke Arabic. Then they settled in Mecca and remained there; Qaṭūrāʾ, their cousins, settled there too. Then God settled Ishmael ﵇ there. He married into Jurhum, so they are the maternal uncles of his children.

Among the descendants of Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah is ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah. They lived among the sand dunes of al-Aḥqāf, and God sent their brother Hūd to them.

Among the descendants of Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah is Thamūd ibn ʿĀbir—also said to be Thamūd ibn Jāthir ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah. He was a cousin of ʿĀd ibn Aram. They lived in al-Ḥijr, and God sent their brother Ṣāliḥ ﵇ to them.

Among the descendants of Aram ibn Shem are Ṭasm and Jadīs, the sons of Lāwudh ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah.

They settled in al-Yamāma. Their brother ʿAmālīq ibn Lāwudh ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah settled in the Ḥaram and the Levant, some in each. Among them were the ʿAmālīq, peoples who spread across the lands; among them were the Pharaohs of Egypt and the tyrants, and among them were the kings of Persia and the people of Khurāsān.

Their brother Umaym ibn Lāwudh ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah settled in the land of Persia.

All the peoples of Persia descend from him:

Among the descendants of Shem was Māsh ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah. He settled in Babylon and had Nimrod ibn Māsh, who built the Tower in Babylon and ruled for five hundred years. In his time, God divided the languages: He made nineteen languages among Shem’s descendants, seventeen among Ham’s, and thirty-six among Japheth’s.

It is said that the Nabataeans are descended from Māsh. They were called Nabataeans (1) because they brought water to the surface.

It is also said that the Nabataeans descend from Shārūkh ibn Arghū ibn Fāligh ibn ʿĀbir ibn Shālakh ibn Arpachshad ibn Shem ibn Noah, and that Nimrod was the brother of Shārūkh ibn Arghū.

All the prophets, both non-Arab and Arab, and all the Arabs, whether Yemenite or Nizārī, descend from Shem ibn Noah.

Hūd ﵇

He was Hūd ibn Shālakh ibn Arpachshad ibn Shem ibn Noah.

Wahb said:

He was Hūd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riyāḥ ibn Ḥārith ibn ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Aram ibn Shem ibn Noah. Of all Aram’s descendants, he most resembled Aram, except for Joseph. He was dark-complexioned, hirsute, and handsome. ʿĀd consisted of thirteen tribes who lived among the sand dunes. Their land was the most fertile of lands, and their numbers and settlements were concentrated in al-Daww (2), al-Dahnāʾ, ʿĀlij, Yabrīn, and Wabār, extending to ʿUmān, Ḥaḍramawt, and Yemen. When God—mighty and sublime is He—became displeased with them, He turned it into wastelands and thickets.

When God destroyed his people, Hūd and those who believed with him went to Mecca and settled there. They remained there until they died. Hūd was a merchant.

Ṣāliḥ ﵇

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

God sent Ṣāliḥ to his people when he was nearing puberty. He was fair-skinned with a reddish tinge, with straight hair. He used to walk barefoot and wore no shoes, as the Messiah walked, and he took neither dwelling nor house. He remained with the she-camel of his Lord wherever it went.

He was Ṣāliḥ son of ʿUbayd son of ʿĀbir son of Iram son of Sām son of Noah. His people lived at al-Ḥijr. Between al-Ḥijr and Qurḥ there were eighteen miles; Qurḥ is Wādī al-Qurā.

When his people said to him, “Bring us a sign,” he took them to a hill. When the she-camel saw it, it began to heave as a woman in labor does, and split open, bringing forth the she-camel.

The one who hamstrung the she-camel was Aḥmar of Thamūd, whose ill omen is proverbial. His name was Qudār son of Sālif. He was red-haired, blond, blue-eyed, sināṭ, and short.1 The other one who hamstrung it was Muṣdaʿ son of Mihrāj. He was thin, tall, reckless, and erratic. When the she-camel was hamstrung, its foal climbed a mountain and then bellowed, whereupon the punishment struck them.

Someone other than Wahb said:

For this reason, the Arabs say, “A foal bellowed above them in the sky,” when they have perished.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

When God destroyed them, Ṣāliḥ said to those who believed with him: “My people, this is a land whose people God has incurred wrath against. So leave it and make for the Sanctuary of God and His protection.” At once they entered the state of consecration for the pilgrimage and donned the ʿabāʾ cloaks as their pilgrimage garments. They set out on red she-camels, bridled with ropes of palm fiber, and then traveled, chanting the pilgrim’s invocation, until they reached Mecca. They remained there until they died. Their graves are west of the Kaʿba, between Dār al-Nadwa and the Ḥijr.

Ṣāliḥ was a merchant.

Abraham the Intimate Friend ﵇

He was Abraham son of Tāraḫ son of Nāḥūr son of Ashragh son of Arghū son of Fāligh son of ʿĀbir son of Shāliḫ son of Arfakhshadh son of Sām son of Noah.

Abū Muḥammad said:

This is how Wahb gave the lineage. I compared it with the lineage in the Torah and found it to agree, except that where it has “Ashragh,” I found “Shārūgh.”

Wahb said:

Abraham was the first to provide hospitality to a guest, the first to prepare tharīd and feed the poor, and the first to trim his moustache, shave with a razor, and undergo circumcision. He was also the first to cut his nails, use a tooth-stick, part his hair, rinse his mouth, clear his nose, and cleanse himself with water. He was the first to grow gray hair, at the age of one hundred and fifty. This was because when Sarah gave birth to Isaac, the Canaanites said, “Do you not marvel at this old man and old woman? They found an abandoned infant and adopted him. God fashioned Isaac to look like Abraham, so that the two could not be told apart. Thus God marked Abraham with gray hair.”

I found in the Torah that Nāḥūr and Hārān were born to Tāraḫ, Abraham’s father. Hārān had three children: Lot, Sarah, and Milcah. Hārān died during the lifetime of his father Tāraḫ, in the land where he had been born. Abraham married Sarah, Hārān’s daughter, and Nāḥūr married Milcah, Hārān’s daughter. Sarah was barren. Tāraḫ took his son Abraham and his grandson Lot and set out with them for the land of Ḥarrān, where they settled. Then Tāraḫ died in the land of Ḥarrān.

Wahb said:

The first to “build Ḥarrān” were two brothers of Abraham, said to be named Hārān—after whom Ḥarrān was named—and Nāhir, who was the father of Rifqā, Isaac’s wife.

Wahb said:

Two thousand two hundred and forty years separated Noah and Abraham. The one who disputed with Abraham about his Lord was Nimrod son of Canaan. He was the first to tyrannize, subjugate, seize by force, and establish evil practices; the first to wear a crown; and the first to devise the science of the stars, study it, and put it into practice. God destroyed him with a mosquito that entered his nostrils. He was tormented by it for forty years, then died.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

Two believers and two unbelievers ruled the earth. The believers were Solomon son of David and Dhū al-Qarnayn; the unbelievers were Nimrod and Bukht Naṣṣar. A fifth from this community will rule it.

He said: When God, Mighty and Glorious, saved Abraham from the fire, he left the land of Babylon—he was at Kūthā— and went to the Holy Land. He set out with Sarah and his nephew Lot. Lot had believed in him, along with a group of his people, and they followed him. They reached Ḥarrān and stayed there for a time. Then they set out for the Jordan and came to a city in which there was a tyrant among the tyrants of Egypt, named Ṣādūf. It was he who made advances toward Sarah, but God prevented him from taking her. God also provided Sarah with Hājar, the mother of Ishmael, and granted her enjoyment of her. Hājar was an Egyptian woman.

Wahb said:

That tyrant left the city, and God gave it to Abraham. Abraham prospered there, and God increased his wealth there. He divided it with Lot, giving him half of it. God sent down twenty scrolls to Abraham.

Abū Muḥammad said:

In the Torah it says that Sarah gave Hājar in marriage to Abraham, saying, “God has denied me children, so go in to my slave woman; perhaps through her we may be comforted by a child.”

Wahb said:

She gave her to him.

In the Torah it says that Hājar gave birth to Ishmael when Abraham was eighty-six years old.

Sarah gave birth to Isaac when Abraham was one hundred years old. Abraham underwent circumcision at the age of ninety-nine, and circumcised Ishmael when he was thirteen, along with some of the children of foreigners. Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years and died in Ḥebron, the village of the giants in the land of Canaan.

Wahb said:

Abraham married a Canaanite woman named Qanṭūrā, who bore him four sons. He married another woman named Ḥajūrā, who bore him seven sons. Thus all of Abraham’s children were thirteen men. Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years.

Wahb said:

He lived two hundred years. He was buried in the field of Ḥebron, which he had bought; Sarah was buried there too.

Ishmael son of Abraham, blessings and ﵇

He said: God commanded Abraham to travel to Mecca with Ishmael and his mother. He told him that He had established the Sacred House for him, that its construction would be carried out by his hands, and that Ishmael would bring forth its water for providing drink. He traveled with the two of them and left them there. A party from Jurhum came and settled in the ravines of Mecca. They gave Ishmael seven she-goats, which became the foundation of his wealth.

Ishmael grew up among their children and learned archery. He spoke their language, then sought a wife from among them, and they married one of their women to him.

Ibn Isḥāq said: “She was the daughter of Muḍāḍ son of ʿAmr al-Jurhumī.”

She bore Ishmael twelve sons. Among them were Qaydār and Nabṭ. Genealogists differ over the lineage of Maʿadd son of ʿAdnān: some say he descended from Qaydār, while others say:

“He descended from Nabṭ.”

Nabṭ was Ishmael’s firstborn, and he succeeded his father as guardian of the House. After Nabṭ, its guardianship passed to Muḍāḍ son of ʿAmr al-Jurhumī, Nabṭ’s maternal grandfather.

When Ishmael’s descendants became numerous, Mecca grew too small for them, and they spread through the lands. They never entered a land without God giving them mastery over its people; they drove out the ʿAmālīq.

Ishmael lived one hundred and thirty-seven years and was buried in the Ḥijr. His mother Hājar was buried there too.

Isaac son of Abraham, blessings and ﵇

He said: Isaac is the one who was to be sacrificed; most people of learning hold this view, and I found him identified as the one to be sacrificed in the Torah.

He said: Muḥammad ibn Khālid ibn Khaddāsh told me: Salm ibn Qutayba told us:

ʿAlī ibn al-Mubārak told us: al-Ḥasan told us, from al-Aḥnaf, from al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, who said:

“The one to be sacrificed was Isaac.”

He said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb told us: Abū Dāwūd told us, from Shuʿba, from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿAbd Allāh, who said:

“The one to be sacrificed was Isaac.”

He said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb told us: Abū Dāwūd told us, from Yazīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Simāk ibn Ḥarb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Muntašir, from Masrūq, who said:

“The one to be sacrificed was Isaac.”

ʿAmr ibn Ḥammād related from Asbāṭ, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murra al-Hamdānī, from Ibn Masʿūd, and from people among the Companions of the Messenger of God, blessings and ﷺ in the full and complete account of Abraham: that the one to be sacrificed was Isaac.

It has reached us from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAmr ibn Abī Sufyān, who said: I heard Kaʿb relate to Abū Hurayra:

“The one to be sacrificed was Isaac.”

Some people say that the one to be sacrificed was Ishmael.

He said: Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Shahīdī told me: Yaḥyā ibn Yamān told us, from Isrāʾīl, from Thuwair, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said:

“The one to be sacrificed was Ishmael.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd told us: Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm told us, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Faḍl, from al-Ḥajjāj ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from the poet al-Farazdaq, who said:

“I heard Abū Hurayra say from the pulpit of the Messenger of God, blessings and ﷺ:

‘The one to be sacrificed was Ishmael.’”

In the Torah, it says that Isaac married Rifqā, daughter of Nāḥūr son of Tāraḫ, and that she was his cousin.

Wahb said:

“She was Rifqā, daughter of Bāhir son of Azrā, his cousin.”

She bore him ʿĪṣū and Jacob, twins in a single womb. ʿĪṣū came out first, then Jacob after him, with his hand clinging to ʿĪṣū’s heel; so he was named Jacob.

Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years. When he died, his two sons buried him in the field Abraham had bought, beside Abraham’s grave, blessings and ﵇.

ʿĪṣū son of Isaac son of Abraham

He said: ʿĪṣū was a red-complexioned man with hair over his body. He had rings of hair upon him and was a hunter. He was the ancestor of the Romans.

The Roman was a sturdy, red-complexioned man, yellow against a white complexion, intensely yellow; for this reason the Romans were called the Banū al-Aṣfar, “the sons of the yellow one.”

ʿĪṣū married his cousin, a daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham, who bore him the Romans, descendants of ʿĪṣū,

and five others.

Everyone in the land of the Romans today is descended from this group. Some people claim that the Spaniards are among his descendants.

Esau lived one hundred and forty-seven years, as did Jacob. They were buried in the field beside Abraham’s grave ﵇.

Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham ﵈

He said: Jacob was Israel, from whom all the tribes were born. He was sparsely haired, thin, grave, and scarcely ever left the tent. The same is said in the Torah. Isaac had instructed him not to marry a Canaanite woman, but to marry a woman from among the daughters of his maternal uncle, Laban son of Nahor son of Azar. Laban lived by the Euphrates. Jacob set out to him, and night overtook him on the way. He spent the night with a stone for a pillow. In a dream, he saw a ladder set up to one of the gates of heaven above his head, with angels descending and ascending upon it. God revealed to him: “I am God; there is no god but Me. I am your God and the God of your forefathers.” He then bequeathed this holy land to him, to his descendants, and to his sons after him; blessed them and him; and placed in them the Scripture, wisdom, and prophecy. “Then I shall be with you and protect you until I bring you back to this place, and make it a house in which you and your descendants will worship Me.” This is the Holy House.

He went to his maternal uncle and asked for his daughter Rachel in marriage. He had two daughters: Leah, the elder, and Rachel, the younger. His uncle said to him, “Do you have any property with which to marry her?” Jacob replied:

“No. I can only serve you as a hired laborer until you have received your daughter’s bride-price.”

“Her bride-price is seven years of service to me,” he said.

Jacob said, “Marry me to Rachel—that is my condition—and I will serve you.”

His uncle said, “Agreed between us.”

Jacob served him for seven years. When he had fulfilled the agreement, his uncle gave him his elder daughter Leah and brought her to him at night. In the morning, Jacob found her to be other than the one he had stipulated. He went to his uncle while he was among his people and said, “You have deceived and cheated me, taken seven years of my labor, and passed off to me a woman who is not my wife.”

His uncle said, “My sister’s son, you wanted to bring disgrace, shame, and reproach upon your maternal uncle—who is also your father. When have you ever seen people marry the younger daughter before the elder?

“Come, then, serve me for another seven years, and I will marry you to her sister.” At that time, people used to marry two sisters at once, until God sent Moses and revealed the Torah to him. Jacob served him for seven years, and he gave him Rachel; then Jacob went in to Rachel.

Leah bore him four of the tribes: Reuben, Judah, Simeon, and Levi.

Rachel bore him Joseph, his brother Benjamin, and their sisters.

When Laban sent his daughters to Jacob, he gave each of them a maidservant. The two women gave the maidservants to Jacob, and each of them bore him three groups from among the tribes.

Then Jacob parted from his uncle and returned until he came to encamp near his brother Esau.

Jacob lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years, and his age was one hundred and forty-seven years. He was buried beside Abraham’s grave ﵉.

Joseph son of Jacob ﵈

From the time Joseph entered Egypt until Moses son of ʿImrān entered it, four hundred years elapsed. Joseph lived twenty-three years after his father’s death.

In the Torah: he lived one hundred and ten years.

Joseph had two sons: Ephraim, the ancestor of Joshua son of Nun son of Ephraim; and the other, Misha.

Misha had a son called Moses, who prophesied before Moses son of ʿImrān. The people of the Torah claim that he was the one who sought al-Khiḍr.

Shuʿayb, Balʿam, and al-Khiḍr ﵈

Wahb ibn Munabbih related:

Shuʿayb and Balʿam were descended from a group of people who believed in Abraham on the day he was burned, and migrated with him to Syria. Abraham married them to daughters of Lot. Every prophet who came before the Children of Israel and after Abraham belonged to that group.

Shuʿayb’s grandmother was Lot’s daughter.

[He was called Shuʿayb because he used to pray, “O God, bless my people.” It is also said that he was Shuʿayb, the orator of the prophets.]

[Balʿam lived in Jericho and Syria, and knew the Greatest Name of God. When he was called upon to invoke a curse against Moses ﵇—and the Children of Israel, God Most High caused him to forget the Name.]

Wahb said:

Midian was not Shuʿayb’s tribe [from among the Companions of the Thicket], but rather a community to whom he was sent.

When Shuʿayb’s people suffered what they suffered, Shuʿayb and those who believed with him from among the Companions of the Thicket went to Mecca. They remained there until they died.

The name of al-Khiḍr was Balyā son of Malkān son of Fāligh son of ʿĀbir son of Shālīḥ son of Arfakhshadh son of Sām son of Noah. His father was a very great king.

Job ﵇

Wahb said:

He was Job son of Mūṣ son of Raʿwīl. His father was among those who believed in Abraham on the day he was burned.

Job lived in the time of Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham. He was Jacob’s son-in-law, having married a daughter of Jacob called Ilyā daughter of Jacob; she was the one whom he struck with the handful of stalks. Job’s mother was the daughter of the Prophet Lot ﷺ. He had al-Bathaniyya, a city in Syria.

Moses and Aaron ﵈

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

He was Moses son of ʿImrān son of Qāhith son of Levi son of Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham.

There was no prophet between the house of Jacob and Job until Moses came.

Moses ﵇ was dark-complexioned, curly-haired, and tall, as if he were one of the men of Shanūʾa. Aaron was taller than Moses, more heavily built, fair-skinned, broader, and three years older than Moses.

There was a birthmark on Aaron’s forehead, a birthmark on the tip of Moses’ nose, and a birthmark on the tip of his tongue. No one before or after him is known to have had a birthmark on the tip of his tongue. It was the impediment that God—Mighty and Glorious—is said to have mentioned.

Their sister Miriam was older than they were. She was married to Caleb son of Jephunneh son of Pharez son of Judah son of Jacob.

He said: The Pharaoh of Moses was the Pharaoh of Joseph. He lived for more than four hundred years, and his name was al-Walīd son of Muṣʿab.

Others reject this and say that he was someone else.

The name of Pharaoh’s wife was Āsiya daughter of Muzāḥim.

Qārūn was Ṣāfir son of Qāhith son of Levi, and was a paternal cousin of Moses son of ʿImrān ﵇.

The Samaritan was Mūsā son of Ẓafar. It is said that he was from the people of Bājarmā. He was among the Children of Israel, from the clan of Moses son of ʿImrān.

He said: Aaron died at the age of one hundred and seventeen years. Moses lived three years after him and died at the same age Aaron had been when he died. Joshua son of Nun succeeded him; he was Joshua son of Nun son of Ephraim son of Joseph son of Jacob ﵈.

Ishmāwīl son of Halqānā ﵇

In Arabic, he is Ismāʿīl. His mother’s name was Ḥanna. He was one of the Children of Israel, and there was no prophet between him and Joshua son of Nun. He is the one God—glorious is His mention—refers to in the Qurʾān: “Their prophet said to them, ‘God has appointed Saul as king over you.’” (2:247)

Saul

Wahb said:

He was from the tribe of Benjamin son of Jacob. The tribes descended from Jacob are like the clans descended from Ishmael. He was poor and tended donkeys. He left his village in search of two donkeys of his. He stopped at Ishmāwīl, who informed them that he was their king and that he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.

They said, “You know that no king has ever come from this tribe, nor has there been any prophecy among them.”

Ishmāwīl said to them, “Are you, or God, more knowledgeable? Do you not know that when God appointed him over you, He knew his lineage?”

David, Solomon, and his descendants ﵈

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

Then God appointed David son of Jesse as successor after Ishmāwīl. He was the seventh of seven brothers, and the youngest of them. He tended his father’s flock. He was short and blue-eyed, with baldness on one part of his head. He had married Saul’s daughter, Saul having stipulated this on the condition that David kill Goliath. She bore him Absalom, his firstborn, who rebelled against his father and sought to remove him from the kingship. Then he married the wife of Uriah son of Ḥannān after Uriah had been killed, and she bore him Solomon son of David.

Kingship and prophecy remained among Solomon’s descendants and their children until al-Aʿraj, one of his descendants. He was lame because of sciatica. The kings coveted Jerusalem because of his chronic illness and weakness, and because he was not a prophet. The king of the Jazīra marched against him. He was called:

Layyaqar. He lived in the wilderness of al-Tharthār, the wilderness of Sinjār, in a city called al-Ḥaḍr, built of stone, and worshipped Venus. He vowed that if he gained Jerusalem, he would sacrifice his son to Venus. Bukht Naṣṣar was his scribe at that time. God sent a wind against him that destroyed his army. He and his scribe escaped until they reached al-Ḥaḍr. His son killed him, and Bukht Naṣṣar, enraged on his account, tricked the son and killed him. Bukht Naṣṣar then ruled, and this was the beginning of his reign. The king of India marched against them, but God Most High destroyed him, and the descendants of Solomon and their peers died out.

Sennacherib, Bukht Naṣṣar, and Jeremiah

Sennacherib, king of Mosul, who lived in Nineveh, marched against them, as did the king of Azerbaijan, whose name was Salmā ʿĀshir—in Arabic, Salmān al-Aʿshar. They fell out and war broke out between them until they were all destroyed. The Children of Israel took as booty what they had with them.

The king of the Romans marched against them, accompanied by the Ashbān and the Ṣaqāliba, as well as the king of al-Andalus. They too quarrelled and fought, and God destroyed some of them by means of others.

Then they innovated and changed things, and some of them turned away from Jerusalem and built alongside it a mosque intended to cause harm. That mosque was shaken down upon them, and they were crushed with a wooden beam.

After that, Bukht Naṣṣar raided them. They turned to God in repentance, and God turned him away from them after they had opened the city and roamed its markets.

This is the first occasion mentioned by God—Mighty and Glorious—when He said: “When the promise of the first of the two came to pass, We sent against you servants of Ours, possessed of great might, and they searched through the homes. It was a promise fulfilled. Then We gave you back the upper hand over them.” (17:5–6) After that, they again innovated. God sent the Prophet Jeremiah to tell them of God’s anger against them. He stood among them bearing God’s revelation, so they beat him, shackled him, and imprisoned him. At that, God sent Bukht Naṣṣar. This was the other occasion mentioned by God—Mighty and Glorious—when He said: “When the promise of the latter came to pass, they were to afflict your faces, enter the mosque as they had entered it the first time, and utterly destroy all that they had conquered.” (17:7) He killed some of them, crucified them, burned them, mutilated them, sold their children and women, and inflicted every kind of mutilation upon them. A group of them went to Egypt and sought refuge with its king. Bukht Naṣṣar then marched against the king of Egypt, and they fought. Bukht Naṣṣar defeated him and took him prisoner. He also took the Children of Israel prisoner, killed his soldiers, and then returned to the land of Babylon.

Jeremiah remained in the land of Egypt and made a garden, planting vegetables there to live on. God revealed to him: “You have concerns and business that keep you from planting and staying in the land of Egypt. How can any land contain you or bear you, when you know of My wrath against the Children of Israel? Let this decree that I have decreed against Ilīyā and its people grieve you, for this is not a time of cultivation, but a time of ruin. Go to this garden of yours: tear down its wall, pull up its vegetables, drain its river, and go to Ilīyā. Let it be your land until My decree reaches its appointed term.”

Jeremiah went out in alarm and fear—it was the season of fruit—and mounted a she-donkey of his.

He took provisions in a basket containing grapes and figs, and took a new waterskin and filled it with water. Then he twisted a new rope and tethered his she-donkey with it. He set out, and when Jerusalem came into view, he saw a great ruin beyond description. He said, “How will God bring this to life after its death?” (2:259) Then God caused him to die for a hundred years.

Then He sent a king of the Persians, called Kūsh, who rebuilt it, and God restored Jeremiah to life.

He was told: “Look at your food and drink: they have not spoiled.” (2:259)

ʿUzayr and Dāniyāl

He said: Among the captives in the hands of Bukht Naṣṣar were ʿUzayr and Dāniyāl.

As for Dāniyāl, he was the one who interpreted Bukht Naṣṣar’s dream for him, and thereby attained the highest rank with him. His tomb was in the region of al-Sūs. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī found him, brought him out, shrouded him, and prayed over him; then he buried him.

[Decay had eaten away part of one side of his beard. He was in a house, inside a stone trough. Beneath the trough were thirty copper jars with their tops sealed with lead, and beneath the jars was a basket in a stone trough. Abū Mūsā did not know what it was, so he asked about it. They said: “We do not know what this is, except that whenever an enemy besieges us and rain is withheld from us, we uncover the head of the trough and uncover his face.” Abū Mūsā wrote to ʿUmar ﵄—about this. ʿUmar wrote back: “The man is Dāniyāl. Bury him where the hands of sinners cannot reach him.” So he shrouded him, diverted the river of Tustar, then placed him in a stone trough and buried him in the river, and then let the water flow over him.]

As for ʿUzayr, when he returned to Syria, he restored the Torah for the Children of Israel after it had been burned, and they knew it. A group of Jews said: “He is the son of God.” He was the one who engaged in much disputation about destiny, so God erased his name from the register of the prophets, and he is not mentioned among them, though he is a messenger.

Isaiah ﷺ

He said: The Children of Israel obeyed God for a time, and God sent them Isaiah son of Amoz as a prophet.

Then transgressions and innovations became widespread among them. So God sent Sennacherib, king of Babylon.

He came and encamped in their midst. They repented to God and turned back to Him. God accepted their repentance and sent plague upon their enemy. By morning, they were dead, and God granted them their army, with everything in it, as spoils. None escaped except their king, Sennacherib, and five men with him. After that, they again committed transgressions, cast aside God’s Book, and vied for kingship. God commanded Isaiah to stand among them and deliver His revelation. When he did so, they killed him. God then set their enemy upon them, who drove them into exile and destroyed them, imposed humiliation and destitution upon them, and took kingship and prophethood away from them. Thus, in every nation they are a people marked by humiliation and abasement until the Day of Resurrection.

Isaiah was the one who foretold the Prophet ﷺ—and described him, and who foretold Jesus.

Ezekiel ﷺ

He was Ezekiel son of Būdhā. He was the one in whose time plague struck his people, and they went out from their homes in their thousands, fearing death. God said to them: “Die.” Then He brought them back to life.

He was from the tribe of Joshua son of Nun. God sent him to the people of Baalbek, who worshiped an idol called Baʿl. Their king was Aḥāb, and his wife was Īzābīl. When he was away, he would appoint her to rule in his place, and she would judge among the people. She was a killer of prophets and had killed many of them. She was the daughter of the king of Ṣaydāʾ, lived a very long life, and married seven kings of the Children of Israel.

She was the one who killed John son of Zechariah. God—Mighty and Majestic—is reported to have said to Elijah: “Ask Me, and I will give to you.” He replied: “Raise me up to You and spare me the taste of death.” God raised him up to Himself after clothing him in feathers, and made him an earthly, heavenly, angelic being who flies with the angels.

Elisha ﷺ

Elisha was Elijah’s disciple. Elijah prayed for him, and God made him a prophet after Elijah and supported him with a spirit like Elijah’s.

Jonah son of Mattā ﷺ

God ﵎ sent, after Elisha, Jonah son of Mattā to the people of Nineveh, in the land of Mosul.

Zechariah and [ʿImrān] ﵉

He said: He was Zechariah son of Ādhin. Zechariah son of Ādhin and ʿImrān son of Māthān, son of al-Yaʿāqīm, were descendants of the prophet David ﵇—from the tribe of Judah son of Jacob, and they lived at the same time. Zechariah married Ashyāʿ, daughter of ʿImrān and sister of Mary daughter of ʿImrān. Mary’s mother was named Ḥannah. John and Jesus were maternal cousins. Zechariah was a carpenter. The Jews spread the claim that he had committed adultery with Mary, and they killed him inside a tree, which they cut down along with him.

[Wahb said:

When he fled, he entered the hollow of a tree. They placed a saw against the tree to cut it down. When the saw reached his body, he groaned. God—Mighty and Majestic—revealed to him: “Either stop groaning or I shall turn the earth upside down.” He fell silent and did not groan until they had cut him in two.]

Jesus and John ﵉

He said: As for John, Aḥāb killed him through the stratagem of his wife Īzābīl, who plotted his killing.

As for Jesus, when his mother gave birth to him, Joseph the carpenter took him and his mother to Egypt, fleeing from Aḥāb, the associate of Īzābīl. This Joseph had proposed marriage to Mary [without her consent], and married her, as is related in the Gospel. When she came to him, he found her pregnant before he had been with her. He was a righteous man and disliked exposing her, so he resolved to send her away secretly. An angel appeared to him in a dream and said: “Joseph son of David, your wife Mary will bear a son called Jesus, who will save his people from their sins.”

In the Gospel: The king whom Mary feared for Jesus’ sake was Herod. Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah—[a place in Syria]—. When Herod died, Joseph saw in a dream that he should take him and his mother to the land of Hebron—[a place in Syria]—. So he set out and settled in a village called Nāṣirah; for that reason they were called Christians.

The Companions of the Cave

Wahb said:

They were young men from the Romans who entered the cave before the Messiah. God—Glorious is He—sealed their ears there. When the Messiah ﷺ—was sent, he told of their story. Then God raised them after the Messiah, during the interval between him and the Prophet ﷺ.

Dhu al-Qarnayn

He was a man from Alexandria named al-Iskandrus. He had a dream in which he saw himself draw near to the sun until he took hold of its two horns, in its east and its west. He recounted his dream to his people, and they called him Dhu al-Qarnayn. He lived during the interval after Jesus ﵇.

George ﵇ The sage Luqmān

Yazīd ibn Hārūn related, from Ḥammād ibn Salamah, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, that he said:

The prophet Luqmān was a tailor.

Wahb said:

I read about ten thousand chapters of his wisdom. People had never heard speech better than his. Then I saw that people had incorporated it into their own speech, used it in their sermons and letters, and drawn upon it to complete their eloquence.

Dhu al-Kifl ﷺ

As for Dhu al-Kifl, I found no mention of him in what Wahb transmitted. He was one of the Children of Israel, sent to a king among them called Canaan. He called him to faith and guaranteed him Paradise, and wrote him a document stating a right that was incumbent upon God—Mighty and Majestic. That king believed. He was called Dhu al-Kifl because of the guarantee.

The number of messengers

The first of the messengers was Adam, and the last was Muḥammad ﷺ and them all. The prophets numbered one hundred and twenty-four thousand; among them, the messengers numbered three hundred and fifteen, though it is also said: three hundred and thirteen messengers. Of them, five were Hebrews: Adam, Seth, Idrīs, Noah, and Abraham; and five were Arabs: Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Ishmael, Shuʿayb, and Muḥammad. The first of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Moses, and the last was Jesus ﵉.

He said: The books sent down to the prophets numbered one hundred and four. Fifty scrolls were sent down to Seth, thirty scrolls to Idrīs, and twenty scrolls to Abraham. To Moses came the Torah, to David the Psalms, to Jesus the Gospel, and to Muḥammad ﷺ and them—the Criterion.

28/ History

Adam lived for a thousand years.

In the Torah, it says that he lived a thousand years minus seventy years. Between Adam’s death and the Flood were two thousand two hundred and forty years; and between the Flood and Noah’s death were three hundred and fifty-two years; between Noah and Abraham were two thousand two hundred and forty years; between Abraham and Moses were seven hundred years; between Moses and David were five hundred years; between David and Jesus were one thousand two hundred years; and between Jesus and Muḥammad ﵉ both—were six hundred and twenty years.

This is the chronology according to some reports.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

There were ten generations between Noah and Adam, and ten generations between Abraham and Noah.

ʿIkrimah said:

There were ten generations between Adam and Noah. All of them followed Islam.

Abū Muḥammad said:

I read in the Gospel that the number of generations from Abraham to David was fourteen, from David to the Babylonian exile fourteen, and from the Babylonian exile to the Messiah fourteen.

Abū Muḥammad said:

I found in books of the histories of the Persians that the period of the kings of the dynasties between Alexander and Ardashīr was four hundred and sixty-five years. Then Ardashīr ruled, followed by their kings down to Yazdegerd, who was killed during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. Their reign lasted four hundred and thirty-odd years. Between Alexander and our Prophet ﷺ—were approximately nine hundred years.

According to Wahb, Alexander came after the Messiah. This conflicts with his statement that six hundred and twenty years lay between Jesus and Muḥammad.

Others say that Alexander came before the Messiah.

The Gospel reports that the Babylonian exile took place fourteen generations after David and fourteen generations before the Messiah.

Genealogists say it took place before Abraham. This shows the extent of the disagreement and discrepancy. God knows best.

Mention of those who followed a religion before the Prophet’s mission ﷺ

Riʾāb ibn al-Barāʾ Waraqah ibn Nawfal

He is Waraqah ibn Nawfal ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā. He was a paternal cousin of Khadījah bt. Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. He had turned away from the worship of idols and become a Christian. Khadījah told him something about the Prophet ﷺ—and he said: “The Great Spirit who used to come to Moses is coming to him.”

Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl

He is the father of Saʿīd ibn Zayd, one of the ten promised Paradise. He had turned away from the worship of idols and sought the true religion, but the Christians killed him in Syria. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “He will be raised as a community on his own.” He is the one who said in the pre-Islamic period: [mutadārik]

I have submitted my face to Him to whomthe rain clouds have submitted, bearing sweet, pure water.

Waraqah ibn Nawfal ibn Asad said of him: [ṭawīl]

You were rightly guided and blessed, son of ʿAmr,for you shunned a furnace blazing with fire,

[for a Lord whose religion is unlike that of any other lord,and your leaving the gardens of the mountains as they are.]

Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt al-Thaqafī

Umayyah had read the scriptures and turned away from the worship of idols. He used to say that a prophet was soon to be sent, and that his time had nearly come. But when he heard that the Prophet ﷺ—had appeared, and learned his story, Umayyah rejected him out of envy. When the Messenger of God ﷺ—was recited his poetry, he said: “His tongue believed, but his heart disbelieved.”

Asʿad Abū Karib al-Ḥimyarī

Asʿad had believed in the Prophet ﷺ—seven hundred years before he was sent. He said: [mutadārik]

[I fought his enemies with the sword,and relieved his heart of every grief.

I bore witness concerning Aḥmad that heis a messenger from God, who created all living beings.

If my life were prolonged until his time,I would be his minister and cousin,

[and I would enjoin obedience to him upon everyoneon earth, Arab and non-Arab alike.

He was the first to cover the House with leather coverings and striped cloaks.

Quss ibn Sāʿidah al-Iyādī

[He was certain of God’s signs and was a judge of the Arabs. The Messenger of God ﷺ—mentioned that he had seen Quss preaching at ʿUkāẓ atop a red camel. Abū Bakr recounted his story and recited his poetry.

30/ Abū Qays Ṣirmah ibn Abī Anas

He was of Banū al-Najjār. He became an ascetic, wore garments of haircloth, abandoned idols, and considered becoming a Christian, but then refrained from doing so. He entered a room in his house and made it a place of worship, admitting neither a menstruating woman nor anyone in a state of major ritual impurity. He said: “I worship the Lord of Abraham.” When the Messenger of God ﷺ—came to Medina, Ṣirmah became Muslim and was excellent in his Islam. He is the one who said of the Messenger of God ﷺ: [ṭawīl]

He dwelt among Quraysh for more than ten years,in Mecca, finding no friend who would stand by him.

[Then, when he came to us and our hearts found peace in him,he was glad and content in Ṭaybah.

He tells us what Noah said to his people,and what Moses said when he answered the caller.

He is also the one who said in the pre-Islamic period: [khafīf]

Glorify God at sunrise every morning,when His sun and every crescent moon have risen.

Children of kin, do not sever your ties;keep them joined, whether short or long.

Children of the boundaries, do not wrong them …For the wrong done to boundaries is a grievous affliction.

Khālid ibn Sinān ibn Ghayth

He was of ʿAbs ibn Bughayḍ.

It is related that the Prophet ﷺ—said: “That was a prophet whom his people neglected.” When Khālid was near death, he said to his people: “When I have been buried, a herd of wild asses from Ḥimyar will come, led by a pale-gray donkey. It will strike my grave with its hoof. When you see that, dig me up, for I will emerge and tell you what is to come until the Day of Resurrection.” When he died, they saw what he had foretold and wanted to dig him up. But some of them disliked the idea and said: “We fear people will reproach us for digging up one of our dead.”

His daughter came to the Messenger of God ﷺ—and heard him reciting: “Say: He is God, One” (Qurʾān 112:1). She said: “My father used to say this.”

Arab Genealogies

The Genealogy of ʿAdnān

People disagreed about the genealogy of ʿAdnān.

Some said: He was ʿAdnān ibn Add ibn Yaḥthūm ibn Muqawwim ibn Nāḥūr ibn Tārikh ibn Yaʿrub ibn Yashjub ibn Nābit ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Abraham.

Others said: He was ʿAdnān ibn Add ibn Ashjab ibn Ayyūb ibn Qaydār ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Abraham.

Others said: He was ʿAdnān ibn Midʿa ibn Mutayʿ ibn Add ibn Kaʿb ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn al-Humaysaʿ ibn Qaydār ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Abraham.

ʿAdnān’s sons were ʿAkk ibn ʿAdnān and Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnān.

Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnān had eight sons. Four whose descendants are known are mentioned:

Quḍāʿah, Iyād, Qanṣ, and Nizār.

As for Quḍāʿah, they went to Yemen and joined Ḥimyar, and so are counted among the Yemenis.

As for Qanṣ, some claim that the family of al-Mundhir, king of al-Ḥīrah, descended from them.

As for Iyād, they are affiliated with the larger tribe, but no well-known tribe descends from them. Some say that Thaqīf were among them; others say that Thaqīf were of Qays ʿAylān.

Nizār’s sons were Muḍar, Rabīʿah, and Anmār.

Anmār’s sons were Khaʿtham and Bajīlah, who settled in Yemen.

As for Muḍar and Rabīʿah, the descendants of Nizār trace their lineage to them; they are the pure line among the descendants of Ismāʿīl ﷺ.

Muḍar ibn Nizār’s sons were Ilyās ibn Muḍar and ʿAylān ibn Muḍar.

As for Ilyās ibn Muḍar, his descendants are called Khindif because Ilyās’s wife was called Khindif. His descendants were therefore named after her, for she was their mother.

His sons were Mudrikah ibn Ilyās, Ṭābikhah ibn Ilyās, and Qamʿah ibn Ilyās.

As for Qamʿah, some genealogists say that Khuzāʿah descended from him. Some claim that they were from Yemen, descendants of ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir [Māʾ al-Samāʾ.

All of Khindif’s descendants traced their lineage back to Mudrikah and Ṭābikhah.

As for ʿAylān ibn Muḍar, he is the ancestor of Qays ʿAylān. Thus all of Muḍar traces back to these two groups:

Khindif and Qays.

Mudrikah ibn Ilyās

As for the descendants of Mudrikah ibn Ilyās, they are Hudhayl, Asad, Kinānah, and Quraysh.

Hudhayl is Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah ibn Ilyās ibn Muḍar. He had three sons: Saʿd, Liḥyān, and ʿUmayr. The numbers are greatest among the descendants of Saʿd.

Saʿd ibn Hudhayl’s sons were Tamīm ibn Saʿd, Ḥurayth ibn Saʿd, Minaʿah ibn Saʿd, Khunāʿah ibn Saʿd, Jihām Saʿd, and Ghanm ibn Saʿd. The numbers are greatest among the descendants of Tamīm.

Tamīm’s sons were Muʿāwiyah ibn Tamīm and al-Ḥārith ibn Tamīm. The numbers are greatest among the descendants of Muʿāwiyah.

As for al-Ḥārith, his clan includes ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, Companion of the Prophet ﷺ.

As for Asad, he is Asad ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah ibn Ilyās ibn Muḍar.

He had two brothers: Kinānah ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah and al-Hawn ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah.

Asad had four sons: Dūdān ibn Asad, Kāhil ibn Asad, ʿAmr ibn Asad, and Ḥamlah ibn Asad. These are the Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah.

From them [the descendants of Asad] [32/] all of Asad branched out. Among their well-known subdivisions are Banū Fuqʿas, Banū al-Ṣaydāʾ, Banū Naṣr ibn Quʿayn, Banū al-Zunyah, Banū Ghāḍirah, and Banū Nuʿāmah.

The descendants of al-Hawn ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah were al-Qārah ibn al-Hawn. Among al-Qārah were ʿAḍl and al-Dayth, who together formed the tribe of al-Hawn ibn Khuzaymah. Al-Qārah were a people of archers, and so it was said:

“Al-Qārah have been fairly matched by whoever shoots at them.”

As for Kinānah, he is Kinānah ibn Khuzaymah.

After his father’s death, he married his father’s wife, Barra bt. Murr, the sister of Tamīm ibn Murr.

Barra bore Kinānah al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah—his mother was Barra—Mālik ibn Kinānah, Milkan ibn Kinānah, and ʿAbd Manāf, who was ʿAlī; sometimes he was called Masʿūd.

As for the descendants of Milkan, a remnant of them survives, but they have no outstanding distinction.

As for the descendants of Mālik, their tribes include Banū Fuqaym and Banū Firās.

The Banū Fuqaym are the intercalators of the months.

Among the Banū Firās was al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Ḥakīm, who lived in Basra. Also among them were:

The Banū Abjar, the physicians of Kufa.

As for ʿAbd Manāf, among his descendants are the Banū Mudlij, the trackers. Among them are also the Banū Jadhīmah, whom Khālid ibn al-Walīd killed at al-Ghamīṣāʾ, after which the Messenger of God ﷺ—paid blood money for them. Among them are also:

The Banū Layth, the clan of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād. Among them are also al-Duʾil, the clan of Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾilī.

Abū Muḥammad said:

In the speech of the Arabs, al-Duʾil is the only name on the pattern of “faʿl.” This pattern is used for verbs, as in “he reviled” and “he struck.”

Abū Ḥātim recited to me, saying: al-Akhfash recited to me: [munsariḥ]

They came with an army whose encampment, if measured,would be no larger than the encampment of the duʾil.

He said: The duʾil is an animal resembling a weasel.

Among them are also the Banū Ṣamrah, the clan of ʿAmr ibn Umayyah al-Ḍamrī, Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Among the descendants of Ḍamrah are Ghifār, the clan of Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī.

Among them are also the Banū ʿUrayj, who are few in number. Abū Nawfal ibn Abī ʿAqrab al-ʿUrayjī was one of them.

Quraysh

As for al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah, he is the ancestor of Quraysh. His sons were Mālik and al-Ṣalt. The descendants of al-Ṣalt went to Yemen—some say he was the ancestor of Khuzāʿah—while Quraysh traced their lineage back to Mālik ibn al-Naḍr, who is the ancestor of all of them.

Mālik ibn al-Naḍr’s sons were Fihr and al-Ḥārith, whose mother was Jarhamī.

As for al-Ḥārith ibn [33/] Mālik, they were among the perfume-appliers. Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ was one of them.

It is said that the Khalaj were among them.

It is also said that they were of ʿAdwān, but ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb affiliated them with al-Ḥārith.

They were called Khalaj because they had been drawn away from ʿAdwān. They are numerous in Medina.

As for Fihr ibn Mālik, the tribes of Quraysh branched out from him, and so they were called the Banū Fihr.

His sons were Ghālib ibn Fihr and Muḥārib ibn Fihr.

As for Muḥārib, among them was Ḍirār ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the poet of Quraysh in the pre-Islamic period.

Among them was also al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Fihrī, whom Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam killed on the day of Marj Rāhiṭ.

As for Ghālib ibn Fihr, his sons were Luʾayy ibn Ghālib and Taym.

As for Taym, they are the Banū al-Adram, among the Bedouin of Quraysh. Not one of them lives in Mecca. A poet said of them: [rajaz]

The Banū al-Adram belong to no one;they are neither of Qays nor of Asad,and Quraysh does not count them among its number.

As for Luʾayy, the number and distinction of Quraysh trace back to him. He had seven sons: Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy, ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy, Sāmah ibn Luʾayy, Saʿd ibn Luʾayy, Khuzaymah ibn Luʾayy, al-Ḥārith ibn Luʾayy, and ʿAwf ibn Luʾayy.

As for ʿĀmir, his sons were Ḥaṣal and Maʿīṣ. Among his descendants were Ibn Umm Maktūm, Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt, and Khadīja bt. Khuwaylid.

Among the descendants of Ḥaṣal were Sahl, Suhayl, and al-Sukrān, the sons of ʿAmr.

As for Sāma b. Luʾayy, he went to ʿUmān and died there; his descendants are there.

As for Saʿd b. Luʾayy, he was the forefather of the Banāna clan, the kinsmen of Thābit al-Bunānī. His descendants were ascribed to her, and she was his wife.

As for Khuzayma b. Luʾayy, among his descendants were ʿĀʾidha—who are among Banū Shaybān—and the poet Miqās al-ʿĀʾidhī, who was one of them.

As for Kaʿb b. Luʾayy, his sons were Murra, Huṣayṣ, and ʿAdī.

As for Banū Huṣayṣ, among them were Banū Sahm and Banū Jumah.

As for ʿAdī, among his descendants were ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb and Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl.

As for Murra, among his descendants were Taym b. Murra—the kinsmen of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq—Ṭalḥa b. ʿUbayd Allāh, ʿUbayd Allāh b. Maʿmar, and the family of al-Munkadir. Among them was Makhzūm b. Murra.

Among Banū Makhzūm were Abū Jahl b. Hishām b. al-Mughīra and the family of al-Mughīra. [Hishām b. al-Mughīra was a chief among his people. Of him the poet says: [metre: wāfir]

The valley of Mecca has become desolate,

as though the earth had no Hishām in it.]

Among them was Kilāb b. Murra. The sons of Kilāb were Zuhra b. Kilāb and Quṣayy b. Kilāb. Zuhra was a woman to whom her descendants, rather than their father, were ascribed; they are the maternal uncles of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

As for Quṣayy b. Kilāb, his name was Zayd. He was called “the Gatherer” because he gathered the tribes of Quraysh, settled them in Mecca, built the Council House, and took the key from Khuzāʿa.

The sons of Quṣayy were ʿAbd Manāf, ʿAbd al-Dār, ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, and ʿAbdā.

As for ʿAbdā, his descendants died out.

As for ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, among his descendants were Khuwaylid b. Asad b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, the grandfather of al-Zubayr, and the father of Khadīja bt. Khuwaylid and Abū Ḥizām b. Khuwaylid.
