As for ʿAbd al-Dār, among his descendants were the family of Abū Ṭalḥa b. ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd al-Dār. They were all killed on the day of Uḥud, except ʿUthmān b. Ṭalḥa, who became Muslim, and to whom the Prophet ﷺ—gave the key of the Kaʿba. His son was Shayba b. ʿUthmān. The key has remained among his descendants to this day.

As for ʿAbd Manāf b. Quṣayy, his name was al-Mughīra. His sons were Hāshim, ʿAbd Shams, al-Muṭṭalib, Nawfal, and Abū ʿAmr.

As for Abū ʿAmr, he left no descendants.

As for Nawfal, among his descendants was Jubayr b. Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī b. Nawfal.

As for al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf, his sons numbered ten, among them al-Ḥārith, ʿAbbād, Makhrama, and Hāshim.

Genealogy of Banū Hāshim

As for Hāshim b. ʿAbd Manāf, his name was ʿAmr, and he died at Gaza, in the land of Syria.

His sons were ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Asad, and others who left no descendants.

As for Asad, his sons were Ḥunayn—who left no descendants and was the maternal uncle of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵁—and Fāṭima bt. Asad, who was the mother of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib.

There is no Hāshimite on earth except one descended from ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib b. Hāshim, because Hāshim had male descendants who left no descendants.

As for ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was called “ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib” because he was in Medina with his maternal uncles. His uncle al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf brought him, and entered Mecca with him behind him. They said, “This is ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.” The name stuck to him and became his usual name, but his name was ʿĀmir—[and it is said: Shaybat al-Ḥamd]—. He lived until he grew old and blind, and died in Mecca while the Messenger of God ﷺ—was eight years and two months old. He had ten sons and six daughters. I have mentioned them in my account of the Prophet ﷺ.

Genealogy of Banū Umayya

As for ʿAbd Shams b. ʿAbd Manāf, he had the following sons: Umayya the Elder, Ḥabīb, ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, Sufyān, Rabīʿa, and three sons called al-ʿAbalāt—because their mother was named ʿAbla. They were Umayya the Younger, ʿAbd Umayya—who died when he was eight years old—and Nawfal.

As for Sufyān, he left no descendants.

As for Rabīʿa, he was the father of ʿUtba and Shayba, the sons of Rabīʿa, and of Hind, the mother of Muʿāwiya, daughter of ʿUtba.

As for ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, his sons were Rabīʿ and Rabīʿa, the “Whelp of al-Baṭḥāʾ.”

As for Rabīʿ, he was Ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ b. al-Rabīʿ, the husband of Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He had no male descendants.

As for Umayya the Younger, among his descendants was al-Thurayyā, whom ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa celebrated in his love poetry.

As for Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams, his son was Rabīʿa—grandfather of ʿĀmir b. Kurayz b. Rabīʿa and Samura b. Ḥabīb. His mother was a Black woman named Zubayba. His maternal half-brother was Abū Jumʿa, grandfather of the poet Kathīr b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Jumʿa.

As for Umayya b. ʿAbd Shams the Elder, his sons were Ḥarb, Abū Ḥarb, Sufyān, Abū Sufyān, ʿAmr, and Abū ʿAmr—these were the ʿAnābis, likened to lions—al-ʿĀṣī, Abū al-ʿĀṣī, al-ʿAyṣ, and Abū al-ʿAyṣ—these were the al-Aʿyāṣ.

As for Ḥarb b. Umayya, he was the father of Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb and of Umm Jamīl bt. Ḥarb, “the carrier of firewood,” the wife of Abū Lahab.

As for Abū al-ʿAyṣ b. Umayya, his son was Usayd, father of ʿAttāb b. Usayd and Khālid b. Usayd. ʿAttāb was the Messenger of God’s governor over Mecca ﷺ.

As for al-ʿĀṣī b. Umayya, his son was Abū Uḥayḥa, whose name was Saʿīd.

As for Abū al-ʿĀṣī, among his descendants were ʿAffān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ, the father of ʿUthmān, and al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ, the father of Marwān b. al-Ḥakam.

As for Abū ʿAmr b. Umayya, among his descendants was Abū Muʿayṭ, father of ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ b. Abī ʿAmr b. Umayya.

Neither ʿAmr b. Umayya, nor Abū Sufyān b. Umayya, nor Abū Ḥarb b. Umayya, nor al-ʿAyṣ b. Umayya left descendants.

These are the descendants of Mudrika b. Ilyās.

The Descendants of Ṭābikha

Then among the descendants of Ṭābikha b. Ilyās was Add b. Ṭābikha.

The sons of Add were Murra b. Add, ʿAbd Manāt b. Add, Ḍabba b. Add, Muzayna b. Add, and Ḥumays b. Add.

As for ʿAbd Manāt b. Add, among his descendants were Taym b. ʿAbd Manāt and its clans; ʿAdī b. ʿAbd Manāt—among them the poet Dhū al-Rumma; ʿIkl and its clans—these three were of al-Ribāb; and Thawr b. ʿAbd Manāt—they are the kinsmen of Sufyān al-Thawrī and al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym.

As for Ḍabba b. Add, his sons were Saʿd, Saʿīd, and Bāsil.

As for Bāsil, he was the forefather of the Daylam. It is said that Bāsil’s bow and saddle remain with the Daylam to this day.

Saʿīd was killed, and left no son.

All of Ḍabba trace their descent to Saʿd b. Ḍabba. They are one of the “embers” among the Arab tribes, and belong to al-Ribāb.

The sons of Saʿd to whom Ḍabba trace their descent were Bakr, Thaʿlaba, and Ṣuraym. Among their clans were Naṣr, Māzin, al-Sayyid, Dhuhl, ʿĀʾidha, Taym Allāt—whose name was Ḥāzim—Dhubyān, ʿAwf, and Shiyīm.

Among Dhuhl were Bajāla, Taym, Ṣubayḥ, Ḍubayʿa, and Kaʿb. These were the Banū Bajāla.

Among Kaʿb were Ḍirār b. ʿAmr—who was the leading house of Ḍabba and the speaker of the saying, “Whoever is gladdened by his sons is distressed by himself.” He had thirteen male children—, Banū Ṣabāḥ—who were known for hunting—, Shaqra, and Hilāl.

As for Muzayna b. Add, they are the Muzayna of Muḍar. Among them were al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin, Maʿqil b. Yasār, Bakr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī, and the poet Zuhayr.

As for Ḥumays b. Add, they are few in number. They are found in Basra among Banū ʿAbd Allāh b. Dārim, and in Kufa among Banū Mujāshiʿ.

As for Murra b. Add, his sons were Thaʿlaba b. Murra—they are Banū Ṭāʿina, named after their mother—, Bakr b. Murra—they are al-Shaʿīrāʾ—, Arāsha b. Murra—they joined Yemen and became part of Judhām and Lakhm, and are said to be called Jadīs—, and al-Ghawth b. Murra, who likewise became part of Yemen.

They are called Banū Ṣūfa, and used to lead the people in the ʿArafāt rite before Banū Ṣafwān. There were also Tamīm b. Murra, whose grave is at Marrān, and his sons: Zayd Manāt b. Tamīm, ʿAmr b. Tamīm, and al-Ḥārith b. Tamīm. Their mother was al-ʿAwrāʾ bt. Ḍabba.

As for al-Ḥārith b. Tamīm, among his descendants was Shaqra.

As for ʿAmr b. Tamīm, his sons were al-ʿAnbar b. ʿAmr, al-Hujaym b. ʿAmr, Usayyid b. ʿAmr—the kinsmen of Abū Ḥāḍir al-Usaydī—, Aktham b. Ṣayfī, Abū Hāla—the husband of Khadīja—, al-Qulayb b. ʿAmr, al-Ḥārith b. ʿAmr—who was al-Ḥabaṭ, and whose descendants are called al-Ḥabaṭāt—, and Mālik b. ʿAmr. Among them were Māzin and al-Ḥirmāz. Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ was descended from Māzin.

As for Zayd Manāt b. Tamīm, his sons were Saʿd b. Zayd Manāt—whose descendants were numerous—, ʿĀmir b. Zayd Manāt—whose descendants were few—and Imruʾ al-Qays b. Zayd Manāt. Among the latter’s descendants was the poet ʿAdī b. Zayd. Among their tribes were Banū ʿUṣayya.

Among Mālik b. Zayd Manāt were Rabīʿat al-Jawʿ, the kinsmen of the poet ʿAlqama b. ʿAbada, and ʿAlqama the eunuch.

Among them were the Barājim: ʿAmr, Qays, Kulfa, Ẓalīm, and Ghālib, the sons of Ḥanẓala b. Mālik.

Among them was Yarbuʿ b. Ḥanẓala, and Kulayb b. Yarbuʿ—the kinsmen of Jarīr—; Riyāḥ b. Yarbuʿ—the kinsmen of the poet al-Aḥwaṣ, Qaʿnab al-Riyāḥī, and Suḥaym b. Wathīl al-Riyāḥī—; Thaʿlaba b. Yarbuʿ—the kinsmen of ʿUtayba b. al-Ḥārith b. Shihāb—; Ghadāna b. Yarbuʿ—the kinsmen of Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd, slayer of Qutayba b. Muslim al-Bāhilī—; and Ḥizām b. Yarbuʿ, the kinsmen of Sajāḥ, who claimed prophethood.

Among them were Banū Dārim b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala; Mujāshiʿ b. Dārim b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala; and Nahshal b. Dārim b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala.

Among them were Banū al-ʿAdawiyya, named after their mother. They were Zayd b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala, Ṣudayy b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala, and Yarbuʿ b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala.

Among them were Banū Ṭahiyya, named after their mother. They were Abū Sūd b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala, ʿAwf b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala, and Jushaysh b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala. Among them was Abū al-Bilād al-Ṭahawī.

As for Saʿd b. Zayd Manāt b. Tamīm, he was al-Fizr. The proverbial saying about him is:

“As the goats of al-Fizr scattered.”

His sons were Kaʿb b. Saʿd, ʿAmr b. Saʿd, al-Ḥārith b. Saʿd, ʿAwāfa b. Saʿd, ʿAbd Shams b. Saʿd—whose name was Maqrūʿ—, Jusham b. Saʿd, Mālik b. Saʿd, ʿAwf b. Saʿd, and Hubayra b. Saʿd.

As for Kaʿb b. Saʿd, his descendants were numerous. Among them were Maqāʿis, who was al-Ḥārith b. ʿAmr b. Kaʿb.

Among them were Banū Ḥammān b. Kaʿb b. Saʿd.

Among them were Banū Munqir b. ʿUbayd b. al-Ḥārith b. ʿAmr b. Kaʿb.

Among them were Banū Murra b. ʿUbayd, the kinsmen of al-Aḥnaf b. Qays and ʿAkrāsh b. Dhuʾayb.

Among them was Rabīʿa b. Kaʿb, the father of al-Mustawghir b. Rabīʿa, who lived for three hundred and twenty years.

Among the descendants of ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb were Bahdalah—the kin-group of al-Zibriqān ibn Badr—and Qurayʿ, the kin-group of Banū Anf al-Nāqah. He was Abū al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Qurayʿ, who moved from tribe to tribe. When they did not praise him, he returned to his people and said, “In every valley are Banū Saʿd.” Among them were the family of ʿAṭārid, the kin-group of Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿAṭāridī, and the family of Ṣafwān [ibn Shajnah], among whom lay the leading of the people out from ʿArafah. Among the descendants of ʿAṭārid were Banū ʿAwf.

The descendants of Ṭābikhah ibn Ilyās ibn Muḍar come to an end here.

As for Qays ʿAylān—who was al-Nās ibn Muḍar—his sons were Saʿd, ʿIkrimah, Aʿṣur, ʿAmr, and Khaṣafah.

Some genealogists claim that ʿIkrimah was the son of Khaṣafah, and that Aʿṣur was the son of Saʿd.

As for ʿAmr ibn Qays, his sons were Fahm and ʿAdwān.

Among Fahm was Taʾabbaṭa Sharran. I do not know their subdivisions.

As for ʿAdwān, among their branches are Banū Khārijah, Banū Wābish, Banū Yashkur, Banū ʿAwf, al-Darʿāʾ, Banū Rihm, Banū Nāj, and, it is said, al-Khalaj.

Among ʿAdwān were ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarb, the arbiter of the Arabs, and Abū Sayyārah, who used to lead the people out from ʿArafah.

ʿAdwān settled Thaqīf in al-Ṭāʾif. Thaqīf had many chieftains, and they scattered because some wronged others.

As for Saʿd ibn Qays, his son was Ghaṭafān—whose mother was Takmah daughter of Murrah.

His maternal brother was Sulaym ibn Manṣūr, and [his brother was] Aʿṣur ibn Saʿd.

The sons of Aʿṣur were Ghanī ibn Aʿṣur, Maʿn ibn Aʿṣur—who was the father of Bāhilah—and Munabbih ibn Aʿṣur, who were al-Ṭafāwah. Bāhilah was a woman of Hamdān, after whom the descendants of Maʿn were named. As for Ghanī, among them were Banū Ḍubaynah, Banū Bahthah, and Banū ʿUbayd, who were allies among Banū Kilāb.

As for al-Ṭafāwah, among them were Banū Ḥayy and Banū Sinān, who were allies among Banū Shaybān.

Among al-Ṭafāwah were also al-Ḥibāl, who were among [the tribe of] al-Hujaym.

As for Maʿn ibn Aʿṣur, his sons were Qutaybah and Wāʾil—their mother was from Fazārah—and Awd, Jaʾāwah—their mother was Bāhilah, a woman of Hamdān—Farrāṣ, and Abū ʿAlīm.

As for Qutaybah ibn Maʿn, among his descendants was Ghanm ibn Qutaybah.

Ghanm’s son was Sihm ibn Ghanm. Among them were Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bakr al-Sahmī. Among them too was Abū Umāmah, a Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Among Banū Qutaybah were Banū Ṣaḥb, who dwell in al-Yamāmah.

Among them too were ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd, Aʿbad, Qaʿnab, Saʿd ibn ʿAbd, and ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd.

Among Banū Saʿd were Banū Aṣmaʿ, the kin-group of al-Aṣmaʿī.

As for Wāʾil ibn Maʿn, among them were Banū Salamah, Banū Hilāl ibn ʿAmr, Banū Zayd, Banū ʿĀmir ibn ʿAwf, and Banū ʿUṣayyah.

Among Banū Hilāl was Qutaybah ibn Muslim al-Bāhilī.

Among Banū Wāʾil was Saḥbān Wāʾil, the orator.

As for Awd ibn Maʿn, among them was the mother of al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays. Among them too were the callers to prayer in the congregational mosque at Baṣrah.

As for Farrāṣ ibn Maʿn, among them was Ibn Aḥmar the poet. Jaʾāwah have descendants remaining, meaning descendants from his line.

As for Banū ʿAlīm, they are numerous in al-Jazīrah. Among them was Bakr ibn Muʿāwiyah, head of the army bureau, who was one of Abū Jaʿfar’s commanders.

As for Ghaṭafān ibn Saʿd, his sons were Rayth and ʿAbd Allāh. Rayth’s sons were Baghīḍ and Ashjaʿ. Baghīḍ’s sons were Dhubyān, ʿAbs, and Anmār.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghaṭafān, they are among Banū ʿAbs.

As for Ashjaʿ ibn Rayth ibn Ghaṭafān, among them were Banū Dahmān.

Ashjaʿ were among those who helped against ʿUthmān ﵁—on the day of the siege of the house.

As for Anmār ibn Baghīḍ, they are few. Among them were Fāṭimah daughter of al-Kharshab, mother of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād and his brothers, al-Kamalah.

As for ʿAbs ibn Baghīḍ, his sons were Qaṭīʿah, Waraqah, and Maʿm. The numbers and distinction lay with Qaṭīʿah. Among them were al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād and his brothers, al-Kamalah.

Among them too were Zuhayr ibn Judhaymah and his brothers. His descendants were Qays ibn Zuhayr, Warqāʾ, and others. Qays ibn Zuhayr was the commander in the war of Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ.

As for Waraqah and Maʿtam, the two sons of ʿAbs, no one of note is known from them.

As for Dhubyān ibn Baghīḍ, his sons were Fazārah, Saʿd, and Hāribah al-Baqʿāʾ. Hāribah have died out, except for a small remnant among Banū Thaʿlabah ibn Saʿd.

As for Fazārah ibn Dhubyān, his sons were ʿAdī, Ẓālim, Māzin, and Shimkh. Their mother was Manūlah.

As for Ẓālim ibn Fazārah, they have died out except for a few. Among them was Naʿāmah, who was known as a fool; his name was Bayhas.

As for Shimkh ibn Fazārah, his sons were Laʾy and Hilāl.

Among Banū Laʾy was Samurah ibn Jundub.

As for Māzin ibn Fazārah, among them were Banū al-ʿAshrāʾ.

Among Banū al-ʿAshrāʾ was Hirm ibn Quṭbah ibn Sayyār, to whom ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl and ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah submitted their dispute.

As for ʿAdī ibn Fazārah, his sons were Thaʿlabah and Saʿd.

Among Saʿd was ʿAmr ibn Hubayrah al-Fazārī.

Among Thaʿlabah was ʿAdī ibn Arṭāh. Among them too was Ḥudhayfah ibn Badr, chief of Ghaṭafān and the leading house of Qays. He was called “the lord of Maʿadd.” His two brothers were Mālik ibn Badr and Ḥamal ibn Badr; his son was Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfah, father of ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn.

Among Banū Badr were Banū Umm Qirfah.

Among Banū Fazārah were Banū Khālidah.

As for Saʿd ibn Dhubyān, his sons were Thaʿlabah and ʿAwf.

Among Thaʿlabah were Banū Jaḥḥāsh, Banū Sayyiʿ, and Banū Ḥashūr.

The leading house and distinction lay among Banū Sayyiʿ.

Among Banū Thaʿlabah were the poets Shammākh and Muzarrid, the two sons of Ḍirār.

The sons of ʿAwf ibn Saʿd were Murrah and ʿĪd. As for ʿĪd, they are few. Among them was the man whom Muḥallim ibn Jaththāmah al-Laythī killed as he was saying, “There is no god but God.” Among Murrah ibn ʿAwf lay distinction and preeminence.

The sons of Murrah ibn ʿAwf were Ghayẓ ibn Murrah, Mālik ibn Murrah, Ṣarimah, Sihm, Banū Ṣārid, and others.

The sons of Ghayẓ ibn Murrah were Nashbah and Yarbuʿ.

Among Yarbuʿ was al-Ḥārith ibn Ẓālim. Among them too was al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānī, and ʿAqīl ibn ʿUllafah.

As for Nashbah ibn Ghayẓ, among his descendants was Hirm ibn Sinān, the generous man whom Zuhayr used to praise, and his brother Khārijah, Baqīr of Banū Ghaṭafān—so called because he was brought out from his mother’s womb after she had died—and his brother, ʿAwf ibn Sinān, whose son was al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf, who secured the blood-money settlement between ʿAbs and Dhubyān.

As for Khaṣafah ibn Qays ʿAylān, his sons were ʿIkrimah and Muḥārib.

Some say that ʿIkrimah was the son of Qays.

As for Muḥārib ibn Khaṣafah, among them were Jasr and Banū al-Khaḍr.

Banū Jasr were allies of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah.

As for ʿIkrimah ibn Khaṣafah, his sons were ʿĀmir, Manṣūr, and Abū Mālik.

As for the sons of Abū Mālik ibn ʿIkrimah ibn Khaṣafah, they are among Banū Taym Allāh, four hundred households.

As for ʿĀmir ibn ʿIkrimah ibn Khaṣafah, they are a numerous group among Banū Sulaym in Baṣrah, and they have descendants remaining in the desert.

As for Manṣūr ibn ʿIkrimah, his sons were Sulaym, Salāmān, Hawāzin, and Māzin.

As for Māzin, among them was ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwān, who laid out the plan of Baṣrah.

As for Sulaym ibn Manṣūr, his son was Bahthah ibn Sulaym.

Bahthah’s sons were Imruʾ al-Qays and ʿAwf.

Among the tribes of Sulaym were Banū Ḥarām, Banū Khifāf, Sammāl, Raʿl, Dhakwān, Maṭrūd, Bahz, Qunfudh, Rifāʿah, ʿUṣayyah, Ẓafar, Bajlah, Ḥabīb ibn Mālik, Banū al-Sharīd, and Banū Qutbah.

As for Bajlah, it left Banū Sulaym and joined Banū ʿUqayl.

Banū al-Sharīd are the leading house of Sulaym. Among them were al-Khansāʾ and her two brothers, Ṣakhr ibn ʿAmr and Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmr.

As for Hawāzin ibn Manṣūr, his sons were Bakr, Sayyiʿ, Ḥarb, and Munabbih. Sayyiʿ and Ḥarb, the two sons of Hawāzin, left no descendants.

As for Munabbih, according to some, he was the father of Thaqīf.

The sons of Bakr ibn Hawāzin were Saʿd ibn Bakr, Muʿāwiyah ibn Bakr, and Zayd ibn Bakr.

As for Zayd ibn Bakr, his brother Muʿāwiyah killed him. He was the first to pay ransom in camels.

As for Saʿd ibn Bakr, they were foster-kin of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Hawāzin were taken captive, and his foster-sister came to him, so he freed them all.

As for Muʿāwiyah ibn Bakr, his sons were Jusham, Naṣr, Ṣaʿṣaʿah, Jasr, al-Sabbāq, Jaḥsh, Jaḥḥāsh, ʿAwf, Daḥwah, and Daḥyah.

As for Daḥwah, Daḥyah, Jaḥsh, and Jaḥḥāsh, we know of no descendants of theirs.

As for ʿAwf, they are called al-Waqʿah. The poet said: [basīṭ]

O sister of Daḥwah—nay, sister of their brothers,From ʿĀmir or Sulūl or al-Waqʿah.

As for Jusham, al-Akhṭal says of them: [ṭawīl]

Jusham are not the worst of tribes, for they areLike quail eggs: neither black nor red.

Among them was Ghaziyyah, the kin-group of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimmah.

As for Banū Naṣr, among them was Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Naṣrī, who commanded Hawāzin on the day of Ḥunayn.

As for Ṣaʿṣaʿah ibn Muʿāwiyah, his sons were ʿĀmir, Murrah, Ghāḍirah, Māzin, and Wāʾilah.

As for Banū Murrah, they are known as Banū Sulūl, after their mother. Among them was Abū Maryam al-Sulūlī.

Among them too was the poet al-ʿUjayr al-Sulūlī.

As for ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah, his sons were Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir—the kin-group of Zaynab daughter of Khuzaymah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ—and Suwāʾah ibn ʿĀmir. Of them al-Akhṭal says: [basīṭ]

My knowledge of Suwāʾah tells me that sheKeeps to the strings and the turbid drink.

And Numayr ibn ʿĀmir, a branch of the Arabs. Among them was Abū Ḥayyah al-Numayrī.

Among them too was al-Rāʿī the poet.

And Rabīʿah ibn ʿĀmir, whose descendants are Banū Majd, named after their mother. The poet Labīd ibn Rabīʿah said: [wāfir]

May my people, Banū Majd, be given drink, and mayNumayr and the tribes of Hilāl be given drink.

They are ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah, Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿah, and Kilāb ibn Rabīʿah.

As for ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah, among his descendants was ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir, the horseman of al-Ḍaḥyāʾ.

Among ʿAmr’s descendants was the poet Khidāsh ibn Zuhayr. Among his descendants too were Banū al-Bakkāʾ ibn ʿĀmir.

Among Banū al-Bakkāʾ was Kharqāʾ, the beloved of Dhū al-Rummah.

As for Kilāb ibn Rabīʿah, there was foolishness among them. His sons were Jaʿfar, Muʿāwiyah, Rabīʿah, Abū Bakr, ʿAmr, al-Waḥīd, [Abū] Ruwās, al-Aḍbaṭ, ʿAbd Allāh, and Kaʿb ibn Kilāb. Their total was ten.

Among the descendants of [Abū] Ruwās was Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ.

Among the descendants of al-Waḥīd was Umm al-Banīn. She was married to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁—and bore him al-ʿAbbās, Jaʿfar, and ʿAbd Allāh.

As for Muʿāwiyah ibn Kilāb, among them were al-Ḍibāb: Ḥisl, Ḥusayl, and Ḍabb, the sons of Muʿāwiyah.

As for ʿAmr ibn Kilāb, they are numerous. Among them is a group called Banū Dūdān. Among ʿAmr’s descendants was Yazīd ibn ʿAmr al-Ṣaʿq.

As for Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb, his sons were al-Aḥwaṣ, Khālid, Mālik, and ʿUtbah, the sons of Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb.

Al-Aḥwaṣ was kunya-named Abū Surayḥ. He commanded Banū ʿĀmir on the day of Jabalah.

Among his descendants was ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah, who contested with ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl before Hirm ibn Quṭbah al-Fazārī.

As for Khālid ibn Jaʿfar, he was the one who killed Zuhayr ibn Judhaymah al-ʿAbsī. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ẓālim al-Murrī killed him.

As for Mālik ibn Jaʿfar, his sons were: ʿĀmir, Ṭufayl, Rabīʿa, ʿUbayda, and Muʿāwiya. Their mother was Umm al-Banīn. About them Labīd said:

[rajaz]

We are the sons of Umm al-Banīn, the four,

He made them four, though they were five, for the sake of the rhyme.

As for Muʿāwiya, he was Muʿawwiḏ al-Ḥukamāʾ.

As for Rabīʿa, he was the father of the poet Labīd.

As for al-Ṭufayl, he was the father of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl.

As for Abū Bakr ibn Kilāb, among his descendants were the Qarṭāt: Qarṭ, Qurayṭ, and Muqarriṭ.

Among them was al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān, whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed over Banū Sulaym.

Among them was al-Muḥalliq ibn Ḥantam, of whom the poet al-Aʿshā said:

[ṭawīl]

And the dew and al-Muḥalliq spent the night by the fire.

The account of Kilāb is concluded.

As for Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿa, his sons were: ʿUqayl, Qushayr, al-Ḥuraysh, Jaʿda, ʿAbd Allāh, and Ḥabīb.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, among his descendants were the Banū al-ʿAjlān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, the clan of the poet Ibn Muqbil.

As for Jaʿda ibn Kaʿb, among his descendants was al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī.

As for al-Ḥuraysh ibn Kaʿb, among his descendants were Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr, Zurāra ibn Awfā, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sabra al-Ḥarashī, whose hand was cut off by the Roman Āṭriyūn.

As for Qushayr ibn Kaʿb, among his descendants were Ghuṭayf and Ghaṭafān.

Among them was Mālik Ḏū al-Ruqayba.

Among them were the Banū Ḍamra, who had many members in Basra.

As for ʿUqayl ibn Kaʿb, among his descendants were Khafāja, among whom were nobles, and among them were the allies.

Among them were the Banū al-Akhyal, the clan of Laylā al-Akhyaliyya. Among them was the poet al-Majnūn.

Among them was Tawba ibn al-Ḥumayyir, the companion of Laylā al-Akhyaliyya.

The descendants of Bakr ibn Hawāzin have come to an end.

Thaqīf

As for Munabbih ibn Hawāzin ibn Manṣūr ibn ʿIkrima ibn Khaṣafa ibn Qays ʿAylān, his sons were:

Qasī, who was Thaqīf. Thaqīf killed Abū Righāl, who was a collector of alms. Thaqīf passed by him and killed him, and it was said, “He was harsh toward him,” so he was named Qasī. The poet said:

[rajaz]

We are Qasī, and Qasā is our father.

Thaqīf’s sons were: Jusham, ʿAwf, and al-Misk.

As for al-Misk, Qāsiṭ married her, and she bore him Wāʾil, the father of Bakr ibn Wāʾil.

As for Jusham, he had a son, Ḥuṭayṭ. Ḥuṭayṭ’s sons were Mālik and Ghāḍira.

As for ʿAwf, they were the Allies, because they made a pact against the Banū Mālik, and Ghāḍira joined the Allies. Thus Thaqīf split into two groups: the Banū Mālik and the Allies.

Among the Banū Mālik was al-Sāʾib ibn al-Aqraʿ. Among them were the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Mālik, who were called al-Atharūn.

Among the Allies were al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd, al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt the poet, Abū Miḥjan the poet, al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada, Muʿattib, ʿAttāb, Abū ʿUtba, and ʿAtbān.

All of Muḍar has come to an end.

Rabīʿa ibn Nizār ibn Maʿadd

The sons of Rabīʿa ibn Nizār ibn Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnān were: Asad ibn Rabīʿa, Akhlab ibn Rabīʿa, and Ḍubayʿa ibn Rabīʿa.

As for Akhlab ibn Rabīʿa, they are among Khuṯʿam. Among them was Anas ibn Mudrik al-Khuṯʿamī, the killer of Sulayk ibn al-Salaka. They are many tribes and clans affiliated with Khuṯʿam.

As for Ḍubayʿa ibn Rabīʿa, his sons were Aḥmas and al-Ḥārith Ḏū al-Qilāda.

Among Aḥmas were a group belonging to the clan of the poet al-Musayyib ibn ʿAlas.

Among them were Bahtha and Dūfan, the clan of the poet al-Mutalammis, and al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dūfan, who was the chief of Ḍubayʿa in the pre-Islamic period.

Among them were the Banū al-Kalba, who were numerous and strong.

Among them were the Banū Shaḥna.

As for Asad ibn Rabīʿa, his sons were: Jadīla ibn Asad—whose mother was Iyādiyya—and ʿAnaza ibn Asad and ʿUmayra ibn Asad, whose mother was Barra daughter of Qays ʿAylān.

As for ʿUmayra ibn Asad, they are among ʿAbd al-Qays. His sons were: Mubashshir, Manṣūr, and Mālik, the sons of ʿUmayra.

As for ʿAnaza ibn Asad, his name was ʿĀmir. He was named ʿAnaza because he killed a man with a spear. It is also said that ʿAnaza was the son of Asad ibn Khuzayma. ʿAnaza’s sons were:

Yadkar ibn ʿAnaza and Yuqaddim ibn ʿAnaza.

As for Jadīla ibn Asad, his son was Daʿmī ibn Jadīla. Daʿmī’s son was Afṣā ibn Daʿmī. Afṣā’s sons were Hanb ibn Afṣā and ʿAbd al-Qays ibn Aqṣā. ʿAbd al-Qays’s son was al-Labūʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Qays—whose mother was Hind daughter of Tamīm daughter of Murra—and his two maternal brothers:

Taghlib and Bakr; and Afṣā ibn ʿAbd al-Qays.

As for al-Labūʾ, they are in Mosul, and there are many of them in Tawwaj.

As for Aqṣā ibn ʿAbd al-Qays, his sons were Shann and Lakīz.

Among Shann’s descendants was al-Dayl ibn Shann. His sons were Saʿd, Juḏayma, ʿĀmir, and Ḥabīb.

Among them were the Banū Bahtha ibn Juḏayma ibn al-Dayl.

As for Lakīz, his sons were Nakira, Ṣabbāḥ, and Wadīʿa.

As for Nakira, they are allies of Juḏayma. Among them were Munabbih ibn Nakira, who are the people of Bahrain, and among whom are great numbers and distinction. Among them were the poet al-Muthaththib al-ʿAbdī, the poet al-Mumazzaq, and the poet al-Mufaḍḍal ibn ʿĀmir, author of the Qaṣīda al-Munṣifa. In Oman there are people of Nakira, and in Yemen there are some of them.

As for Wadīʿa, his sons were ʿAmr ibn Wadīʿa, Ghanm ibn Wadīʿa, and Dahn ibn Wadīʿa.

As for Dahn ibn Wadīʿa, they are Wāʾila. They were affiliated with their mother, and among them was [ʿAmmār al-Dahnī].

As for Ghanm ibn Wadīʿa, his sons were ʿAmr ibn Ghanm and Ghawf ibn Ghanm.

As for ʿAmr ibn Wadīʿa, his sons were Anmār, ʿAjl, Muḥārib, al-Dayl, al-ʿAwq, and Imruʾ al-Qays.

Among the descendants of al-Dayl were the people of Oman, among them the Banū Ṣawḥān and Miṣqala ibn Ruqba, the orator.

Among them were the family of al-Muʿaḏḏal ibn ʿAylān in Basra.

As for al-ʿAwq, they are the ʿAwqa, a small Omani group.

As for Anmār, among them were ʿAṣr, the clan of al-Ashajj al-ʿAbdī; and among them were Ẓafar, the clan of Ṣuḥār al-ʿAbdī.

Among Anmār were the Banū Juḏayma. Among Juḏayma was Mahū, who bought flatulence for two cloaks of Ḥabra cloth.

As for Muḥārib ibn ʿAmr, his sons were Ḥaṭama and Ẓafar, the two sons of Muḥārib.

As for Hanb ibn Afṣā, his sons were Qāsiṭ ibn Hanb, ʿAmr ibn Hanb, and Jundab ibn Hanb.

As for ʿAmr ibn Hanb, among his descendants were ʿUtayb [page marker] ibn ʿAmr—they are among the Banū Shaybān—and ʿUtayb had many descendants in Basra. Jundab is also among the Banū Shaybān.

As for Qāsiṭ ibn Hanb, his sons were ʿAmr ibn Qāsiṭ, al-Namir ibn Qāsiṭ, and Wāʾil ibn Qāsiṭ. Their mother was al-Misk daughter of Thaqīf.

As for ʿAmr ibn Qāsiṭ, among his descendants were Ghuṭayfa, who had many members in the Jazīra among the Banū Taghlib.

As for al-Namir ibn Qāsiṭ, his sons were Taym Allāh, Aws Allāh, and ʿĀʾidh Allāh. Their mother was Hind daughter of Tamīm ibn Murra. Their maternal brothers were Bakr and Taghlib. Their other maternal brother was al-Labūʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Qays.

As for Taym Allāh, his sons were al-Khazraj and al-Ḥārith.

Al-Khazraj’s son was Saʿd. Saʿd’s son was ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd al-Ḍaḥḥiyān, because at midday he would arbitrate for his people and settle disputes among them; he was also the holder of their fourth share. [ʿĀmir’s sons were Rabīʿa and Rubayʿa]. Among his descendants was Hilāl ibn Rabīʿa ibn Zayd Manāt ibn ʿĀmir. Among them was Abū Ḥawṭ al-Ḥaẓāʾir. He was called Ḥawṭ al-Ḥaẓāʾir because al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays had gathered Bakr’s captives in enclosures to burn them. He interceded with him on their behalf, and al-Mundhir accepted his intercession.

Among them was Kaʿb ibn al-Ḥārith.

Among them was [Ibn] al-Kayyis al-Namirī.

Among them was Ibn al-Qirriyya. [Al-Qirriyya means “the crop”].

As for Wāʾil ibn Qāsiṭ, his sons were Bakr ibn Wāʾil, Taghlib ibn Wāʾil, and ʿAnz ibn Wāʾil. Their mother was Hind daughter of Tamīm ibn Murra.

As for ʿAnz Wāʾil, his sons were Arāsha and Rufayda. Among Arāsha’s descendants were Ashjaʿ and Ghaḍāḍa.

As for Taghlib ibn Wāʾil, his sons were Ghanm ibn Taghlib, Aws ibn Taghlib, and ʿImrān ibn Taghlib.

As for Ghanm ibn Taghlib, among his descendants was Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmr ibn Ghanm. Al-Akhṭal says of them: [wāfir]

When Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmr settled

by the watering places, the dogs were strangled.

Among them were the Arāqim, namely: Jusham, Mālik, ʿAmr, Thaʿlaba, al-Ḥārith, and Muʿāwiya, the sons of Bakr ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿAmr.

Among the Banū Taghlib were ʿAkkab. Among them were the Banū ʿAdī ibn Usāma. Among them were the Banū Kināna.

They are called the Quraysh of Taghlib, and they are the Banū ʿAkkab. Among them was Jusham ibn Bakr.

Among the Banū Jusham were the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Zuhayr, the clan of Kulayb ibn Rabīʿa, of whom it is said: “Mightier than Kulayb Wāʾil.” His brother was al-Muhalhil. He was the one who stirred up the war between Bakr and Taghlib, which lasted forty years.

Among the Banū Zuhayr were the Banū ʿAttāb. Among them was ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm.

Among the Banū Jusham were Fadūkas, the clan of the poet al-Akhṭal.

Bakr ibn Wāʾil

The sons of Bakr ibn Wāʾil were ʿAlī ibn Bakr, Yashkur ibn Bakr, and Badan ibn Bakr. Their mother was Hind daughter of Tamīm ibn Murra. She was called the Mother of the Tribes.

As for Yashkur ibn Bakr, his sons were Kaʿb ibn Yashkur, Kināna ibn Yashkur, and Ḥarb ibn Yashkur. Among Kaʿb’s descendants were great numbers and distinction.

Among the descendants of Kaʿb ibn Yashkur were Ḥubayb and al-ʿAtīk. Among them were the Banū ʿAnbar ibn Ghanm ibn Ḥabīb, Thaʿlaba, Jusham, and ʿAdī ibn Jusham.

This concludes Yashkur.

As for ʿAlī ibn Bakr ibn Wāʾil, his son was Ṣaʿb. Ṣaʿb’s sons were al-Lujaym ibn Ṣaʿb, ʿUkāba ibn Ṣaʿb, and Mālik ibn Ṣaʿb.

As for Mālik, among his descendants were the Banū Zamān, including al-Find al-Zamānī. Their numbers are among the Banū Ḥanīfa.

As for Lujaym ibn Ṣaʿb, his son was ʿAjl ibn Lujaym, and two others who left no descendants.

As for ʿAjl, his sons were Rabīʿa, Ḍubayʿa, Saʿd, and Kaʿb.

As for Saʿd and Ḍubayʿa, they were few.

As for Rabīʿa, among his descendants were Abū al-Najm, the rajaz poet of ʿAjl, and al-ʿAdīl ibn al-Farakh. Among them was Daghah the foolhardy woman. She was married to Jundab ibn al-ʿAnbar, and bore him ʿAdī ibn Jundab.

As for Saʿd ibn ʿAjl, most of their descendants are among his line. Among them were al-Aghlab, the rajaz poet, and Abū Dulaf. Among them was al-Furāt ibn Ḥayyān, who was a Companion.

The account of ʿAjl has come to an end.

As for Ḥanīfa ibn Lujaym, his sons were al-Duʾl ibn Ḥanīfa, ʿAdī ibn Ḥanīfa, ʿĀmir ibn Ḥanīfa, and ʿAbd Manāt ibn Ḥanīfa.

As for ʿAbd Manāt, they were few.

Among the descendants of ʿAdī ibn Ḥanīfa was Musaylima the Liar.

Among al-Duʾl were the Banū Haffān. Among them was Hawdha ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥanafī, the Crowned One.

The account of Ḥanīfa has come to an end.

As for ʿUkāba ibn Ṣaʿb, his sons were Qays and Thaʿlaba.

As for Qays ibn ʿUkāba, they were few, and their numbers are among the Banū Ḏuhl.

As for Thaʿlaba ibn ʿUkāba, he is called al-Ḥiṣn. Al-Aʿshā said: [ṭawīl]

What harm would it have done her had she mingled in their homes

with the Banū al-Ḥiṣn, had the tribes not been at odds?

The sons of Thaʿlaba were Ḏuhl ibn Thaʿlaba, Shaybān ibn Thaʿlaba, Qays ibn Thaʿlaba, Taym Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba, Atīd ibn Thaʿlaba, and Ḍanna ibn Thaʿlaba.

As for Ḍanna, they joined Yemen and became part of the Banū ʿUḏra.

As for Atīd, they are among the Banū Shaybān.

As for Taym Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba, they are the Lahāzim, allies of the Banū ʿAjl.

The sons of Taym Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba were Mālik, al-Ḥārith, ʿĀmir, Hilāl, Ḏuhl, Zamān, Māzin, and Ḥāṭiba. These are called the Allies, [except for] al-Ḥārith, ʿĀmir, and Mālik. The others are called Allies because they made a pact against these three.

As for Qays ibn Thaʿlaba, his sons were Ḍubayʿa, Taym, and Saʿd.

Ḍubayʿa had many descendants. Among them was al-Aʿshā Maymūn ibn Qays. Among them was Rabīʿa al-Jaḥdar, who was the horseman of Bakr ibn Wāʾil on the day of the Shaving of the Forelocks. Among them were Murra ibn ʿAbbād, al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbbād, and Jarīr ibn ʿAbbād, to whom the traditionist al-Jarīrī is affiliated.

As for “Taym ibn Qays” and “Saʿd ibn Qays,” they are the two Ḥirqas.

As for “Dhuhl ibn Thaʿlabah ibn ʿUkābah,” he fathered Shaybān and ʿĀmir.

As for “ʿĀmir,” they are called al-Wakham.

As for “Shaybān ibn Dhuhl,” his descendants are Sadūs ibn Shaybān—in whose line the numbers lie—and ʿAmr, Māzin, ʿAlbāʾ, Mālik, ʿĀmir, and Zayd Manāt.

As for “ʿAlbāʾ ibn Shaybān,” they are few.

Among the descendants of “ʿAmr ibn Shaybān” was al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Shawr, of whom the poet says: [wāfir]

I was once the companion of al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Shawr,

and no companion of al-Qaʿqāʿ is ever wretched.

Among them was Daghfal the genealogist.

As for “Sadūs ibn Shaybān,” he held the position of deputy to Ākil al-Murār, and he had ten children, among them al-Ḥārith ibn Sadūs, who had twenty-one sons. The poet said of him:

Had my Lord wished, the penis of your father

would have been long, like the penis of al-Ḥārith ibn Sadūs.

As for “Shaybān ibn Thaʿlabah ibn ʿUkābah,” his descendants are Dhuhl, Taym, Thaʿlabah, and ʿAwf.

As for “ʿAwf,” he left no descendants.

As for “Thaʿlabah,” among them was Miṣqal ibn Hubayrah al-Shaybānī.

As for “Taym ibn Shaybān,” they are known for generosity and eminence. Among the Banū Taym were al-Aṣmaʿān; in the pre-Islamic period, people used to say “the Day of the Two Aṣmaʿs.”

As for “Dhuhl ibn Shaybān,” his descendants were Murrah ibn Dhuhl ibn Shaybān, in whose line the numbers, the household, and the chieftainship lay; Rabīʿah ibn Dhuhl; Muḥallim ibn Dhuhl; and al-Ḥārith ibn Dhuhl. Their mother was Ruqāsh.

And ʿAbd Ghanm ibn Dhuhl, ʿAwf ibn Dhuhl, Ṣubayḥ, and Shaybān, whose mother was al-Wārithah, from Banū Yashkur. They are attributed to her and are called “the Banū al-Wārithah.”

And ʿAmr, whose mother was Jadhrah, a captive woman from Yemen; they are called “the Banū Jadhrah,” and they are few.

Among the notable men of the Banū Shaybān was ʿAwf ibn Muḥallim ibn Dhuhl, of whom it was said:

“There is no free man in ʿAwf’s valley.” Among them were al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Shārī, al-Buṭayn ibn Zayd al-Shārī, and Shabīb and Qaʿnab, the two Khārijites.

Among them were Hāniʾ ibn Masʿūd, the commander at the Day of Dhū Qār, and his brother Qays ibn Masʿūd.

Among them was Jassās, the killer of Kulayb.

Among them were Suwayd ibn Sulaym al-Shārī and al-Muthannā ibn Ḥārithah, who conquered al-Sawād. When al-Muthannā died, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ married his wife “Salmā.” She looked at the people of al-Qādisiyyah and said, “The men are evenly matched, but they have no Muthannā.” Saʿd slapped her.

Among them were al-Ḥawfizān ibn Shurayk and Maṭar ibn Shurayk.

Among the descendants of “Maṭar” were Maʿn ibn Zāʾidah and Yazīd ibn Mazīd.

Among them was Qays ibn Masʿūd al-Shaybānī, chief of Bakr ibn Wāʾil, and his son Basṭām ibn Qays.

Among them were the Banū al-Shaqīqah, named after their mother. All of these trace back to “Dhuhl ibn Shaybān.”

All of “Nizār” has now been covered.

Genealogy of Yemen

He said: The genealogists agree that Yemen descends from Qaḥṭān, whose genealogy has already been established earlier in the book.

They say: Qaḥṭān fathered Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān. Yaʿrub fathered Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub.

Yashjub fathered Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub.

Some say that “Sabaʾ” was named ʿĀmir.

“Sabaʾ” fathered Ḥimyar ibn Sabaʾ, Kahlan ibn Sabaʾ, ʿAmr ibn Sabaʾ, al-Ashʿar ibn Sabaʾ, Anmār ibn Sabaʾ, ʿĀmilah ibn Sabaʾ, and Murrah ibn Sabaʾ.

As for “ʿAmr ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered ʿAdī ibn ʿAmr. “ʿAdī” fathered Lakhm ibn ʿAdī and Judhām ibn ʿAdī.

Among “Lakhm” were Ḥadas ibn Lakhm, comprising many tribes.

Some people say that they descend from Arāshah ibn Murrah ibn Add ibn Ṭābikhah ibn al-Yās, because “Arāshah” joined the Yemenites and became part of “Judhām.”

Among “Lakhm” were Ghanm ibn Lakhm, comprising many tribes.

Some people say that they are from “Muḍar.”

Among “Lakhm” were the Banū al-Dār ibn Hāniʾ, who are the Dāriyyūn. Tamīm al-Dārī was one of them.

Among “Judhām” were Ḥarām ibn Judhām and Ḥashm ibn Judhām.

“Ḥarām” fathered Ghaṭafān ibn Ḥarām and Mālik ibn Ḥarām.

Among “Ghaṭafān” were Naḍlah, the Banū al-Aḥnaf, the Banū al-Ḍabīb, the Banū Hadālah, the Banū Nafāthah, the Banū Ḍulayʿ, the Banū ʿĀʾidhah, the Banū Shabrah, the Banū ʿAbd Allāh, the Banū al-Khaḍrāʾ, the Banū Sulaym, the Banū Bajālah, the Banū Ghanm, and the Banū Fākih.

Some people claim that “Ghaṭafān ibn Ḥarām” are from Qays ʿAylān, who came to Yemen.

“Mālik ibn Ḥarām ibn Judhām” fathered Saʿd ibn Mālik and Wāʾil ibn Mālik.

The descendants of “Saʿd ibn Mālik” comprise many clans.

Among them are the Banū ʿAwf, the Banū ʿĀʾidhah, the Banū Fuhayrah, the Banū Ṣabḥah, the Banū al-Akhnas, the Banū Ḥayy, and others.

The descendants of “Wāʾil ibn Mālik” comprise many clans.

“Ḥashm ibn Judhām” fathered five lineages, among them Ḥaṭmah.

The genealogists of “Muḍar” claim that they are from the Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah.

As for “al-Ashʿar ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered the Ashʿarites, the kin of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

As for “Anmār ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered a son whose descendants formed alliances with Khathʿam and Bajīlah.

The genealogists of “Muḍar” claim that “Khathʿam” and “Bajīlah” are the sons of Anmār ibn Nizār, and that “Anmār ibn Sabaʾ” attached their lineage to “Sabaʾ” by using their father’s name.

Others said:

Khathʿam and Bajīlah are the sons of ʿAmr ibn al-Ghawth, the brother of al-Azd ibn al-Ghawth; and Bajīlah is a woman.

Among the clans of “Bajīlah” are Qasr, the kin of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī; and the Banū Aḥmas, the kin of Shibl ibn Maʿbad. Their other clans are not well known.

As for “ʿĀmilah ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered tribes of Yemen, and they are few.

The genealogists of “Muḍar” claim that they descend from Qāsiṭ ibn Wāʾil. Al-Aʿshā said: [mutaqārib]

O ʿĀmil, how long will you wander

far from your noblest father?

Your father is Qāsiṭ, so return

to the most ancient and earliest lineage.

As for “Ḥimyar ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered Mālik ibn Ḥimyar, ʿĀmir ibn Ḥimyar, Saʿd ibn Ḥimyar, Wāʾilah ibn Ḥimyar, and ʿAmr ibn Ḥimyar.

“ʿĀmir ibn Ḥimyar” fathered Dahmān ibn ʿĀmir. Dahmān fathered Yaḥṣub, in its entirety.

“Saʿd ibn Ḥimyar” fathered Ansalaf and Aslam.

“ʿAmr ibn Ḥimyar” fathered al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr. “Al-Ḥārith” fathered Dhū Rayʿīn.

“Mālik ibn Ḥimyar” fathered Quḍāʿah ibn Mālik.

Among the tribes of “Quḍāʿah” was Kalb ibn Wabrah. Among their clans were the Banū ʿAdī ibn Janāb, the Banū ʿAlīm ibn Janāb, and others—Zuhayr mentioned them.

Among them were the Banū al-ʿUbayd. Al-Aʿshā said: [wāfir]

[The Banū of the sacred month are not my kin,

nor am I of the noble Banū al-ʿUbayd.]

Among them were Rufaydah, Miṣād, the Banū al-Qayn, Sulayḥ, Tanūkh, Jarm ibn Rabbān, Rāsib ibn Jarm, Bahrāʾ, Balī, Mahrah, ʿUdrah, Saʿd Hudhaym—Hudhaym was an Abyssinian slave who brought up “Saʿd,” and so Saʿd was attributed to him—Ḍannah ibn Saʿd, Salāmān ibn Saʿd, Juhaynah ibn Saʿd, and Nahd ibn Saʿd.

Among “Quḍāʿah” were the Tubbaʿs. Among them were Dhū al-Kalāʿ, Dhū Nuwās, Dhū Aṣbaḥ—to whom the Aṣbaḥī whips are attributed—Dhū Jadān, Dhū Fāʾish, and Dhū Yazan. Also Jerash, al-Shaḥūl, and many clans.

“Wāʾilah ibn Ḥimyar” fathered al-Sakāsik ibn Wāʾilah; among “Ḥimyar,” the numbers lie with the Sakāsik.

As for “Kahlan ibn Sabaʾ,” he fathered Zayd ibn Kahlan. “Zayd” fathered Mālik ibn Zayd and Add ibn Zayd.

“Add” fathered Ṭayyiʾ ibn Add and al-Ghawth ibn Add.

Among “Ṭayyiʾ” were the Banū Nabḥān ibn ʿAmr, the Banū Thaʿl ibn ʿAmr, and Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

Among them were Jarm ibn ʿAmr and the Banū Sunbus. The poet said: [mutaqārib]

Then the Sunbusī hunter came upon her.

The Banū “Taym ibn Thaʿlabah,” of whom Imruʾ al-Qays says: [wāfir]

The Banū Taym are lamps in the darkness.

The clans of “Ṭayyiʾ” are numerous, but the majority of lineages are attributed to “Ṭayyiʾ,” the forefather.

“Mālik ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan” fathered Yaḥābir ibn Mālik—who is Murād—Martaʿ ibn Mālik, Qarn ibn Mālik, and Khiyār ibn Mālik.

“Martaʿ ibn Mālik” fathered Thawr ibn Martaʿ.

“Thawr” fathered Kindah ibn Thawr and Yazīd ibn Thawr.

“Yazīd” fathered Ṣadāʾ ibn Yazīd.

“Kindah” fathered Tajīb and al-Sakūn.

“Khiyār ibn Mālik” fathered Rabīʿah ibn Khiyār.

“Rabīʿah ibn Khiyār” fathered Awsalah ibn Rabīʿah; they are Hamdān.

Among “Hamdān” were al-Subayʿ, the kin of Abū Isḥāq al-Subayʿī, and Widāʿah, the kin of Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ.

“Yaḥābir ibn Mālik” fathered Madhḥij ibn Yaḥābir.

“Madhḥij” fathered Murād, Saʿd al-ʿAshīrah, Khālid, and ʿAns.

As for “ʿAns,” they are the kin of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī, who claimed prophethood in Yemen.

“Saʿd al-ʿAshīrah ibn Madhḥij” fathered Jaʿfī ibn Saʿd, Janb ibn Saʿd, al-Ḥakam ibn Saʿd, ʿĀʾidh Allāh ibn Saʿd, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd, al-Labūʾ ibn Saʿd, Khārijah ibn Saʿd, Asad ibn Saʿd, ʿAmr ibn Saʿd, Jaml ibn Saʿd, and al-Ṣaʿb ibn Saʿd.

As for “Jaʿfī ibn Saʿd,” among them were Marrān and Ḥarīm, the two sons of Jaʿfī. Labīd said:

[kāmil]

I have certainly wept on the Day of al-Nakhīl and before it,

Marrān, from among our days, and Ḥarīm.

As for “al-Ṣaʿb ibn Saʿd,” among them were Zubayd ibn al-Ṣaʿb, the kin of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Zubaydī, and Awd ibn Ṣaʿb.

As for “Khārijah,” among them was Jadīlah ibn Khārijah, who belongs to Ṭayyiʾ.

As for “ʿAmr ibn Saʿd,” he is the father of Khawlān ibn ʿAmr.

As for “al-Ḥakam,” it is of them that it was said: “They came—the Ḥakam.”

As for “Janb,” Muhalhil says of them: [majzūʾ [??] basīṭ]

Marry her: the Aqārim have lost her;

among Janb, the bridal gift was hides.

As for “Jaml,” among them was Hind ibn ʿAmr al-Jamalī, who was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and was killed. His killer said:

I killed ʿAlbāʾ and Hind al-Jamalī.

“Mazād ibn Madhḥij” fathered Anʿam ibn Murād and Yaḥābir ibn Murād. They had Yaghūth at Jerash. “Khālid ibn Madhḥij” fathered ʿIllah ibn Khālid. “ʿIllah” fathered ʿAmr ibn ʿIllah.

ʿAmr fathered Jisr ibn ʿAmr and Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr.

As for “Jisr,” he is the father of al-Nakhaʿ ibn Jisr, the kin of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

As for “Kaʿb,” among them were the Banū al-Nār, the Banū al-Ḥammās—the kin of al-Najāshī, the poet—and the Banū Qinān.

“Qarn ibn Mālik ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan”—whose name was Nabt—fathered al-Ghawth. Al-Ghawth fathered al-Azd. Al-Azd fathered Māzin, ʿAmr, Daws, Naṣr, Mālik, Qidār, al-Hanū, Midʿān, Zahrān, ʿĀmir, and ʿAbd Allāh.

As for “Māzin,” they are Ghassān. Ghassān is a body of water to which they are attributed.

Among them were the Banū Jafnah—the kin of the kings—and the family of ʿAnqāʾ, the family of Muḥarriq, Tanūkh, and Kaʿb, the kin of Jābilah ibn al-Ayham al-Ghassānī.

It used to be said: “Māzin Ghassān are the lords of kings; Ḥimyar are the lords of the Arabs; Kindah are kings; Madhḥij are the lancers; Hamdān are the saddles of horses; and al-Azd are the lionhearted people.”

As for “Midʿān,” among them were Salāmān.

As for “Zahrān,” among them was Daws ibn ʿAdthān, the kin of Abū Hurayrah.

Among them were Jadhīmah ibn Mālik ibn Fahm ibn Ghanm ibn Daws, the companion of “al-Zabbāʾ”—he was Jadhīmah al-Abrash—and Jadhm ibn Mālik, the kin of the Jahāḍim. Among them was the jurist Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim; and Sulaymah ibn Mālik, the kin of Abū Ḥamzah the Khārijite; and the Banū Hanāʾah ibn Mālik, the kin of ʿUqbah ibn Salm; and Maʿn ibn Mālik, the kin of Masʿūd ibn ʿAmr.

Among them was a clan called Yaḥmad. Among them was al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, the author of the science of prosody, from a branch called the Farāhīd. One says, “So-and-so is al-Farhūdī.”

Among “Zahrān” were the al-Ghaṭārīf: the Banū Yashkur and al-Jadrah.

As for “ʿĀmir ibn al-Azd,” among them were the Banū Lahb ibn ʿĀmir, the physiognomists.

Among them were Ghāmid.

As for “ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Azd,” his descendants were numerous, among them the Qasāmil.

Among them were the Azd of al-ʿAtīk, the kin of al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufrah.

Among them were Bāriq ibn ʿAwf, Shahrān ibn Bāriq, Ṭāḥiyah ibn Sūd, and Haddād.

Among them was ʿAmr Muzayqiyāʾ ibn ʿĀmir. The Anṣār descend from him: al-Aws and al-Khazraj, the sons of Ḥārithah ibn Thaʿlabah al-ʿAnqāʾ ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir.

Among them were ʿImrān ibn ʿAmr and Khuzāʿah, who descend from ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir.

Among “Khuzāʿah” was a clan called the Banū Qumayr, the kin of Qubayṣah ibn Dhuʾayb and the kin of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mālik.

Among them were the Banū Ḥalīl, the kin of the Banū Kurz, the physiognomists.

Among them were the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, Kaʿb, Mulayḥ, ʿAdī, Saʿd, Aslam, and Jashm.

The Genealogy of al-Aws and al-Khazraj

They are al-Aws and al-Khazraj, the two sons of Ḥāritha son of Thaʿlaba son of ʿAmr son of ʿĀmir son of Ḥāritha son of Imruʾ al-Qays son of Thaʿlaba Māzin son of ʿAbd Allāh son of al-Azd son of al-Ghawth son of al-Nabt son of Mālik son of Zayd son of Kahlan son of Sabaʾ. They are the two sons of Qayla, being ascribed to their mother, and they are the Anṣār.

Al-Khazraj son of Ḥāritha had five sons: Jashm son of al-Khazraj and ʿAwf son of al-Khazraj, who were the two Khurṭumān; and it was said: [rajaz]

If honor delights you, then vaunt Jashm!

Al-Ḥārith son of al-Khazraj, ʿAmr son of al-Khazraj, and Kaʿb son of al-Khazraj.

As for Jashm son of al-Khazraj, among them were the Banū Tazīd. Among the Banū Tazīd son of Jashm were the Banū Salima and their clans.

Among the Banū Jashm were the Banū Bayāḍa.

As for ʿAwf son of al-Khazraj, among them were the Banū Ḥublā—the people of ʿAbd Allāh son of Ubayy son of Salūl—and the Qawāqil. In the pre-Islamic period, when a man sought protection in Yathrib, he was told:

“Call out ‘qawqil,’ and then you are safe.”

Among them were the Banū Sālim.

As for ʿAmr son of al-Khazraj, among them were the Najjār. The name of the Najjār was Taym Allāt son of Thaʿlaba. He was given this name because he cut a man’s face with an adze. It is also said that he was given it because he was circumcised with an adze.

As for Kaʿb son of al-Khazraj, among them were the clans of Sāʿida, the people of Saʿd son of ʿUbāda.

The Genealogy of al-Aws son of Ḥāritha

He said: Al-Aws son of Ḥāritha had Mālik son of al-Aws. From Mālik all the tribes and clans of al-Aws branched out.

Mālik son of al-Aws had ʿAmr son of Mālik—they are al-Nabīt—and ʿAbd al-Ashhal, and the Banū Ẓafar—the name of Ẓafar was Kaʿb son of al-Khazraj—and these are:

Khazraj among the al-Aws; and the Banū Ḥāritha son of al-Ḥārith son of al-Khazraj. These are the al-Nabīt of al-Aws.

ʿAwf son of Mālik, among whom were the Banū ʿAmr son of ʿAwf, the people of Qubāʾ. Among them were Jaḥjabā.

Murra son of Mālik—they are the Jaʿādira, and they are called Aws Allāh.

Sālim son of Mālik; they are the Banū Wāqif.

Al-Silm son of Mālik; they are the people of Saʿd son of Khaythama.

ʿAbd Allāh son of Mālik; they are the Banū Khaṭma.

The genealogies are concluded.

Naming Those Who Married Their Father’s Wife after Him

Barra—Barra daughter of Murra was the sister of Tamīm son of Murra. She was married to Khuzayma son of Mudrika son of Ilyās son of Muḍar. His son Kināna son of Khuzayma then married her, and she bore him al-Naḍr son of Kināna and other offspring of his, except for ʿAbd Manāt son of Kināna.

Nājiya—Nājiya daughter of Jarm son of Rabbān, of Quḍāʿa, was married to Sāma son of Luʾayy. She bore him Ghālib son of Sāma. Then he died, and his son al-Ḥārith son of Sāma married her.

Wāqida—Wāqida was of the Banū Māzin son of Ṣaʿṣaʿa and was with ʿAbd Manāf. She bore him Nawfal and Abū ʿAmr. He died, and his son Hāshim son of ʿAbd Manāf married her. She bore him Khālida and Ḍaʿīfa.

Āmina—Āmina daughter of Abān son of Kulayb was with Umayya son of ʿAbd Shams. She bore him the Aʿyāṣ. Then he died, and his son Abū ʿAmr son of Umayya married her. She bore him Abū Muʿayṭ.

Mālikah—Mālikah daughter of Sinān son of Ḥāritha al-Murrī, the sister of Hirm son of Sinān, was married to Zabān son of Sayyār son of ʿAmr al-Fazārī. After him, his son Manẓūr son of Zabān married her. She bore him Khawla daughter of Manẓūr and Hāshim son of Manẓūr. Al-Ḥasan son of ʿAlī son of Abū Ṭālib ﵁—married Khawla, and she bore him al-Ḥasan son of al-Ḥasan. Then Muḥammad son of Ṭalḥa son of ʿUbayd Allāh married her after him, and she bore Ibrāhīm son of Muḥammad, who was al-Aʿraj.

A woman of the Anṣār: she was the wife of Isāf son of Zayd son of Isāf. Isāf married her after his father.

A woman of Fahm: she was married to Nufayl son of ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, the grandfather of ʿUmar son of al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. After him, ʿAmr son of Nufayl married her, and she bore him Zayd. His mother was:

Umm al-Khaṭṭāb. This Zayd was the father of Saʿīd son of Zayd son of ʿAmr son of Nufayl.

Names Shared among the Tribes

[Sadūs: among Rabīʿa. He was Sadūs son of Shaybān, of Bakr son of Wāʾil.

Among them was Suwayd son of Manjūf.

And Sadūs, with an unraised sīn: among Tamīm. He was Sadūs son of Dārim.

Muḥārib son of Fihr son of Mālik son of al-Naḍr, among Quraysh.

Muḥārib son of Khaṣafa, among Qays ʿAylān.

Muḥārib son of ʿAmr son of Wadīʿa, among ʿAbd al-Qays.

Ghāḍira, among the Banū Asad son of Khuzayma.

And Ghāḍira, among the Banū Ṣaʿṣaʿa son of Muʿāwiya.

Ghāḍira also, among Thaqīf.

Taym son of Murra, among Quraysh, the people of Abū Bakr.

And Taym son of Ghālib son of Fihr, also among Quraysh: they are the Banū al-Adram.

Taym son of ʿAbd Manāt son of Add son of Ṭābikha, among Muḍar.

Taym, among Ḍabba.

Taym, among Qays son of Thaʿlaba.

Taym, among Shaybān.

Taym Allāh son of Thaʿlaba, among ʿUkāba.

Taym Allāh, among al-Namir son of Qāsiṭ.

Taym Allāh, among Ḍabba.

Kilāb son of Murra, among Quraysh.

Kilāb son of Rabīʿa son of ʿĀmir son of Ṣaʿṣaʿa, among Qays.

ʿAdī son of Kaʿb, among Quraysh, the people of ʿUmar son of al-Khaṭṭāb.

ʿAdī son of ʿAbd Manāt, among al-Ribāb, the people of Dhū al-Rumma.

ʿAdī, among Fazāra.

ʿAdī, among the Banū Ḥanīfa.

Dhuhl son of Mālik, among Ḍabba.

Dhuhl son of Thaʿlaba, among ʿUkāba.

Dhuhl, among the Banū Shaybān.

Ḍubayʿa, among the Banū Ḍabba.

Ḍubayʿa, among the Banū ʿIjl.

Ḍubayʿa, among Qays son of Thaʿlaba; they are the people of al-Aʿshā.

Al-Duʾal, among Ḥanīfa [son of Bakr son of Wāʾil. Among them were Qatāda son of Maslama and Hawdha son of ʿAlī, the possessor of the crown, whom the poet al-Aʿshā of Bakr son of Wāʾil praised.

Al-Duʾal, among the Banū Kināna.

Al-Duʾil, among the Banū ʿAbd al-Qays.

Among them also was al-Duʾil son of ʿAmr son of Wadīʿa.

Al-Duʾil, among Ḍubayʿa.

Al-Duʾil, among Kināna, the people of Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī.

Māzin, among Taym.

Māzin, among Qays ʿAylān; they are the people of ʿUtba son of Ghazwān.

Māzin, among the Banū Ṣaʿṣaʿa son of Muʿāwiya.

Māzin, among the Banū Shaybān.

Sahm, among Quraysh.

Sahm, among Bāhila.

Saʿd, among Dhubyān.

Saʿd son of Bakr, the wet nurses of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Saʿd, among ʿIjl.

Saʿd, among Zayd Manāt son of Tamīm.

Jashm, among Muʿāwiya son of Bakr.

Jashm, among Thaqīf.

Jashm, among the Arāqim.

The Banū Ḍamra, among Kināna.

The Banū Ḍamra, among Qushayr.

Dūdān, among the Banū Asad.

Dūdān, among the Banū Kilāb son of Rabīʿa.

Sulaym, among Qays ʿAylān.

Sulaym, among Judhām, of Yemen.

Judayla, among Rabīʿa.

Judayla, among Ṭayyiʾ.

[Judayla, among Qays ʿAylān.

Al-Khazraj, among the Anṣār.

Al-Khazraj, among al-Namir son of Qāsiṭ.

Asad, son of Khuzayma son of Mudrika.

Asad, son of Rabīʿa son of Nizār.

Shaqra, son of Ḍabba.

Shaqra, among the Banū Tamīm.

The Greater Rabīʿa: he was Rabīʿa son of Mālik son of Zayd Manāt, and was nicknamed Rabīʿa al-Jūʿ (“Rabīʿa of Hunger”).

The Middle Rabīʿa: he was Rabīʿa son of Ḥanẓala son of Mālik son of Zayd Manāt.

The Lesser Rabīʿa: he was Rabīʿa son of Mālik son of Ḥanẓala.

Each one of them was the uncle of another.

The Genealogy of the Messenger of God ﷺ

He was Muḥammad son of ʿAbd Allāh son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib son of Hāshim son of ʿAbd Manāf son of Quṣayy son of Kilāb son of Murra son of Kaʿb son of Luʾayy son of Ghālib son of Fahw2 son of Mālik son of al-Naḍr son of Kināna son of Khuzayma son of Mudrika son of Ilyās son of Muḍar son of Nizār son of Maʿadd son of ʿAdnān.

Genealogists differed about those after ʿAdnān. I have set this out in the Book of Genealogy.

The name of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was ʿĀmir, and the name of his father Hāshim was ʿAmr. He was named Hāshim because he crumbled the tharīd and fed people.

The name of ʿAbd Manāf was al-Mughīra. The name of Quṣayy was Zayd. He was called Mujammiʿ (“the Gatherer”) because he gathered the tribes of Quraysh and settled them in Mecca.

The Prophet’s Father, Uncles, and Aunts ﷺ

Abū Muḥammad said:

ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib son of Hāshim had ten sons and six daughters of his own. Their names were:

ʿAbd Allāh son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet’s father ﷺ.

Al-Zubayr son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Abū Ṭālib son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; his name was ʿAbd Manāf.

Al-ʿAbbās son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Ḍirār son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Ḥamza son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Muqawwim son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Abū Lahab son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; his name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

Al-Ḥārith son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Ghaydāq son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; his name was Ḥajal.

The Names of His Aunts ﷺ

ʿĀtika daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Umayma daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Bayḍāʾ daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. She was Umm Ḥakīm.

And Barraʾ daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

And Ṣafiyya daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

And Arwā daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

[The Mothers

These sons and daughters had six mothers, whose names were:

Fāṭima daughter of ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿImrān ibn Makhzūm. Among her children were ʿAbd Allāh, the father of the Prophet ﷺ—al-Zubayr, Abū Ṭālib, ʿĀtika, Umayma, al-Bayḍāʾ, and Barraʾ—seven.

And al-Namiriyya, a woman of Banū al-Namir ibn Qāsiṭ, whose name was Nutayla [daughter of Kulayb ibn Mālik ibn Junāb. Among her children were al-ʿAbbās and Ḍirār—two.

And Hāla daughter of Wuhayb ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra. Among her children were Ḥamza, al-Muqawwim, and Ṣafiyya—three.

And Lubnā, a woman of Khuzāʿa. Her child was Abū Lahab alone.

And Ṣafiyya, a woman of Banū Ṣaʿṣaʿa. Her children were al-Ḥārith and Arwā—two.

And another woman, of Khuzāʿa, whose name was not preserved. Her child was al-Ghaydāq alone.

[Later I was told that her name was Mumtiʿa daughter of ʿAmr.]

The Maternal Uncles of His Uncles and His Father ﷺ

As for ʿAbd Allāh, the father of the Prophet ﷺ—he had no child besides the Messenger of God ﷺ—neither male nor female. His maternal uncles were in Medina, so he went to them and died there while still a young man.

As for al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was one of the leading men of Quraysh, and he used to compose poetry. He is the one who said: [wāfir]

Were it not for the Ḥums, men would not wear

Garments of honor until they die.

Abū Muḥammad said:

The Ḥums are Kināna and Quraysh.

He was known by the kunya Abū Ṭāhir. Among his descendants were ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, who lived to see Islam, became Muslim, and left no descendants; Ḍubāʿa daughter of al-Zubayr, who was married to al-Miqdād; and Umm al-Ḥakam, who was married to Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib had no surviving descendants through his sons.

As for Abū Ṭālib ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he had ʿAlī, Jaʿfar, ʿAqīl, Ṭālib, Umm Hāniʾ—whose name was Fākhita—and Jumāna.

Their mother was Fāṭima daughter of Asad ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf.

ʿAqīl was ten years older than Jaʿfar. They all had descendants except Ṭālib, who left none.

Their mother, Fāṭima daughter of Asad, became Muslim. She was the first Hāshimite woman to bear a child to a Hāshimite.

Abū Ṭālib died three years and four months before the Messenger of God ﷺ—emigrated to Medina.

As for al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, his kunya was Abū al-Faḍl. He held responsibility for the provision of water and for Zamzam; the Prophet ﷺ—entrusted these to him on the day Mecca was conquered. He was with the Prophet ﷺ—at al-ʿAqaba, where he made the pact with the Anṣār and took charge of that matter.

He died in Medina during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, having lost his sight. He was eighty-nine years old.

He had been born three years before the [Year of the] Elephant, and so was older than the Prophet ﷺ.

ʿUthmān performed the funeral prayer over him, and his son ʿAbd Allāh entered his grave.

His children were ʿAbd Allāh, al-Faḍl, ʿUbayd Allāh, Qutham, Maʿbad, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and Umm Ḥabīb.

Their mother was Umm al-Faḍl daughter of al-Ḥārith [ibn Ḥazn al-Hilāliyya, the sister of Maymūna daughter of al-Ḥārith, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. Umm al-Faḍl’s name was Lubāba. Tammām, Kathīr, al-Ḥārith, Āmina, and Ṣafiyya were by slave mothers.

As for al-Faḍl, his kunya was Abū Muḥammad. He was the eldest of his children, and he was the one by whom al-ʿAbbās was known by his kunya.

He died in Syria during the plague of ʿAmwās. He left no descendants except a daughter called Umm Kulthūm, who was married to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās, he was generous and munificent. [He had many slaves.

He used to say to his slaves: “Whoever among you brings me a guest is free”.

He was ʿAlī’s governor in Yemen, and he became blind at the end of his life.

ʿUbayd Allāh’s children were ʿAbd Allāh, al-ʿAbbās, and Jaʿfar.

As for ʿAbd Allāh, his children were al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn. Their mother was Asmāʾ daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās.

ʿĀʾisha al-Ḥārithiyya was married to ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās, and she bore him two sons in Yemen. Muʿāwiya sent Busr ibn Arṭāʾ in his place, so ʿUbayd Allāh fled, and Busr seized his two sons and killed them. Their mother is the one who says: [basīṭ]

O you who have news of my two sons,

Like two pearls from which the shell has shattered,

As for Maʿbad ibn al-ʿAbbās, he went on a campaign to Ifrīqiya during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, and was killed there. His concubine was taken while pregnant and gave birth to a girl. The girl was rescued and married to Yazīd al-Ḥimyarī. Maʿbad’s son was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maʿbad. ʿAbd Allāh’s sons were al-ʿAbbās, al-ʿAbbās, and al-ʿAbbās—three. One of them was made black in Medina in the days when Abū al-ʿAbbās rose to power, and he took it.

He left no descendants.

As for al-Ḥārith ibn al-ʿAbbās, he had descendants. Among them was al-Sarī ibn ʿAbd Allāh, governor of al-Yamāma.

As for Qutham ibn al-ʿAbbās, he was killed at Samarqand.

Abū Ṣāliḥ, the author of the commentary, said:

“We have never seen the graves of the sons of any mother so widely separated as those of the sons of Umm al-Faḍl, from among the Banū al-ʿAbbās. Al-Faḍl died in Syria; ʿAbd Allāh died in al-Ṭāʾif; ʿUbayd Allāh died in Medina; Qutham died in Samarqand; and Maʿbad was killed in Ifrīqiya.”

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās, his kunya was Abū al-ʿAbbās. He lived to the age of seventy and died in al-Ṭāʾif during the conflict of Ibn al-Zubayr. He had lost his sight. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya performed the funeral prayer over him, said four takbīrs, and had a tent pitched over his grave.

Al-Wāqidī said: “Ibn ʿAbbās died in the year sixty-eight in al-Ṭāʾif, at the age of seventy-two. He used to dye his beard yellow.”

ʿAbd Allāh’s children were ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAbbās, Muḥammad, al-Faḍl, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿUbayd Allāh, and Lubāba—their mother was Zarʿa daughter of Mishraḥ al-Kindiyya—and Asmāʾ, by a slave mother.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh, Muḥammad, and al-Faḍl, they left no descendants.

As for ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he was among the most devout and forbearing of people, and among those who prayed most. He used to pray one thousand rakʿas every day and night. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad. He died at al-Sharāh in the year one hundred and seventeen, at the age of eighty.

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He was born on the night ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵇—was killed, and died in the year one hundred and eighteen.”

Ibn al-Kalbī said: “Al-Walīd had ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh flogged seven hundred times because of instigation.”

—And he related his story—

ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s children were Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī—his mother was al-ʿĀliya daughter of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās, whose mother was ʿĀʾisha daughter of ʿAbd al-Madān al-Ḥārithiyya—and Dāwūd and ʿĪsā, by a slave mother; Sulaymān and Ṣāliḥ, by a slave mother named Saʿdā; Ismāʿīl and ʿAbd al-Ṣamad, by a slave mother; Yaʿqūb, by a slave mother; and ʿAbd Allāh and ʿUbayd Allāh—their mother was Umm Abīhā, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, whose mother was Laylā daughter of Masʿūd ibn Khālid al-Nahshalī—and Amīna, Umm ʿĪsā, and Lubāba, by various slave mothers.

As for Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, he was among the most handsome of people and the most exalted in rank. There were fourteen years between him and his father.

ʿAlī dyed his hair black, while Muḥammad dyed his red, so that anyone who did not know them would think that Muḥammad was ʿAlī. He died in the year one hundred and twenty-two. The Mahdī was born in that year.

It is said that he died in the year one hundred and twenty-five at al-Sharāh, in the land of Syria. He was sixty years old. The caliphs are among his descendants.

We shall mention them and his brothers when we begin to discuss them, after mentioning the caliphs of the Banū Umayya, if God wills.

As for Ḍirār ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he died before Islam, left no descendants, and used to compose poetry.

As for Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, his kunya was Abū ʿUmāra [and Abū Yaʿlā]. He was the Lion of God and the Lion of His Messenger ﷺ. At Badr he killed Shayba ibn Rabīʿa, Ṭuʿayma ibn ʿAdī, and Sibāʿ al-Khuzāʿī. At Uḥud, Waḥshī, the slave of Ṭuʿayma, struck him with a spear and killed him. He had been nursed by the Prophet ﷺ—and by Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzūmī. A woman of Mecca called Thuwayba had nursed them.

Ḥamza had a son called ʿUmāra, by a woman of Banū al-Najjār; he left no descendants. He also had a daughter called Umm Abīhā, whose mother was Zaynab daughter of ʿUmays al-Khathʿamiyya. She was married to ʿUmar ibn Abī Salama al-Makhzūmī.

As for al-Muqawwim ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he did not live to see Islam and left no descendants. He had a daughter called Hind, who was married to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Masrūḥ, the brother of Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr ibn Hawāzin.

As for Abū Lahab ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, his name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā. His kunya was Abū ʿUtba.

He was cross-eyed. It is said that he was called Abū Lahab because of his good looks. He contracted al-ʿadasa and died in Mecca. He was the thief of the Kaʿba’s gazelle, which was made of gold.

His children were ʿUtba, ʿUtayba, Muʿattib, and daughters. Their mother was Umm Jamīl daughter of Ḥarb ibn Umayya, the firewood carrier. She was the sister of Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and the paternal aunt of Muʿāwiya.

As for ʿUtba, the Messenger of God ﷺ—had married his daughter Ruqayya to him. Abū Lahab ordered him to divorce her, and he did so. The Messenger of God ﷺ—prayed against him, saying: “O God, set one of Your dogs upon him.” A lion devoured him on one of his journeys. His kunya was Abū Wāsiʿa. He had many descendants among sons and daughters, Among them were Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Khidāsh ibn ʿUtba, governor of Mecca, and al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUtba ibn Abī Lahab, the poet. He is the one who said: [ramal]

I am al-Akhḍar; whoever knows me

Knows al-Akhḍar of skin among the Arabs.

Abū Muḥammad said: “Al-khuḍra means blackness; he meant dark-complexioned.”

Al-Faḍl was a supporter, and he had a story concerning lending money to people, which we have mentioned in the book ʿUyūn al-Akhbār. As for Muʿattib, he became Muslim and fought at Ḥunayn alongside the Prophet ﷺ. He had many descendants.

As for ʿUtayba, he married Umm Kulthūm daughter of the Prophet ﷺ—and separated from her before consummating the marriage.

As for al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was the eldest of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s children. He was with him when Zamzam was dug, and it was by him that ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was known by his kunya. His children were Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith, al-Mughīra ibn al-Ḥārith, Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith, Arwā, Rabīʿa, and ʿAbd Shams.

As for Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith, he was the Prophet’s foster-brother ﷺ. Ḥalīma nursed him with her milk for several days, and he was close to the Messenger of God ﷺ. When the latter was sent [as a prophet], Abū Sufyān became his enemy and satirized him. Then he became Muslim in the year of the Conquest and fought at Ḥunayn. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “I hope he will be a successor to Ḥamza.” He also said of him: “Abū Sufyān is the chief of the young men of the people of Paradise.” He died in Medina. The cause was a wart on his head: a barber shaved it at Minā and cut it. He said to his family: “Do not weep for me, for since becoming Muslim I have not stained myself with a sin.” He died in the year twenty and was buried at al-Baqīʿ. He left no descendants.

As for Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was the oldest of the Banū Hāshim to become Muslim. He was older than Ḥamza, al-ʿAbbās, and all his brothers. He was captured at Badr and ransomed by al-ʿAbbās. He became Muslim and emigrated at the time of the Trench. He had many descendants. Among them was ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal, whose nickname was Babba. He was deaf. He joined Ibn al-Ashʿath; when the latter was defeated, he fled to ʿUmān and died there.

As for ʿAbd Shams ibn al-Ḥārith, the Messenger of God ﷺ—named him ʿAbd Allāh. He died at al-Ṣafrāʾ during the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Prophet buried him in his own shirt. His descendants in Syria are called al-Mawza, because they are few and hardly ever number more than three.

Among the descendants of Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith was al-Mughīra, who was judge of Medina during the caliphate of ʿUthmān. He fought alongside ʿAlī ﵇—at Ṣiffīn, and ʿAlī ﵁—advised him to marry Ummāma daughter of Abū al-ʿĀṣ after him. Her mother was Zaynab daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said: “I fear that Muʿāwiya will marry her.” Al-Mughīra married her, and she bore him Yaḥyā, by whom he was known by his kunya. By other women he had ʿAbd al-Malik, ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, Saʿīd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, [So-and-so, and so-and-so. All of these were by women other than Ummāma daughter of Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

As for Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was a Companion.

The Prophet ﷺ—said: “Rabīʿa is an excellent man, if only he would shorten his hair and raise his garment.”

He was ʿUthmān’s partner in trade.

Rabīʿa had sons and daughters. Among them was al-ʿAbbās ibn Rabīʿa, who held a position of standing. ʿUthmān ﵁—granted him an estate in Baṣra and gave him one hundred thousand dirhams.

He fought at Ṣiffīn alongside ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵇—and is the man mentioned in the report of Abū al-Agharr al-Tamīmī. He was married to Umm Firās, daughter of Ḥassān ibn Thābit. She bore him children, and he had many descendants.

[As for al-Ghaydāq ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, he was Ḥajal, and left no descendants.

The account of the Prophet’s paternal uncles ﷺ—is concluded.

An Account of His Paternal Aunts ﷺ

As for ʿĀtika daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, she was married to Abū Umayya ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī.

Umayma daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to Jaḥsh ibn Riʾāb al-Asadī.

Al-Bayḍāʾ daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to Kurayz ibn Rabīʿa ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿAbd Shams.

Barraʾ daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to ʿAbd al-Asad ibn Hilāl al-Makhzūmī. She bore him Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, to whom Umm Salama was married before she married the Prophet ﷺ. Then Abū Ruhm ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy, married her afterward, and she bore him Abū Sabra ibn Abī Ruhm.

Ṣafiyya daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥarb ibn Umayya. Then al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwaylid married her afterward. She was the mother of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām.

Arwā bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to ʿUmayr b. ʿAbd b. Quṣayy b. Kilāb.

Of the Prophet’s paternal aunts ﷺ only Ṣafiyya, the mother of al-Zubayr, accepted Islam.

There are differing accounts concerning Arwā. Some say that she accepted Islam as well. Ṣafiyya died during the caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁.

The Mother of the Prophet ﷺ

[Abū Muḥammad said:

As for the mother of the Prophet ﷺ she was Āmina bt. Wahb b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Zuhra b. Kilāb b. Murra b. Kaʿb b. Luʾayy b. Ghālib b. Fihr b. Mālik b. al-Naḍr b. Kināna b. Khuzayma b. Mudrika b. Ilyās b. Muḍar.

We do not know of any brother of Āmina who would have been an uncle of the Prophet ﷺ. But the Banū Zuhra say: “We are the maternal uncles of the Messenger of God ﷺ” because Āmina was one of them.

The Prophet’s grandmothers ﷺ

[Abū Muḥammad said:

As for the Prophet’s paternal grandmother closest to him, she was Fāṭima bt. ʿAmr b. ʿĀʾidh b. ʿImrān b. Makhzūm. She was the mother of ʿAbd Allāh, the father of the Prophet ﷺ.

The mother of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib b. Hāshim was Salmā bt. ʿAmr, of the Banū al-Najjār. His maternal grandmother was also from them, as was his maternal great-grandmother. Before Hāshim b. ʿAbd Manāf married her, Salmā was married to Uḥayḥa b. al-Jallāḥ, and bore him ʿAmr b. Uḥayḥa, who was ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s maternal half-brother. The mother of Hāshim b. ʿAbd Manāf was ʿĀtika bt. Murra b. Hilāl b. Fālij b. Dhakwān, of the Banū Sulaym.

Abū al-Yaqẓān also reported that the mother of ʿAbd Manāf was Ḥayyī bt. Ḥalīl al-Khuzāʿiyya.

The key to the House was in the hands of Ḥalīl al-Khuzāʿī, and Quṣayy b. Kilāb took it from him.

The mother of Quṣayy was Fāṭima bt. Saʿd, of the Azd of al-Sarāt.

The mother of Kilāb was Nuʿaym bt. Sarīr b. Thaʿlaba b. Mālik b. Kināna.

The mother of Murra was Waḥshiyya bt. Shaybān b. Muḥārib b. Fihr.

The mother of Kaʿb was Salmā bt. Muḥārib b. Fihr.

The mother of Luʾayy was Waḥshiyya bt. Mudlij b. Murra b. ʿAbd Manāt b. Kināna.

The mother of Ghālib was Salmā bt. Saʿd b. Hadhīl b. Mudrika.

The mother of Fihr was Jandala bt. al-Ḥārith al-Jurhumiyya.

The mother of Mālik was Hind bt. ʿAdwān b. ʿAmr, of Qays ʿAylān.

The mother of al-Naḍr was Barra bt. Murra, who was the sister of Tamīm b. Murra. She had been married to his father, Kināna, and after his father’s death Tamīm married her. Thus Tamīm was the maternal uncle of Quraysh, since Quraysh descends from al-Naḍr, who was called “Quraysh.”

The Prophet’s maternal grandmothers ﷺ

[Abū Muḥammad said:

The mother of Āmina bt. Wahb was Barra bt. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd al-Dār.

The mother of Barra was Umm Ḥabīb bt. Asad b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. Quṣayy b. Kilāb b. Murra.

The mother of Umm Ḥabīb was Barra bt. ʿAwf b. ʿUbayd b. ʿUwayj b. ʿAdī b. Kaʿb b. Luʾayy b. Ghālib.

The mother of Barra bt. ʿAwf was Qulāba bt. al-Ḥārith b. Liḥyān b. Hadhīl.

The mother of Qulāba bt. al-Ḥārith was Hind bt. Yarbuʿ, of Thaqīf.

As for the mother of Wahb, the Prophet’s maternal grandfather ﷺ she was ʿĀtika bt. al-Awqaṣ b. Murra b. Hilāl b. Fālij b. Dhakwān, of Sulaym.

ʿAbd Manāf, the father of Wahb, had a mother named Zuhra, after whom her children were named rather than after their father. I do not know the father’s name; she has been assigned the place of the father in the genealogical account.

Zuhra b. Kilāb was the brother of Quṣayy b. Kilāb, and their mother was Fāṭima bt. Saʿd, of the Azd of al-Sarāt.

The Prophet’s foster mothers ﷺ

The Messenger of God ﷺ was sent out to be nursed among the Banū Saʿd b. Bakr of Hawāzin. His wet nurse was named Ḥalīma bt. Abī Dhuʾayb.

The name of Abū Dhuʾayb was ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥārith, of Saʿd b. Bakr.

The name of his foster father was al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, of Saʿd b. Bakr.

His foster siblings were ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥārith and Judāma bt. al-Ḥārith—she was al-Shaymāʾ, a nickname that superseded her given name.

The Messenger of God ﷺ stayed among them for five years, then they returned him to his mother.

The Prophet ﷺ said: “I am the most eloquent of the Arabs, even though I am Qurashī and grew up among the Banū Saʿd b. Bakr.”

The Wives of the Prophet ﷺ

The first of his wives ﷺ was Khadīja bt. Khuwaylid b. Asad b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. Quṣayy.

Her mother was Fāṭima bt. Zāʾida al-Aṣamm, of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy.

Her mother was Hāla bt. ʿAbd Manāf, of the Banū al-Ḥārith, who were of the Banū Muʿayṣ.

Khadīja was the mother of all the Prophet’s children ﷺ except Ibrāhīm, whose mother was Māriya al-Qibṭiyya.

Khadīja had been married to ʿAtīq b. Khālid al-Makhzūmī, and bore him a daughter. After him, Abū Hāla Zurāra b. Nabbāsh al-Usaydī married her. He was a Tamīmī, of the Banū Ḥabīb b. Jarwa, and died in Mecca in the pre-Islamic period. She bore him Hind b. Abī Hāla. After him, the Messenger of God ﷺ married her. He married no other woman while she was alive. He raised her son Hind, who was his stepson. Hind used to say: “I am the noblest of people in father, mother, brother, and sister: my father is the Messenger of God ﷺ; my mother is Khadīja; my sister is Fāṭima; and my brother is al-Qāsim.”

Hind had a son, the stepson of the Messenger of God ﷺ whom he also named Hind. He died in the devastating plague.

The Prophet ﷺ married her when he was twenty-five years old. She remained with him until she died, twenty-four years and some months later. She died three days after the death of his uncle Abū Ṭālib.

Abū Muḥammad said:

After Khadīja, the Prophet ﷺ married Sawda bt. Zamʿa [b. Qays b. ʿAbd Shams b. ʿAbd Wudd b. Naṣr b. Mālik b. Ḥisl b. ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy].

She had been married to al-Sakrān b. ʿAmr, who was one of those who migrated to Abyssinia. He died without leaving descendants.

The Messenger of God ﷺ married her after him. She was the first of his wives whom he married after Khadīja.

Abū Muḥammad said:

Then the Prophet ﷺ married ʿĀʾisha bt. Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁. She was a virgin, and he married no other virgin. He married her in Mecca when she was six years old, and consummated the marriage in Medina when she was nine, seven months after his arrival in Medina. When the Messenger of God ﷺ died, she was eighteen. She was kunya-named Umm ʿAbd Allāh.

Ibn Qutayba said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb told me: Mālik b. Suʿayr told me: al-Aʿmash told me, from Ibrāhīm, from al-Aswad, from ʿĀʾisha, who said:

“The Messenger of God ﷺ married me when I was nine”—she meant: “he consummated the marriage with me”—“and I remained with him for nine years.”

She lived into the caliphate of Muʿāwiya and died in the year fifty-eight, when she was nearly seventy. She was asked, “Shall we bury you beside the Messenger of God ﷺ?” She replied, “I have done things since his death, so bury me with my sisters.” She was buried in al-Baqīʿ and appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr as her executor.

Among ʿĀʾisha’s freedmen was ʿAlqama b. Abī ʿAlqama, from whom Mālik b. Anas transmitted.

ʿAlqama taught grammar and prosody. He died at the beginning of the caliphate of al-Manṣūr.

Among her freedmen was Abū al-Sāʾib, from whom reports were also transmitted. His name was ʿUthmān.

The Messenger of God ﷺ married Ḥafṣa bt. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. She had been married to Khunays, the brother of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ married her. Khunays had been the Prophet’s envoy to Kisrā, and left no descendants.

Ḥafṣa was the sister of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar, sharing both parents. She died in Medina during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁.

The Prophet ﷺ married Zaynab bt. Khuzayma, of the Banū ʿAbd Manāf b. Hilāl b. ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. She had been married to ʿUbayda b. al-Ḥārith b. al-Muṭṭalib. The Prophet ﷺ then married her. She was called “Mother of the Poor.” She died before him.

The Prophet ﷺ married Zaynab bt. Jaḥsh b. Riʾāb b. Yaʿmar b. Ṣabra b. Murra b. Kathīr b. Ghanm b. Dūdān b. Asad b. Khuzayma.

She was the daughter of the Prophet’s paternal aunt. Her mother was Umayma bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

She was the first of his wives to die after his death, during the caliphate of ʿUmar. She was the first to be carried in a bier—and she was a well-built woman. When ʿUmar saw the bier, he said: “What an excellent litter for a woman riding in a howdah!”

The Prophet ﷺ married Umm Ḥabība bt. Abī Sufyān b. Ḥarb. She had been married to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Jaḥsh al-Asadī, who became a Christian and died in Abyssinia. The Messenger of God ﷺ married her after him. The couch on which the Prophet ﷺ was carried lay in her house; it remains in Medina with one of her freedmen.

She lived into the caliphate of Muʿāwiya.

The Prophet ﷺ married Umm Salama bt. Abī Umayya b. al-Mughīra b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. Makhzūm. Before him, she had been married to Abū Salama b. ʿAbd al-Asad. She had by him Zaynab bt. Abī Salama and ʿUmar b. Abī Salama, the stepson of the Prophet ﷺ.

ʿUmar was with ʿAlī on the day of the Battle of the Camel. ʿAlī appointed him governor of Bahrayn, and he left descendants in Medina.

Umm Salama was a cousin of Abū Jahl. Her brother ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Umayya had been one of the most hostile Qurayshites toward the Prophet ﷺ. He then accepted Islam and was martyred on the day of al-Ṭāʾif.

Umm Salama died in the year fifty-nine, a year and some days after ʿĀʾisha.

Khayra, the mother of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, was a freedwoman of Umm Salama.

Shayba b. Naṣṣāḥ b. Sarjis b. Yaʿqūb was a freedman of Umm Salama. In his time he was the leading reciter of Medina. Among her freedmen was Abū Maymūna. Nāfiʿ b. Abī Nuʿaym studied with him.

The Prophet ﷺ married Maymūna bt. al-Ḥārith. She descended from ʿAbd Allāh b. Hilāl b. ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. He consummated the marriage with her at Sarif—which is ten miles from Mecca—and she also died at Sarif, in the year thirty-eight, and was buried there.

Before he married her, she had been married to Abū Sabra b. Abī Rahm al-ʿĀmirī.

Maymūna’s mother was a woman from Jurash called Hind bt. ʿAmr.

She bore daughters by two men, among them Maymūna bt. al-Ḥārith, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

Among them was Umm al-Faḍl Lubāba bt. al-Ḥārith, who was married to al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

There was also Zaynab bt. ʿUmays al-Khathʿamiyya, who was married to Ḥamza;

Salmā bt. ʿUmays, who was married to Shaddād b. al-Hād;

and Asmāʾ bt. ʿUmays al-Khathʿamiyya, who was married to Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib. After Jaʿfar died, Abū Bakr married her; then ʿAlī married her. She bore children to all of them.

Their mother, the woman of Jurash, was said to be “the noblest old woman on earth in her sons-in-law.”

Yasār was Maymūna’s freedman. His sons were ʿAṭāʾ, Sulaymān, Muslim, and ʿAbd al-Malik; all were jurists.

The Prophet ﷺ married Ṣafiyya bt. Ḥuyayy b. Akhṭab al-Naḍīrī [b. Saʿya b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUbayd b. Kaʿb b. al-Khazraj b. Abī Ḥabīb b. al-Naḍīr b. al-Naḥḥām b. Yanḥūm, of the descendants of Aaron.

She had been married to a man from the Jews of Khaybar called Sallām b. Mishkam al-Quraẓī.

Then Kināna b. al-Rabīʿ b. Abī al-Ḥuqayq married her. The Messenger of God ﷺ struck off his head for an act that made his blood lawful, and took his family captive and married her.

She died in the year thirty-six. (1) The Prophet ﷺ married Juwayriya bt. al-Ḥārith [b. Abī Ḍirār b. Ḥabīb b. ʿĀʾidh b. Mālik b. Jadhīma, al-Muṣṭaliqiyya.

The Prophet raided Banū al-Muṣṭaliq while they were off their guard [and unaware of the army], and their livestock was being watered at the water. Among those taken was Juwayriya bt. al-Ḥārith, and he married her.

She died in the year fifty-six.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said: The Messenger of God ﷺ—married ʿAmra, who was from Banū al-Quraṭāt, themselves from Banū Bakr b. Kilāb. Her father described her, then said:

“I would add that she has never been ill.” The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “There is no good in her for God.” He divorced her without consummating the marriage.

A woman whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—married and took into his household, then divorced without having intercourse with her.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He had married Umayma bt. al-Nuʿmān b. Sharāḥīl al-Jawniyya. When he went in to her, he said to her: “Give yourself to me.” She said: “Does a queen give herself to a commoner?” He reached out his hand to place it upon her, so that she might calm down. She said: “I seek refuge in God from you.” He said to her: “You have sought refuge in One who grants refuge.”
