Then he sent her away and gave her a parting gift.

It is said that the one who said, “I seek refuge in God from you,” was Malīka al-Laythiyya.

Others said she was Fāṭima bt. al-Ḍaḥḥāk, whom he had married after the death of his daughter Zaynab.

A woman whom he ﷺ—proposed to, but was turned away from.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ—proposed to a woman from Banū Murra b. ʿAwf b. Saʿd b. Dhubyān, asking her father for her hand. He said: “She has leprosy”—though he was lying—so the Messenger went back.

He found that she was indeed leprous.

It is said that her son was Shabīb b. al-Barṣāʾ b. al-Ḥārith b. ʿAwf al-Murrī, the guarantor between ʿAbs and Dhubyān.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

The woman who gave herself to the Prophet ﷺ—was Khawla bt. Ḥakīm al-Sulamiyya.

Someone else said: She was Umm Sharīk al-Azdiyya.

[It is said: She was Fāṭima bt. Shurayḥ, from Quraysh. It is also said: She was Ghaziyya bt. Dūdān b. ʿAwf b. ʿAmr b. Khālid b. Ḍibāb b. Ḥujayr b. ʿAdī b. Muʿayṣ b. ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy, Umm Sharīk.

The children of the Prophet ﷺ

The Messenger of God ﷺ—had the following children by Khadīja: al-Qāsim, after whom he was given his teknonym; al-Ṭayyib; Fāṭima; Zaynab; Ruqayya; and Umm Kulthūm.

By Māriya the Copt, he had Ibrāhīm.

As for al-Qāsim and al-Ṭayyib, they died as young children in Mecca.

Mujāhid said: “Al-Qāsim lived seven nights, then died.”

As for Zaynab, she was married to Abū al-ʿĀṣ b. al-Rabīʿ b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. ʿAbd Shams.

Abū al-ʿĀṣ’s name was al-Qāsim—it is also said, Muqassim—and his mother was Hāla bt. Khuwaylid b. Asad b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, the sister of Khadīja bt. Khuwaylid. Abū al-ʿĀṣ b. al-Rabīʿ was Zaynab’s maternal cousin, and he was her husband. He had married her while he was still an unbeliever. Quraysh said to him: “Divorce her—”

“—and we will marry you the daughter of Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ,” but he refused. Abū al-ʿĀṣ was captured at Badr, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—released him as a favor, without ransom. Zaynab went to al-Ṭāʾif. Then she came to the Prophet ﷺ—in Medina. Abū al-ʿĀṣ came to Medina and embraced Islam, becoming a good Muslim.

Zaynab died in Medina seven years and two months after the Prophet ﷺ—had gone there.

Abū al-ʿĀṣ married the daughter of Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ. He died in Medina, having appointed al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām as his executor.

[By Zaynab, the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—he had a daughter called Umāma. She married al-Mughīra b. Nawfal and bore him Yaḥyā, who left no descendants.

As for Ruqayya, she married ʿUtba b. Abī Lahab. His father ordered him to divorce her, and he did so before consummating the marriage. She married ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān in Mecca and died there one year, ten months, and twenty days after his arrival in Medina. She bore ʿUthmān ʿAbd Allāh, who died as a young child before reaching six years of age. A rooster pecked him in the eye; he fell ill and died.

As for Umm Kulthūm, she married ʿUtayba b. Abī Lahab and separated from him before the marriage was consummated. After Ruqayya, she married ʿUthmān. She died eight years, two months, and ten days after his arrival in Medina.

As for Fāṭima, she married ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib in Medina, one year after his arrival. He consummated the marriage about a year after that. She died one hundred days after the death of the Prophet ﷺ]

—in Medina. She bore ʿAlī al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, Muḥassin, Umm Kulthūm the elder, and Zaynab the elder. We shall mention them when we discuss ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, along with his other children. As for Ibrāhīm, the son of Māriya the Copt, he was born in Medina eight years after the Prophet ﷺ—arrived there. He lived one year, ten months, and eight days.

His mother Māriya was a gift from al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Alexandria, to the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Muḥammad said: Muḥammad b. Ziyād al-Ziyādī told me. He said: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna told us, from Bashīr b. al-Muhājir al-Ghanawī, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Burayda al-Khuṣayb, from his father, who said:

The ruler of the Copts gave the Messenger of God ﷺ—two enslaved sisters and a mule. He used to ride the mule in Medina. He took one of the two women into his household, and she bore him Ibrāhīm; he gave the other to Ḥassān b. Thābit.

Someone else said: The woman’s name was Sīrīn, and she was the mother of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥassān. It is said that Māriya, the mother of his child, died five years after him.

The freedmen of the Messenger of God ﷺ

Abū Muḥammad said:

Zayd b. Ḥāritha, and Umm Ayman, his wife.

Abū Muḥammad said: Zayd b. Akhzam al-Ṭāʾī told me: I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. Dāwūd say:

Umm Ayman was among those whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—inherited from his father. Her name was Baraka. The Messenger of God ﷺ—set her free. She married ʿUbayd al-Khazrajī in Mecca. She bore him Ayman. Then Khadīja came to own Zayd b. Ḥāritha: Ḥakīm b. Ḥizām had bought him for her at the market of ʿUkāẓ for four hundred dirhams. After marrying her, the Messenger of God ﷺ—asked her to give Zayd b. Ḥāritha to him. She gave him to him, and he set him free and married him to Umm Ayman. She bore him Usāma b. Zayd. Usāma and Ayman were maternal brothers.

Ayman had a son called Jubayr.

One of the transmitters of reports said:

He was Zayd b. Ḥāritha b. Shurāḥīl, from Kalb. He was captured in a raid, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—set him free. He used to be called Zayd b. Muḥammad, until the verse was revealed: “Call them by their fathers’ names” (Qurʾān 33:5). He was among those whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed to command the army at the Battle of Muʾta, where he was martyred. The Battle of Muʾta took place in the year eight.

Umm Ayman, his wife, had been the Prophet’s nurse. He was killed at the age of fifty-five. He was short and dark, with a very dark complexion, and had a snub nose. His teknonym was Abū Usāma.

Usāma b. Zayd b. Ḥāritha, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

He had two sons from whom reports are transmitted: Muḥammad b. Usāma and al-Ḥasan b. Usāma.

Abū Ghaziyya Muḥammad b. Mūsā, from Banū Māzin b. al-Najjār, was descended through his mothers from Usāma b. Zayd b. Ḥāritha.

Abū Rāfiʿ, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

His name was Aslam; they agree on that, but disagree about his story.

Some said he belonged to al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, who gave him to the Prophet ﷺ. When al-ʿAbbās embraced Islam, Abū Rāfiʿ brought the Prophet the news of his conversion. The Prophet set Abū Rāfiʿ free and married him to his freedwoman Salmā, who bore him ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Rāfiʿ.

He remained a scribe for ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib throughout his caliphate.

Others said he belonged to Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ, except for one share among the shares. Saʿīd set him free, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—bought that share and set him free.

He had two sons: ʿUbayd Allāh, who wrote for ʿAlī and transmitted ḥadīth from him, and ʿAbd Allāh, who was a man of standing.

When ʿAmr b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ became governor of Medina, he sent for ʿUbayd Allāh and asked him: “Whose freedman are you?” He replied: “The freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.” He struck him two hundred lashes, then his brother interceded for him.

Others said: Abū Rāfiʿ had been a servant of Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ. His sons inherited him; some set him free after the advent of Islam, while others held on to him. Abū Rāfiʿ went to the Prophet ﷺ—to seek his help against those who had not set him free. The Prophet spoke to them about him, and they gave him to the Messenger of God ﷺ—who set him free.

Safīna, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

He was a black man born among the Arabs of the desert. They disagreed about his name.

Some said his name was Mihrān, and his teknonym was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Others said his name was Rabāḥ, and that the Messenger of God ﷺ—named him Safīna. This was because, on a journey, everyone who grew tired would put some of his belongings on him, whether a shield or a sword, until he was carrying a great deal. The Prophet passed by him and said: “You are a ship.”

They also disagreed about his story. Some said the Messenger of God ﷺ—bought him and set him free.

Others said that Umm Salama bought him and set him free, on condition that he serve the Prophet ﷺ—as long as he lived.

[ Aḥmad b. Mūsā told us: ʿĀṣim b. ʿAlī told us: Ḥashraj b. Nubāta told us: Saʿīd b. Jumhān told us. He said:

I said to Safīna: “Why were you named Safīna?” He replied: “We were with the Messenger of God ﷺ—and their baggage became too heavy for them. I got down and said: ‘Load it onto my back.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: ‘Carry it, for you are a ship.’ Had I carried the load of one camel, or two camels, that day, it would not have weighed me down afterward”.

Thawbān, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and he was from the Sarāt region.

They said that he was from Ḥimyar, had been captured in a raid, and was bought and set free by the Prophet ﷺ. He remained with him until the Prophet ﷺ—died. Then he moved to Syria and settled in Ḥimṣ, where he had a property endowed as a charitable gift. He died in the year fifty-four, during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya.

Yasār, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Yasār was a Nubian captured during the raid against Banū ʿAbd b. Thaʿlaba. The Prophet set him free. He was the man killed by the ʿUraniyyūn, who raided the Prophet’s milch camels, cut off his hand and foot, and thrust thorns into his tongue and eyes until he died. They drove off the herd, and he was brought into Medina dead.

Shaqrān, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

His name was Ṣāliḥ; it is said that his father was called ʿAdī.

They disagreed about his story. Some said he belonged to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf, from whom the Prophet bought him and set him free.

Abū Muḥammad said: Zayd b. Akhzam told me: I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. Dāwūd say:

Shaqrān was among those whom the Prophet inherited from his father.

Abū Kabsha, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

His name was Sulaym. He was born in the land of Daws; it is also said that he was born in Mecca.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—bought him and set him free.

Abū Kabsha died on the first day of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb’s accession as caliph ﵁.

Abū Ḍamīra, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

He was among the spoils that God granted to His Messenger. He was an Arab. The Prophet ﷺ—set him free and wrote him a document, which remained in the hands of his descendants, instructing that care be given to him and his household.

Among his descendants was Ḥusayn b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḍamīra. He came as a delegation to al-Mahdī with the document.

Al-Mahdī kissed it, placed it on his eyes, and gave him three hundred dinars.

Midʿam, a freedman of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Midʿam had been a slave of Rifāʿa b. Zayd al-Judhāmī. He gave him to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

It is said that this is the man about whom the Prophet ﷺ—said [when he was unloading his baggage, an arrow came from somewhere and killed him. The people said: “Good news for him: Paradise!” The Prophet ﷺ—said: “No! The cloak he stole at Khaybar is burning him in the Fire of Hell.”]

Abū Muwayhiba, a freedman of the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Muwayhiba was born among the people of Muzayna. The Prophet bought him and set him free. He was the one whom the Prophet took to al-Baqīʿ, saying: “I have been commanded to seek forgiveness for them.”]

Al-Nabīh, a client of the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Nabīh was born in al-Sarāt. The Messenger of God ﷺ—bought him and freed him.

Faḍālah, a client of the Prophet ﷺ.

This Faḍālah was a client of the Prophet ﷺ—and settled in Syria.

The horses and mounts of the Messenger of God ﷺ

The horse of the Messenger of God ﷺ—at the Battle of Uḥud was al-Sakb. The horse of Abū Burdah ibn Niyār that day was called Malāwiḥ.

Al-Murtaʾij was the horse of the Messenger of God ﷺ—which he bought from a Bedouin. Khuzaymah ibn Thābit alone testified on his behalf, and he accepted his testimony alone.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—had a horse called Lizāz, a horse called al-Ẓarb, a horse called al-Laḥīf, and a horse called al-Ward.

The mule gifted to him by al-Muqawqis was called Duldul, and it remained alive until the time of Muʿāwiyah.

He had a donkey called Yaʿfūr.

Among his she-camels were al-Qaṣwāʾ, al-Jadʿāʾ, and al-ʿAḍbāʾ.

His milch camels, which ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn al-Fazārī raided at al-Ghābah, numbered twenty.

The circumstances of the Messenger ﷺ

His birth, the beginning of his mission, his campaigns and expeditions, until he passed away ﷺ

They said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ—was born in the Year of the Elephant. There were twenty years between the Year of the Elephant and the Year of the Fijār.

His mother entrusted him to his foster mothers among Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr. He remained with them for five years, then they returned him to her. One year later, his mother took him to her maternal uncles in Medina, and she died at al-Abwāʾ. After his mother’s death, Umm Ayman, his nurse, brought him back to Mecca.

ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib died when he was eight years and two months old.

He went with his uncle Abū Ṭālib to Syria on a trading journey when he was twelve years old.

He witnessed the Fijār when he was twenty years old.

He went to Syria on a trading journey for Khadījah when he was twenty-five years old, and married her two months and some days later.

The Kaʿbah was rebuilt, and Quraysh accepted his judgment concerning it, when he was thirty-five years old.

He was commissioned as a prophet ﷺ—when he was forty years old, five years after the Kaʿbah was rebuilt.

Twenty days after the beginning of his mission, Quraysh saw stars being pelted.

His uncle Abū Ṭālib died when he was forty-nine years and eight months old.

Khadījah died three days after Abū Ṭālib. Three months after Khadījah’s death, he then went to al-Ṭāʾif with Zayd ibn Ḥārithah. He stayed there for a month, then returned to Mecca under the protection of Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdī.

He was taken by night to Jerusalem a year and a half after his return to Mecca. Then God Almighty commanded him to emigrate and prescribed fighting for him. He ordered his Companions to emigrate, and they set out in groups.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—set out with Abū Bakr, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah, Abū Bakr’s client, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Arqam—also said to be Arqaṭ, and also said to be Urayqiṭ—al-Daylī. He left ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵇—in charge of deposits people had entrusted to him, until he had returned them; then ʿAlī followed him.

He emigrated to Medina when he was fifty-three years old. Concerning this, Ḥassān ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī said—according to Abū al-Yaqẓān’s account—as follows: [ṭawīl]

He dwelt among Quraysh for some ten years,reminding them, whenever he met a kindly friend.

At the festival gatherings he presented himselfto the people, but found none to shelter him, nor one to answer.

Then when he came to us, and the hearts found rest in him,he awoke glad, content with Ṭaybah.

He said: As for Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, he stated that the first line belonged to Ṣarimah ibn Abī Anas al-Anṣārī.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—entered Medina on Monday, when twelve nights of Rabīʿ al-Awwal had passed. The calendar was reckoned from the month of Rabīʿ al-Awwal, then shifted to Muḥarram, because it is the first month of the year.

He stayed at Qubāʾ with Kulthūm ibn al-Hidm, of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf of the Aws. Then Kulthūm died, and he moved to Saʿd ibn Khaythamah al-Awsī. He stayed there for a month and four days, until the resident prayer had been completed.

Five months after completing the prayer, he established bonds of brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers.

Six months later, he led the campaign of Waddān.

Then, a month and three days later, he led a campaign against a Quraysh caravan.

Then he went out in pursuit of Karz, reaching Badr after twenty days.

The direction of prayer was then turned toward the Kaʿbah.

Then he led the campaign of Badr.

The Battle of Badr

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

Badr was a man of Ghifār, from the clan of Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, from a branch called Banū al-Nār. The watering place was named after him.

Al-Shaʿbī said: “Badr” was the well of a man called Badr, but he did not identify him further.

He said: The polytheists numbered nine hundred and fifty men, while the Muslims numbered three hundred and some ten. Groups of men took turns riding one camel. Of the Muslims, two hundred and seventy were Helpers; the rest were from among the other people.

The standard of the Messenger of God ﷺ—was white, and his banner was black, made from a mantle belonging to ʿĀʾishah, patterned with figures.

That day his banner was with ʿAlī, and his standard was with Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr.

He said: Not a single clan of Quraysh was left without some men going out among the polytheists, except Banū ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb, from whom not one man went out. Some men of Zuhrah had gone out, but al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq al-Thaqafī, who was their ally, stood among them and advised them to turn back. They returned, and none of them witnessed Badr.

He was called al-Akhnas because he turned Banū Zuhrah back on the day of Badr. He was a Thaqafī, counted among Banū Zuhrah, and al-Akhnas did not become Muslim.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

The jurist ʿUthmān al-Battī of Basra was one of his clients.

Names of those who stayed behind at Badr

Among the Emigrants and Helpers, those known to have had an excuse:

ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān stayed behind from Badr to attend to Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Messenger of God ﷺ—awarded him a share equal to that of a participant. ʿUthmān said:

“Was there also a reward for me, Messenger of God?” He said: “And your reward.”

Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh was in Syria, so he stayed behind from Badr. He arrived after the Messenger of God ﷺ—had returned and spoke with him, whereupon the Messenger awarded him a share. Ṭalḥah said: “Was there also a reward for me, Messenger of God?” He said: “And your reward.”

Saʿīd ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl was also in Syria. He arrived after the Messenger of God ﷺ—had returned from Badr, and the Messenger awarded him his share. Saʿīd said: “Was there also a reward for me, Messenger of God?” He said: “And your reward.”

Abū Lubābah and al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib, both of the Helpers, had set out with the Messenger of God ﷺ—but he sent them back and appointed Abū Lubābah to govern Medina. He awarded them both shares alongside the participants of Badr.

The Quraysh who provided food during the campaign of Badr

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir ibn Nawfal, Ṭuʿaymah ibn ʿAdī, Abū al-Bakhtarī ibn Hishām, Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kaldah, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Munabbih and Nubayh, the sons of al-Ḥajjāj, and Suhayl ibn ʿAmr.

[Concerning them was revealed: “Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to bar people from the way of God. They will spend it, then it will become a source of regret for them, and they will be overcome.” (Qurʾān 8:36)

The number of those killed and captured on the day of Badr

The number of polytheists killed on the day of Badr was fifty men. Forty-four men were captured.

Among those captured were al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, captured by Abū al-Yusr Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr; ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib—both had gone out under duress—and Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Among the captives were ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ and al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kaldah. The Messenger of God ﷺ—killed them at al-Ṣafrāʾ. Ibn al-Mubārak related from Shuʿbah, from Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that he said:

The Prophet ﷺ—executed three men on the day of Badr: ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, Ṭuʿaymah ibn Abī ʿAdī, and al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said to al-ʿAbbās: “Ransom yourself, your two nephews, ʿAqīl and Nawfal, and your ally, for you are a man of means.”

He said: “Messenger of God, I was a Muslim, but the people forced me to go out.”

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “God knows best about your Islam.

“If what you say is true, God will reward you for it. But as things stood outwardly, you were against us.” He said:

“But I have no money.” He said: “Then where is the money you left with Umm al-Faḍl in Mecca when you set out, while there was no one else with the two of you? You said to her, ‘If I am struck down on this journey, then such-and-such is for al-Faḍl, and such-and-such for ʿAbd Allāh.’”

Al-ʿAbbās said: “By Him who sent you with the truth as a prophet, no one knew of this but her. I know that you are the Messenger of God.” He ransomed himself for one hundred ūqiyyahs, and each of his two nephews for forty ūqiyyahs.

This is how Ibn Isḥāq reported it.

He said: “You have left me begging people with my hand.”

Al-ʿAbbās became Muslim and ordered ʿAqīl to become Muslim. No other captives became Muslim besides them.

That day ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib killed al-ʿĀṣ ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, and ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, their ally, from Banū Anmār ibn Baghīḍ.

ʿAlī also killed Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, the brother of al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwaylid.

There are differing accounts concerning Ṭuʿaymah ibn ʿAdī. Some said that ʿAlī killed him.

Others said that Ḥamzah killed him. Still others said that the Messenger of God ﷺ—executed him.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb killed his maternal uncle, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām ibn al-Mughīrah.

Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib killed Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad ibn Hilāl al-Makhzūmī.

ʿUbaydah ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib killed ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām killed ʿUbaydah ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayyah.

Muʿādh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ al-Anṣārī killed Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, striking his leg with his sword and cutting it off; then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd finished him off.

ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir killed ʿAlī ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

The killers of the rest of those killed among the Helpers are unknown.

Mention of the Muslims who were martyred on the day of Badr

Fourteen Muslims were martyred on the day of Badr. Among them were: ʿUbaydah ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Muṭṭalib, the killer of ʿUtbah; Mihjaʿ, the client of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb; Dhū al-Shimālayn; ʿUmayr ibn Abī Waqqāṣ al-Zuhrī, the brother of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ al-Zuhrī; ʿĀqil ibn al-Bukayr—also said to be called ʿĀqil and Ghāfil—and Ṣafwān ibn al-Bayḍāʾ. The rest were Helpers.

The Battle of Badr took place in the month of Ramaḍān in the second year, on the night when seventeen nights of the month had passed.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—returned to Medina, and his daughter Ruqayyah died.

ʿAlī consummated his marriage with Fāṭimah sixteen days after Ruqayyah’s death.

ʿUthmān married his daughter Umm Kulthūm and consummated the marriage five and a half months after ʿAlī had consummated his marriage with Fāṭimah.

Two months later, the Messenger of God ﷺ—married Ḥafṣah.

Twenty days after that, he married Zaynab bint Khuzaymah.

Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī was born five days later. This is according to some reports. If this is correct, then when the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, al-Ḥasan was seven years old.

In Ibn Isḥāq’s account—as I suppose—she gave birth to al-Ḥasan after Khaybar, in the year six. As for al-Ḥusayn, he was born ten months and twenty-two days after al-Ḥasan. Fāṭimah ﵂ had conceived him one month and twenty-two days after giving birth to al-Ḥasan. She nursed him while pregnant, then nursed them both together.

The Battle of Uḥud

Ibn Isḥāq said:

The Battle of Uḥud took place in the year three, in Shawwāl.

He said: When Quraysh set out to fight the Messenger of God ﷺ—the Messenger of God ﷺ—and the Muslims went out until they encamped among the dwellings of Banū Ḥārithah. They stayed there.

They remained there for the rest of that day and night. Then, on the following day, he set out with a thousand of his Companions. When they were partway along the road, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl broke away with a third of the people, saying: “By God, we do not know why we should get ourselves killed!” Banū Ḥāritha and Banū Salima were on the point of turning back, but God—mighty and majestic—is their protector. The Messenger of God ﷺ—went on. A horse swished its tail and struck the tassel of a sword, drawing it from its scabbard. The Messenger of God ﷺ—said to the owner of the sword—who loved auspicious omens and did not practice divination—“Unsheathe your sword, for I see that swords will be drawn today.” The Quraysh numbered three thousand that day, while the Messenger of God ﷺ—had seven hundred. That day he wore one coat of mail over another. He took a sword, brandished it, and said: “Who will take it with its due?”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: “I will.” But he turned away from him. Al-Zubayr said: “I will.” But he turned away from him.

The two of them felt slighted. Abū Dujāna Simāk ibn Kharasha then stood up and said: “And what is its due, Messenger of God?” He replied: “Strike with it until it bends.” He said: “I will take it with its due,” and the Messenger gave it to him. The commander of the archers that day was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jubayr, the brother of Khawwāt ibn Jubayr, the man of the two wineskins. The polytheists were being routed until the archers disobeyed the Messenger of God ﷺ—who had ordered them to hold their position. They turned toward the spoils, and the Muslims were struck down; some of them fled.

Number of the Muslims Martyred at Uḥud

Four men from among the Emigrants were martyred at Uḥud: Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh, Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, and Shammās ibn ʿUthmān ibn al-Sharīd.

Sixty-one men from among the Anṣār were martyred.

Number of the Polytheists Killed at Uḥud

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib killed Ṭalḥa ibn Abī Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Dār in single combat. He was the standard-bearer of the polytheists. ʿAlī also killed Abū al-Ḥakam ibn al-Akhans ibn Sharīq al-Thaqafī, an ally of Banū Zuhra, and Abū Umayya ibn Abī Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Mughīra.

Ḥamza killed ʿUthmān ibn Abī Ṭalḥa and Sibāʿ ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ killed Abū Saʿd ibn Abī Ṭalḥa.

ʿĀṣim ibn Thābit killed Musāfiʿ ibn Ṭalḥa, Kilāb ibn Ṭalḥa, al-Jullās ibn Ṭalḥa, and al-Ḥārith ibn Ṭalḥa.

This is the account of some of them. As for Ibn Isḥāq, he says that al-Jullās and al-Ḥārith were killed by Quzmān, an ally of Banū Ẓafar.

He says: Quzmān killed that day Arṭāh ibn Sharḥabīl ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn ʿAbd al-Dār, a black slave of his named Ṣuʾāb, and al-Qāsiṭ ibn Shurayḥ ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn ʿAbd al-Dār; Hishām ibn Abī Umayya ibn al-Mughīra; al-Walīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām; Khālid ibn al-Aʿlam; ʿUbayda ibn Jābir; and Shayba ibn Mālik ibn al-Muḍarrib.

This Quzmān was a hypocrite. He was the one who said: “By God, I fought only out of zeal for my people”.

He was wounded, and when his wound became severe, he killed himself. It was of him that the Prophet ﷺ—said:

“God supports this religion through a wicked man.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf killed Usayd ibn Abī Ṭalḥa.

Thus, ten men from Banū ʿAbd al-Dār and one of their freedmen were killed that day.

Of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār ibn Quṣayy, only Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr accompanied the Prophet ﷺ. He was martyred that day and was the standard-bearer of the Messenger of God ﷺ. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning Banū ʿAbd al-Dār: “Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb, who do not understand” (Qurʾān 8:22).

The Day of the Trench and What Followed

The Day of the Trench took place in the year four.

The Day of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq and the Day of Banū Liḥyān took place in Shaʿbān of the year five.

The Day of Khaybar took place in the year six. The Messenger of God ﷺ—besieged them for more than ten nights. Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib came to him from the Negus.

The people of Fadak made peace with him that year, giving him half their produce. It was his alone, because the Muslims had not brought horses or camels against it.

That year the Messenger of God ﷺ—set out to perform the lesser pilgrimage, but the polytheists turned him back. He had brought with him seventy sacrificial camels, but they prevented him from reaching the place where the offering was to be made. The Muslims pledged allegiance to him beneath the tree in the Pledge of Good Pleasure. The people numbered seven hundred. This was the ʿUmra of al-Ḥudaybiya.

He said: Zayd ibn Akhzam related to me: Abū Dāwūd related to us, from Qurra ibn Khālid, from Qatāda, who said: I asked Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib:

“How many were they at the Pledge of Good Pleasure?” He said: “Fifteen hundred.” I said: “But Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh said that they were fourteen hundred.” He replied: “May ﵀; he was mistaken. He is the one who told me that they were fifteen hundred.”

The first to pledge allegiance was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. The pledge came about because of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁. The Messenger had sent him to Mecca to tell the Quraysh that he had not come to wage war, but the Quraysh detained him there. The Messenger of God ﷺ—was told that ʿUthmān had been killed. He called the people to pledge allegiance to fight the enemy, then word reached him that what had been reported about ʿUthmān was false.

In the year eight, the Messenger of God ﷺ—sent an expedition to Muʾta and appointed Zayd ibn Ḥāritha as its commander. He said: “If Zayd is killed, then Jaʿfar is to take command; and if Jaʿfar is killed, then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa is to command the people.” They numbered three thousand.

Zayd ibn Ḥāritha, Jaʿfar, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa were killed. Khālid ibn al-Walīd then took command of the people and saved them by maneuvering with them—that is, he used them as a shield.

In the year eight, he had a son, Ibrāhīm. The Negus died, and his daughter Umm Kulthūm died.

In the year eight, God granted him the conquest of Mecca in the month of Ramaḍān. He stayed there for fifteen nights, shortening the prayer.

Then, in Shawwāl of the year eight, he set out for Ḥunayn and appointed ʿAttāb ibn Asīd as his deputy in Mecca. The people performed the pilgrimage according to their customary stations while still in polytheism. The Messenger of God ﷺ—met a force from Hawāzin at Ḥunayn in the middle of Shawwāl. God—mighty and majestic—routed them and granted him their wealth and women as booty.

Those who stood firm with the Messenger of God ﷺ—on the Day of Ḥunayn, after the people had been routed, were: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, who held the bridle of his mule; Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and his son; al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; Ayman ibn ʿUbayd—who was the son of Umm Ayman, the freedwoman and nurse of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He and Ibn Abī Sufyān were killed that day; Ibn Abī Sufyān left no descendants. Also among them were Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: [long meter]

We helped the Messenger of God in battle, seven,

while those who fled from among them scattered away.

Our eighth met death with his sword,

uncomplaining of what had befallen him for God’s sake.

He meant Ayman ibn ʿUbayd.

After Ḥunayn, the Messenger of God ﷺ—set out for al-Ṭāʾif. He besieged them for a month, then withdrew without conquering it. He performed the lesser pilgrimage from al-Jiʿrāna in Dhū al-Qaʿda of the year eight.

Then he turned back toward Medina, entered it, and remained there until Rajab of the year nine.

Then he set out for the land of the Romans. The furthest point he reached was Tabūk, where he stayed and built a mosque, which still stands there to this day.

On that journey, God granted him the conquest of Dūmat al-Jandal. He sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd there, and its ruler, Ukaydir, came to him and made peace with him on condition of paying the poll tax.

Then he came to Medina and remained there until the pilgrimage season of the year nine. He sent Abū Bakr as commander of the pilgrims, and Abū Bakr led the people through their pilgrimage. It was the first pilgrimage performed in Islam.

The Sūrat Barāʾa was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ—after Abū Bakr had set out. He therefore sent it with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and ordered him to proclaim it to the people when Abū Bakr had completed the pilgrimage.

Abū Bakr and ʿAlī ﵄—then returned to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

The year ten began, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—spent it in Medina. Delegations of the Arabs came to him from every direction. He sent his envoys to the kings of the earth, and people entered Islam in throngs. “When God’s help and victory come” (Qurʾān 110:1) was revealed to him. He knew then that his own death had been announced to him. When the pilgrimage season came, the Messenger of God ﷺ—set out five nights before the end of Dhū al-Qaʿda. He led the people through their pilgrimage and taught them its rites. Then he returned to Medina and remained there for the rest of Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year ten, Muḥarram, Ṣafar, and twelve nights of Rabīʿ al-Awwal in the year eleven. Then God took him to Himself on Monday.

He had lived in Medina for ten years until his death, and had reached the age of sixty-three.

It is said that he ﷺ—was born on a Monday, was commissioned on a Monday, entered Medina on a Monday, and died on a Monday. He was buried on the night of Wednesday in ʿĀʾisha’s chamber, where he had died.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib entered the grave.

It is also said that Qutham ibn al-ʿAbbās entered with them.

The Banū Zuhra said: “We are his maternal uncles; let one of our men enter.” So they admitted ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf.

It is said that Usāma ibn Zayd entered with him.

Al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba said: “I was the last of you to be with him”—because he had dropped his ring into the grave and then retrieved it.

Zayd ibn Akhzam related to me: ʿUthmān ibn Farqad related to me: I heard Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad relate from his father. He said:

The man who made the niche in the grave of the Messenger of God ﷺ—was Abū Ṭalḥa, and the man who laid the cloth beneath him was Shaqrān.

Jaʿfar said: Ibn Abī Rāfiʿ told me:

I heard Shaqrān say: “By God, I was the one who placed the cloth beneath the Messenger of God ﷺ—in the grave.”

Reports about Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

Abū Bakr’s name was ʿAbd Allāh. His father, Abū Quḥāfa, was named ʿUthmān. Abū Bakr’s name in the pre-Islamic period was ʿAbd al-Kaʿba, but the Messenger of God ﷺ—named him ʿAbd Allāh and gave him the epithet ʿAtīq because of the beauty of his face.

It is said that he was called ʿAtīq because the Messenger of God ﷺ—said to him: “You are freed from the Fire.” He was called Ṣiddīq because he affirmed the account of the Night Journey.

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿĀmir ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Taym ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna.

Abū Bakr was affiliated with Taym of Quraysh, and so was called al-Taymī. In genealogical degree, he was like the Messenger of God ﷺ—for he and the Messenger of God share Murra ibn Kaʿb as a common ancestor, with six forefathers between each of them and Murra.

Abū Bakr’s Father and Mother

They said:

Abū Quḥāfa accepted Islam on the day Mecca was conquered. He was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ—and his head was as white as thughāma. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “Would you not have left the old man in his house, so that we might go to him out of respect for Abū Bakr?” He told them to dye his white hair. Abū Quḥāfa pledged allegiance to him, came to Medina, and remained there until he died during the caliphate of ʿUmar.

Abū Bakr had died before him. Abū Quḥāfa bequeathed him one-sixth of his estate, but he returned it to Abū Bakr’s children.

Abū Quḥāfa died in the year fourteen, during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He was ninety-seven years old when he died.

Abū Bakr’s mother was Salmā bt. Ṣakhr ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Taym. She was Abū Quḥāfa’s paternal uncle’s daughter and was known by the kunya Umm al-Khayr.

Abū Quḥāfa had the following children: Abū Bakr, Umm Farwa, and Qurayba.

As for Umm Farwa, she married a man from al-Azd and bore him a daughter. Then she married Tamīm al-Dārī. Then she married al-Ashʿath ibn Qays.

As for Qurayba, she was married to Saʿd ibn Qays ibn ʿUbāda.

Abū Bakr’s Conversion to Islam and Disagreement about It

Ibn Isḥāq said:

The first of the Messenger of God’s Companions to follow him and believe in him was:

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁—who was nine years old; then Zayd ibn Ḥāritha; then Abū Bakr ibn Abī Quḥāfa.

Then a group of Muslims accepted Islam, among them ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb related to me, saying: Nūḥ ibn Qays related to us, saying: Sulaymān Abū Fāṭimah related to us, from Muʿādhah bt. ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAdawiyyah, who said:

I heard ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on the pulpit in Baṣrah saying: “I am the foremost of the truthful. I believed before Abū Bakr believed, and I embraced Islam before Abū Bakr embraced Islam.” He said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb related to me, saying: Abū Dāwūd related to us, saying: Shuʿbah related to us, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: I heard Ḥabbah al-ʿUranī say:

I heard ʿAlī say: “I was the first to pray with the Messenger of God ﷺ.” He said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb related to me, saying: Abū Dāwūd related to us, saying: Shuʿbah related to us, saying: al-Jarīrī related to us, saying: I heard Abū Naḍrah say:

Abū Bakr said, concerning the caliphate: “Who is more entitled to it than I? Was I not the first to embrace Islam?”

Abū Bakr’s Appearance

ʿĀʾishah ﵂—described him, saying: “My father was fair-complexioned and thin, with sparse hair on his cheeks, stooping, and his waist-wrapper would not stay in place but slipped down from his hips. His face was lean, his eyes sunken, his forehead prominent, and his knuckles bare.”

She also said: “He used to dye his hair with henna and katam.”

The Pledge to Abū Bakr, His Caliphate, and His Death

Abū Bakr was pledged allegiance on the day the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, at the portico of Banū Sāʿidah ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Khazraj. Then, on Tuesday, the day after that, the general pledge of allegiance was made. The Arabs apostatized, with the exception of a few, by withholding the alms-tax, and he fought them until they returned to order. He sent ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to lead the people on the pilgrimage in the year eleven. Yamāmah was conquered, and Musaylimah the Liar and al-Aswad ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAnsī were killed in Ṣanʿāʾ. Abū Bakr led the people on the pilgrimage in the year twelve, then returned to Medina and sent the armies to Syria. The battle of Ajnādayn took place in Jumādā al-Ūlā of the year thirteen.

They disagreed about the cause of the illness from which he died and about the day on which he died.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said, on the authority of Salām ibn Abī Muṭīʿ: “He was poisoned and died on Monday, toward its end.”

Another authority said:

The cause of his illness was that he bathed on a cold day, developed a fever, and was ill for fifteen days. When he became gravely ill, ʿUmar led the people in prayer.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

He died on Friday, with nine nights remaining in Jumādā al-Ākhirah, in the year thirteen.

His rule lasted two years, three months, and nine nights. He had instructed that his wife, Asmāʾ bt. ʿUmays, wash him. When he died, he was carried on the bed on which the Prophet ﷺ—used to sleep, which was ʿĀʾishah’s bed. A man from the clients of Muʿāwiyah bought it for four thousand dirhams and made it available to the people; it is in Medina. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb performed the funeral prayer over him.

ʿUmar, Ṭalḥah, ʿUthmān, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr descended into his grave. He was buried with the Prophet ﷺ—in ʿĀʾishah’s room ﵂.

He had said to ʿĀʾishah: “Look, my daughter: whatever has increased in Abū Bakr’s wealth since we took charge of this affair, return it to the Muslims. By God, nothing of their wealth has come to us except what we ate in our bellies of their coarse food and what we wore on our backs of their rough clothes.” She looked and found a young camel, a worn velvet cloak worth no more than five dirhams, and a stuffed cushion.3

When the messenger brought these things to ʿUmar ﵁—ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf said to ʿUmar:

“Commander of the Faithful, are you going to take this away from Abū Bakr’s children?” He said: “No, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah. Abū Bakr would not have incurred sin over it in his lifetime, and I will bear it after his death. May God have mercy on Abū Bakr: he has burdened those who came after him with hardship.”

Abū Bakr’s Age

They agree that he was sixty-three years old. The Messenger of God was therefore older than Abū Bakr by the number of years of his caliphate.

Muḥammad ibn Ziyād related to me, saying: ʿAbd al-Wārith ibn Saʿīd related to me, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Ṣuhayb, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

The Prophet ﷺ came to Medina with Abū Bakr riding behind him. Abū Bakr was an old man recognizable to people, while the Prophet of God ﷺ—was a young man whom they did not recognize. A man would meet Abū Bakr and say:

“Abū Bakr, who is this man in front of you?” He would reply: “He is showing me the way.” The observer would think that he meant he was guiding him along the road, whereas he meant the way of goodness.

This report indicates that Abū Bakr was much older than the Prophet ﷺ. What is generally known among the historians is what we related first.

Abū Bakr’s Children by Birth and Their Descendants

Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁—had ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr and Asmāʾ bt. Abī Bakr. Their mother was Qutaylah, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy.

He also had ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and ʿĀʾishah. Their mother was Umm Rūmān, daughter of ʿUmayr ibn ʿĀmir, of Banū Firās ibn Ghanm ibn Kinānah. Umm Rūmān had been married to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Sakhbarah, and bore him al-Ṭufayl ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith. Abū al-Ṭufayl came from al-Sarāh and entered into an alliance with Abū Bakr; his wife, Umm Rūmān, was with him. Then he died, and Abū Bakr married her. Thus al-Ṭufayl was ʿĀʾishah’s maternal half-brother.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr; his mother was Asmāʾ bt. ʿUmays.

Umm Kulthūm; her mother was the daughter of Zayd ibn Khārijah, one of the Anṣār.

As for ʿAbd Allāh, he was present with the Prophet ﷺ—at the battle of al-Ṭāʾif, where he was wounded. He lived until his father’s caliphate, and died during it, leaving seven dinars, which Abū Bakr considered a great amount. [page marker in source: / ٨٧/]

ʿAbd Allāh had a son, Ismāʿīl, who died without descendants.

As for Asmāʾ, she was Dhāt al-Niṭāqayn. Al-Zubayr married her in Mecca, and she bore him several children. He divorced her, and she remained in Mecca with her son ʿAbd Allāh until he was killed. She lived to be one hundred years old, until she went blind, and died in Mecca.

As for ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet ﷺ—married her; her story has been related in the accounts of his wives.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr, he was present at Badr with the polytheists, then embraced Islam and became an excellent Muslim. He died suddenly in the year fifty-three, at a mountain near Mecca. ʿĀʾishah bt. Abī Bakr brought him into the sanctuary and buried him, and emancipated a slave on his behalf. He had been present with her at the Battle of the Camel. His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had Muḥammad, ʿAbd Allāh, and Ḥafṣah.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he had Ṭalḥah—whose mother was ʿĀʾishah bt. Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, whose mother was Umm Kulthūm bt. Abī Bakr. Ṭalḥah was generous. Ṭalḥah had Muḥammad, who was governor of Mecca. Ṭalḥah had many descendants, who live near Medina. ʿĀʾishah bt. Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah was married to Sulaymān ibn ʿAlī.

As for Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he had ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad, whose descendants are known as the House of Abū ʿAtīq. They are among the descendants of Abū Bakr. This is because a number of Abū Bakr’s descendants were vying with one another. One of them said: “I am the son of al-Ṣiddīq.” Another said: “I am the son of the second of two.” Someone else said: “I am the son of the companion of the cave.” Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: “I am the son of Abū ʿAtīq.” He and his descendants have been known by that name to this day.

As for Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr, his teknonym was Abū al-Qāsim, and he was among the ascetics of Quraysh.

He was among those who helped kill ʿUthmān. Then ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib appointed him governor of Egypt. There, a supporter of Muʿāwiyah fought him, overcame him, and killed him.

Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr had al-Qāsim, by an umm walad. He was a jurist in the Ḥijāz, distinguished, and died at Qudayd in the year one hundred and eight.

Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad had ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim and Umm Farwah.

As for Umm Farwah, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib married her, [and she bore him Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was among the most distinguished of Quraysh. His teknonym was Abū Muḥammad, and he had a small number of descendants in Medina.

As for Umm Kulthūm bt. Abī Bakr, ʿUmar asked ʿĀʾishah for her hand, and ʿĀʾishah agreed to the match, but Umm Kulthūm disliked him. She contrived matters until he refrained from pursuing her. Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh married her, and she bore him Zakariyyāʾ and ʿĀʾishah. Then he was killed, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Rabīʿah al-Makhzūmī married her.

[Among the clan of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁—was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān, a generous man and a leader among his people. He died in Mecca in the pre-Islamic period.

Abū Bakr’s Clients and His Descendants ﵁

Bilāl the caller to prayer—he was Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ, and his mother was Ḥamāmah. He was one of those born in Mecca, belonging to a man from Banū Jumah. Abū Bakr bought him for five ūqiyyahs and emancipated him. He was tortured for God’s sake.

Bilāl was present at Badr and all the campaigns. He was the first to call the adhān for the Messenger of God ﷺ. When the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, he went to Abū Bakr and asked permission to go to Syria. Abū Bakr gave him permission, and he remained there. He did not call the adhān after the Prophet ﷺ.

When ʿUmar came to Syria, he met him and ordered him to call the adhān, so Bilāl did. ʿUmar and the Muslims wept. Bilāl’s military register was in Khathʿam, so every Abyssinian in Syria was registered with Khathʿam. He died there.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Bilāl was among those born in al-Sarāh, between Yemen and al-Ṭāʾif. His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was a very dark-complexioned, thin, tall man, stooping, with abundant hair, sparse hair on his cheeks, and much gray in it. He did not dye his gray hair. He died in Damascus in the year twenty, aged a little over sixty. [His grave is in Damascus.

ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah—among Abū Bakr’s clients was ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah. He belonged to al-Ṭufayl ibn al-Ḥārith, ʿĀʾishah’s maternal half-brother through her mother, Umm Rūmān. ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah embraced Islam, and Abū Bakr bought and emancipated him. He was among those tortured for God’s sake.

More than one person related to us, among them al-Riyāshī: Abū Bakr emancipated seven people, all of whom were tortured for God’s sake: Bilāl, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah, Zunnayrah, Umm ʿUbayṣ, a bondwoman from Banū ʿAmr ibn Muʾammal, al-Nahdiyyah, and her daughter.

ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah was with the Messenger of God ﷺ—when he emigrated to Medina, serving him. He was present at Badr and Biʾr Maʿūnah, where he was martyred that day. [page marker in source: / ٨٩/] Among Abū Bakr’s clients was Ṣafiyyah, the mother of Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn.

Among Abū Bakr’s clients was Abū Nāfiʿ, the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr. He had amassed considerable wealth. It is he who is meant by the saying: “Good fortune like Abū Nāfiʿ’s good fortune.” He lived in Baṣrah, where he had a well-known house. Ibn Mufarrigh al-Ḥimyarī said of him: [long]

May God give rain to land and a house I left behind,beside my house, Maʿqil ibn Yasār.

Abū Nāfiʿ is a neighbor there, as is Ibn Barthan—what a neighbor of disgrace and lowliness you are!

Ibn Barthan was a client of Banū Ḍubayʿah. Someone said to Abū Nāfiʿ: “He has satirized you.” He said: “If he satirizes me, will I die, or will my son Ṭalḥah die?” They said: “No.” He said: “Then I do not care.”

Among Abū Bakr’s clients was Murrah ibn Abī ʿUthmān, the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr. ʿĀʾishah wrote to Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān, entrusting him to his care. Ziyād was pleased by her letter, treated him generously, and granted him the “Canal of Murrah” in Baṣrah. The canal is named after him, and he has many descendants in Baṣrah.

Among the clients of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad was Sulaymān ibn Bilāl. He was a handsome Berber.

He held the office of Medina’s land-tax administration, and reports of ḥadīth were transmitted from him. He died in Medina in the year one hundred and seventy-two, during the caliphate of Hārūn al-Rashīd.

Reports concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁

He was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Nufayl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Qurṭ ibn Riyāḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rizāḥ ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna. ʿUmar was affiliated with ʿAdī, and was therefore called al-ʿAdawī.

Abū ʿUmar, his mother, and his brother Zayd and his mother

Al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Nufayl was one of the men of Quraysh. His mother was a woman from Fahm. She was married to Nufayl, and after Nufayl’s death she married his son ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, to whom she bore Zayd. Thus Zayd’s mother was Umm al-Khaṭṭāb. This Zayd was the father of Saʿīd ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, one of the ten whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—gave the glad tidings of Paradise.

Al-Khaṭṭāb had two sons: Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

As for Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, his mother was Asmāʾ, of Banū Asad ibn Khuzayma. He embraced Islam before ʿUmar did. He fought at Badr, and there was a coat of mail between him and ʿUmar. Each of them said, “By God, no one but you shall wear it.” Then he fought at the Battle of Uḥud, where he stood firm among four men and did not flee with those who fled. He fought on the day of Musaylima in the year twelve.

He was killed. It is said that his killer was Abū Maryam al-Ḥanafī. It is also said that Salama, the brother of Abū Maryam, killed him.

Zayd was surnamed Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. His children were ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—whose mother was the daughter of Abū Lubāba al-Anṣārī—and Asmāʾ.

As for Asmāʾ, she married ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and he was killed while she was still his wife.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, his children were ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—who was lame—ʿAbd Allāh, and his mother Fāṭima bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd was an official of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

His children were Ibrāhīm, ʿAbd al-Malik, ʿAbd al-Kabīr, ʿUmar, Zayd, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Muḥammad.

As for Ibrāhīm, he had a son, Isḥāq, known as al-Khaṭṭābī.

His descendants in Baṣra were numerous and held high standing. The other descendants of ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd held governorships.

As for ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he was surnamed Abū Ḥafṣ. His mother was Ḥantama bint Hishām ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī.

He was called al-Fārūq, “the Discerner,” because he proclaimed Islam openly and called people to it while they were concealing it, and so he distinguished truth from falsehood. There were thirty-nine Muslim men and women in Mecca, and ʿUmar brought their number to forty.

Ibn Masʿūd said: “We have remained mighty ever since ʿUmar embraced Islam.”

The appearance of ʿUmar ﵁

They differed about his complexion. Some of the Ḥijāzīs related that he was white, very pale, tall, bald, and touched with redness.

The Kūfans related that he was dark, of a deep-brown complexion, and that he used to dye his beard yellow with henna.

It is related through more than one chain that he was left-handed but also able to use his right hand—that is, he worked with both hands, and was ambidextrous.

He said: Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me: al-Aṣmaʿī related to us: Shuʿba related to us, from Simāk ibn Ḥarb: “ʿUmar was bow-legged, as if he were riding while people walked, and as if he were one of the men of Banū Sadūs.”

“Bow-legged” means that a man’s heels draw close together when he walks.

The caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

Abū Bakr ﵁—appointed ʿUmar as his successor and made him caliph after him.

During the years of his rule, God granted him the conquest of Jerusalem, Damascus—which was taken by treaty through Khālid ibn al-Walīd—Maysān, Dastumaysān, Abzaqbād, and al-Yarmūk.

Then came the battle of al-Jābiya and al-Ahwāz and its districts, under the command of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

The battle of Jalūlāʾ took place in the year nineteen, under the command of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ al-Zuhrī.

In that year the battle of Qaysāriyya also took place, under the command of Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān.

Then came the battle at the Gate of Babylon in the year twenty, under the command of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.

The battle of Nihāwand took place in the year twenty-one, under the command of al-Nuʿmān ibn Muqarrin al-Muzanī.

Arrajān, in al-Ahwāz, was conquered in the year twenty-two, under the command of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba.

The first campaign at Iṣṭakhr and the campaign at Hamadhān took place in the year twenty-three.

As for the Year of the Ashes and the Plague of ʿAmwās, they occurred in the year eighteen.

ʿUmar led the people on the pilgrimage for ten consecutive years. Then he returned to Medina, where he was killed by Fīrūz, Abū Luʾluʾa, the slave of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, on Monday, four nights remaining in Dhū al-Ḥijja, at the close of the year twenty-three.

Al-Wāqidī said:

ʿUmar was stabbed on Wednesday, with seven nights remaining in Dhū al-Ḥijja. He lived for three days, then died with four nights remaining in Dhū al-Ḥijja. Ṣuhayb led the funeral prayer over him. He was buried in ʿĀʾisha’s chamber, alongside the Messenger of God ﷺ—and Abū Bakr.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

His caliphate lasted ten years, six months, and five nights.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s age ﵁

They differed about his age.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

He died at the age of fifty-five.

This is also the view of Abū al-Yaqẓān.

Al-Wāqidī related from Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ, from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, who said:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb died at the age of sixty-three. I think this can only be a mistake. The correct view is the first one.

Zayd ibn Akhzam related to me: Abū Qutayba related to us, from Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim, from Ayyūb, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was killed at the age of fifty-five.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s children and their descendants

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s children were ʿAbd Allāh and Ḥafṣa—their mother was Zaynab bint Maẓʿūn—ʿUbayd Allāh—whose mother was Mulayka bint Jarwal al-Khuzāʿī—and ʿĀṣim—whose mother was Jamīla bint ʿĀṣim ibn Thābit, Ḥimā al-Dabr—Fāṭima and Zayd—their mother was Umm Kulthūm bint ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, born to Fāṭima, the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. It is said that ʿUmar’s daughter by Umm Kulthūm was named Ruqayya, and that ʿUmar married her to Ibrāhīm ibn Nuʿaym al-Naḥḥām. She died while married to him and left no children. He also had Mujabbar—whose name was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—Abū Shaḥma—also named ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—Fāṭima, and other daughters.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ﵃

As for ʿAbd Allāh, he was surnamed Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He embraced Islam with his father in Mecca while still a boy. He took part in all the campaigns after Badr and Uḥud, and lived into the time of ʿAbd al-Malik.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

They claim that al-Ḥajjāj secretly sent a man, who poisoned the tip of his spear, jostled him on the road, and stabbed him in the back of his foot. Al-Ḥajjāj came in to see him and said, “Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who struck you?”

He said, “Why do you say that? May God have mercy on you.” He replied, “You carried weapons in a town where weapons were not carried.” He died. The funeral prayer was performed for him at al-Radm, and he was buried in the enclosure of Ḥurmāz.

Others besides Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He died in Mecca and was buried at Fakhkh, at the age of eighty-four.

He used to dye his beard yellow. He was the last of the Companions to die in Mecca.

The children of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ﵃

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar’s children were ʿAbd Allāh—whose mother was Ṣafiyya bint Abī ʿUbayd, the sister of al-Mukhtār—Sālim—whose mother was a bondwoman—and ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, Bilāl, Wāqid, and daughters. One of the daughters was married to ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, and another to ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, he was one of the notable men of Quraysh and his father’s testamentary executor. He had descendants in Medina.

Among them was ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. He governed Kirmān for al-Mahdī, then Mūsā appointed him over Medina.

Among them was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He was one of the most ascetic, devout, and excellent of people. He died in a desert region near Medina.

As for Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he was surnamed Abū ʿAmr and was among the best and most learned in jurisprudence of people. His father was reproached for his love of him, and would say: [ṭawīl]

“They reproach me for Sālim, and I reproach them;

Sālim is like a skin between the eye and the nose.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

Sālim was surnamed Abū al-Mundhir. He died in Medina in the year one hundred and six, and Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik led the funeral prayer over him.

As for ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, he had a son, Muḥammad, whose descendants were in Kūfa.

As for Wāqid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, he fell from his camel while in a state of consecration for pilgrimage and died. Wāqid’s son was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Wāqid, one of the notable men of Quraysh. A poet said of him: [ṭawīl]

“I love every slender woman among women

who has ʿAbbād’s beauty and Ibn Wāqid’s figure.”

He means ʿAbbād ibn Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr.

As for Bilāl ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, he had a scar on his forehead. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar used to say to him:

“Bilāl, I hope you will be the most scarred of the Banū ʿUmar.” He died young, leaving no descendants.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he was very strong-handed. When ʿUmar was killed, he drew his sword and killed the daughter of Abū Luʾluʾa, al-Hurmuzān, and Jufayna—a foreign man—and said, “I will not leave a single foreigner alive.” ʿAlī wanted to kill him in retribution for those he had killed, but he fled to Muʿāwiya and fought alongside him at Ṣiffīn, where he was killed.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar’s children were Abū Bakr, ʿUthmān, Umm ʿĪsā, and others.

Abū Bakr’s child was Umm Salama, who was married to al-Ḥajjāj.

ʿUthmān’s daughter was Umm ʿUthmān, who was married to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

As for ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he was virtuous and good. He died in the year seventy, before ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr was killed. His brother ʿAbd Allāh elegized him in verse: [ṭawīl]

“If only death had left ʿĀṣim behind,

we would have lived together, or it would have taken us both.”

ʿĀṣim’s children were Ḥafṣ, ʿUmar, Ḥafṣa, Umm ʿĀṣim, and Umm Miskīn.

As for Umm ʿĀṣim, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān married her, and she bore him ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. She died while married to him, and he then married her sister Ḥafṣa. Hence it is said: “Ḥafṣa is not among the children of Umm ʿĀṣim.” As for Umm Miskīn, Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya married and divorced her; ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād then married her.

As for Ḥafṣ ibn ʿĀṣim, his children were ʿUmar and Umm ʿĀṣim. ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ’s child was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī, who is cited as a transmitter of ḥadīth.

As for Abū Shaḥma ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿUmar inflicted the legal punishment on him for drinking wine, and he died. He left no descendants.

As for Zayd ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he was struck by a stone in a war between Banū ʿUwayj and Banū Rizāḥ, and died. He left no descendants. It is said that he and his mother, Umm Kulthūm, died at the same hour, so neither inherited from the other. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar led the funeral prayers for them. He placed Zayd first and Umm Kulthūm afterward, and the practice of placing men first was thereby established.

As for Mujabbar ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he had children, but they died out, and none of them remained.

The Clients of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁

Among the clients of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was Mālik al-Dār. ʿUmar had appointed him over a public treasury, where he distributed something among the people. The mother of his children was Ḥubbā, who had nursed ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. She was beautiful. ʿUthmān said to her, “I want to grant you something. Which would you prefer: a fifth from five fifths, or a sixth from six sixths?” She said: “A sixth.”

So he granted it to her, and Mālik al-Dār claimed affiliation with Yemen.

Among the clients of Mālik al-Dār was Dhakwān, who was held in great esteem and had governed some administrative districts. He was the one who traveled from Mecca to Medina in a single day and night.

Among the clients of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was Mihjaʿ, a client of ʿUmar. He was killed on the day of Badr.

Another of his clients was Aslam.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said:

“Aslam was an Abyssinian of the Bajāwa tribe, and was known by the kunya Abū Zayd. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb bought him in the year twelve. In that same year, al-Ashʿath ibn Qays was brought before Abū Bakr in chains. Aslam said: ‘I heard him speaking to Abū Bakr.’”

He died during the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He transmitted many reports from ʿUmar, and his son Zayd ibn Aslam transmitted many reports from his father.

Another of his clients was Nāfiʿ, the client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.

Nāfiʿ was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was from Aburshahr. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar acquired him on one of his campaigns. He had the following children: Abū Bakr, ʿAbd Allāh, and ʿUmar.

Reports have been transmitted from them.

Another of his clients was Hunayy.

Hunayy, the client of ʿUmar, is the one who reported that Abū Bakr designated no land as protected except al-Baqīʿ, which he protected for the horses used on campaigns.

Among the clients of ʿUmar was al-Mubārak ibn Faḍāla ibn Abī Umayya. His grandfather, Abū Umayya, had been a contractually manumitted client of ʿUmar, and his name was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Many reports were transmitted from al-Mubārak. He died in the year 165. Al-Mubārak had two brothers from whom reports were transmitted: al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Faḍāla and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Faḍāla.

Reports of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁

The Lineage of ʿUthmān

He was ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna. He was known by the kunyas Abū ʿAmr, Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and Abū Laylā.

Abū ʿUthmān and His Mother

ʿAffān had set out on a trading journey to Syria and died there.

It is said that he was killed at al-Ghumayṣāʾ, along with al-Fākih ibn al-Mughīra.

ʿAffān’s children were ʿUthmān, Āmina, and Arnab. Their mother was Arwā bint Kurayz ibn Rabīʿa ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿAbd Shams. Her mother was al-Bayḍāʾ bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Thus ʿUthmān’s mother was a cousin of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

ʿUthmān’s Appearance and Reports about Him

Al-Wāqidī said: “ʿUthmān was a man of neither short nor tall stature, handsome, with delicate skin, a large and abundant beard, dark complexion, and abundant hair on his head. He used to bind his teeth with gold.”

Another added:

“He was bald, with a prominent nose, and had a lock of hair hanging below his ears. Because of the abundance of hair on his head and beard, his enemies called him Naʿthal. The Messenger of God ﷺ—married his two daughters to him: Ruqayya and Umm Kulthūm.

“He was beloved among Quraysh. One of them said of him: [rajaz, in shortened form]

I love you, by the Merciful,

As Quraysh love ʿUthmān,

When he calls for the scales.

“He was among the earliest Emigrants. He had married Ruqayya, the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—while he was in Mecca, and emigrated with her to the land of Abyssinia. The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: ‘The two of them were the first to emigrate for God’s sake—mighty and majestic is He—after Abraham and Lot ﵉.’ Then he emigrated to Medina, so he had two emigrations.

“He bought the Well of Rūma, which belonged to a Jew who sold its water to the Muslims. The Prophet ﷺ—said: ‘Who will buy Rūma and make it available to the Muslims, so that he may draw water from it with his bucket alongside theirs, and have a drinking place there in Paradise?’ ʿUthmān went to the Jewish owner and bargained with him for it, but he refused to sell the whole well.

“So ʿUthmān bought half of it for twelve dirhams and made it available to the Muslims. ʿUthmān said: ‘If you wish, I can have one day and you one day; or, if you wish, shall I put two qarns against my share?’ The Jew said: ‘I shall have one day and you one day.’”

On ʿUthmān’s day, the Muslims would draw enough water for two days. When the Jew saw this, he said to ʿUthmān: “You have ruined my well for me. Buy the other half.” So ʿUthmān bought it for eight thousand dirhams.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “Who will add to our mosque?” ʿUthmān bought the site of five pillars and added it to the mosque.

ʿUthmān equipped the Army of Hardship with nine hundred and fifty camels, bringing the total to one thousand with fifty horses.

He did not take part in Badr because the Messenger of God ﷺ had left him behind to care for his daughter Ruqayya, who was gravely ill. She died, and he buried her.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—assigned him his share and reward.

He did not take part in the Pledge of Good Pleasure because the Messenger of God ﷺ—sent him to Mecca to inform its people that he had not come to fight. The Messenger of God ﷺ—pledged on ʿUthmān’s behalf with his left hand.

He took part in the day of Uḥud, then fled and went as far as al-Ghāba, a journey of three days. The verse was revealed concerning him and his companions: “Those of you who turned back on the day the two armies met—it was Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. Yet God has pardoned them; God is forgiving, forbearing” (3:155).

The Caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁

ʿUthmān was pledged allegiance to at the beginning of Muḥarram in the year 24. He was then sixty-nine years old.

The first campaign undertaken during his caliphate was against Rayy, with Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī commanding the armies. Next came Alexandria, then Sābūr, then Ifrīqiya, then Cyprus, on the shores of the Sea of the Romans, then Iṣṭakhr al-Ākhira and Fāris al-Ūlā, then Jūr and Fāris al-Ākhira, then Ṭabaristān and Dārābjird, Kirmān, and Sijistān; then the Asāwira at sea; then Ifrīqiya; then the fortresses of Cyprus; then the coast of Jordan. After that, Marw was taken by ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir in the year 34.

Then ʿUthmān was besieged in Dhu al-Ḥijja of the year 35. Among the things for which ʿUthmān was blamed was that he gave refuge to al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ and gave him one hundred thousand dirhams [as they claimed].

The Messenger of God ﷺ—had banished him, and neither Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar had given him refuge.

They said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ—gave Mahzūr, the site of the market of Medina, as a charitable endowment for the Muslims. But ʿUthmān granted it to al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥakam, the brother of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. He also granted Fadak to Marwān, though it was the charitable endowment of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

“He conquered Ifrīqiya and took the fifth [as they claimed], then gave all of it to Marwān.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥanbal al-Jumaḥī, whom ʿUthmān had sent away, and who was a poet, said: [mutāqārib]

I swear by God, Lord of humankind:

God left nothing without purpose;

Rather, you were created for us as a trial,

So that we might be tested by you, or you by us.

The two trustworthy men made clear

The signposts of the path of guidance.

Neither took a dirham by stealth,

Nor placed a dirham in the service of desire.

You gave Marwān the people’s fifth—

How far your stride falls short of those who strove!

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Asīd asked him for a gift, and he gave him four hundred thousand dirhams [as they claimed].

He sent Abū Dharr to al-Rabadha. He sent ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd al-Qays from Basra to Syria. A group of people from Egypt then marched against him, among them Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, with a troop; Kināna ibn Bishr al-Tujībī, with a troop; and Ibn ʿUdays al-Balawī, with a troop.

From among the people of Basra were Ḥakīm ibn Jabala al-ʿAbdī, Sadūs ibn ʿUbayd al-Shannī, and a number of people from Kufa, among them al-Ashtar ibn al-Ḥārith al-Nakhaʿī. They demanded that he make amends, and he did so, appeasing and satisfying them.

Then, after they had departed, heading for Egypt, they found a letter from ʿUthmān [in the handwriting of his scribe], bearing his seal, addressed to the governor of Egypt: “When the people arrive, strike off their heads.” They brought it back to ʿUthmān, who swore to them that he had neither ordered it nor known of it. They said: “This is a grave matter for you: your seal has been taken without your knowledge, and your inner circle has been compromised! If you have been overpowered in your affairs, then step down.”

He refused to step down or fight them. He forbade fighting and closed his door. They besieged him for more than twenty days. He was in the house with six hundred men. Then they entered upon him through the house of the Banū Ḥazm al-Anṣārī. Niyār ibn ʿIyāḍ al-Aslamī struck him in the face with a barbed arrowhead, and blood ran onto the Qurʾān in his lap. Then Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr took hold of his beard, and ʿUthmān said:

“Leave my beard to me.”

He was killed in Dhu al-Ḥijja of the year 35.

That year, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās led the pilgrimage for the people, while ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib led the people in prayer in Medina and addressed them.

ʿUthmān had led the pilgrimage for the people ten years in succession. The day on which he was killed is disputed.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

“He was killed on Wednesday after the afternoon prayer and buried on Saturday before noon.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He was killed on Friday, when eight nights of Dhu al-Ḥijja had passed, in the year 35. He was then eighty-two years old.”

He said: “This is the account on which there is no disagreement.”

He was buried at night in al-Baqīʿ. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim performed the funeral prayer over him, and they concealed his grave.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

“He was killed on Friday in the year 35, and buried in a place called Ḥashsh Kawkab. ʿUthmān had bought it and added it to al-Baqīʿ.

“Al-ḥashsh means a garden; its plural is ḥashshān. Kawkab was a man of the Anṣār.”

Abū Muḥammad said:

“I found that the poets say he was killed on the day of sacrifice. About this, al-Farazdaq ibn Ghālib said: [kāmil]

ʿUthmān, when they killed him and violated

His blood on the morning of the Night of Sacrifice.

Another poet said: [basīṭ]

They sacrificed a white-haired man, whose forehead bore the mark of prostration;

He spent the night in praise and recitation of the Qurʾān.

Ayman ibn Khuraym said: [basīṭ]

May the slayers of ʿUthmān be bereft at noon! ... What unlawful slaughter—woe to them—did they commit?

They sacrificed ʿUthmān in the sacred month and feared not

For the aspiration of unbelief toward which they aspired.

What practice of unbelief did their first man institute,

And what gate of unbelief did they open for their ruler?

The swords of the Muslims intercepted them

At the end of their thirst, as a water-drawing beast is led to water.

What did they intend? May God frustrate their efforts,

By spilling that pure blood which they shed.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

“His rule lasted twelve years, less twelve nights.”

The Children of ʿUthmān ﵁

ʿUthmān’s children were: ʿAbd Allāh the elder—his mother was Fākhita bint Ghazwān; ʿAbd Allāh the younger—his mother was Ruqayya, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ; ʿAmr, Abān, Khālid, ʿUmar, Saʿīd, al-Walīd, Umm Saʿīd, al-Mughīra, ʿAbd al-Malik, Umm Abān, Umm ʿAmr, and ʿĀʾisha.

As for ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, he was the eldest of ʿUthmān’s sons and the noblest in lineage. He died at Minā.

His children were: ʿUthmān the elder, Khālid, ʿAbd Allāh the elder—whose mother was Ḥafṣa, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—ʿUthmān the younger, ʿAbd Allāh the younger, Bukayr, al-Mughīra, ʿAnbasa, and al-Walīd.

As for ʿAbd Allāh the elder, he was one of the most handsome of men, and was nicknamed al-Muṭarraf because of his beauty. Of him, Mudrik ibn Ḥiṣn says: [wāfir]

Whenever I enter the house of Ibn ʿAmr,it is as though I enter the chamber of a veiled beauty, full of charms.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr the elder had the following children: Khālid, ʿĀʾisha, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Āmina, and Umm ʿAbd Allāh.

By Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, he had Muḥammad the younger, al-Qāsim, and Ruqayya.

By other women, he had Muḥammad the elder, ʿUmar, and Saʿda.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr the younger was one of the most handsome of men. He was nicknamed al-Dībāj because of his beauty. He had standing and nobility, and it was said of him: “The namesake of the Prophet ﷺ; one of his descendants; and the seed of the wronged caliph.”

He married often and divorced often. One of his wives said: “He is like this world: its delights do not last, and its calamities cannot be trusted.”

Abū Jaʿfar seized him along with the Fāṭimids. Then he ordered him to be secretly beheaded, and sent his head to India, claiming that it was the head of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan al-Fāṭimī.

Muḥammad had descendants. Among them were a woman, with whom the Messenger of God ﷺ fathered a child, and Abū Bakr, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr. She was Ḥafṣa, daughter of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān. Her mother was Khadīja, daughter of ʿUthmān ibn ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr. ʿUrwa’s mother was:

Asmāʾ, daughter of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq.

Muḥammad’s mother was Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Al-Ḥusayn’s mother was:

Fāṭima, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, had as her mother:

Umm Isḥāq, daughter of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān’s mother was Ḥafṣa, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

As for al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, he had no descendants.

As for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he had a son, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, the poet known as al-ʿArjī. He used to reside in al-ʿArj—which is a place near al-Ṭāʾif—and he satirized Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām al-Makhzūmī. Ibrāhīm seized and imprisoned him, and he died in prison. He is the one who said in prison: [wāfir]

As though I had never been a man of standing among them,nor had my lineage been among the house of ʿAmr.

They cast me aside—what a young man they cast aside,for a day of battle and the defense of a frontier!

As for Abān ibn ʿUthmān, he fought at the Battle of the Camel with ʿĀʾisha, and was the second of those to flee. His mother was the daughter of Jundub ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥamma al-Dawsī, and she was foolish. She would put a beetle in her mouth and say, “I challenge you: what is in my mouth?” She was also the mother of ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān.

Abān was a leper, cross-eyed, and nicknamed Baqīʿ.

Umm Kulthūm, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, was his wife. Al-Ḥajjāj married her after him.

His descendants were numerous. Among them was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abān, who was devout and from whom ḥadīth was transmitted.

As for Khālid ibn ʿUthmān, he had ʿUthmān’s codex, which had been in ʿUthmān’s lap when he was killed. It then passed into the hands of his descendants, who have since died out. As for ʿUmar ibn ʿUthmān, he had Zayd, ʿĀṣim, and Umm Ayyūb. Umm Ayyūb was married to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

Zayd ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿUthmān married Sukayna, daughter of al-Ḥusayn.

ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar was one of the stingiest of men. It was of him that the following was said: [ṭawīl]

Set out, for darkness has fallen upon you;may the one who hopes for hospitality from ʿĀṣim be ruined.

I knew of no offense I had committed against him,except that I had visited him without fasting.

As for Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān, he was one-eyed and stingy. He was killed. The reason for his killing was that he had been Muʿāwiya’s governor in Khurāsān. Muʿāwiya dismissed him, and he brought with him to Medina hostages from among the sons of the Sogdians who were in his custody. He set them to work for him on land with mattocks. One day they shut the garden gate, rose against him, and killed him. They were pursued, and killed themselves.

As for al-Walīd ibn ʿUthmān, he was a man of wine and youthful revelry. His father ʿUthmān was killed while he was being perfumed in his bridal chamber.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān, whose mother was Ruqayya, the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ he died as a child. They reported that he reached the age of six, when a rooster pecked him in the eye. He fell ill and died.

As for ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUthmān, he too died while still a boy.

102/ ʿUthmān’s clients ﵁

Among ʿUthmān’s clients were Kaysān Abū Firwa and his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Firwa. The latter held great standing and was an associate of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr. When Muṣʿab was killed, he took ten thousand dirhams from the money that had been with him and went with them to Medina.

Their number in Medina was great, and their standing was high.

Among ʿUthmān’s clients were also ʿImrān ibn Abān and his descendants, and Abū al-Zinād and his descendants.

Reports about ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁

The lineage of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁

He is ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Abū Ṭālib’s name was ʿAbd Manāf ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim. His kunya was Abū al-Ḥasan.

His father, brothers, and sisters

Abū Ṭālib’s children were ʿAqīl, Jaʿfar, ʿAlī, Ṭālib, Umm Hānī—whose name was Fākhita—and Jumāna.

Their mother was Fāṭima, daughter of Asad ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf. Her mother was Ḥubbā, daughter of Hurm ibn Rawāḥa, from Quraysh, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy.

Their mother, Fāṭima daughter of Asad ibn Hāshim, accepted Islam. She was the first Hāshimite woman to bear a child to a Hāshimite man.

As for ʿAqīl, his kunya was Abū Yazīd. He was captured on the day of Badr. Al-ʿAbbās ransomed him for four thousand dirhams, according to what Abū al-Yaqẓān relates.

ʿAqīl and Ṭālib inherited from Abū Ṭālib, but ʿAlī and Jaʿfar did not inherit from him because they were Muslims.

ʿAqīl was ten years older than Jaʿfar, and Jaʿfar was ten years older than ʿAlī.

ʿAqīl accepted Islam, joined Muʿāwiya, and left his brother ʿAlī. He died after becoming blind, during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya. He had a spacious house in al-Baqīʿ with many people in it. ʿAqīl had accused a man of Quraysh of adultery, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb imposed the prescribed punishment on him.

ʿAqīl’s children were Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh, Muḥammad, Ramla, and ʿUbayd Allāh—by a concubine.

Some say:

The mother of Muslim ibn ʿAqīl was a Nabataean woman, from the family of Farzandā.

And ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Ḥamza, ʿAlī, Jaʿfar, ʿUthmān, Zaynab, Asmāʾ, and Umm Hānī—by various concubines.

And Yazīd, Saʿd, Jaʿfar the elder, and Abū Saʿīd.

As for Asmāʾ, she married ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The sons of ʿAqīl went out with al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and nine men of them were killed. Muslim ibn ʿAqīl was the bravest of them. He was at the head of al-Ḥusayn’s vanguard, and ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād had him executed. The poet said: [khafīf]

O eye, pour forth tears and wailing,and mourn, if you mourn, the family of the Messenger.

Seven of them, all of ʿAlī’s loins,were struck down, and nine from ʿAqīl.

Muslim ibn ʿAqīl’s children were ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim and ʿAlī ibn Muslim—their mother was Ruqayya, daughter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—Muslim ibn Muslim, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl’s children were al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad—their mother was Zaynab the younger, daughter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
