As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl, he was a jurist from whom reports were transmitted, and he was cross-eyed.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAqīl, he had Muḥammad, Ruqayya, and Umm Kulthūm. Their mother was Maymūna, daughter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

As for Abū Saʿīd ibn ʿAqīl, he had a son, Muḥammad.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAqīl, he had a son, Saʿīd. His mother was Khadīja, daughter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

As for Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib, he was the possessor of the two migrations and the two wings. He was martyred on the day of Muʾta, when both his hands were severed. God—Mighty and Glorious—is exalted—replaced them with two wings with which he flies in Paradise.

That day, they found fifty-four sword blows on his front, and forty wounds from spear thrusts and arrow shots.

He returned from Abyssinia to the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of the conquest of Khaybar. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “I do not know which of the two things makes me happier: Jaʿfar’s arrival or the conquest of Khaybar.” The Messenger of God ﷺ assigned him a house in Medina beside the mosque.

Abū Hurayra said:

No one after the Messenger of God ﷺ ever rode a camel litter, wore sandals, or walked upon the earth who was better than Jaʿfar.

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Jaʿfar’s children were ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, ʿAwn ibn Jaʿfar, and Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar. Their mother was Asmāʾ, daughter of ʿUmays al-Khathʿamiyya.

As for Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, he had al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and Ṭalḥa. Ṭalḥa had Fāṭima, whose mother was Umm Kulthūm, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. Her mother was Zaynab, daughter of ʿAlī. Her mother was Fāṭima, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Fāṭima married Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, then Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh married her. He had no descendants.

Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar was martyred at Tustar. As for ʿAwn ibn Jaʿfar, he too was killed at Tustar. He had no descendants, except that a man called al-Masāwir came to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar and said, “I am the son of ʿAwn.” ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar acknowledged him and gave him ten thousand dirhams. They reported that he married him to a daughter of his who was blind, but she bore him no children. Then the descendants of ʿAbd Allāh disavowed him thereafter. Today they are in al-Madāʾin: no noble family gives them a woman in marriage, none marries into their family, and they are not called Qurashīs.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, his kunya was Abū Jaʿfar. He was born in Abyssinia and was the most generous of the Arabs. He died in Medina, having reached an advanced age.

Someone else said:

This is Abū al-Yaqẓān’s account.

He died and was buried at al-Abwāʾ in the year ninety. It is said that he was ten years old when the Prophet ﷺ died; thus, it would seem that he was born in the year of the Hijra and died at the age of ninety.

Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik prayed over him.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar’s children were Jaʿfar the elder, ʿAlī, ʿAwn the elder, ʿAbbās, and Umm Kulthūm—their mother was Zaynab, daughter of ʿAlī. Her mother was Fāṭima, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and Muḥammad, ʿUbayd Allāh, and Abū Bakr—their mother was al-Ḥawṣāʾ, daughter of Khaṣafa of Banū Taym Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba—and Ṣāliḥ, Mūsā, Hārūn, Yaḥyā, and Umm Abīhā—their mother was Laylā, daughter of Masʿūd ibn Khālid al-Nahshalī, who was married to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁ before him—and Muʿāwiya, Isḥāq, Ismāʿīl, and al-Qāsim—by various concubines—and al-Ḥasan, ʿAwn the younger—whose mother was Jumāna, daughter of al-Musayyib al-Fazārī—and Jaʿfar.

As for Umm Kulthūm, she was married to al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib.

Then al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf married her. Then Abān ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁ married her.

As for Umm Abīhā, she was married to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He divorced her, then ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās married her, and she died with him. The reason for her divorce was that he bit into an apple and tossed it to her—ʿAbd al-Malik had bad breath—so she asked for a knife.

He said, “What are you doing?” She replied, “Removing the filth from it.” So he separated from her.

The descendants among ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar’s children came from ʿAlī, Muʿāwiya, Isḥāq, and Ismāʿīl.

As for Muʿāwiya, he used to call [someone] stingy. His children were ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿāwiya and Muḥammad ibn Muʿāwiya—their mother was Umm ʿAwn, a descendant of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib—and Yazīd, al-Ḥasan, and Ṣāliḥ—their mother was Fāṭima, daughter of al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī—and ʿAlī, by a concubine.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿāwiya, he sought the caliphate and rose in revolt at Iṣfahān and in parts of Fārs.

Abū Muslim killed him. He had no descendants.

As for Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had him flogged with the prescribed punishment when he was governor of al-Madāʾin. He said to ʿUmar: “You would like there to be no Qurashī left on earth who has not been subjected to the prescribed punishment.”

That was because his father, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, had been subjected to the prescribed punishment.

Isḥāq had a son, al-Qāsim. His mother was Umm Ḥakīm, daughter of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁.

The caliphate of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁

Ibn Isḥāq said:

When ʿUthmān was killed, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁ received the people’s pledge of allegiance in the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The people of Baṣra pledged allegiance to him. In Medina, those who pledged allegiance to him were Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr. ʿĀʾisha had left Medina on pilgrimage while ʿUthmān was besieged.

She then departed from the pilgrimage. When she was at Sarif, news reached her of ʿUthmān’s killing and ʿAlī’s receiving the pledge of allegiance. She turned back to Mecca, and Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz, and Yaʿlā ibn Munya—the governor of Yemen—joined her there. Once they had all gathered in Mecca, they consulted about what they intended to do in seeking vengeance for ʿUthmān. They considered going to Syria, since Muʿāwiya was there. But ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir turned them away from that course and directed them to Baṣra. They set out for it. They seized ʿUthmān ibn Ḥunayf, ʿAlī’s governor there, imprisoned him, and killed fifty men who were with him over the treasury and other matters of his administration. They committed further outrages. When ʿAlī heard of their movement, he set out hastily toward them and called on the people of Kūfa for support. Then he marched with them to Baṣra. They numbered some ten thousand men, and Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, and ʿĀʾisha came out against him with the people of Baṣra. They fought fiercely. Ṭalḥa was killed— Those who were with him were routed. Al-Zubayr turned back and was killed at Wādī al-Sibāʿ by ʿAmr ibn Jurmūz. ʿĀʾisha was surrounded and taken. ʿAlī entered al-Baṣra with those who were with him, and the people of al-Baṣra pledged allegiance to him.

ʿUthmān ibn Ḥunayf was released. He did not remain there long before departing for al-Kūfa. He appointed ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās over al-Baṣra, and prepared for war against Muʿāwiya.

He marched with the people of al-ʿIrāq and those from among the rest of the people who followed him. Muʿāwiya came with the people of al-Shām and those who followed him. Then came the Battle of Ṣiffīn, followed by the two arbitrators. ʿAlī remained at war until he was killed—may ﵇—and did not perform the pilgrimage in any of those years because he was occupied with war. He was killed on Friday night, nineteen nights having passed of the month of Ramaḍān, in the year forty. His rule lasted five years less three months. He was killed by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muljam al-Murādī.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was buried at night, and his grave was concealed.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

Al-Ḥasan prayed over him. He was buried in al-Kūfa, by the congregational mosque, in the governor’s palace.

ʿAlī’s appearance and age ﵁

They differed about his age.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

He was killed when he was sixty-three years old.

Another said:

He was killed when he was fifty-eight years old.

They differed about his appearance.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was dark-complexioned, very dark, large-bellied, large-eyed, and bald; he was closer to short than tall.

Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ related from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Ḥārith, who said:

ʿAlī ﵇—was short, bald, stooping, large-bellied, flat-nosed, with slender forearms. He never wrestled anyone without throwing him. He could leap powerfully and struck with great force.

Another said:

A woman saw him and said, “Who is this, who looks as though he was broken and then mended?”

The children of ʿAlī ﵁

ʿAlī had al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, Muḥassin, Umm Kulthūm the Elder, and Zaynab the Elder—their mother was Fāṭima, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—[page 107] and Muḥammad—his mother was Khawla, daughter of Iyās ibn Jaʿfar, the neighbor of al-Ṣafāʾ; she was al-Ḥanafiyya. It is said that she was Khawla, daughter of Jaʿfar ibn Qays. It is also said that she was a captive woman from al-Yamāma, who came into ʿAlī’s possession; and that she was a black Sindī slave woman belonging to Banū Ḥanīfa, not one of their own people. Khālid ibn al-Walīd had made peace with them concerning their slaves, not concerning their persons—then ʿUbayd Allāh and Abū Bakr—their mother was Laylā, daughter of Masʿūd ibn Khālid al-Nahshalī—and ʿUmar and Ruqayya—their mother was Taghlibiyya.

Khālid ibn al-Walīd had taken her captive during the apostasy wars. ʿAlī bought her—and Yaḥyā—his mother was Asmāʾ daughter of ʿUmays—and Jaʿfar, al-ʿAbbās, and ʿAbd Allāh—their mother was Umm al-Banīn, daughter of Ḥarām al-Wuḥaydiyya—and Ramla and Umm al-Ḥasan—their mother was Umm Saʿīd, daughter of ʿUrwa ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafī—and Umm Kulthūm the Younger, Zaynab the Younger, Jumāna, Maymūna, Khadīja, Fāṭima, Umm al-Kirām, Nafīsa, Umm Salama, Umāma, and Umm Abīhā—by various slave women who bore him children.

The daughters of ʿAlī ﵁

As for Zaynab the Elder, daughter of Fāṭima, she was married to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar.

She bore him children whom we have already mentioned.

As for Umm Kulthūm the Elder, daughter of Fāṭima, she was married to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and bore him children whom we have already mentioned. When ʿUmar was killed, Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib married her, and she died while married to him.

The rest of ʿAlī’s daughters married descendants of ʿAqīl and descendants of al-ʿAbbās, except Umm al-Ḥasan, who was married to Jaʿda ibn Hubayra al-Makhzūmī, and Fāṭima, who was married to Saʿīd ibn al-Aswad, of Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Asad.

As for Muḥassin ibn ʿAlī, he died young.

As for al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, he was called Abū Muḥammad. When ʿAlī was killed, allegiance was pledged to al-Ḥasan in al-Kūfa, while allegiance was pledged to Muʿāwiya in al-Shām and Bayt al-Maqdis. Muʿāwiya marched toward al-Kūfa, and al-Ḥasan marched against him. They met at Maskin, in the territory of al-Kūfa. Al-Ḥasan made peace with Muʿāwiya, pledged allegiance to him, and entered al-Kūfa with him. Then Muʿāwiya left al-Kūfa for al-Shām, [page 108] appointing al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba over al-Kūfa and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir over al-Baṣra; afterward he placed both under Ziyād. Al-Ḥasan departed for al-Madīna, where he died.

It is said that his wife, Jaʿda, daughter of al-Ashʿath ibn Qays, poisoned him.

He died in the month of Rabīʿ al-Awwal in the year forty-nine, at the age of forty-seven. Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, governor of al-Madīna, prayed over him.

Al-Ḥasan had Ḥasan—his mother was Khawla, daughter of Manẓūr ibn Zabban al-Fazāriyya—Zayd and Umm al-Ḥasan—their mother was a daughter of ʿUqba ibn Masʿūd al-Badrī—ʿUmar—his mother was a woman of Thaqīf—al-Ḥusayn al-Athram—by a slave woman—and Ṭalḥa—his mother was Umm Isḥāq, daughter of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh.

Umm ʿAbd Allāh was by a slave woman.

As for al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, he had ʿAbd Allāh, al-Ḥasan, Ibrāhīm, Jaʿfar, Dāwūd, and Muḥammad.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan was called Abū Muḥammad. He was virtuous and distinguished. One day he was seen wiping over his leather socks. He was asked, “You wipe over them?” He replied, “Yes. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb did so, and whoever places ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb between himself and God has made himself secure.”

He was with Abū al-ʿAbbās, who honored him and took comfort in his company.

One day Abū al-ʿAbbās brought out a casket of jewels and shared them with him. He showed him a building he had built and said, “What do you think of this?” He replied: [in the wāfir meter]

Have you not seen Ḥawshab, now buildingPalaces whose benefit is for the Banū Baqīla,Hoping to live as long as Noah,While God’s command comes anew each night?

Abū al-ʿAbbās said to him, “You recite this after seeing what I have done for you?” He replied, “By God, I meant no harm by it; these verses simply came to mind. If the Commander of the Faithful would overlook what I have done!” He said, “I have done so.” Then he sent him back to al-Madīna.

When Abū Jaʿfar came to power, he pressed his pursuit of the two sons of ʿAbd Allāh, Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm. They went into hiding in the desert. Abū Jaʿfar ordered that their father, ʿAbd Allāh, and his brothers—Ḥasan, Dāwūd, and Ibrāhīm—be seized, bound tightly, and sent to him. They met him on the road to Mecca at al-Rabdha, in chains. ʿAbd Allāh asked Abū Jaʿfar to grant him an audience, but he refused.

ʿAbd Allāh did not see him again before he died. He died in prison, and they died there too. His two sons, Ibrāhīm and Muḥammad, rebelled against Abū Jaʿfar, [page 109] and gained control of al-Madīna, Mecca, and al-Baṣra.

ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā was sent against them. He killed Muḥammad in al-Madīna and Ibrāhīm at Bākhamrā, sixteen parasangs from al-Kūfa.

Their brother Idrīs ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan was the one who went to al-Andalus and the Berbers and gained control over them.

As for al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, he was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He set out intending to go to al-Kūfa. ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād sent ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ against him, and Sinān ibn Abī Anas al-Nakhaʿī killed him in the year sixty-one, on the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ. He was fifty-eight years old—it is also said, fifty-six years old—and he dyed his hair black.

Al-Ḥusayn had ʿAlī—his mother was a daughter of Murra ibn ʿUrwa ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafī—ʿAlī the Younger—by a slave woman—Fāṭima—her mother was Umm Isḥāq, daughter of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh—and Sukayna—her mother was al-Rabāb, daughter of Imruʾ al-Qays al-Kalbiyya. Al-Ḥusayn said of her:

[in the wāfir meter]

By your life, I love a houseWhere Sukayna and al-Rabāb dwell.

As for Fāṭima, she was married to al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. After his death, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān married her.

As for Sukayna, Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr married her, and she outlived him. Then ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām married her, and she bore him Qurayn, who had descendants.

Then al-Aṣbagh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān married her, but he divorced her before consummating the marriage.

Then Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān married her. Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ordered him to divorce her, and he did. She died in al-Madīna during the caliphate of Hishām.

This is the account of Abū al-Yaqẓān.

Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī said: Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥassān and others told me; they said:

Sukayna was married to ʿAmr ibn Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām. After him, ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān married her, and after him Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr married her.

Ibn al-Kalbī said:

The first of Sukayna’s husbands was al-Aṣbagh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the brother of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He died in Egypt before seeing her. Then Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān married her; after him Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr married her; and after him ʿAbd Allāh [page 110] ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām married her. She bore him ʿUthmān, known as Qurayn. She had borne Muṣʿab a daughter. Then Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, the grandfather of the jurist Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd, married her.

As for ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn the Younger, al-Ḥusayn had no descendants except through him. It is said that his mother was a Sindī woman called Sulāfa—it is also said, Ghazāla. After al-Ḥusayn, Zubayd married her, a client of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī. She bore him ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zubayd, who was ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn’s maternal brother.

ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad related from ʿUthmān ibn ʿUthmān, who said:

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn married his mother to his client. He freed a slave woman of his and married her. ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to him, reproaching him for that, and ʿAlī wrote back: “You have a good example in the Messenger of God. The Messenger of God ﷺ freed Ṣafiyya, daughter of Ḥuyayy, and married her; and Zayd ibn Ḥāritha freed and married Zaynab, daughter of Jaḥsh, his paternal aunt’s daughter.” ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn died in al-Madīna in the year ninety-four. He was called Abū al-Ḥasan.

He was buried in al-Baqīʿ. He was virtuous and distinguished.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn had al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, ʿAlī ibn ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī—their mother was Umm ʿAbd Allāh, daughter of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī—ʿUmar and Zayd—by a slave woman called Ḥaydān—Khadīja—by a slave woman—and Umm Mūsā, Umm Ḥasan, and Umm Kulthūm—by slave women.

As for Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, he was called Abū Jaʿfar and was learned in jurisprudence. He died in al-Madīna in the year one hundred and seventeen.

Muḥammad had Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad—their mother was Umm Farwa, daughter of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr. Her mother was Asmāʾ, daughter of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr.

Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and the Jaʿfariyya are named after him. He died in al-Madīna in the year one hundred and forty-six, and had descendants.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad was nicknamed Daqdaq. He died in al-Madīna and had descendants.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī had descendants.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn was called Abū al-Ḥasan. His mother was a Sindī woman. He rebelled during the caliphate of Hishām, in the year one hundred and twenty-two. Yūsuf [page 111] ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafī sent al-ʿAbbās al-Murrī against him. One of their men shot him with an arrow; he died and was crucified.

Zayd had Yaḥyā—his mother was Rayṭa, daughter of Abū Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya—ʿĪsā, Ḥusayn, and Muḥammad—by slave women.

Yaḥyā was killed in the time of Naṣr ibn Sayyār at al-Jūzjān. He had no descendants.

ʿĪsā ibn Zayd died in al-Kūfa and had descendants, among them Aḥmad ibn ʿĪsā.

Ḥusayn ibn Zayd was blind. His daughter Maymūna was married to al-Mahdī, and he had a son.

ʿAlī ibn ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn was nicknamed al-Afṭas and had descendants.

Umm Mūsā, daughter of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, married Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās. After her, her sister Umm Ḥasan married him. Their sister Khadīja married Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the son of al-Ḥanafiyya, was called Abū al-Qāsim. He moved to al-Ṭāʾif as a fugitive from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr and died there in the year eighty-one, at the age of sixty-five.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib had al-Ḥasan, ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Hāshim, Jaʿfar the Elder, Ḥamza, ʿAlī—by a slave woman—Jaʿfar the Younger, and ʿAwn—their mother was Umm Jaʿfar—and al-Qāsim and Ibrāhīm.

As for Abū Hāshim, he was highly esteemed, and the Shīʿa were devoted to him. When he was near death in al-Shām, he bequeathed his cause to Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās and said to him, “You are the one who will hold this authority, and it will be among your descendants.” He handed him his books and directed the Shīʿa to him. Abū Hāshim had no descendants.

Neither ʿAlī nor Ḥamza had descendants.

Ibrāhīm was nicknamed Shiʿra.

As for al-Qāsim, he was kept back from the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ and was unable to enter it.

As for ʿUmar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ḥadīth was transmitted from him, and he related reports from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

He had Muḥammad and Umm Mūsā—their mother was Asmāʾ, daughter of ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib.

Muḥammad had ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh, and ʿUbayd Allāh—[page 112] their mother was Khadīja, daughter of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī—and Jaʿfar—his mother was Umm Hāshim, daughter of Jaʿfar ibn Jaʿda ibn Hubayra al-Makhzūmī.

ʿUmar had descendants in al-Madīna.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was killed with al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Al-ʿAbbās had ʿUbayd Allāh—his mother was Lubāba, daughter of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās—and Ḥasan, by a slave woman; he had descendants.

Al-Mukhtār killed ʿUbayd Allāh, who had no descendants.

Jaʿfar ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib had no descendants.

The clients of the family of Abū Ṭālib

Abū Muḥammad said:

Among them was Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from whom al-Awzāʿī relates. He was a client of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Yaḥyā died in the year one hundred and twenty-nine.

Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: “No one remains on the face of the earth like Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr.”

His son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā related reports from his father.

Among them was Abū Usāma Ḥammād ibn Usāma, a client of al-Ḥasan ibn Saʿd, who was a client of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; thus he was the client of a client. He died in al-Kūfa in the year two hundred and one, at the age of eighty.

Accounts of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām ﵁

The lineage of al-Zubayr

He was al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwailid ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna.

His mother was Ṣafiyya bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the paternal aunt of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He was surnamed Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

Khuwailid was killed in the pre-Islamic period. Khuwailid had Khadīja, whose mother was:

Fāṭima bt. Zāʾida ibn al-Aṣamm. She was the wife of the Prophet ﷺ—and the paternal aunt of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwailid. His mother was from Banū Māzin ibn Manṣūr.

Al-ʿAwwām was killed on the Day of al-Fijār.

He had Naufal ibn Khuwailid, who was called “the Lion of Quraysh.” ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib killed him on the Day of Badr, and he left no descendants.

He also had Ḥizām ibn Khuwailid, who was the father of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām.

Ḥakīm was surnamed Abū Khālid. He was present at Badr with the polytheists, but was neither killed nor taken captive. He then embraced Islam and was a good Muslim. When he swore an oath and made it emphatic, he would say:

By Him who saved me on the Day of Badr.

He had ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥakīm and Hishām ibn Ḥakīm. Hishām was a Companion, and left no descendants.

As for ʿAbd Allāh, he was killed on the Day of the Camel alongside ʿĀʾisha. He had ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

ʿUthmān had ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān, the husband of Sukayna bt. al-Ḥusayn. She bore him a son called Qarīn, who has descendants.

Al-ʿAwwām ibn Khuwailid had al-Zubayr and al-Sāʾib; al-Sāʾib’s mother, too, was Ṣafiyya bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Al-Sāʾib was present at Uḥud and the Trench, and was killed on the Day of al-Yamāma. He also had ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Aswad, Aṣram, and Yaʿlā. None of them left descendants except al-Zubayr.

Al-Zubayr was the Messenger of God’s ḥawārī, one of the ten who were named for Paradise, and one of the members of the council of consultation. The Messenger of God ﷺ—granted him an area the size of his horse’s stride. He rode until his horse was exhausted, then cast his whip.

He was killed on the Day of the Camel, in Jumādā al-Ūlā of the year thirty-six. He was then sixty-four years old.

This is al-Wāqidī’s account. Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was killed when he was sixty years old. Ibn Jurmūz killed him at Wādī al-Sibāʿ, and his grave is there.

The appearance of al-Zubayr ﵁

Al-Wāqidī said:

Al-Zubayr was neither tall nor short, tending toward lightness of build. He had a light beard, a dark complexion, and much hair; he did not dye his grey hair.

Ibn Abī al-Zinād related, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father:

Al-Zubayr was so tall that, when he rode a mount, his feet dragged on the ground. He was blue-eyed and very hairy. When I was a boy, I would sometimes take hold of the hair on his shoulder and stand upright.

The children of al-Zubayr ﵁

Al-Zubayr had ʿAbd Allāh, ʿĀṣim, ʿUrwa, al-Mundhir, and Umm al-Ḥasan—their mother was:

Asmāʾ bt. Abī Bakr, “She of the Two Girdles.” He also had Muṣʿab, Ḥamza, Ramla, Khālid, ʿAmr, ʿUbayda, Jaʿfar, Khadīja, ʿĀʾisha, and others, making a total of nine daughters.

As for Ramla, she was married to Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. About her, he said:

[long metre]

The horses of women wander freely, but I seeNo anklet of Ramla’s wandering, nor heart.

For love of her, I love all the sons of al-ʿAwwām,And for her sake I have loved her maternal uncles, Kalb.

As for Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, he was one of the young men of Quraysh and was amorous. He was the one who said:

[ kāmil metre ]

The Qurashī’s place in the gathering is a due right,So consider the matter of the noble, accomplished man.

What do you command concerning Jaʿfar and a needHe seeks in private, humbly and earnestly?

He has descendants in Medina.

As for Ḥamza ibn al-Zubayr, he was killed with ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca. He left no descendants.

As for ʿAmr ibn al-Zubayr, he was surnamed Abū al-Zubayr. He was a man of standing and generosity. He opposed his brother ʿAbd Allāh and fought him. Then he came to him under the protection of his brother ʿUbayda, and ʿAbd Allāh killed him. He has descendants.

His son ʿAmr ibn ʿAmr is the one about whom al-Ḥuzayn al-Dīlī said: [wāfir metre]

Were meanness up among the Pleiades,ʿAmr ibn ʿAmr would reach its very head.

As for ʿUbayda ibn al-Zubayr, he was the one who said to ʿAmr ibn al-Zubayr, when the latter fought ʿAbd Allāh:

“Go with me to him, and you are under my protection. If he grants you safe-conduct, well and good; otherwise I will return you to a place of safety.”

He went with him. ʿAbd Allāh did not honor his safe-conduct: he exacted retaliation from him, until ʿAmr died. ʿUbayda has descendants.

As for Khālid ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAbd Allāh appointed him governor over Yemen. He has descendants, among them Khālid ibn ʿUthmān ibn Khālid ibn al-Zubayr. He went out with Muḥammad al-Ḥasanī, and Abū Ḥafṣ captured him and crucified him.

As for ʿĀṣim ibn al-Zubayr, he died as a boy. He left no descendants.

As for ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, he was an eminent jurist. He was surnamed Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Gangrene affected his leg in Syria while he was with al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. His leg was amputated with al-Walīd present. Al-Walīd did not stir and did not realize it was being cut until it was cauterized.

He noticed the smell of the cauterization. He lived for eight years afterward. In Medina he dug a well called:

The Well of ʿUrwa. There is no sweeter well in Medina. He died at an estate of his near Medina in the year ninety-three—it is also said that he died in the year ninety-four. That year was called “the Year of the Jurists,” because so many of them died in it.

ʿUrwa had Muḥammad, Yaḥyā, ʿUthmān, ʿAmr, and ʿAbd Allāh, Muṣʿab, ʿUbayd Allāh, and Hishām. The mother of Hishām ibn ʿUrwa was an enslaved woman named Sāra.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUrwa, he was among the most eloquent and articulate of people, and in eloquence he was likened to Khālid ibn Ṣafwān. He was told: “You have left Medina, the abode of the Hijra. If you returned, you would meet people, and people would meet you!” He replied, “And where are the people? People are only of two kinds: one who rejoices at a misfortune, or one who envies a blessing.”

He became blind before his death. He has descendants in Medina.

As for Muḥammad ibn ʿUrwa, he was among the most handsome of people. He left no male descendants.

As for ʿUthmān, he was a forceful orator. He has descendants in Medina.

As for Yaḥyā ibn ʿUrwa, he had knowledge of genealogy and the historical campaigns of the people. He mentioned Ibrāhīm ibn Hishām, the governor of Medina under Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Hishām ordered that he be beaten. He died after the beating. He has descendants in Medina.

As for ʿAmr ibn ʿUrwa, he was killed with Ibn al-Zubayr and left no descendants.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUrwa, he has descendants in Medina.

As for Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, he was a jurist. He came to Kufa in the days of Abū Jaʿfar, and the Kufans heard traditions from him. He died there in the year one hundred and forty-six. He has descendants in Medina and Basra, and was surnamed Abū al-Mundhir.

As for al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr, he was surnamed Abū ʿUthmān. He was a chief, forbearing man, and was killed with Ibn al-Zubayr. Among his descendants was Muḥammad ibn al-Mundhir, who was called “the Chief of Quraysh.”

He was surnamed Abū Zayd. When he passed along the road, fires were put out in deference to him. One day, a sandal strap of his broke. He said, “Like this, with my foot!” He pulled off the other sandal and went on, leaving them both without turning back.

He was the one who said: “A people’s fools have never become few without that people being humbled.” He has descendants.

As for Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, he was surnamed Abū ʿAbd Allāh—it is also said that he was surnamed:

Abū ʿĪsā—and he was the most generous of the Arabs. His brother ʿAbd Allāh appointed him over the two Iraqs. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān marched against him and sent his brother Muḥammad ibn Marwān at the head of his vanguard. Muṣʿab met him and fought him. Muṣʿab was killed.

Muṣʿab had ʿĪsā, ʿUkāsha, ʿUmar, Jaʿfar, Ḥamza, Saʿd, Muṣʿab—whose laqab was Ḥuṣayn—and Muḥammad.

As for ʿĪsā, he was killed with his father. He left no descendants.

As for ʿUkāsha, he has descendants in Medina. His son Muṣʿab ibn ʿUkāsha was killed on the Day of Qudayd. As for Jaʿfar, he married Malīka bt. al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. She bore him daughters. He has descendants from another wife.

As for Ḥamza, he and his son ʿUmāra were killed on the Day of Qudayd. He has descendants in Medina.

He had been drinking, so one of the governors of Medina seized him, administered the prescribed punishment, and displayed him before the people.

The Day of Qudayd was the day on which Abū Ḥamza the Khārijite was killed. He had set out from Yemen, gained control of Mecca and Medina, then headed toward Syria, where he was killed.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, he was surnamed Abū Bakr and Abū Khubayb. He was born twenty months after the Hijra.

This is al-Wāqidī’s account. Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was the first child born in Medina in Islam. He rebuilt the Kaʿba and gave it two doors.

He sought the caliphate and gained control of the Ḥijāz, Iraq, Yemen, and Egypt. He remained in that position for nine years.

Al-Ḥajjāj marched against him and besieged him in Mecca. Then a missile struck him, and he died of it.

He was miserly. A poet said of him: [long metre]

I saw Abū Bakr—your Lord prevailsIn His command—as he sought the caliphate with dates.

He was killed at the age of sixty-three. He was crucified where he had been struck.

ʿAbd Allāh had Ḥamza, Khubayb, Thābit, Mūsā, ʿAbbād, Qays, ʿĀmir, ʿAbd Allāh, and daughters.

As for Ḥamza, he was the most generous of the Arabs. He was his father’s governor over Basra and has descendants in Medina.

As for Khubayb, he was sterile.

As for Thābit, he was eloquent and fluent, yet miserable. He has descendants. Among them was al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṣʿab ibn Thābit, governor of Hārūn [al-Rashīd] over Medina and Yemen.

As for Mūsā, he has descendants in Medina. Among them was Ṣadīq ibn Mūsā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, who was one of the notables of Quraysh.

As for ʿAbbād, he has a son in Medina.

Qays left no descendants.

As for ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he was among the most devout people of his time. He would not marry off his daughters. He was the one whose sandal was stolen, whereupon he swore he would not buy another sandal, for fear that a Muslim might steal it and incur sin by stealing it.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he was the one among them who most resembled his father.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr married his daughters to the sons of his brother.

117 / The clients of al-Zubayr and his family

Al-Bahī, who related from ʿĀʾisha, was a client of al-Zubayr. His name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yasār, and he was surnamed Abū Muḥammad. He settled in Kufa, and the Kufans related from him.

Among them was Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj, the Qurʾān-reciter. He was Ḥumayd ibn Qays, a client of the family of al-Zubayr.

He was the Qurʾān-reciter of the people of Kufa, prolific in hadith, an expert in inheritance law, and an arithmetician. He studied recitation with Mujāhid.

His brother ʿUmar ibn Qays was considered weak in hadith. Once he jested with Mālik ibn Anas, saying: “Sometimes he errs, and sometimes he does not get it right.” That was in the presence of the governor of Mecca. Mālik said to him, “That is how people are.” He did not understand the remark; ʿUmar had only caught him off guard. Mālik was later alerted to the matter and said, “I will never speak to him again.”

As for Abū al-Zubayr, who related from Jābir, his name was Muḥammad ibn Muslim. He was a client of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām ibn Khuwailid, the cousin of al-Zubayr.

Accounts of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ﵁

The lineage of Ṭalḥa

He was Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Taym ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna.

He was surnamed Abū Muḥammad. He was called Ṭalḥa the Good, Ṭalḥa the Bountiful, and Ṭalḥa of the Ṭalḥas.

He is not the Ṭalḥa of the Ṭalḥas about whom it is said: [wāfir metre]

May God have mercy on bones they buriedIn Sijistān: Ṭalḥa of the Ṭalḥas.

Rather, that man was from Khuzāʿa.

Ṭalḥa was among the earliest emigrants, one of the ten named for Paradise, and one of the members of the council of consultation. He did not attend the day of consultation, being absent. He stood firm with the Messenger of God ﷺ—on the Day of Uḥud, shielding him with his hand from a blow intended for him; his hand was crippled. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “Ṭalḥa has earned [Paradise].” The Messenger of God ﷺ—paired him in brotherhood with Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. He was strongly opposed to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.

His mother was al-Ṣaʿbah daughter of al-Ḥaḍramī. Before she became the wife of ʿUbayd Allāh, she had been married to Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, who divorced her. He then longed for her again and said: [mut aqārib]

As people see it, I and al-Ṣaʿbahare far apart, though love is near.

If there is no deeply rooted lineage,the maiden has beauty and grace.

O people of Quṣayy, marvel!The gazelle’s fosterling has become a lizard.

When Ṭalḥah came to al-Baṣrah to fight ʿAlī, he took part in the Day of the Camel. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam saw him. Marwān bore a grudge against him over what he had done in the affair of ʿUthmān ﵁—and shot him with an arrow, striking his leg. He drove it into the horse’s flank, grasped its rein at the neck—that is, the horse’s neck—and said, “By God, I have never seen the fall of elders more wasted.” He died and was buried at the Qurrat bridge.

Thirty years after his death, ʿĀʾishah saw him in a dream, complaining to her of al-nazz4 She had him brought out while his body was still fresh. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Salāmah al-Taymī undertook to exhume him, and he was buried in his house, in the Hijriyyīn quarter of al-Baṣrah. His grave there is well known.

Ṭalḥah had two brothers: ʿUthmān ibn ʿUbayd Allāh and Mālik ibn ʿUbayd Allāh.

As for ʿUthmān, he held a position of standing among Quraysh in the Jāhiliyyah and lived to see Islam. He took Ṭalḥah and Abū Bakr and bound the two of them together with a rope; for this reason they were called “the two companions.” One of the family of al-Zubayr said of a man descended from Ṭalḥah, whose son was Abū Bakr:

O Ṭalḥ, son of the two companions who,with the Prophet, humbled every tyrant;

this one, named for his good deeds, is an extraamong all people; and this one is the companion of the cave.

ʿUthmān had descendants, and Mālik also had descendants in Mecca.

Ṭalḥah’s age and appearance ﵁

They differed concerning Ṭalḥah’s age.

Abū al-Yaqaẓān said:

He was killed at the age of sixty.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was killed at the age of sixty-four, in Jumādā al-Ūlā, in the year thirty-six.

It is related from one of his descendants that he was killed at the age of sixty-two.

They also differed concerning his appearance. Some said:

He was dark-complexioned, very hairy, neither lank-haired nor tightly curled, handsome of face, with a slender nose. When he walked, he walked quickly, and he did not dye his white hair.

Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥah said: “My father was fair, with a reddish hue, of medium stature, nearer to short than tall, broad-chested, broad-shouldered. When he turned, he turned his whole body. His feet were large, with no arch to them; a man whose feet have no arch is araḥḥ5”

Al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn related from Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ, from ʿImrān ibn Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥah, from his father, who said:

Ṭalḥah had a silver ring on his hand, set with a red ruby. His income each day was a full thousand dirhams.

The children of Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh

Ṭalḥah had ten sons and four daughters, by different mothers. Among them was Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah—his mother was Ḥamnah daughter of Jaḥsh, whose mother was Umaymah daughter of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet’s paternal aunt ﷺ. He was devout and was called “the one who prostrates”; he was known by the teknonym Abū al-Qāsim. He took part in the Day of the Camel. ʿAlī restrained people from attacking him, saying, “Beware of the man in the burnoose!” But a man killed him and began to recite [ṭawīl]:

A disheveled man, devoutly standing in prayer,a Muslim, causing little harm, as the eye can see.

I thrust a spear through the two sides of his shirt;he fell dead, face down, hands and mouth to the ground,

for no reason other than that he did not followʿAlī; whoever does not follow the truth will regret it.

He was calling on me by “Ḥāʾ Mīm” while the spear was lodged in him …Why did he not recite “Ḥāʾ Mīm” before advancing?

Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah’s son was Ibrāhīm. He was bald, lame, and a notable man, called “the Lion of the Ḥijāz.” ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr appointed him over the tax revenues of al-Kūfah. He died in Mecca while in the state of consecration.

Among Ibrāhīm’s descendants were ʿImrān and Yaʿqūb, sons of Ibrāhīm. Their mother was a daughter of Ismāʿīl ibn Ṭalḥah, whose mother was Lubābah daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās.

ʿImrān’s son was Muḥammad ibn ʿImrān, judge of al-Madīnah for Abū Jaʿfar. He was miserly. When reproached for his miserliness, he said, “I do not withhold from what is right, nor do I dissolve into what is false.”

Among them was ʿImrān ibn Ṭalḥah. His mother was Ḥamnah, and he was married to Umm Kulthūm, daughter of al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās. He had no descendants.

Among them was ʿĪsā ibn Ṭalḥah. He was ascetic and miserly, and he went as a delegate to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

He spoke with him about dismissing al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, together with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, until al-Ḥajjāj was dismissed from the Ḥijāz. ʿĪsā died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and he had descendants.

Among them was Yaḥyā ibn Ṭalḥah, one of the best of Ṭalḥah’s descendants. His son Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ṭalḥah transmitted jurisprudence from him. Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā’s mother was Umm Iyās daughter of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

Among them was Ismāʿīl ibn Ṭalḥah. He was a man of high standing, and he was married to Lubābah daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās.

Among them was Isḥāq ibn Ṭalḥah. Muʿāwiyah appointed him over Khurāsān as a partner to Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. He died in al-Rayy, and his descendants were numerous.

Among them was Yaʿqūb ibn Ṭalḥah. He was killed on the Day of al-Ḥarrah, and he had descendants.

Among them was Abū Yaʿrah, Abū Jaʿfar’s governor over al-Baḥrayn.

Among them was Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥah, one of the best of his descendants, a man of standing and distinction. He died in al-Kūfah in the year one hundred and four. His teknonym was Abū ʿĪsā. He used to bind his teeth with gold and dye his hair black. His son Muḥammad ibn Mūsā’s mother was a daughter of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān sent him against Shabīb the Khārijite, and Shabīb killed him.

ʿImrān ibn Mūsā’s mother was a concubine. He was generous and had descendants.

Among them was Zakariyyā ibn Ṭalḥah. His mother was Umm Kulthūm daughter of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq. His full sister was ʿĀʾishah daughter of Ṭalḥah. He was generous and had descendants.

Among them was Ṣāliḥ ibn Ṭalḥah. His mother was of the Taghlib.

Among his daughters:

Umm Isḥāq daughter of Ṭalḥah was married to al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. She bore him Ṭalḥah ibn al-Ḥasan, who died as a small child. Then al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī married her, and she bore him Fāṭimah daughter of al-Ḥusayn—who was the mother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan. Then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAtīq married her, and she bore him Umayyah.

Another of his daughters was ʿĀʾishah daughter of Ṭalḥah. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr married her. Then Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr married her and gave her a thousand thousand dirhams. Anas ibn Zunaym al-Daylī said to his brother [kāmil]:

Convey a message to the Commander of the Faithfulfrom one who counsels you and seeks no deception:

A maiden’s bride-price is a full thousand thousand,while the commanders of the armies spend the night hungry.

Were I to speak my mind to Abū Ḥafṣand recount the tale of their affair, he would be alarmed.

That is, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. When Muṣʿab was killed, ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar al-Taymī married her. She bore children only to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr.

Among his daughters were al-Ṣaʿbah, by a concubine, and Maryam, by a concubine.

Ṭalḥah’s clients ﵁

Among his clients was Muslim ibn Yasār. In his time, no one was considered his equal. When he grew angry and his anger became intense, he would say, “May God separate me from you.” When he said this, they knew that nothing more would follow.

He used to say, “I dislike touching my private parts with my right hand, while I hope to receive my book in that hand.”

He passed by a mosque, and the muezzin gave the call to prayer, so he turned back. The muezzin asked him, “What made you turn back?” He replied:

“You made me turn back.”

He never cursed anything. If he was angry with an animal, he would say, “May you have eaten a deadly poison.”

He died in the year one hundred, or one hundred and one.

His son was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Yasār, who transmitted traditions from him.

Another of Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh’s clients was Abū Nuʿaym al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn ibn Ḥammād, the traditionist. He transmitted from al-Aʿmash and al-Thawrī. He died in al-Kūfah in the year two hundred and nineteen.

As for Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, he was the client of Ṭalḥah of the Ṭalḥahs, not Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Taymī.

Reports concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf ﵁

The lineage of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf

Abū Muḥammad said:

He was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd ʿAwf ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilāb ibn Murrah ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah.

His name in the Jāhiliyyah was ʿAbd al-Ḥārith—and it is also said, ʿAbd ʿAmr—but the Prophet ﷺ named him ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. His father, ʿAwf, was killed in the Jāhiliyyah at al-Ghumayṣāʾ, by Banū Jadhīmah.

His mother was named al-Shifāʾ, and she too was of the Zuhrah.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had brothers. One was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf, one of the eminent men of Quraysh. His son was Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf, who had descendants in al-Madīnah. Another was al-Aswad ibn ʿAwf, who was a Companion. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—found him in Mecca drinking wine and ordered that the prescribed punishment be administered to him. He took part in the Day of the Camel with ʿĀʾishah and was killed; he had descendants.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He was one of the ten promised Paradise, and one of the six nominated for the consultative council. He had mottling6 The Prophet ﷺ therefore granted him permission to wear silk.

Al-Wāqidī said:

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf was born ten years after the Elephant. He died in the year thirty-two, at the age of seventy-five.

Abū al-Yaqaẓān said:

He died during the caliphate of ʿUthmān. His estate was divided into sixteen shares, and each of his wives received eighty thousand dirhams. In a single day he freed thirty slaves, and he bequeathed that ʿUthmān should lead the funeral prayer over him.

The appearance of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf ﵁

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was a tall man, handsome of face, with delicate skin and a slight stoop, fair with a reddish hue. He did not dye the hair of his head or beard.

Sahlah daughter of ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī said:

He was large-eyed, with an aquiline nose, and long upper incisors. At times they would badly cut his lip. He had hair reaching below his ears and a long neck. When you looked at the image of his face, it was as though there were bubbles of water in it. He had large palms and thick fingers.

The children of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf ﵁

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s children included Muḥammad, Ibrāhīm, Ḥumayd, and Zayd—their mother was Umm Kulthūm daughter of ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ; Abū Salamah, the jurist—his mother was Tamāḍur daughter of al-Aṣbagh al-Kalbī; Muṣʿab—his mother was Yemeni; Suhayl—his mother was Yemeni; ʿUthmān, al-Miswar, ʿUmar, and others, as well as daughters.

As for Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was intensely jealous. He had a son, ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, whose descendants continued.

As for Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was the chief of the people and was short. He married Sukaynah daughter of al-Ḥusayn, but the Banū Hāshim did not approve, so she separated from him. His teknonym was Abū Isḥāq. He died in the year ninety-six, at the age of seventy-five.

Ibrāhīm’s son was Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm. His mother was a daughter of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. He was judge of al-Madīnah in the time of Hishām and had descendants. Mūsā Shahawāt said of him [khafīf]:

People guard themselves against his obscenity and harmjust as they guard themselves against a donkey’s urine.

Do not let a prostration between his eyes deceive you:beware of it, and flee from it.

It is related that he flogged a man who came in to see him. The man asked, “For what have you flogged me?” He replied, “For ugliness.” Someone in al-Madīnah said of this:

The judge Saʿd floggedIbn Salm for ugliness.

So God granted Saʿdevery need from the ruler.

Saʿd died in al-Madīnah in the year one hundred and twenty-seven, at the age of ninety-two.

His son Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd, Abū Isḥāq, was in charge of the treasury in Baghdad. He was strict in matters of tradition and died in Baghdad in the year one hundred and eighty-three.

As for Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he had wealth and standing, and traditions were transmitted from him. His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Among his descendants was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥumayd, one of the eminent men of Quraysh in al-Madīnah. He died in al-Madīnah in the year ninety-five, at the age of seventy-three.

Some said:

He died in the year one hundred and five.

As for Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was a jurist, and traditions were transmitted from him.

His name was ʿAbd Allāh. His son ʿUmar ibn Abī Salamah was killed by Abū Jaʿfar in Syria. ʿUmar was with the sons of one of his sisters, who were Banū Umayyah, and was killed along with them.

Abū Salamah died in the year ninety-four, at the age of seventy-two.

It is said that he died in the year one hundred and four.

As for Muṣʿab ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was brave.

ʿAbd al-Malik asked a man from Syria, “Which horseman have you ever met who was the fiercest?”

He replied, “Muṣʿab.”

He was killed alongside Ibn al-Zubayr. Before that, he had served as Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam’s chief of police in al-Madīnah. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said of him [majzūʾ al-khafīf]:

Muṣʿab stood between passionand the night’s journey;

and whips in the hands of menwere brandished.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Muṣʿab ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān killed five of al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Numayr’s men with his own hand, then returned with his sword bent, saying: [Basīṭ]

We bring them forth white, and send them backred, their blades bent after being straightened.

Al-Wāqidī used to say that he died, and was not killed.

As for Suhayl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he married al-Thurayyā, a woman of the lesser Umayyads. She is the woman celebrated in the love poems of ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿah. He said:

[Khafīf]

O you who married al-Thurayyā to Suhayl,may your life be blessed! How can the two meet?She is a Syrian when she sets out,and Suhayl, when he sets out, is a Yemeni.

Suhayl had descendants in Medina, among them ʿUtayr ibn Suhayl, who was a drinker. The poet says of him: [Ṭawīl]

When you drink with ʿUtayr and generous Jabīr,and pass the glass to Khālid,

Jabīr was the son of Umm Ayman, the Prophet’s nursemaid ﷺ—and Khālid was the son of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī.

As for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was one of Quraysh’s brave men. He was among those who acted against al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, until ʿAbd al-Malik removed him from Medina.

Among his descendants was Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Abū Jaʿfar’s judge over Medina; he had descendants.

Zayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had no descendants.

Al-Miswar ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was killed on the Day of al-Ḥarrah (1). ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had descendants in Baṣra.

Reports about Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ ﵁

Saʿd’s lineage

Abū Muḥammad said: He was Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Uhayb ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilāb ibn Murrah ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah. He was known by the teknonym Abū Isḥāq.

His mother was Ḥamnah bint Sufyān ibn Umayyah ibn ʿAbd Shams. He had two brothers: ʿUtbah and ʿUmayr.

Among the descendants of ʿUtbah was Hāshim ibn ʿUtbah al-Mirqāl. He was one-eyed and was with ʿAlī on the Day of Ṣiffīn. He was among the bravest of men. He was the one who said: [Rajaz]

One-eyed, seeking a place for his people,he has endured life until he is weary.He must either be bound or be the one who binds.7

As for ʿUmayr ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, he was martyred at Badr.

Saʿd was one of the ten who were promised Paradise, and one of the members of the council.

He was the best archer among men. The Prophet ﷺ—prayed for him, saying: “O God, answer his prayer and make his shooting true.” The Prophet ﷺ—brought his own parents together for Saʿd, saying:

“Shoot, Saʿd; may my father and mother be your ransom.” And he said: “This is my maternal uncle; let every man bring his maternal uncle.” ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb appointed him governor of Kūfah. He was in command of the people at al-Qādisiyyah (2), but he suffered from an ailment caused by wounds he had sustained, so he did not attend the battle. He appointed a deputy, and God granted the Muslims victory. A man from Bajīlah said:

Do you not see that God made His religion victorious,while Saʿd, confined, was at the gate of al-Qādisiyyah? (1)

We returned, and many women had been widowed,but among Saʿd’s women there was no widow.

Saʿd said: “O God, spare us his hand and his tongue.” The man was struck by a projectile and became mute, and his hand withered.

Then the people of Kūfah complained about Saʿd, and ʿUmar dismissed him. Later, ʿUthmān appointed him governor of Kūfah in his place, then dismissed him.

He appointed al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah over it. When al-Walīd arrived, Saʿd said to him:

“Abū Wahb, have you become more prosperous since we left, or have we grown foolish since you came?” Al-Walīd replied: “We have not prospered, Abū Isḥāq, nor have you grown foolish; the people have kept things for themselves.”

Saʿd died in his palace at al-ʿAqīq, ten miles from Medina. [He was buried in al-Baqīʿ with his companions.] He died in the year 55, the last of the ten to die. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, who was then governor of Medina for Muʿāwiyah, performed the funeral prayer over him. He was in his seventies [or in his eighties]. He used to say: “I embraced Islam when I was nineteen years old.”

Saʿd’s appearance ﵁

Al-Wāqidī said:

ʿĀʾishah, daughter of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ ﵁—said: “My father was short and stout (1), thickset, large-headed, and had rough fingers.”

ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd said:

“Saʿd had curly hair, a hairy body, and was dark-complexioned and tall. He lost his sight toward the end of his life.”

Saʿd’s descendants

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ ﵁—had among his children ʿUmar, Muḥammad, ʿĀmir, Mūsā, Muṣʿab, ʿĀʾishah, and others [sons and daughters].

As for ʿUmar ibn Saʿd, he was the killer of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ﵄. ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād had sent him to fight al-Ḥusayn.

During the days of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd, he sent Abū ʿAmrah, a client of Bajīlah, to ʿUmar ibn Saʿd.

Al-Mukhtār said to him: “Do you recognize this head?” He replied: “Yes, this is the head of Abū Ḥafṣ”. Al-Mukhtār said: “Then send Ḥafṣ to join Abū Ḥafṣ”. He was killed. ʿUmar had descendants in Kūfah.

As for Muḥammad ibn Saʿd, he went out with Ibn al-Ashʿath (1). Al-Ḥajjāj killed him by execution. His son Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad ibn Saʿd was among Quraysh’s jurists and men of distinction.

As for ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, he transmitted ḥadīth from him, and died in the year 104.

As for Muṣʿab ibn Saʿd, they said that he wept when his father died. His father said to him: “Why are you weeping, my son? I adjure my Lord not to punish me.”

Muṣʿab died in the year 103. Ḥadīth was transmitted from him.

As for Mūsā ibn Saʿd, he had descendants, among them Najjād ibn Mūsā.

Reports about Saʿīd ibn Zayd ﵁

Saʿīd’s lineage

Abū Muḥammad said: He was Saʿīd ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Qurṭ ibn Riyāḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Razāḥ ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—was his father’s cousin.

Nufayl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā had two sons: ʿAmr ibn Nufayl and al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Nufayl.

Al-Khaṭṭāb’s mother was a woman from Fahm. After his father’s death, ʿAmr ibn Nufayl married his father’s wife, and she bore him Zayd ibn ʿAmr. His mother was al-Khaṭṭāb’s mother. Zayd turned away from the worship of idols and sought the religion until he met a man in al-Jazīrah, who described to him the religion of Abraham ﵇—and said: “Return to your land; the coming of a prophet is near. When he appears, follow him.” Zayd remained alive until he met the Prophet ﷺ—and told him his story. He said: “I returned, but I saw nothing.” This was before revelation had come to the Prophet ﷺ. Then Zayd returned to Syria, where the Christians killed him. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “He will be raised as a community on his own on the Day of Resurrection.” Waraqah ibn Nawfal said of him: [Ṭawīl]

You found the right way and did well, son of ʿAmr,for you shunned a blazing furnace of fire.

Zayd ibn ʿAmr also said these words in the pre-Islamic age: [Ṭawīl]

I have submitted my face to Himto whom the rain clouds submit, bearing pure, sweet water.

Zayd’s children were Saʿīd ibn Zayd and ʿĀtikah bint Zayd.

As for ʿĀtikah, she was married to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—then married her, and afterward al-Zubayr married her.

As for Saʿīd ibn Zayd, he was known by the teknonym Abū al-Aʿwar and was among the earliest emigrants. He embraced Islam before ʿUmar and was one of the ten who were promised Paradise. He lived into the caliphate of Muʿāwiyah. He had many descendants in Kūfah. One of his daughters was married to al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, another to al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, and another to ʿĀṣim ibn al-Mundhir.

Among his descendants was Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd, who composed poetry. He said to Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah on the Day of al-Ḥarrah: [Khafīf]

You are not one of us, nor is your maternal uncle one of us,O you who squander prayer for the sake of desires!

Saʿīd’s appearance ﵁

Al-Wāqidī said:

“Saʿīd ibn Zayd ﵁—was dark-complexioned, tall, and hairy.”

He died in the year 51, then in his seventies. His grave is in Medina, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ descended into his grave.

Another said: “He was among those who settled in Kūfah, and his grave is there.”

Reports about Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was Abū ʿUbaydah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jarrāḥ, and was ascribed to his grandfather. His name was ʿĀmir, and he was from Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah.

Banū Fihr are Quraysh, and the tribes of Quraysh branched out from Fihr.

His mother was from Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr, and she had embraced Islam. Abū ʿUbaydah married her after the advent of Islam.

Al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr belonged to al-Muṭayyibīn, and Abū ʿUbaydah was one of the eminent Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “Every community has a trusted man, and the trusted man of this community is Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ.” Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq said on the day of the Saqīfah of Banū Sāʿidah: “I am content for you with either of my two companions: Abū ʿUbaydah or ʿUmar. As for Abū ʿUbaydah, I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say: ‘Every community has a trusted man, and the trusted man of this community is Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ.’ As for ʿUmar, I heard him say: ‘O God, strengthen this religion through ʿUmar or Abū Jahl.’” Abū ʿUbaydah died in Syria during the plague of ʿAmwās. He had no descendants.

Abū ʿUbaydah’s appearance ﵁

Al-Wāqidī said:

“Abū ʿUbaydah was a lean man, with a thin face, a sparse beard, tall, stooped, and with his two front teeth broken. He dyed his hair with henna and katam.”

Another said:

“The reason his front teeth were broken was that on the Day of Uḥud he pulled arrowheads from the forehead of the Messenger of God ﷺ—with his two front teeth, and they fell out. No man with broken front teeth was ever seen more handsome than Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ.”

[A man with broken front teeth is one whose front teeth are broken.]

Al-Wāqidī related, on the authority of a man from his people:

“He witnessed Badr when he was forty-one years old. He died in the year 18, aged fifty-eight.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd ﵁

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd was from Hudhayl. Among his clan were the Banū ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Tamīm ibn Saʿd ibn Hudhayl. He was an ally of the Banū Zuhra. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

He fought with the Messenger of God ﷺ—at Badr, attended the Pledge of al-Riḍwān, and took part in all the campaigns.

He was in charge of adjudication in Kūfa and its treasury under ʿUmar, and during the early part of ʿUthmān’s caliphate. He then went to Medina, where he died in the year thirty-two, when he was in his early sixties. He was buried in al-Baqīʿ.

Description of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd ﵁

He was a thin, short man, so short that someone sitting nearly concealed him. He was very dark-complexioned, and his hair reached his collarbones; he wore it behind his ears. He did not dye his gray hair, and he wore an iron signet ring.

The descendants of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd ﵁

Among the descendants of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd were ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and Abū ʿUbayda ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he had Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who was in charge of adjudication in Kūfa, and Maʿn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Maʿn had al-Qāsim ibn Maʿn, who was in charge of adjudication in Kūfa and never received a stipend before he died. He was learned in jurisprudence, hadith, poetry, genealogy, and the histories of the people. He was called the Shaʿbī of his age.

As for ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allāh, he had descendants, among them Abū ʿUmays ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, who died in Baghdad, and his brother ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Masʿūdī. The latter’s memory became confused in his old age, and he died in Baghdad. He was the elder al-Masʿūdī. The younger was ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abī ʿUbayda.

ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd, brother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd ﵁

ʿAbd Allāh had a brother named ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd, who shared both his parents. He was an early convert to Islam, but did not transmit anything from the Prophet ﷺ. He died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He had a son named ʿAbd Allāh, known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who lived in Kūfa. He died there during the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He transmitted many hadiths and gave many legal opinions; he was a jurist.

Among his descendants was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, who was a learned man. He was the one from whom al-Zuhrī transmitted. Al-Zuhrī used to rise for him when he came out, but when he thought he had exhausted what he had to offer, he did not rise for him. The man said to him: “You are still on rugged ground, so rise.” [Al-ʿazāz is ground that is hard. The meaning is: “You are still out in the borderlands.”] He died in the year ninety-eight.

Among his descendants was ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd. He was an ascetic and a learned man. At first he professed irjāʾ [deferred judgment], but then recanted, saying: [wāfir meter]

The first thing from which we part, without a doubt,

Is what the Murjiʾites say.

They said: “A believer whose blood is inviolable,”

Though the blood of believers is forbidden to shed.

They said: “A believer from among the people of injustice,”

Though believers are not people of injustice.

He held a position of favor with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. Jarīr said of him: [basīṭ meter]

O reader, with your turban hanging loose,

This is your time; mine has passed away.

Tell our caliph, if you should meet him,

That I am at the door, bound fast in a tether.

ʿAwn had many eloquent, fine sayings. He left his son a lengthy testament, whose opening words were:

“My son, be one whose distance from those who keep their distance from him is marked by certainty and integrity.”

His brother ʿUbayd Allāh was reproached for composing poetry. He said: “One afflicted in the chest must needs give vent.”

Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

His name was Jundub ibn al-Sakan, and his sobriquet was Barīr.

Al-Wāqidī said:

His name was Barīr ibn Junāda.

Others said:

Jundub ibn Junāda.

He said: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb told me: Abū ʿAttāb Sahl ibn Ḥammād told us: ʿAmr ibn Thābit informed us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Ḥanash ibn al-Muʿtamir, who said:

I came upon Abū Dharr holding the ring of the door of the Kaʿba, and he was saying: “I am Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī. Whoever does not know me, I am Jundub, the Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say: ‘The likeness of my household is the likeness of Noah’s Ark: whoever boards it is saved.’”

He was from Ghifār, and Ghifār is a tribe of Kināna. Ghifār was the son of Milīl ibn Ḍamra ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Kināna ibn Khuzayma.

Abū Dharr accepted Islam in Mecca. He did not take part in Badr, Uḥud, or the Campaign of the Trench, because when he accepted Islam he returned to the land of his people and stayed there until these campaigns had passed. Then he came to Medina to the Messenger of God ﷺ. ʿUthmān had sent him to al-Rabdha, where he died in the year thirty-two. He left no descendants.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ṣāmit, the son of Abū Dharr’s brother, was known by the teknonym Abū Naṣr.

Muʿādh ibn Jabal ﵁

He was Muʿādh ibn Jabal ibn ʿAmr ibn Aws ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿAdī, and he was from the Khazraj.

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

His mother was Hind daughter of Sahl, from Juhayna. His maternal brother was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jarīr ibn Qays, a veteran of Badr.

Some said that he had no children at all.

Others said that he had the following children: Umm ʿAbd Allāh, who was among those who pledged allegiance, and two sons, one named ʿAbd al-Raḥmān—the other was not named. He and his two sons died in the plague of ʿAmwās, after Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ. He left no descendants. He died in the region of Jordan.

They differed about his age.

It is related from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib that he said:

“Muʿādh died at the age of thirty-three.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

“Muʿādh took part in Badr when he was twenty years old—or twenty-one—and died in the year eighteen/171, at the age of thirty-eight.”

They differed about his complexion.

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He was fair-complexioned, tall, with fine hair, large eyes, and tightly curled hair. He was among the most handsome of men.”

Someone else said: “He was dark-complexioned, handsome, with gleaming front teeth.”

ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit ﵁

He was ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit ibn Qays, from the Khazraj. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Walīd.

His mother was Qurra al-ʿAyn daughter of ʿUbāda ibn Naḍla, a woman of the Khazraj. ʿUbāda was one of the twelve leaders. He took part in Badr and all the campaigns, and he attended al-ʿAqaba with the seventy.

His brother Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit took part in Badr. He was the first to practice ẓihār in Islam.

He suffered from episodes of mental disturbance. During one of his lucid intervals, he quarreled with his wife Khawla and said: “You are to me like my mother’s back.” Then he regretted it—the story continues.

ʿUbāda was tall, handsome, and imposing. He died at al-Ramla, in Syria, in the year thirty-four, when he was seventy-two years old.

His son al-Walīd ibn ʿUbāda was born in the final period of the Prophet’s lifetime ﷺ. He died in Syria during the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. He was a reliable transmitter who related few hadiths.

He had descendants.

ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir ﵁

He was ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir ibn ʿĀmir ibn Mālik ibn ʿAns. ʿAns was a branch of Madhḥij in Yemen, the clan of the lying claimant to prophethood al-ʿAnsī.

They were brothers of Murād, from Madhḥij, and of Saʿd al-ʿAshīra, from Madhḥij.

Yāsir came from Yemen and entered into an alliance with Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī. Abū Ḥudhayfa married him to a female slave of his named Sumayya, who bore him ʿAmmār. Abū Ḥudhayfa then freed him. Yāsir and his son ʿAmmār remained with Abū Ḥudhayfa until he died.

Then God brought Islam, and Yāsir, ʿAmmār, Sumayya, and his brother ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yāsir accepted Islam. After Yāsir, al-Azraq took Sumayya as his wife. Al-Azraq was a Roman youth enslaved by al-Ḥārith ibn Kalda. He was among those who went out to the Prophet ﷺ—on the day of al-Ṭāʾif with the enslaved people of al-Ṭāʾif, among whom was Abū Bakra. The Messenger of God ﷺ—freed them. Sumayya bore al-Azraq Salama ibn al-Azraq, who was ʿAmmār’s maternal half-brother. Later, Salama’s descendants claimed that they were from Ghassān and were allies of the Banū Umayya; they became prominent in Mecca.

Al-Azraq and his descendants married into the Banū Umayya, and they had children by them.

Sumayya, the mother of ʿAmmār, was the first woman martyred in Islam. Abū Jahl stabbed her with a spear, and she died.

ʿAmmār fought at Ṣiffīn alongside ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁. He was killed and buried there. ʿAlī prayed over him, did not wash him, and pronounced four takbīrs over him.

Al-Ziyādī told me: ʿAbd al-Wārith ibn Saʿīd told us: Rabīʿa ibn Kulthūm ibn Jabr told us: my father told me: Abū al-Ghādiya told me:

“I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say: ‘Take care: do not become unbelievers after me, striking one another’s necks.’” Abū al-Ghādiya said:

“I heard ʿAmmār mention ʿUthmān in the mosque—he was called a coward among us—and say: ‘This Naʿthal does such-and-such, and such-and-such,’ criticizing him. ‘If I had found supporters against him that day, I would have trampled him until I killed him.’ Then, while I was at Ṣiffīn, there he was at the front of the battalion. A man struck him in the knee, and his helmet came away from his head. I struck his head, and behold, ʿAmmār’s head had come off.” My father said:

“I have never seen an older man more astray than he: he relates that he heard the Prophet ﷺ—say what he said, then he strikes off ʿAmmār’s head.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

“ʿAmmār was a dark-complexioned, tall, lanky man, with gray-blue eyes and a broad space between his shoulders. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Yaqẓān.”

Someone else said:

“ʿAmmār’s ear was cut off on the day of al-Yamāma. He was killed in the year thirty-seven, at the age of ninety-three.”

ʿAmmār had a son named Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār, who transmitted from him.

Saʿd al-Qaraẓ, ʿAmmār’s freedman, used to give the call to prayer at Qubāʾ during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and Abū Bakr’s. When ʿUmar became caliph, he settled him in Medina, and he used to give the call to prayer in the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ. His descendants still give the call to prayer in the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ—to this day.

Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda ﵁

He was Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda ibn Dulaym, of Banū Sāʿida, of the Khazraj. He was known by the teknonym Abū Thābit. In the pre-Islamic period he could write, was skilled at swimming and archery, and was called “the Perfect.”

He did not witness Badr because he had been bitten. He then witnessed all the campaigns.

After the death of the Messenger of God ﷺ—he went to Syria and died in Ḥawrān, two and a half years into ʿUmar’s caliphate. The cause of his death was that he sat to urinate in a tunnel and was stung. He died immediately, and his skin turned green.

One of his descendants said: “We knew nothing of his death in Medina until we heard that some young men had heard someone calling out from a well, saying: [majzūʾ al-madīd]

We have killed the lord of the Khazraj,Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda;We shot him with two arrowsAnd did not miss his heart.

It is also said that he was bitten. This is the correct account.

Among his descendants was Qays ibn Saʿd, known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Malik, who related traditions from the Messenger of God ﷺ. He died in Medina at the end of Muʿāwiya’s caliphate.

Saʿīd ibn Saʿd was married to a daughter of Abū al-Dardāʾ, and had children by her.

Zayd ibn Thābit ﵁

He was Zayd ibn Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk, one of the Anṣār, of Banū Ghānim ibn Mālik ibn al-Najjār. He was known by the teknonym Abū Saʿīd; it is also said that he was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

His father was killed at the Battle of Buʿāth when Zayd was six years old. The Messenger of God ﷺ—came to Medina when Zayd was eleven. The last recension of the Qurʾān made by the Messenger of God was according to Zayd’s codex, which is the closest of the codices to our own. Zayd also served as a scribe for ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵄.

He died in the year 45, and Marwān performed the funeral prayer over him.

He had a brother called Yazīd ibn Thābit.

His son Khārija ibn Zayd, known by the teknonym Abū Zayd, said: “I saw in a dream that I had built seventy steps. When I had finished them, they collapsed. This is my seventieth year, which I have now completed.” He died that year, the year 100, in Medina.

Seven of Zayd ibn Thābit’s biological sons were killed on the Day of al-Ḥarra. He has descendants in Medina.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb ﵁

He was one of the Anṣār and was known by the teknonym Abū al-Mundhir. He could write in the pre-Islamic period and wrote the revelation for the Messenger of God ﷺ. He was short and stout, and white-haired, with a white beard; he did not dye his gray hair.

There is disagreement about when he died. Some said that he died during ʿUmar’s caliphate, in the year 22. ʿUmar said: “Today the master of the Muslims has died.”

Others said that he died in the year 30, during ʿUthmān’s caliphate.

He had sons, among them al-Ṭufayl ibn Ubayy and Muḥammad ibn Ubayy. al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was al-Miqdād ibn ʿAmr ibn Thaʿlaba, from Yemen.

Al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra claimed him as his son because al-Miqdād was his ally, and so he was ascribed to him; later, he returned to his own lineage.

He was the horseman of the Messenger of God ﷺ—at Badr. He was married to Ḍubāʿa bt. al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the daughter of the Prophet’s paternal uncle ﷺ.

He was a tall, dark-complexioned man with a belly and abundant hair on his head. He dyed his beard yellow. He was wide-eyed, with eyebrows that met, and a hooked nose. He was known by the teknonym Abū Maʿbad. He died at al-Ḥarf, and was carried on men’s shoulders until he was buried in Medina in the year 30, at the age of seventy or thereabouts.

Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was Ḥudhayfa ibn Ḥisl ibn Jābir. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Ḥisl was nicknamed al-Yamān.

He said: “He was of Banū ʿAbs, but was counted among Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal.”

Ten men of Banū ʿAbs accepted Islam with the Messenger of God ﷺ—and al-Yamān was the tenth. The Muslims mistakenly killed him on the day of Uḥud, while Ḥudhayfa was crying, “My father! My father!”

Another authority said:

He was Ḥudhayfa ibn Ḥisl ibn Jābir ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarwa. Jarwa was al-Yamān. He had caused a death among his people and fled to Medina, where he entered into an alliance with Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal. His people called him al-Yamān because he had allied himself with the Yemenites.

Ashʿath related from al-Ḥasan, who said:

Ḥudhayfa was a man of ʿAbs. The Messenger of God ﷺ—gave him a choice, saying: “If you wish, you may be one of the Emigrants; if you wish, you may be one of the Anṣār.” He replied:

“Of the Anṣār.” He said: “Then you are one of them.” Ḥudhayfa has descendants among the Anṣār. Ḥudhayfa did not witness Badr.

His brother Ṣafwān ibn al-Yamān witnessed Uḥud but did not witness Badr.

Ḥudhayfa died in Kūfa after ʿUthmān’s death.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He died at al-Madāʾin in the year 36. News of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān’s death reached him, but he did not live to see the Battle of the Camel—which took place ten nights into Jumādā al-Ūlā in the year 36.

His sister was Laylā bt. al-Yamān, the mother of Salama ibn Thābit ibn Waqsh; another sister was Fāṭima bt. al-Yamān.

Ṣuhayb ibn Sinān ﵁

He was Ṣuhayb ibn Sinān ibn Mālik, a veteran of Badr. All the Medinans establish his lineage among the Namir ibn Qāsiṭ. His mother was Salmā, of Māzin Tamīm.

Some said that his father, Sinān ibn Mālik, was Kisrā’s governor over al-Ubulla, and that their homes were in the land of al-Mawṣil and the adjacent Jazīra. The Byzantines raided that region and took Ṣuhayb captive when he was a small boy, and he grew up among the Byzantines. The Kalb then bought him from them and brought him to Mecca, where ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān bought him.

It is said that Ibn Judʿān freed him and sent him to the Prophet ﷺ.

His descendants say that he fled from the Byzantines and came to Mecca, where he entered into an alliance with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān.

He said: Ziyād ibn Yaḥyā related to me, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal related to us, saying:

Yūnus related to us, from al-Ḥasan, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “I am the foremost of the Arabs; Ṣuhayb is the foremost of the Byzantines; Salmān is the foremost of the Persians; and Bilāl is the foremost of the Abyssinians.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

Ṣuhayb was a ruddy man, very red in complexion, neither tall nor short, though nearer to short. He had abundant hair on his head and dyed it with henna and katam. He was fond of joking. The Prophet ﷺ—said to him: “You eat dates while you have sore eyes!” He replied: “Messenger of God, I chew them on the other side.” The Prophet ﷺ—laughed. Ṣuhayb died in Medina in Shawwāl of the year 38, at the age of seventy, and was buried in al-Baqīʿ.

His sons were Ḥamza, Ṣayfī, and ʿUmāra, the sons of Ṣuhayb.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī ﵁

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays, one of the Ashʿarites of Yemen.

He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ—with a group of Ashʿarites, and they accepted Islam. His first campaign was Khaybar.

His mother was called Ṭufayya.

[Abū Muḥammad said: “Al-ṭufiyya is the spathe of the doum palm”.]

She was of ʿAkk. His mother Ṭufayya accepted Islam and died in Medina.

Abū Mūsā had brothers who accepted Islam, among them Abū ʿĀmir ibn Qays, who was killed on the day of Awṭās; Abū Burda ibn Qays; and Abū Ruhm ibn Qays. Abū Ruhm related nothing from the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Mūsā was slight of build, short, and thin-haired. [Al-thaṭṭ means one with sparse hair; al-sanāṭ means hairless.] He had a beautiful voice when reciting the Qurʾān.

He died in the year 52; it is also said, in the year 42.

He had sons, among them Abū Burda ibn Abī Mūsā, who served as a judge. His son was Bilāl ibn Abī Burda, who also served as a judge.

Abū Burda’s name was ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh. Abū Burda died in the year 103.

Among them also was Mūsā ibn Mūsā, whose mother was Umm Kulthūm bt. al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Among them also was Abū Bakr ibn Abī Mūsā, whose name was his teknonym. He was older than Abū Burda.

Khālid ibn al-Walīd ﵁

He was Khālid ibn al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, of Banū Makhzūm. His mother was Lubāba al-Ṣughrā bt. al-Ḥārith al-Hilāliyya, the sister of Maymūna, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ—and of Lubāba al-Kubrā, who was Umm al-Faḍl, the wife of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and the mother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās, al-Faḍl, ʿUbayd Allāh, and others of his children.

Khālid was known by the teknonym Abū Sulaymān. He did not witness Badr, Uḥud, or the Trench; in all of these he was with the polytheists. He accepted Islam in the year 8, along with ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥa.

Khālid killed Musaylima the Liar and Mālik ibn Nuwayra, and defeated Ṭulayḥa the Liar. He killed Banū Jadhīma—who were of Kināna—at al-Ghumayṣāʾ. The Messenger of God ﷺ—paid blood money for them and said: “O God, I disavow before You what Khālid has done.” Khālid conquered ʿAyn al-Tamr and most of Syria. He protected the Muslims at Muʾta. He died at Ḥimṣ in the year 21.

He had many children in Syria. The plague killed forty of them, and they died out.

Khālid ibn al-Walīd used to say: “I have encountered so many armies in battle, and there is no place on my body without a sword blow, a spear thrust, or an arrow wound. And here I am, dying in my bed, a natural death, like a donkey. May the eyes of cowards never sleep!”

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī ﵁

He was Saʿd ibn Mālik, affiliated with al-Khudra, a people from Yemen.

His maternal half-brother was Qatāda ibn al-Nuʿmān. Qatāda was one of the renowned archers among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Abū Saʿīd died in the year 74, in which Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ also died.

His children included ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Saʿīd, and Bashīr.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad and died in Medina in the year 112.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s sons were ʿAbd Allāh and Rabiḥ, whose name was Saʿīd. Rabiḥ is considered weak by the traditionists, is not reliable, and has many traditions.

Abū al-Dardāʾ ﵁

He was ʿUwaymir ibn Mālik—it is also said, ʿUwaymir ibn Zayd, and it is also said, ʿUwaymir ibn ʿĀmir—of Balḥārith ibn al-Khazraj. He was the last person in his household to accept Islam. Before his conversion, he was a merchant. He died in Syria in the year 32, and his descendants are in Syria.

ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī ﵁

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. The Prophet ﷺ—appointed him over al-Ṭāʾif, and he remained there until several years of ʿUmar’s caliphate had passed. ʿUmar appointed him over ʿUmān and al-Baḥrayn. He went to Tuwaj and fought Sahrak, whom he killed. ʿUthmān settled in al-Baṣra, and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān granted him twelve thousand jarībs.

He died during Muʿāwiya’s caliphate. He had distinguished descendants.

Muḥammad ibn Maslama ﵁

He was Muḥammad ibn Maslama ibn Salama, of the Banū Ḥāritha ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj, an ally of the Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal. He was called “the horseman of the Messenger of God” ﷺ. During the expedition of Qarqarat al-Kudr, the Prophet appointed him over Medina.

He was dark-skinned, tall, large-built, and bald. He was present with the Messenger of God ﷺ—at Badr and at all the other battles. After the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, he took a wooden sword and put it in a scabbard. He did not take part in the Battle of the Camel or at Ṣiffīn, nor did he fight in any civil strife.
