He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He settled in Medina and died there in Ṣafar, in the year forty-six—or forty-three. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam led the prayer over him.

He had ten sons and six daughters.

Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān ﵁

He was Mālik ibn al-Tayyihān, of the Balī ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥāf, of Quḍāʿa, and an ally of the Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal.

Some say that he was himself of the Aws. He used to estimate the dates on the palm trees for the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Some people have reported that he took part at Ṣiffīn with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The learned do not know of this, nor do they accept it as established.

He died in Medina during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—in the year twenty. He left no surviving descendants.

His brother was ʿUbayd ibn al-Tayyihān, though his name is disputed: some say ʿUbayd, and some say ʿUtayk.

Salmān al-Fārisī ﵁

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

Some say that he was from Iṣfahān; others say that he was from Fārs, from Rāmhurmuz. Iṣfahān borders Fārs.

He was not present at Badr or Uḥud, because at the time of both he was enslaved.

The first expedition he took part in was the Battle of the Trench, in the fifth year after the Hijra. He lived to an advanced age.

He died at the beginning of ʿUthmān’s caliphate.

Some reports say that he died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—in al-Madāʾin.

Abū Ṭalḥa al-Anṣārī ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

He was Zayd ibn Sahl, the man who said: [rajaz]

I am Abū Ṭalḥa, and Zayd is my name;Each day, with my weapon, I make my prey.

The Prophet ﷺ—said: “The voice of Abū Ṭalḥa in the army is better than a thousand men.”

He was one of the archers. On the day of Ḥunayn, he killed twenty men and took their spoils.

He was dark-complexioned and of medium height, and he did not dye his gray hair.

He died in Medina in the year thirty-four. ʿUthmān led the prayer over him.

The people of al-Baṣra report that he sailed on the sea and died there, and that they buried him on an island.

Umm Sulaym bint Milḥān was married to Abū Ṭalḥa. She was the mother of Anas ibn Mālik. Her brother was Ḥarām ibn Milḥān.

Abū Dujāna al-Anṣārī ﵁

He was Simāk ibn Kharasha. He was present on the day of Musaylima and took part in killing Musaylima; then he was killed that same day. He had descendants in Medina and Iraq.

Abū Usayd al-Sāʿidī ﵁

He was Mālik ibn Rabīʿa.

He was short and stocky, with abundant hair on his head; his head and beard were white. He lost his sight and died at the age of seventy-eight, in the year sixty. He had descendants in Medina and Baghdad.

Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

He was Hushaym ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf. He was among those who migrated to Abyssinia in both migrations, and a child was born to him there.

Abū Ḥudhayfa was tall, handsome, athʿal8, and cross-eyed.

He was killed on the day of al-Yamāma. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān took responsibility for Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥudhayfa, who remained in his care. When ʿUthmān was besieged, Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥudhayfa was among those who rose against him, assisted in the attack, and incited the people of Egypt until they marched against him.

When ʿUthmān was killed, Muḥammad fled to Syria. There, Rashdīn, a client of Muʿāwiya, found and killed him.

The descendants of Abū Ḥudhayfa have died out; none remain. The descendants of his father, ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, have also died out, except for the descendants of al-Mughīra ibn ʿImrān ibn ʿĀṣim ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who are in Syria.

Sālim, client of Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ﵁

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. [He was a veteran of Badr.]

The Prophet ﷺ—established a bond of brotherhood between him and Abū Bakr. Sālim’s clientage originally belonged to the wife of Abū Ḥudhayfa, who was an Anṣārī woman; she made him Abū Ḥudhayfa’s client.

Some say he was Sālim ibn Maʿqil, from Iṣṭakhr. He was the client of Buthayna al-Anṣārīya, and so he is counted among the Anṣār because she freed him, and among the Emigrants because he was affiliated as a client to Abū Ḥudhayfa.

Buthayna was married to Abū Ḥudhayfa. She freed Sālim unconditionally, as a sāʾiba, and he then attached himself to Abū Ḥudhayfa, who adopted him. A sāʾiba is someone from whom none of his property or other possessions returns to the person who freed him.

Abū Ḥudhayfa married him to his brother’s daughter, Fāṭima bint al-Walīd ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.

Some say that the woman who freed him was the wife of Abū Ḥudhayfa, whose name was Salmā, of the Khaṭma.

He was martyred on the day of al-Yamāma. He left no descendants.

ʿUkāsha ibn Miḥṣan ﵁

He was ʿUkāsha ibn Miḥṣan ibn Ḥarthān, of Asad ibn Khuzayma. His kunya was Abū Miḥṣan.

His sister was Umm Qays bint Miḥṣan, who came to the Prophet ﷺ—with a son on whom she had hung something for al-ʿudhara; al-ʿudhara is a sore throat.

ʿUkāsha was one of the most handsome of men. The Messenger of God ﷺ—gave him the good news of Paradise.

He was killed at Buzākha during the caliphate of Abū Bakr.

His brother Abū Sinān ibn Miḥṣan was present at Badr, Uḥud, and the Trench.

He was the first to pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God ﷺ—at the Pledge of Good Pleasure.

Al-Wāqidī said:

The first to pledge allegiance to him at the Pledge of Good Pleasure was his son Sinān ibn Abī Sinān al-Asadī.

It is also said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.

Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī ﵁

He was Khālid ibn Zayd ibn Kulayb.

He was with ʿAlī ﵁—at Ḥarūrāʾ. He campaigned with Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya and died at Constantinople. He was buried at the foot of the city wall, and his grave was concealed.

Mujāhid said:

Yazīd ordered the horses to be brought. They kept coming toward him and turning away until they had concealed him. The people of Constantinople looked out and said, “You have had quite an affair tonight.” They replied, “Yes. This is one of the leading Companions of our Prophet ﷺ—and among the earliest to embrace Islam. We buried him where you saw. By God, if he is exhumed, not a single bell will ring in the land of the Arabs for as long as our kingdom endures.”

Mujāhid said:

When they suffered drought, they would uncover his grave, and rain would fall upon them. He had descendants in Medina.

ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān ﵁

He was ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jābir, of the Banū Māzin, the brothers of Sulaym ibn Manṣūr ibn ʿIkrima ibn Khaṣafa ibn Qays ʿAylān.

He was among the earliest Emigrants and among those present at Badr. He was one of the well-known archers.

He was the one who conquered al-Ubulla and laid out al-Baṣra. He ordered Miḥjan ibn al-Adraʿ to lay out the mosque of al-Baṣra.

He was a tall man. He arrived in Medina during the Hijra at the age of forty, and died at the age of fifty-seven, on the road to Mecca at Maʿdin Banū Sulaym, during ʿUmar’s caliphate, in the year seventeen.

His client Khabbāb was present at Badr.

Yaʿlā ibn Munya ﵁

He was Yaʿlā ibn Munya, one of the warriors. His mother was Munya, after whom he was named. She was Munya bint al-Ḥārith ibn Jābir, of the Banū Māzin ibn Manṣūr. Munya was the paternal aunt of ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān.

His father’s name was Umayya ibn Abī ʿUbayda, of the Banū Zayd Mālik ibn Ḥanẓala.

Yaʿlā brought his father to the Prophet ﷺ—and said, “Messenger of God, accept his pledge to emigrate.” He replied, “There is no emigration after the Conquest.” Abū Bakr ﵁—appointed Yaʿlā over Yemen. He married the daughter of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām and the daughter of Abū Lahab.

Yaʿlā arrived during ʿUthmān’s caliphate, and Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb came to him and gave him ten thousand dirhams. On the day of the Camel, Yaʿlā put ʿĀʾisha on a camel called ʿAskar; it was ʿĀʾisha’s camel. He equipped seventy men at his own expense. When ʿAlī heard that they had arrived in al-Baṣra, he said, “I am beset by the bravest of men”—meaning al-Zubayr—“the most forthright of men”—meaning Ṭalḥa—“the most obeyed of people”—meaning ʿĀʾisha—“and the wealthiest of people”—meaning Yaʿlā ibn Munya.

He had a son called ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaʿlā, who lived at ʿAlīb, near Mecca. He was a poet, and he said this poem in mourning his wife Zaynab: [ṭawīl]

Your face is too dear to be touched by the dust;So do not be gone—every living soul will pass away.

The doors grew strange when you entered them,And they said, “Look, Zaynab has departed today.”

Would I go, having left Zaynab willingly,While my soul is with me and I have not found her where I go?

Among Yaʿlā’s clients were people in Yemen called the Banū Shihāb. They held rank and standing, and were Arabs of Khawlān. Yaʿlā took them captive, and they claimed affiliation with Yemen.

Among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—was Yaʿlā ibn Murra, of Thaqīf. He was the one whom the Prophet ordered to cut down the trees of al-Ṭāʾif.

Abū Hurayra ﵁

They disagreed about his name and gave many accounts.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr.

Someone other than him said:

He was ʿAbd ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Ghanm. It is also said: ʿAbd Shams. And it is said: ʿUmayr ibn ʿĀmir.

It is also said: Sukayn.

He belonged to a tribe from Yemen called Daws. It was Daws ibn ʿAdthān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zahrān, of the Azd.

His mother was Umayma bint Ṣafīḥ ibn al-Ḥārith, of Daws. His mother became Muslim.

His maternal uncle was Saʿd ibn Ṣafīḥ, one of the fiercest men of his time.

Abū Hurayra said: “I grew up an orphan, emigrated as a poor man, and worked for Busra bint Ghazwān, for food for my belly and9 my feet. I would serve when they stopped, and sing to the camels when they rode. Then God gave her to me in marriage. Praise be to God, who made religion a support and made Abū Hurayra a leader.”

Abū Hurayra said: “I was given the kunya Abū Hurayra because of a little kitten I used to play with.”

He arrived in Medina in the year seven, when the Prophet ﷺ—was at Khaybar. He travelled to Khaybar, then came to Medina with the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Hurayra was dark-complexioned, broad between the shoulders, with two braids and widely spaced front teeth. He dyed his beard yellow and let it grow, trimmed his moustache closely, and was a jokester.

ʿAffān related from Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Thābit, from Abū Rāfiʿ, who said:

Marwān would sometimes appoint Abū Hurayra as his deputy over Medina. Abū Hurayra would ride a donkey fitted with a coarse saddlecloth, with a halter made of palm fibre on its head. He would ride along and meet a man, saying:

“Make way, make way! The governor has arrived.”

Sometimes he would come upon the boys at night while they were playing a game called “the crow”. They would notice nothing until he threw himself among them and kicked with his feet; the boys would be frightened and run away.

Sometimes he would invite me to supper at night and say, “Leave the ribs for the governor.” I would look, and there would be bread soaked in oil.

He died in the year fifty-nine. It is also said: in the year fifty-seven.

ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir al-Juhanī ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAmr; it is also said that his kunya was Abū Ḥammād. He embraced Islam after the Prophet ﷺ—arrived in Medina. He practiced archery frequently, because of something he had heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ. When he died, he left behind seventy bows, with their quivers and arrows.

He fought at Ṣiffīn with Muʿāwiyah, then moved to Egypt and settled there, building a house there. He used to dye his hair black and say:

[Ṭawīl]

Its upper parts change, while its roots refuse [to change].

He died toward the end of Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate.

Zayd ibn Khālid al-Juhanī ﵁

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān; it is also said that he was known by the kunya Abū Ṭalḥah. They disagreed about the place where he died.

Some said that he died in Medina in the year seventy-eight, aged eighty-five.

Others said that he died in Kufa, toward the end of Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Unays al-Anṣārī ﵁

His kunya was Abū Yaḥyā. He was known as al-Juhanī, though he was not a Juhanī; rather, he belonged to Wabrah, of Quḍāʿah. Juhaynah, too, belonged to Quḍāʿah. He was an ally of Banū Salimah.

He was present at al-ʿAqabah and Uḥud. They disagreed about whether he had been present at Badr.

His home was at Aʿrāf, one postal stage from Medina. The Messenger of God ﷺ—gave him a staff and said: “It is a sign between me and you. On that day, few people will carry walking sticks.” He is the one associated with what is called “the Night of the Bedouin” and “the Night of the Juhanī.” The Messenger of God ﷺ—had ordered him to leave his desert home for his mosque, and to pray there on the night of the twenty-third. He would come in the evening of the twenty-third night, after performing the afternoon prayer, and would not leave except when he had some need, until he had performed the dawn prayer; then he would go home to his family. Hence it was called “the Night of the Juhanī.”

He is the one who related from the Messenger of God ﷺ—concerning the Night of Decree, that he said: “Seek it tonight,” and that night was the twenty-third. He died in Medina during Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate. al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām ibn al-Mughīrah ﵁

He was the brother of Abū Jahl ibn Hishām. He fought at Badr with the polytheists, then fled. It was of him that Ḥassān ibn Thābit said: [Kāmil]

If what you have told me is a lie,then you escaped as al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām escaped.

He left his loved ones, and did not fight on their behalf;he escaped with a swift horse and its bridle.

Al-Ḥārith excused his flight, saying:

God knows that I did not give up fighting themuntil they had driven my dapple-gray horse to a lather.

I knew that if I fought a single one of them,I would be killed, and my presence would not harm my enemy.

So I turned away from them, though my loved ones were among them,hoping to spare them the punishment of a ruinous day.

He embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered. He was among those whose hearts were reconciled to Islam, then became a good Muslim. In ʿUmar’s time, he set out for Syria with his family and property. The people of Mecca followed him, weeping; he was moved and wept, then said: “But if we wanted to exchange one home for another, and one neighbor for another, we would not choose anyone in your place, “but this is the journey to God.” He continued striving in the cause of God until he died in the plague of ʿAmwās, in the year eighteen.

His son was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad, and his name had been Ibrāhīm. During ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s rule, he came before him at a time when ʿUmar wished to change the Muslims’ names to the names of prophets. He named him ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and that name has remained his to this day.

ʿĀʾishah ﵂—said: “It would be dearer to me to have stayed at home instead of setting out for Baṣrah than to have had ten children by the Messenger of God ﷺ—all of them like ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith.”

He had been with her at the Battle of the Camel. He was a distinguished and generous man, and died in Medina during Muʿāwiyah’s caliphate.

His son was Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām; his name was his kunya. He was called “the ascetic of Quraysh” on account of his excellence and frequent prayers. He was considered too young to fight on the day of the Camel and was sent back, along with ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr. He later lost his sight. He entered his bathhouse and died there suddenly in Medina in the year ninety-four, the Year of the Jurists.

Shaddād ibn al-Hādī al-Laythī ﵁

He was Shaddād ibn Usāmah. He was called al-Hādī because at night he would light a fire for travelers on the road. Salmā bint ʿUmays, the sister of Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays, was married to him, and bore him ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād, who was a jurist and transmitter of hadith. He was a maternal cousin of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and Khālid ibn al-Walīd, because ʿAbd Allāh’s mother and Khālid’s mother were sisters of Asmāʾ and Salmā, the daughters of ʿUmays.

ʿAttāb ibn Asīd ﵁

He was ʿAttāb ibn Asīd ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayyah. He embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered. When the Prophet ﷺ—set out for Ḥunayn, he appointed him over Mecca. He remained in charge of it until the Prophet ﷺ—died, and through Abū Bakr’s caliphate.

He and Abū Bakr died at the same time; neither knew of the other’s death.

His full brother Khālid ibn Asīd also embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered. He had great pride, so the Prophet ﷺ—said: “O God, increase him in pride.” This has persisted among his descendants to this day.

He had descendants.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAttāb ibn Asīd was the chief of Quraysh. He was likened to the chief bee, for he was their leader. He fought at the Battle of the Camel with ʿĀʾishah. An eagle carried off his palm; she was struck that day at al-Yamāmah and was recognized by his signet ring.10

al-ʿAlāʾ al-Ḥaḍramī ﵁

His father al-Ḥaḍramī’s name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḍimād, and he was from Ḥaḍramawt. He was an ally of Banū Umayyah. His brother Maymūn ibn al-Ḥaḍramī owned the well of Maymūn, which is in the lowland of Mecca; he had dug it in the pre-Islamic period.

Al-ʿAlāʾ was the one who crossed over to the people of Dārīn on his horse, fought them, killed them, and took their children captive. He conquered Asyāfā in Persia.11

He died during ʿUmar’s caliphate at Tiyās, in the land of Tamīm. It is said that his prayers were answered.

Suhayl ibn ʿAmr ﵁

His kunya was Abū Zayd. He belonged to Banū Ḥiṣl ibn ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy, of Quraysh.

He went to Ḥunayn with the Messenger of God ﷺ—while still a polytheist, and embraced Islam at al-Jiʿrānah. He was among those whose hearts were reconciled to Islam, then became a good Muslim. During ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s caliphate, he went to Syria to fight in the cause of God and died there in the plague of ʿAmwās. He was cleft-lipped. He had no male descendants. “Cleft-lipped” means one whose lip is split; aflaḥ has the same meaning. His brother al-Sakrān ibn ʿAmr was among the emigrants to Abyssinia.

Sawdah had been married to him. When he died, the Prophet ﷺ—married her. Al-Sakrān, too, had no descendants; their descendants came only from their brother Sahl ibn ʿAmr, who lived in Medina.

Sahl ibn ʿAmr embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered and died in Medina.

Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim ﵁

He was Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdī ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Quṣayy. He embraced Islam in the year of the conquest, in Medina, and his kunya was Abū Muḥammad.

He was among those whose hearts were reconciled to Islam, then became a good Muslim. He was one of the leading Muslims of the conquest in Medina. He died in the year fifty-nine. According to some, Abū Hurayrah died that year too.

His son Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim was haughty. One day he sat in the circle of al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥaraqī, who was teaching people to recite. When he finished, Nāfiʿ said, “Do you know why I sat with you?” They said, “You sat to listen.” He said, “No, by God. I wanted to humble myself before God by sitting with you.”

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ ﵁

He was ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil ibn Hāshim ibn [Saʿīd ibn Sahm ibn Huṣayṣ ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah.

His father al-ʿĀṣ was among those who mocked the Prophet, and concerning him the verse was revealed: “Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off” (Qurʾān 108:3). “Cut off” means one who has no child; the meaning was that his name would be cut off. His mother was al-Nābighah, of ʿAnazah.

Al-ʿĀṣ had two sons: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ. Hishām was one of the best of the Muslims. He was killed on one of the days of al-Yarmūk and left no descendants. ʿAmr was asked, “Are you better, or Hishām?” He replied, “I will tell you; then judge for yourselves: his mother was Umm Ḥarmlah bint Hishām ibn al-Mughīrah, “who was the maternal aunt of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb; my mother was from ʿAnazah. He was dearer to my father than I was, and you know what a father’s insight into his child is like. He embraced Islam before me. We raced toward God, and he was martyred on the day of al-Yarmūk, while I lived on after him.”

As for ʿAmr, his kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He embraced Islam in the year eight, along with Khālid ibn al-Walīd.

Muʿāwiyah appointed him over Egypt for three years. Then, a day before the end of Ramaḍān, he was overtaken by death. He said:

“O God, I have no acquittal by which to excuse myself, nor strength by which to prevail. You commanded me, and I disobeyed; You forbade me, and I did what was forbidden. O God, here is my hand up to my chin.” Then he gave instructions: “Dig the ground for me; press the earth down firmly.” Then he put his finger in his mouth and died. He was seventy-three years old. He was buried on the day of the Festival of Breaking the Fast.

There was disagreement about when he died. It was said: in the year forty-two; and it was said: in the year fifty-one. His son ʿAbd Allāh prayed over him, then led the people in the Festival Prayer.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ ﵁

His kunya was Abū Muḥammad. He embraced Islam before his father and fought at Ṣiffīn with him. He wielded two swords. His residence was Mecca, then he travelled to Syria and stayed there,

until Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah died. He then died in Mecca in the year sixty-five, aged seventy-two. It is also said that he died in Egypt and was buried in his small house.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr was twelve years older than his father.

[Abū Muḥammad said:

He said: Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh related to us; he said: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam related to us; he said:

al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ related to us, saying:

“We had a bondwoman who was twenty-one years old, and she was a grandmother.”

ʿAmrah bint ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was married to him, and bore him Muḥammad. Muḥammad’s son was Shuʿayb. Shuʿayb’s son was ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb—who was a distinguished man and would sometimes distribute fifty thousand from his grandfather’s charity in a single gathering—and Shuʿayb ibn Shuʿayb, who was also a distinguished man.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr was ruddy, large-bellied, and tall. He went blind toward the end of his life and could read Syriac.

ʿAmr had another son called Muḥammad.

Among ʿAmr’s clients was Wardān, a man of judgment and reflection. He had descendants in Egypt, and there was a market there known as Wardān’s Market.

Abū Bakrah ﵁

He was Nufayʿ ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kaldah, and was affiliated with him. Al-Ḥārith ibn Kaldah was the physician of the Arabs. He was sterile and had no children. He embraced Islam and died during ʿUmar’s caliphate.

Abū Bakrah’s mother was Sumayyah, from Zandaward. Kisrā had given her to Abū al-Khayr, a king of the kings of Yemen. When he returned to Yemen, he fell ill at al-Ṭāʾif, and al-Ḥārith treated him, so he gave her to al-Ḥārith. When the Messenger of God ﷺ—besieged the people of al-Ṭāʾif, he said: “Any slave who comes down to me is free.” Abū Bakrah, whose name was Nufayʿ, came down. His brother Nāfiʿ wanted to lower himself down, but al-Ḥārith said to him, “You are my son, so stay.” He stayed, and both brothers were affiliated with al-Ḥārith. Their mother Sumayyah was also the mother of Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān. Ardat bint al-Ḥārith claimed affiliation with al-Ḥārith. She was married to ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwān. When ʿUtbah was appointed governor of Baṣrah, he took her with him, and her brothers Nāfiʿ, Nufayʿ, and Ziyād went with her. When Abū Bakrah embraced Islam and became a good Muslim, he stopped claiming affiliation with al-Ḥārith. He used to say, “I am the client of the Messenger of God ﷺ.” Al-Ḥārith died, but Abū Bakrah did not take his inheritance. Sumayyah’s husband was called Masrūḥ.

Abū Bakrah left forty children, male and female, and seven of them left descendants:

ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUbayd Allāh, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Muslim, Rawwād, and ʿUtbah.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakra, he was the first child born in Baṣra. The first child born in Kūfa was Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr, of Banū al-Bakkāʾ, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿa.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh, he was the most generous of people and the bravest of them, and he was very dark-complexioned. ʿUbayd Allāh allotted ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar seven hundred jarībs in a single grant. ʿUmar swore that he would never see him without taking hold of his stirrup, and that he would not marry off a child until ʿUbayd Allāh had arranged the marriage.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān used to say: “The dark-complexioned one is the master of the people of the East”—meaning ʿUbayd Allāh. It is also said that “the dark-complexioned one” means a black animal, to which he was compared.

In the year seventy-eight, al-Ḥajjāj appointed him governor of Sijistān. He raided enemy territory, and his companions were struck by severe hunger and afflicted by famine, until a loaf of bread cost seventy dirhams.

148/ There ʿUbayd Allāh died, and many people perished with him. They suffered what no army had ever suffered. The poet Aʿshā Hamdān said: [Kāmil]

Have you heard of the army that was torn apartAnd struck by the crooked vicissitudes of time?

At Kābul they remained, eating their finest mounts,In the worst of places, at the worst of halts.

No army in the lands suffered what they suffered;For their like, tell the mourners to weep aloud.

ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasa ﵁

He was of Banū Sulaym, and was known by the kunya Abū Najīḥ. He was called “a quarter of Islam,” because when he embraced Islam, the Prophet ﷺ—was asked: “Who has followed you in this affair?” The Messenger of God ﷺ—replied: “A free man and a slave.” The free man was Abū Bakr, and the slave was Bilāl. ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasa used to say: “I remember when I was a quarter of Islam.”

When ʿAmr embraced Islam, he returned to his homeland, the land of Banū Sulaym, and remained there until Badr, Uḥud, the Trench, al-Ḥudaybiya, and Khaybar had all passed. Then he came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. After the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, he settled in Syria.

Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind man ﵁

Some people say his name was ʿAbd Allāh; others say it was ʿAmr.

He was the son of Qays, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy. His mother was Umm Maktūm, whose name was ʿĀtika, a Makhzūmī woman.

He came to Medina as an emigrant shortly after Badr, having lost his sight. The Messenger of God ﷺ—used to leave him in charge of Medina to lead the people in prayer during most of his military expeditions.

He took part in al-Qādisiyya, carrying a black standard and wearing armor. Then he returned to Medina and died there.

Sahl ibn Ḥunayf ﵁

He was one of the Anṣār, of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, and was known by the kunya Abū Saʿīd. He fought at Ṣiffīn with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. He lived in Kūfa and died there in the year thirty-eight. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib performed the funeral prayer over him and pronounced the takbīr six times, saying: “He was one of those who fought at Badr.”

His son Abū Umāma ibn Sahl transmitted many ḥadīths. His name was Asʿad; he was named after his grandfather, his mother’s father, Asʿad ibn Zurāra.

Sahl had other sons, and descendants in Medina and Baghdad.

149/ Tamīm al-Dārī ﵁

He was Tamīm ibn Aws, of Banū al-Dār ibn Hāniʾ, of Lakhm, of Yemen.

He was known by the kunya Abū Ruqayya.

He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ—with his brother Nuʿaym ibn Aws and a group of Banū al-Dār—it is said they were ten—in the year nine, and they embraced Islam.

ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥamiq ﵁

He was of Khuzāʿa. He pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God ﷺ—at the Farewell Pilgrimage, accompanied him thereafter, and narrated a ḥadīth from him.

He was among the residents of Kūfa and one of the partisans of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. He was among those who marched against ʿUthmān. He fought alongside ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in his campaigns, and supported Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī. Then he fled to Mosul and entered a cave, where a snake bit him and killed him. They sent men to the cave to search for him and found him dead. The governor of Mosul took his head and carried it to Ziyād, who sent it on to Muʿāwiya. This was the first head carried from one town to another in Islam.

Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAmr, and was of Bajīla.

He came to the Prophet ﷺ—in Ramaḍān of the year ten, pledged allegiance to him, and embraced Islam.

ʿUmar used to say: “Jarīr is the Joseph of this community,” because of his handsome appearance.

The Prophet ﷺ—said of him: “There is a touch of kingship in his face.” He was so tall that he could twist at the top of a camel’s hump; his sandal was a cubit long. At night he would dye his beard with saffron, and wash it in the morning, whereupon it emerged the color of gold.

He kept apart from ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya, and lived in the Jazīra and its environs until he died at al-Sharāt in the year fifty-four, during the governorship of al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays over Kūfa.

Jarīr had two sons who narrated from him: Ibrāhīm and Abān, the sons of Jarīr. Ibrāhīm lived long enough to meet Sharīk. Abū Zurʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarīr al-Bajalī narrated from his grandfather and from Abū Hurayra.

[He had a son called ʿAmr, but no one narrated from him.]

ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth ﵁

He was of Banū Makhzūm.

He married a daughter of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim on terms set by ʿAdī, who stipulated four hundred dirhams. He also married a daughter of Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī.

He had descendants in Kūfa and was renowned.

Among his clients was ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ.

He was generous 150/ and brave. Al-Mahdī appointed him governor of Ṭabaristān. Bashshār said of him:

[Mutqārib]

When grave affairs keep you awake,Rouse ʿAmr to face them, then sleep.

His generosity called me to ʿUmar,And his clan’s words—a boundless sea.

Were it not for what they say, I would notPraise a sweet basil before smelling it.

The mother of ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth was a daughter of Hishām ibn Khalaf al-Kinānī. Hishām was a man of distinction in the pre-Islamic era. He was the one who urinated on the head of al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir. Al-Nuʿmān followed the religion of the Arabs and went on pilgrimage. When he reached Mecca, Hishām saw him and asked, “Is this the king of the Arabs?” They said, “Yes.” So he urinated on his head to humiliate him. Al-Nuʿmān then turned away from the religion of the Arabs and became a Christian.

ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth had a brother called Saʿīd ibn Ḥurayth.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr ﵁

He was one of the Anṣār, and was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. His mother was ʿAmra bt. Rawāḥa, the sister of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa. Of her, the poet said: [Mutqārib]

ʿAmra is among the noblest of women,Her sleeves wafting with musk.

He heard someone reciting this and they silenced the man. Al-Nuʿmān said: “He said nothing but the truth, and said nothing wrong.”

He was treacherously killed in Syria, between Salīma and Ḥimṣ.

Al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh, and was of Thaqīf. His paternal uncle was ʿUrwa ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafī.

ʿUrwa embraced Islam during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and called his people to Islam, but they killed him. The Prophet ﷺ—said: “This man resembles the believer of the family of Yā Sīn.”

Al-Mughīra accompanied a group of polytheists to Egypt, treacherously killed them, and took what they had with them. Then he came to the Prophet ﷺ—and embraced Islam. He witnessed the Pledge of al-Riḍwān, al-Yamāma, the conquests of Syria, al-Yarmūk, and al-Qādisiyya.

ʿUmar ﵁ appointed him governor of Baṣra. He conquered Maysān, Dast Maysān, Abzqubādh, Sūq al-Ahwāz, and Hamadhān; he took part in the conquest of Nihāwand, and commanded the left wing of al-Nuʿmān ibn 151/ Muqarrin. He was the first to establish the register of Baṣra. It is said that he married eighty women. One of his wives was told, “He is one-eyed and ugly.” She replied: “By God, he is a Yemeni honey-cake in a poor wrapping.”

He died in Kūfa while serving as its governor, during the plague in the year fifty. When death came upon him, he said: “O God, this is my right hand: with it I pledged allegiance to Your Prophet and fought in Your path.”

He had the following sons: ʿUrwa ibn al-Mughīra—known by the kunya Abū Yaʿqūb. He was governor of Kūfa and was a virtuous man—al-ʿAqqār, Yaʿfūr, and Ḥamza. Reports have been narrated from all of them.

Khālid ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayya ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān [Sukhaym ibn Ḥafṣ ibn Qādim al-ʿAjīfī] and others reported:

He embraced Islam before Abū Bakr did, because of a vision he had seen. The Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed him to collect alms from Banū Zubayd. The ṣamṣāma, the sword of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, came into his possession and remained with the family of Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ until al-Mahdī bought it from them for twenty thousand dirhams.

Khālid was killed on the day of al-Yarmūk. His brother al-ʿĀṣ ibn Saʿīd was killed as a polytheist on the day of Badr; his opponent was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁.

His son Saʿīd was a boy, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—clothed him in a robe. It was because of this robe that garments called Saʿīdī came by their name.

Saʿīd was the first to brand camels on the bone. He had around twenty sons and twenty daughters.

Among his descendants was ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Ashdaq, whom ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān killed.

Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ died in the year fifty-nine. Muʿāwiya asked his son ʿAmr al-Ashdaq, who was still a child: “To whom did your father entrust you?” He replied: “He entrusted me to myself; he did not entrust me to anyone.”

Among the descendants of ʿAmr was Ismāʿīl ibn Umayya ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd. He narrated ḥadīths, and died in the year one hundred and forty.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal ﵁

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal ibn ʿAbd Nahm. The sons of ʿAbd Nahm were Mughaffal, Khuzāʿī, and ʿAbd Allāh Dhū al-Najjādayn, by one mother, whose name was ʿAbla bt. Muʿāwiya ibn Muʿāwiya al-Muzanī.

He was of Muḍar’s Muzayna. They are also called Banū ʿUthmān. Muzayna “joined up”—that is, became a thousand strong—on the day Mecca was conquered. Sulaym joined up as well.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khuzāʿī ibn Ziyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal reported that his kunya was Abū Saʿīd.

He died in Baṣra in the last part of Muʿāwiya’s caliphate, during the governorship of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād.

He instructed that Ibn Ziyād not perform the funeral prayer over him, and that Abū Barza al-Aslamī should perform it.

He had ten children, 152/ among them Saʿīd, Ḥassān the elder, Ḥassān the younger, Ziyād, Ṭāriq, and al-Mughīra.

Maʿqil ibn Yasār ﵁

He was also of Muḍar’s Muzayna, and was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was the one who opened the mouth of the Maʿqil canal. Ziyād had dug it, and, seeking good fortune from Maʿqil’s companionship, ordered him to open it. It was therefore named after him. The Maʿqilī date is also named after him.

He died in the last part of Muʿāwiya’s caliphate, and had descendants in Baṣra.

Among his clients was Ḥabīb al-Muʿallim, who was Ḥabīb ibn Zayd, the client of Maʿqil ibn Yasār.

Maʿqil ibn Sinān ﵁

He was of Ashjaʿ. He took part in the conquest with the Prophet ﷺ—and lived until the day of al-Ḥarra. Muslim ibn ʿUqba killed him that day; Nawfal ibn Musāḥiq was responsible for his killing, because he had once heard him speak of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya as a wine-drinker and criticize him, and he had held a grudge against him for it.

ʿĀʾidh ibn ʿAmr ﵁

He too was of Muḍar’s Muzayna. ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād said to him: “You are among the rabble of the companions of Muḥammad.” ʿĀʾidh replied: “Is there rabble among the companions of Muḥammad ﷺ?” He had a house in Baṣra in the quarter of Muzayna.

Bilāl ibn al-Ḥārith ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and was also of Muḍar’s Muzayna.

He was the one to whom the Prophet ﷺ—granted the mines of al-Qabaliyya. He died in the year sixty, aged eighty.

His son Ḥassān ibn Bilāl was the first to introduce irjāʾ in Baṣra.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Muqarrin ﵁

He belonged to the Aws, and the Aws were of Muzayna, except that they were not descendants of ʿUthmān. Their number was small.

He conquered Nihāwand for ʿUmar and was killed there. His grave is there, at a place called al-Asfīdhbān. Also there are the grave of Ṭalḥa ibn Khuwaylid, the grave of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, and the graves of a group of Muslims.

He had two brothers: Suwayd ibn Muqarrin and Miqran ibn Muqarrin. All of them narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ and their residence was Kūfa.

Miqran ibn Muqarrin was the father of ʿAmra al-Muzanī.

153/ Ḥanẓala the Scribe

He was Ḥanẓala ibn Rabīʿa ibn Ṣayfī, the nephew of Aktham ibn Ṣayfī, the sage of the Arabs.

He was from Banū Tamīm, from a clan called Banū Sharīf.

Aktham lived to see the Prophet’s mission ﷺ and urged his people to go to him and hasten to reach him. He did not become Muslim, and lived to the age of one hundred and ninety. He said: [long metre]

A man who has lived through ninety yearsand on to a hundred, yet does not weary of life, is ignorant.

Aktham had descendants in Kūfa, and died in the desert.

As for Ḥanẓala the Scribe, he used to write for the Messenger of God ﷺ. He lived on into the time of Muʿāwiya and died without descendants.

Some say that he was Ḥanẓala ibn al-Rabīʿ, and that he once wrote a document for the Prophet ﷺ and was therefore called “the Scribe.” Writing was uncommon among the Arabs. He was a Companion.

His brother, Rabāḥ ibn Rabīʿa ibn Ṣayfī, was also a Companion. One day, the Prophet ﷺ set aside a day for the Jews and a day for the Christians. Rabāḥ said, “If only we had a day!” Then Sūrat al-Jumuʿa was revealed.

Burayda al-Aslamī ﵁

He was Burayda ibn al-Ḥuṣayb, and was the chief of Aslam. When the Messenger of God ﷺ migrated, he passed by Kurāʿ al-Ghamīm. Burayda was there, and the Messenger of God ﷺ called them to Islam, so they became Muslims. Then Burayda came to the Messenger of God ﷺ in Medina while he was building the mosque.

Burayda died in the caliphate of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya at Marw.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ ﵁

He was the one who used to write for the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ would dictate to him “Mighty, Wise,” but he would write “Forgiving, Merciful.” Concerning him was revealed:

“And who says, ‘I shall send down the like of what God has sent down’” (Q 6:93). The Prophet ﷺ declared his blood forfeit on the day Mecca was conquered.

He was the foster-brother of ʿUthmān, who brought him to the Prophet ﷺ and kept pleading for him until he granted him safety.

ʿUthmān appointed him over Egypt, and he was the one who conquered Ifrīqiya.

His father, Saʿd, was one of the hypocrites.

Qays ibn ʿĀṣim al-Munqirī ﵁

He was Qays ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sinān ibn Khālid ibn Munqir, and his teknonym was Abū ʿAlī.

He was the one of whom the Messenger of God ﷺ said, “The chief of the people of the desert.” He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with the delegation of Banū Tamīm after the conquest of Mecca, and became Muslim.

He was a noble chief. Concerning him the poet said: [long metre]

Qays’s death was not the death of one man;rather, it was a people’s edifice that collapsed.

Among his children were Ṭalaba, al-Qaʿqāʿ, Shammākh, and others. It is said that they were thirty-three sons.

Mayya, beloved of Dhū al-Rumma, was descended from Ṭalaba.

Al-Zibriqān ibn Badr ﵁

His name was Ḥuṣayn ibn Badr ibn Khalaf ibn Bahdala ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd.

He was called al-Zibriqān because of his beauty, and he was known as “the moon of Najd.”

His children were ʿAbbās—after whom he was given his teknonym—ʿAyyāsh, Abū Shadhara, and daughters.

His descendants in the desert were numerous.

The Messenger of God ﷺ appointed al-Zibriqān over the alms of his people. When the Prophet ﷺ died, al-Zibriqān brought them to Abū Bakr. They numbered seven hundred camels.

ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn ﵁

He was ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr. His name had been Ḥudhayfa, but he was afflicted with a weakness of the eye, which made it protrude, and so he was called ʿUyayna.

His teknonym was Abū Mālik.

His grandfather, Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, was the chief of Ghatafān.

He was called “the lord of Maʿadd.”

Likewise, his son Ḥiṣn led Asad and Ghatafān.

The Banū ʿAbs killed Ḥudhayfa, and the Banū ʿUqayl killed Ḥiṣn.

His son Khārija ibn Ḥiṣn was the chief of the people of Kūfa.

Al-Wāqidī said: The lands of Badr ibn ʿAmr suffered drought until nothing of their property remained except the stray animals. They were told of a cloud that had settled at Taghlimayn, toward Baṭn Nakhl. ʿUyayna set out with the family of Badr until he came within sight of Baṭn Nakhl. Then he became apprehensive of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, and went to Medina. He came to the Prophet ﷺ who called him to Islam. He did not distance himself, but did not enter into it either. He said, “I wish to draw near to your protection, so make a truce with me.”

The Prophet made a truce with him for three months. When the term ended, he and his people returned to their lands, having fattened their animals and increased their milk yield. The hooves had grown strong from eating ṣillyān grass, and they were pleased with the appearance of the land. So ʿUyayna raided with those animals and seized the Prophet’s milch camels, which were at al-Ghāba. Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf said to him, “How badly you have repaid Muḥammad! You fattened your animals in his land, then raided him!” He said, “That is what you see.” The Prophet ﷺ said of him, “The fool who is obeyed.” Then he became Muslim and was among those whose hearts were reconciled. He apostatized when the Arabs apostatized and joined Ṭulayḥa ibn Khuwaylid when he claimed prophethood, believing in him. When Ṭulayḥa was defeated and fled, Khālid ibn al-Walīd seized ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn and sent him in chains to Abū Bakr ﵁. He brought him to Medina, where the boys of Medina began prodding him with palm branches and beating him, saying, “Enemy of God! You have disbelieved in God after your faith!” He would reply, “By God, I had never believed.” When Abū Bakr spoke with him, he returned to Islam. Abū Bakr accepted this from him and wrote him a guarantee of safety.

During ʿUthmān’s caliphate, he came to see him and said, “Ibn ʿAffān, govern us according to the practice of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, for he gave to us and made us rich, and he made us fear him, so we became mindful of God.” ʿUthmān said to him, “By God, even so, you would not be satisfied with ʿUmar’s practice. Will you stay for the evening meal?” He said, “I am fasting.” ʿUthmān asked, “Are you fasting continuously?” He said, “What is continuous fasting?”

ʿUthmān said, “You fast through your day and your night, until evening.” He replied, “No, but I find fasting at night easier for me than fasting during the day.”

ʿUyayna was the one who raided the market of ʿUkāẓ; this was the Second Fijār.

He had descendants. He became blind at the end of his life.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura ﵁

He was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿAbd Shams. He had been called ʿAbd Kulāl.

The Prophet ﷺ named him ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and said to him, “Do not seek authority, for if it is given to you without your asking for it, you will be helped in carrying it out.” ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir appointed him over Sijistān, which he conquered; he also conquered Kābul.

He had a brother named ʿAmr ibn Samura, whom the Prophet ﷺ had his hand cut off for theft. The two of them had descendants. Manṣūr ibn Zādhān was his client.

Samura ibn Jundub ﵁

His teknonym was Abū Sulaymān. He was from Banū Laʾy ibn Shimkh ibn Fazāra. He attended Uḥud while still a boy.

It is said that he was one of the ten of whom the Messenger of God ﷺ said:

“The last of you to die will be in the Fire.” He was cross-eyed, and his mother was black.

Ziyād appointed him over Baṣra, and he died in Kūfa in the year sixty-something.

His descendants were there.

Samura ibn Junāda ibn Jundub ﵁

Among the Companions was another man called Samura ibn Junāda ibn Jundub. Some people thought he was the first Samura, but that is not so.

He was Abū Jābir ibn Samura al-Sawāʾī, from Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa.

His son Jābir ibn Samura narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ. He died in Kūfa during the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

On the day of al-Madāʾin, Saʿd gave him two young slaves from among the sons of the Persian kings. One was Badhīma, the father of ʿAlī ibn Badhīma, who is a transmitter; the other was Abū Zuhayr, the grandfather of al-Muṭṭalib ibn Ziyād ibn Abī Zuhayr. Jābir emancipated them both.

Abū Maḥdhūra ﵁

He was Salmān ibn Samura—and it is said that he was Samura ibn Muʿayr ibn Lawdhān ibn ʿUwayj ibn Saʿd ibn Jumah. His mother was from Khuzāʿa.

This Samura was the Messenger of God’s caller to prayer ﷺ. When he gave the call, ʿUmar said to him, “Were you not afraid your marīṭā would split?” Marīṭā means the lower part of the belly, from the navel to the pubic area.

He had a brother named Anīs ibn Muʿayr, who was killed as an unbeliever at Badr.

Abū Maḥdhūra became Muslim after Ḥunayn, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to give the call to prayer in Mecca. The call to prayer has remained in his family in the Sacred Mosque to this day. He died in the year fifty-nine.

Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj ﵁

He was one of the Anṣār, from the Aws. His teknonym was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He attended Uḥud and the Trench. He used to trim his moustache very closely, as though it had been shaved, and he trimmed his beard and dyed it yellow.

He died from a wound he had sustained in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. It flared up again in the year seventy-three, when he was eighty-six years old.

His brother Rifaʿa ibn Khadīj had been a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ. His paternal uncle Ẓahīr ibn Rāfiʿ and his son Usayd ibn Ẓahīr both narrated from the Prophet ﷺ.

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī ﵁

He was Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr. His father was killed at Uḥud. Jābir was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He attended al-ʿAqaba with the seventy from among the Anṣār, and was the youngest of them then. He did not attend Badr or Uḥud, but attended the campaigns that followed.

It is related in some ḥadīth from him that he said, “I was one of my companions’ provisions at Badr.”

This is an error, because the authorities on the campaigns unanimously agree that he did not attend Badr.

He died in Medina in the year seventy-eight, at the age of ninety-four. By then he had lost his sight. Abān ibn ʿUthmān, who was then governor of Medina, performed the prayer over him.

He was among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who died late in Medina.

He had two sons who narrated ḥadīth from him: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jābir and Muḥammad ibn Jābir. The ḥadīth authorities consider both weak.

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rīʾāb ﵁

Among the Companions was another man called Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rīʾāb. He narrated a few ḥadīths.

Anas ibn Mālik ﵁

He was one of the Anṣār. His mother was Umm Sulaym bint Milḥān, the wife of Abū Ṭalḥa.

His brother al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik narrated from the Prophet ﷺ. Anas’s mother brought him to the Prophet ﷺ when he arrived in Medina. Anas was eight years old, and served him until the Prophet ﷺ passed away. The Prophet prayed for him, saying, “O God, grant him wealth and children, and bless him.” Anas said, “I am among the Anṣār with the greatest wealth and the most children.”

I was informed that by the time al-Ḥajjāj came to Baṣra, more than a hundred and twenty of his own descendants had been buried.

Al-Ḥirmāzī said:

Three men of Baṣra did not die until each had seen a hundred male descendants of his own: Khalīfa ibn Badr, Abū Bakra, and Anas ibn Mālik.

Anas lived to an advanced age. He was the last of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ—to die in al-Baṣra. His death occurred in the year ninety-one. It is also said:

In the year ninety-three, two years before al-Ḥajjāj died.

Among the descendants of Anas who transmitted ḥadīth were Mūsā ibn Anas, Mālik ibn Anas, al-Naḍr ibn Anas, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Anas.

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, the freedman of Anas, was the scribe of Anas ibn Mālik in Fārs.

[Of him the poet says: [kāmil]]

He refuses to answer, and does not reply, out of awe;

Those who ask lower their chins,

The guidance of piety, and the might of the rule of piety;

He is obeyed, though he holds no sovereignty.

ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn al-Khuzāʿī ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū Nuǧayd. He embraced Islam early and died in al-Baṣra during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya, in the year fifty-two.

Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī ﵁

He was Ṣudayy ibn ʿAǧlān. He was among those who fought with ʿAlī at Ṣiffīn, and settled in Syria. He is counted among the Companions who died late.

He died in the year eighty-six, aged ninety-one. He used to dye his beard yellow.

Among the Anṣār were Abū Umāma Asʿad ibn Zurāra, and Abū Umāma al-Ḥārithī, Thaʿlaba ibn Sahl.

ʿIkrāsh ibn Dhuʾayb ﵁

He was from Banū Tamīm, from Banū al-Nazzāl ibn Murra ibn ʿUbayd. Banū Murra ibn ʿUbayd sent him with the alms due on their property to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

He fought at the Battle of the Camel alongside ʿĀʾisha. Al-Aḥnaf, who was of his clan, said: “It is as if you are about to bring him here dead, or with a wound that will not leave him until he dies!” He was struck once on the nose; he lived another hundred years, carrying the mark of the blow.

He was known by the kunya Abū al-Ṣahbāʾ. His sons were ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUbayd Allāh, and ʿAbd al-Salām.

ʿAbd Allāh is the one who transmits ḥadīth from his father about his arrival before the Messenger of God ﷺ—with camels like the veins of the arṭā shrub, and about eating with him.

ʿUbayd Allāh is the one whom Abū al-Naḍr, the freedman of ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, mentions in these lines:

Tell Sawwār, when

You come to him, and Ibn ʿAlātha:

In the morning ʿUbayd Allāh added

Three strings.

ʿUbayd Allāh had descendants in al-Baṣra. He is the one who said: “An age treacherous, and an heir shafūn; so do not trust the treacherous, and be an heir shafūn.”12

Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām ﵁

He was Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad, the cousin of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām and the nephew of Khadīja bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ḥakīm said: “I was born thirteen years before the Elephant, and I was old enough to understand, when ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib intended to sacrifice his son ʿAbd Allāh, after his vow had fallen upon him. That was five years before the birth of the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

Ḥakīm fought alongside his son at al-Fiǧār, and his father Ḥizām was killed at the later al-Fiǧār.

Ḥakīm was known by the kunya Abū Khālid. He embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered, and his sons embraced Islam that day too: Hishām ibn Ḥakīm, Khālid ibn Ḥakīm, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥakīm. All of them were Companions of the Prophet ﷺ—and transmitted from him.

Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām lived sixty years in the pre-Islamic age and sixty years in Islam. He was among those whose hearts were reconciled, but later became a good Muslim. He died in Medina in the year fifty-four. He sold a house of his to Muʿāwiya for sixty thousand dinars. Someone said to him:

“Muʿāwiya has cheated you!” He replied: “By God, I bought it in the pre-Islamic age for a wineskin of wine. I call you to witness that it is now for the sake of God. See which of us has been cheated.”

Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

He was ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy. He, too, lived one hundred and twenty years: sixty in the pre-Islamic age and sixty in Islam. He died in Medina in the year fifty-four, during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya. He had descendants.

Ḥuwayṭib had sold a house of his to Muʿāwiya for forty thousand dinars. Someone said to him: “Abū Muḥammad, forty thousand dinars!” He replied: “And what are forty thousand dinars to a man who has five dependants?”

He was among those whose hearts were reconciled, but later became a good Muslim.

Ḥassān ibn Thābit ibn al-Mundhir ﵁

Abū Muḥammad said:

He was one of the Anṣār, and was known by the kunya Abū al-Walīd. His mother, al-Furayʿa, was from Khazraǧ.

He was among the earliest to embrace Islam, but did not take part in any expedition with the Prophet ﷺ—because he was a coward. He had a forelock that he let hang between his eyes, and, because his tongue was so long, he could touch the tip of his nose with it. He lived sixty years in the pre-Islamic age and sixty years in Islam.

He was apparently a contemporary of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām and Ḥuwayṭib. He died around the same time as they did.

His son was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān, born to a sister of Māriya al-Qibṭiyya, the mother of Ibrāhīm, the son of the Messenger of God ﷺ. She was called Shīrīn. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was a poet. His son was Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. His line died out, and none of his descendants remained.

Ḥassān had two brothers called Aws ibn Thābit and Ubayy ibn Thābit.

Aws was the father of Shaddād ibn Aws, who transmitted religious learning. Shaddād died in Palestine in the year fifty-eight. His descendants were in Jerusalem; among them was Yaʿlā ibn Shaddād, a reliable transmitter from whom ḥadīth is related.

Ubayy ibn Thābit was known as Abū Shaykh. He was killed at Biʾr Maʿūna and left no descendants.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Among this generation of long-lived men who died in the year fifty-four were Saʿīd ibn Yarbuʿ, Abū Hūd, who lived to the age of one hundred and twenty, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal, who lived to the age of one hundred and fifteen.

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī ﵁

He was known by the kunya Abū Ṭarīf. He was so tall that, when he rode a horse, his feet nearly dragged on the ground. He came before ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who seemed to treat him brusquely, and said to him:

“Do you not know me?” He replied: “Indeed, by God, I know you—may God grant you the finest recognition. You embraced Islam when they disbelieved, recognized the truth when they denied it, kept faith when they betrayed it, and came forward when they turned away.” He said:

“That is enough for me, Commander of the Faithful, enough!” He fought with ʿAlī ﵁—at the Battle of the Camel, where one of his eyes was gouged out. His son Muḥammad was killed that day, and his other son was killed with the Khāriǧites.

He fought with ʿAlī at Ṣiffīn and died in the time of al-Mukhtār, aged one hundred and twenty. He left instructions that al-Mukhtār was not to perform the funeral prayer over him.

He had no surviving descendants except through his two daughters, Asada and ʿAmra. The descendants of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī came only through his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥātim; they live along the river at Karbalāʾ.

ʿAmr ibn al-Masīḥ al-Ṭāʾī ﵁

He came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ—and embraced Islam. He was the finest archer among all the Arabs. He is the one of whom Imruʾ al-Qays says: [madīd]

Many an archer from Banū Thaʿl

Draws his hands out from beneath his cloak.

He lived one hundred and fifty years. I do not know whether he died before the Prophet ﷺ—or after him.

Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiya ﵁

He was Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmr al-Duʾalī. His father Muʿāwiya led Banū al-Duʾal on the day of the First al-Fiǧār. To him Taʾabbaṭa Sharran refers in these words:

Neither ʿĀmir nor al-Naffāthī Nawfal His son Aslam ibn Nawfal was the most generous of the Arabs.

Nawfal lived sixty years in the pre-Islamic age and sixty years in Islam. He embraced Islam, took part in the events after the Battle of the Trench, and transmitted ḥadīth from the Prophet ﷺ.

He died in Medina during the caliphate of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.

ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashǧaʿī ﵁

He was ʿAwf ibn Mālik. He embraced Islam and fought on the day of Ḥunayn. He carried the banner of Ashǧaʿ on the day Mecca was conquered. During the caliphate of Abū Bakr ﵁—he moved to Syria and settled in Ḥimṣ, where he remained until the beginning of the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik. He died in the year seventy-three.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAmr.

161/ Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Naṣrī ﵁

He was from Naṣr ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Bakr ibn Hawāzin. He was the leader of the polytheists on the day of Ḥunayn, then embraced Islam. The Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed him over his people and gave him one hundred camels. He was among those whose hearts were reconciled. He had descendants.

Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf ﵁

He was from Banū Murra ibn Nashba and was known by the kunya Abū Asmāʾ. He was the guarantor who paid the blood money in the war of Dāḥis. He was one of the leaders of the polytheists on the day of the Confederates, but later embraced Islam and became a good Muslim. The Messenger of God ﷺ—sent with him one of the Anṣār, under his protection, to call his people to Islam. They killed the Anṣārī, so he sent seventy camels as blood money for him. The Messenger of God ﷺ—gave them to the heirs of the Anṣārī.

He had descendants.

Muʿayqīb ﵁

He was Muʿayqīb ibn Abī Fāṭima al-Dawsī, from al-Azd. He was among those who embraced Islam early in Mecca, then migrated to the land of Abyssinia. It is also said that he instead returned to his homeland, then came with Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and the Ashʿarites to the Messenger of God ﷺ—at Khaybar, where he took part in the campaign. He lived until the caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁. He was in charge of the seal of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and served as a scribe to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. He was among ʿUmar’s trusted stewards of the public treasury. He contracted leprosy.

Khāriǧa ibn Zayd said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—said to Muʿayqīb, as he ate with him: “Eat from what is nearest you. If what afflicts you afflicted someone else, I would speak to him only with a spear’s length between us.”

Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt ﵁

He was from Banū Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm and was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was taken captive and sold in Mecca. Umm Anmār—who was Umm Sibāʿ al-Khuzāʿiyya, an ally of Banū Zuhra—bought him and freed him. It is also said that Khabbāb’s mother and the mother of Sibāʿ ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā al-Khuzāʿī were one and the same, and that she was a circumciser in Mecca.

Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said to Sibāʿ ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, whose mother was Umm Anmār:

“Come here, son of the woman who cuts women’s clitorises.” So Khabbāb joined the household of Sibāʿ and, for this reason, claimed the protection of Banū Zuhra.

Khabbāb was a young man, and he had developed vitiligo.

His son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khabbāb was the one whom the Khāriǧites killed. His blood flowed like a sandal strap, ma-imdhaqarr.13 They cut open the belly of the mother of his child. He was staying in a village, and for this reason ʿAlī ﵁—deemed it lawful to fight them.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Khabbāb was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He died in al-Kūfa in the year thirty-seven, aged sixty-three. He was the first person whom ʿAlī buried in al-Kūfa; ʿAlī prayed over him on his return from Ṣiffīn.

He had descendants.

Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was a freedman of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd ibn Zuhayr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy. ʿUbayd Allāh made him a contract of manumission, which he fulfilled on the day of the conquest. He came originally from a clan of al-Azd called al-Namir, from Lakhm.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd was killed as an unbeliever at Badr, by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He was from Lakhm and an ally of Banū Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad. He died in Medina in the year thirty. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁—performed the funeral prayer over him. He was then sixty-five years old.

He was sparse-bearded, stooped, and well-built.

Someone else said:

Ḥāṭib was a merchant who sold food and other goods. When he died, he left four thousand dinars, dirhams, and other property.

His freedman was Saʿd ibn Khawlā, the freedman of Niʿma. He fought at Badr and Uḥud and was killed at Uḥud.

He had a son called ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥāṭib, who transmitted ḥadīth from him. He was born in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and transmitted from ʿUmar. He died in Medina in the year sixty-eight. He was reliable and transmitted few ḥadīths.

Ḥāṭib had descendants in Medina.

al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ ibn Abī ʿAmr ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams.

Abū ʿAmr had been a slave called Dhakwān. Umayya claimed him as his son and gave him the kunya Abū ʿAmr. He then married Umayya’s wife, Āmina bint Abān, the mother of the ʿAyāṣ.

Al-Walīd was kunya’d Abū Wahb. He was the maternal brother of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān: their mother was Arwāʾ bt. Kurayz.

He embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Mecca. The Messenger of God ﷺ—sent him as a collector of alms [muṣaddiq] to Banū al-Muṣṭaliq. He came back and said, “They have refused to pay the alms”—but he was lying. The Messenger of God ﷺ—then ordered arms to be taken against them. God, Mighty and Glorious, revealed to him: “O you who believe, if a transgressor brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance” (Qurʾān 49:6). An exchange of words took place between him and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. He said, “I am more capable than you of turning back a battalion and striking the crown of a bold champion.” God, Mighty and Glorious, then revealed: “Is one who is a believer like one who is a transgressor? They are not equal” (Qurʾān 32:18).

Ibn al-Kalbī said:

Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams went to Syria and stayed there for ten years. He had intercourse with a Jewish slave woman belonging to Lakhm, from Ṣaffūriyya. She was called Tarnā, and she had a Jewish husband from Ṣaffūriyya. She bore him Dhakwān, whom Umayya claimed as his son and formally acknowledged; he gave him the kunya Abū ʿAmr. He then brought him to Mecca. For this reason, on the day the Prophet ﷺ—ordered ʿUqba to be killed, he said to him, “You are only a Jew from Ṣaffūriyya.” ʿUmar ﵁—appointed him collector of alms from Banū Taghlib. ʿUthmān appointed him governor of Kūfa after Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. He led the people of Kūfa in prayer while drunk and said, “Shall I give you more?” They testified before ʿUthmān that he had drunk wine, so ʿUthmān dismissed him and had him flogged.

He remained in Medina until ʿAlī was pledged allegiance. Then he went to al-Raqqa and settled there, keeping apart from both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

He died in the region of al-Raqqa, and his grave is on the al-Balīkh.

His descendants were in al-Raqqa and Kūfa. Among them was Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba.

He was called Dhū al-Shāma, and was accused of heresy.

His brother ʿUmāra ibn ʿUqba embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Mecca. Among his descendants was Mudrik ibn ʿUmāra, from whom Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid transmitted.

His brother Khālid ibn ʿUqba was one of their notables. He embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Mecca and, from among Banū Umayya, attended the funeral of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ﵄.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ﵁

Abū al-Yaqẓān said: He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz ibn Rabīʿa ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿAbd Shams.

His father, ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz, embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Mecca and lived until the caliphate of ʿUthmān. He came to Baṣra to visit his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir, who was its governor under ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁.

ʿĀmir’s mother was al-Bayḍāʾ bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

He was weak-minded. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib brought him to himself and touched him, then said, “By the bones of Hāshim, no child born to ʿAbd Manāf is more foolish than he.”

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir, his father brought him to the Prophet ﷺ—and the Prophet rubbed his palate. The child yawned, so the Prophet spat into his mouth, and he swallowed the Prophet’s saliva. The Prophet ﷺ—said, “I hope he will be God-fearing.” His kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He conquered most of Persia, Khurāsān, Sijistān, and Kābul. He established himself at al-Nibāj and planted there; it came to be called “the Nibāj of Ibn ʿĀmir.” He established himself at al-Quraytayn and planted palm trees there. He caused springs to flow, known as the Springs of Ibn ʿĀmir, a night’s journey from al-Nibāj on the road to Medina. He dug al-Ḥafīr, then dug al-Samīna. Near Qubāʾ, he built a palace and put Zanj there to work. They died, so he abandoned it. At ʿArafāt he made watering basins and planted palm trees. At Baṣra he dug two canals, one to the east and the other known as Umm ʿAbd Allāh. Umm ʿAbd Allāh was his mother; her name was Dajjāja bt. Asmāʾ bt. al-Ṣalt al-Sulamī. The Umm ʿAbd Allāh basin at Baṣra is named after her. She died at Baṣra.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir dug the canal of al-Ubulla. He used to say, “If I were left to it, a woman would set out in her howdah on her mount, finding water and a market every day, until she reached Mecca.”

He died at Mecca and was buried at ʿArafāt. He had many descendants. He died in the year 59, a year before Muʿāwiya’s death. [I have been told that] he transmitted only one hadith from the Messenger of God ﷺ: “Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr.”

He appointed ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr as his executor. Ibn ʿUmar was present when he died and praised him for the watering basins he had built at ʿArafāt and for his works in the land. He looked at them. Ibn ʿUmar said, “When one’s earnings are wholesome, one’s spending is blessed. We shall return and see.”

Among the clients of the family of Kurayz was Ṭuways, client of Arwāʾ bt. Kurayz, the mother of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁. His name was ʿAbd al-Malik, and his kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Naʿīm. Ṭuways was seen throwing sugar colored with saffron at the pebbles [during the pilgrimage rite]. He was asked, “What is that?” He replied, “Satan once did me a favor, and I wanted to repay him for it.”

Dhū al-Yadayn ﵁

He was ʿUmayr ibn ʿAbd ʿAmr, from Khuzāʿa. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad. He worked with both hands, so he was called Dhū al-Yadayn, “the man with two hands.” He was also called Dhū al-Shimālayn, “the man with two left hands.” It is also said that his name was al-Khirbāq and that his hands were long.

He is the man mentioned in the hadith in which it is related that the Messenger of God ﷺ—spoke after the prayer and then made up what he had missed.

He is not Dhū al-Shimālayn, who was martyred at Badr.

Dhū al-Bijādayn ﵁

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Nahm. He was named Dhū al-Bijādayn because, when he wished to set out for the Messenger of God ﷺ—his mother cut one of her cloaks, a coarse wrap, in two. He wrapped one piece around his waist and draped the other over his shoulders.

He died during the Prophet’s lifetime ﷺ.

ʿUmayr, client of Ābī al-Laḥm al-Ghifārī ﵁

ʿUmayr, the client of Ābī al-Laḥm, transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. Ābī al-Laḥm had refused to eat what was slaughtered at the stone idols, so he was named Ābī al-Laḥm, “the one who refused meat.”

ʿUmayr said, “I was present at Ḥunayn while I was a slave. The Prophet ﷺ—gave me a sword and some of the baggage, but he did not allot me a share.”

Juhjah al-Ghifārī ﵁

He was Juhjah ibn Saʿīd al-Ghifārī. He was one of the poor Emigrants and a hired worker of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He seized ʿUthmān’s staff while ʿUthmān was on the pulpit and broke it across his knee. Gangrene then set into his knee.

He had eaten with the Prophet ﷺ—while he was an unbeliever, and ate a great deal. Then he ate with him after embracing Islam, and ate little. The Prophet ﷺ—said:

“The believer eats in one stomach, and the unbeliever eats in seven stomachs.”

Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ al-Aslamī ﵁

His kunya was Abū Iyās, and he was among the renowned archers. He died in the year 74, aged eighty.

His brother was Ahbān ibn al-Akwaʿ, the one who spoke with the wolf.

Al-Wāqidī said:

The one who spoke with the wolf was Ahbān ibn Aws al-Aslamī.

Ahbān embraced Islam, accompanied the Prophet ﷺ—and settled in Kūfa. He died during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān.

His son, Iyās ibn Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ, was kunya’d Abū Bakr. He died in Medina in the year 119, aged seventy-seven.

Al-Furāt ibn Ḥayyān ﵁

He was from ʿIjl, of Banū Saʿd, the clan of Ḥanẓala ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Sayyār. He was the best guide and knew the roads better than anyone. He used to travel with Quraysh’s caravans to Syria. Ḥassān ibn Thābit said of him: [ṭawīl]

If on our journeys and in our searchwe meet al-Furāt ibn Ḥayyān, he will be a pledge for a doomed man.

Al-Furāt embraced Islam and was a good Muslim. On the day of Ḥunayn, when the Messenger of God ﷺ—gave gifts to those whose hearts were to be reconciled, he said, “Among people are some whom we leave to their faith; among them is al-Furāt ibn Ḥayyān.”

Sharḥabīl ibn Ḥasana ﵁

He was named after his mother. His father was ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muṭāʿ ibn ʿAmr, from Yemen and an ally of Banū Zuhra. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He died in the plague of ʿAmwās in the year 18, aged sixty-four.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Buḥayna ﵁

He was named after his mother, Buḥayna, daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. His father, Mālik, was from Azd.

Khafāf ibn Nudba ﵁

He was named after his mother, who was black. Khafāf was one of the Arabs’ “black ravens,” on account of his dark complexion. His father was ʿUmayr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Sharīd al-Sulamī, who was a poet.

He took part with the Prophet ﷺ—in the conquest of Mecca, carrying the banner of Banū Sulaym, and lived until the time of ʿUmar.

Abū Lubāba al-Anṣārī ﵁

His kunya was taken from a daughter of his called Lubāba, who was married to Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and bore him children. His name was Bashīr ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir—though it is also said to have been Rifāʿa ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir. Abū Lubāba died after ʿUthmān was killed. It is also said: before ʿAlī.

He had descendants through his son al-Sāʾib.

Al-Maʿārif by Ibn Qutayba

Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib al-Anṣārī ﵁

His kunya was Abū ʿUmāra. Al-Barāʾ was the sister’s son of Abū Burda ibn Niyār.

Abū Burda’s name was Hāniʾ, and he was from Quḍāʿa.

Abū Burda had descendants.

Al-Barāʾ had two sons who transmitted hadith from him: Yazīd ibn al-Barāʾ and Suwayd ibn al-Barāʾ.

Suwayd governed ʿUmān and was among the best of governors.

ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī ﵁

He was from al-ʿAjlān, of Banū Quḍāʿa. He died aged 115 during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya.

His brother Maʿn ibn ʿAdī had descendants and was killed at al-Yamāma.

Among ʿĀṣim’s descendants was Abū al-Baddāḥ ibn ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī al-ʿAjlānī, a nickname that became his usual name. His kunya was Abū ʿAmr, and hadith was transmitted from him. He died in the year 117, aged eighty-four.

Abū ʿAbs ibn Jabr ﵁

His name was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and he was from Khazraj. Abū ʿAbs wrote in Arabic before Islam. He died in the year 34 and was buried in al-Baqīʿ. He used to dye his hair with henna.

He had many descendants in Medina and Baghdad.

Khawwāt ibn Jubayr ibn al-Nuʿmān ﵁

He was from Khazraj. His kunya was Abū Ṣāliḥ—though it is also said his kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. In the pre-Islamic period, he was the man of the two wine-skins.

He died in Medina in the year 40 and had descendants. His brother was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jubayr, commander of the archers on the day of Uḥud. ʿAbd Allāh was killed that day and left no descendants.

Abū al-Yusr ﵁

He was Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr, one of the Anṣār. He was short and stout. He captured al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib at Badr and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ. He died in the year 55, during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya. He had descendants in Medina.

Abū Marthad al-Ghanawī ﵁

He was Kannāz ibn Ḥuṣayn, from Ghanī. He was the same age as Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—made him brothers with ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit.

He also made his son Marthad brothers with Ibn al-Ṣāmit, the brother of ʿUbāda.

Abū Marthad was tall, with abundant hair on his head. He died in the year 12 during the caliphate of Abū Bakr ﵁—aged sixty-six.

His son Marthad was killed as a martyr during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ—on the day of al-Rajīʿ. He was the commander of the detachment.

Misṭaḥ ibn Athātha ﵁

He was Misṭaḥ ibn Athātha ibn ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manāf. His kunya was Abū ʿAbbād. He took part at Badr, Uḥud, and all the campaigns.

Abū Bakr used to provide for him. He was the one who slandered ʿĀʾisha ﵂.

The man whom she was accused of being with was Ṣafwān ibn al-Muʿaṭṭal. [God, Exalted, cleared her of that.]

Suwaybiṭ ﵁

He was Suwaybiṭ ibn Saʿd ibn Ḥarmala, of ʿAbd al-Dār ibn Quṣayy. He was among those who migrated to Abyssinia. He took part at Badr and Uḥud and was a joker. He was the man whose story made the Prophet ﷺ—and his Companions laugh for a year. This happened when he went with Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁—on a trading journey to Buṣrā. Nuʿaymān was with them, and he too had taken part at Badr. He was in charge of the provisions. Suwaybiṭ said to him, “Feed me.” Nuʿaymān replied, “Wait until Abū Bakr comes.” Suwaybiṭ said, “By God, I’ll make you regret that!” They passed by some people, and Suwaybiṭ said to them:

“Will you buy a slave from me?”

They said, “Yes.”

He said, “He is a slave who talks, and he will tell you that he is free. If you are going to let him go when he says that to you, then don’t spoil my slave for me.”

They said, “We’ll buy him from you.” So they bought him for ten she-camels. Then they came and put a rope around his neck. Nuʿaymān said, “This man is making fun of you. I am free.” They replied, “We know your story,”

They went off with him. When Abū Bakr arrived, they told him, so he followed them, returned the camels to them, and took him back. When they came before the Prophet ﷺ—they told him, and he and his Companions laughed about it for a year.

Nuʿaymān was also a joker. The Prophet ﷺ—had him flogged four times for drinking wine. Once he passed by Makhrama ibn Nawfal, who had lost his sight. Makhrama said, “Is there no one to lead me so that I may urinate?” Nuʿaymān took his hand. When they reached the rear of the mosque, he said, “Here—urinate.” Makhrama urinated, and someone shouted at him. He said, “Who led me?” They said, “Nuʿaymān.” He said, “I owe it to God to strike him with this stick of mine.” When the news reached Nuʿaymān, he came to him and said, “Would you like to see Nuʿaymān?” He said, “Yes.” He said, “Then get up.” He got up and went with him. Nuʿaymān took him to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁—while he was praying, and said, “There you are—the man.”

Makhrama grasped the stick with both hands and struck him. The people said, “Commander of the Faithful!” He said, “Who led me?”

They said, “Nuʿaymān.” He said, “I shall never go to Nuʿaymān again.”

Diḥya ibn Khalīfa ﵁

He was Diḥya ibn Khalīfa ibn ʿĀmir, of the Khazraj. He embraced Islam early but did not take part in [the battle of] Badr. Because of his beauty and handsomeness, he was likened to Gabriel ﵇. Whenever he came to Medina, there was no young woman who did not go out to look at him. He lived until the time of Muʿāwiya.

ʿArāba al-Awsī ﵁

He was ʿArāba ibn Aws al-Qayẓī, whom al-Shammākh praised, saying:

[Wāfir]

I saw ʿArāba al-Awsī aspireto good deeds, with no peer beside him.

Whenever a banner was raised for glory,ʿArāba took it in his right hand.

ʿArāba took part in the day of Uḥud, but was deemed too young and sent back.

Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥamza

He was Waḥshī ibn Ḥarb, and was known by the kunya Abū Dasma. He was one of the Black men of Mecca and a slave of Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim. He killed Ḥamza, then came to the Prophet ﷺ—as a Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ—said to him, “Keep your face out of my sight.” He said:

“Whenever I saw him on the road, I took another route.” He went to Syria and settled in Ḥimṣ. He used to drink wine and wear safflower-dyed garments. He was the first man in Syria to be flogged for drinking wine. He left descendants in Syria.

Ḥaml ibn Mālik ibn al-Nābigha

He was from Hudhayl. He embraced Islam, then returned to the lands of his people, and later moved to Baṣra, where he built a house in the quarter of Hudhayl. After him, his house passed to ʿUmar ibn Mihrān the secretary.

Mujālid and Mujāshiʿ, sons of Masʿūd ﵄

They were from Sulaym. Mujālid suffered from a severe limp. His brother Mujāshiʿ ibn Masʿūd was one of the Emigrants.

After the conquest of Mecca, Mujāshiʿ brought his brother to the Prophet ﷺ—to pledge allegiance to him on the basis of emigration. The Prophet said, “There is no emigration after the conquest.”

Mujāshiʿ had a horse called al-Dabsāʾ, which he raced. It is said that he won fifty thousand dirhams in a single race.

He took part in the Battle of the Camel with ʿĀʾisha ﵂—and was killed. He left descendants in Baṣra.

ʿAlqama ibn ʿUlātha ﵁

He was the man who engaged ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl in a contest of boasts. Al-Aʿshā said of him: [Sarīʿ]

ʿAlqama, what are you beside ʿĀmir,the breaker of bowstrings and the avenger?

He had come in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ—and embraced Islam, but then apostatized and joined Caesar. Afterward he turned back and embraced Islam. ʿUmar appointed him governor of Ḥawrān, where he died.

Labīd ibn Rabīʿa, the poet ﵁

He was Labīd ibn Rabīʿa ibn Mālik ibn Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb.

Labīd came with the delegation of Banū Kilāb to the Prophet ﷺ—and he and they embraced Islam. They returned to their lands, and after his conversion he composed no poetry. Later, he and his sons came to Kūfa, but his sons returned to the desert as Bedouins.

Labīd remained there until he died, and was buried in the open country of Banū Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb.

He died on the night Muʿāwiya camped at al-Nukhayla to make peace with al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ﵄. It is also said that he died later.

He died at the age of one hundred and fifty-seven.

The delegate of al-Muntafiq

It is said that he was Laqīṭ ibn Ṣabra; it is also said that he was Laqīṭ ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Muntafiq, of Banū ʿUqayl. He was known by the kunya Abū Razīn.

They are unanimous that he was from ʿUqayl.

Muknaf ibn Zayd al-Khayl al-Ṭāʾī ﵁

Muknaf was the eldest of his father’s sons, and his father was known by his name. He embraced Islam and accompanied the Prophet ﷺ. He took part in the fighting against the apostates alongside Khālid ibn al-Walīd, as did his brother Ḥurayth ibn Zayd al-Khayl, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ—who also took part in the fighting against the apostates.

As for Zayd al-Khayl, he came to the Prophet ﷺ—who renamed him Zayd al-Khayr and granted him two tracts of land.

Medina was unhealthy. When Zayd left the Prophet, he said, “Zayd will not escape Umm Mildam.” When he reached his homeland, he died.

Ḥammād al-Rāwiya was a client of Muknaf.

Al-Ashʿath ibn Qays ﵁

His name was Maʿdīkarib ibn Qays. He was called al-Ashʿath because of his disheveled hair. He was from Kinda. Murād had killed his father, so he set out to avenge him, but was captured. He ransomed himself for three thousand camels. He came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ—with seventy men from Kinda and embraced Islam.

He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad.

When the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, al-Ashʿath refused to pledge allegiance to Abū Bakr ﵁. Abū Bakr’s governor fought him until he sought a guarantee of safety, accepting Abū Bakr’s judgment. The governor sent him to Abū Bakr. Al-Ashʿath asked Abū Bakr to keep him for his wars and to marry him to his sister, Umm Farwa. Abū Bakr did so.

He died in the year forty.

His son was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ashʿath, who rebelled against al-Ḥajjāj; the Qurʾān reciters and scholars joined him.

ʿIkrima ibn Abī Jahl ﵁

He embraced Islam after the conquest and was killed on the day of Yarmūk, during the caliphate of Abū Bakr ﵁. He left no descendants.

Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī ﵁

He was the man whom Muʿāwiya killed. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He had come in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ—and embraced Islam. He took part in [the battle of] al-Qādisiyya, the Battle of the Camel, and Ṣiffīn, alongside ʿAlī. Muʿāwiya killed him, along with a number of others, at Marj ʿAdhrāʾ. He had two sons who were partisans of ʿAlī, named ʿUbayd Allāh and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr had them executed. Ḥujr was killed in the year fifty-three.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwsaja al-Bajalī ﵁

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwsaja al-Bajalī was the Messenger of the Prophet ﷺ—to Banū Ḥāritha ibn ʿAmr ibn Qurayṭ. He carried a letter from him, inviting them to Islam.

They took the letter, washed it, and used it to patch the bottom of their bucket. They refused to answer him.

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said, “What is the matter with them? May God take away their reason! They are people of trembling, foolishness, and confused speech!”

Fīrūz al-Daylamī
