He was one of the sons of the Persians whom Kisrā had sent to Yemen. They drove the Abyssinians out of Yemen and gained control of it. Fīrūz was the man who killed al-Aswad ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAnsī, the false prophet in Yemen. The Messenger of God ﷺ—said, “The righteous man, Fīrūz al-Daylamī, killed him.” Fīrūz had come in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ—and related traditions from him in which he is mentioned. He is accordingly called al-Daylamī al-Ḥimyarī. He was called Ḥimyarī because he settled among Ḥimyar.

Fīrūz died during the caliphate of ʿUthmān.

Al-ʿAjlānī

The man who performed the mutual imprecation before the Messenger of God ﷺ—between himself and his wife.

He was ʿUwaymir ibn al-Ḥārith.

ʿIkrima said:

“I saw the son of the mutual imprecation as governor of Egypt, and no one claimed him as a son.”

### Al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī

He embraced Islam before the conquest of Mecca. On the day Mecca was conquered, he was present with the Messenger of God ﷺ—with more than nine hundred men, mounted on horses and carrying lances and shields. He used to return to the lands of his people and lived neither in Mecca nor in Medina.

His son Jalthama related traditions from the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Barza al-Aslamī ﵁

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Naḍla. It is also said that he was Naḍla ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

He died in Khurāsān while on campaign.

Al-Khashkhāsh

He was al-Khashkhāsh ibn Khalaf. His father was known as al-Mujaffar.14

He was from Banū al-ʿAnbar.

He was the man to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—said, “Do not let your left hand wrong your right.”

He had two sons, Mālik and ʿUbayd, who held governorships. Mālik had a son named Ḥuṣayn, who governed Maysān for Ziyād and remained in office there for forty years. He had another son, named al-Ḥurr. Among his descendants was Muʿādh ibn al-ʿAnbarī, who served as judge of Baṣra for al-Rashīd.

Among the clients of the house of al-Khashkhāsh was Fīrūz, the most eminent client in Iraq. He held governorships and joined Ibn al-Ashʿath’s rebellion. Al-Ḥajjāj said, “Whoever brings me Fīrūz’s head will have ten thousand dirhams.” Fīrūz said, “Whoever brings me al-Ḥajjāj’s head will have one hundred thousand dirhams.” When Ibn al-Ashʿath was defeated, Fīrūz fled to Khurāsān. Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab captured him and sent him to al-Ḥajjāj. Al-Ḥajjāj said to him, “Tell me where your wealth is.” Fīrūz said, “Will you guarantee my safety?” He replied, “No.” Fīrūz called out, “Anyone who has money belonging to Fīrūz may keep it; I release him from any obligation to return it.” Al-Ḥajjāj ordered that reeds be split for him and tied around him. Then he had them peeled off one by one until his body was cut open. He poured vinegar and salt over him until he died.

### ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār

He was ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār ibn Abī Ḥimār ibn Nājiya ibn ʿIqāl al-Dārimī. Abū Ḥimār ibn Nājiya ibn ʿIqāl al-Dārimī was the brother of Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Nājiya, the grandfather of the poet al-Farazdaq.

ʿIyāḍ was the man who presented a gift to the Prophet ﷺ—while he was still an unbeliever.

The Prophet said, “I do not accept provisions from unbelievers.” We know of no descendants of his.

Al-Ashajj al-ʿAbdī

He was al-Mundhir ibn ʿĀʾidh, from ʿAṣr. ʿAmr ibn Qays was his sister’s son.

He was the first man from Rabīʿa to embrace Islam. Al-Ashajj had sent him to the Messenger of God ﷺ—to learn about him. When he met the Prophet ﷺ—he believed in him and went to al-Ashajj to tell him about him. Al-Ashajj embraced Islam and came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said, “There are two qualities in you that God loves: forbearance and modesty.”

Al-Jārūd al-ʿAbdī

He was Bishr ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥunash ibn al-Muʿallā, from ʿAbd al-Qays. He was known by the kunya Abū Ghiyāth. He was called al-Jārūd because he fled with his camels to his maternal uncles, Banū Shaybān. The camels had a disease, and it spread among his maternal uncles’ camels and destroyed them. Therefore the poet said:

[Ṭawīl]

Al-Jārūd stripped the young camels of Bakr ibn Wāʾil

Al-Jārūd embraced Islam during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ—and engaged the enemy at ʿAqabat al-Ṭīn, where he was killed. It was therefore named ʿAqabat al-Jārūd.

His son was ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jārūd, nicknamed “Bird of the Neck” because he was short.

He was the leader of ʿAbd al-Qays, and the tribesmen of Baṣra gathered around him, along with the people of The people of Kūfa appointed him to lead them at Rastuqādh. They fought al-Ḥajjāj, who defeated them. Al-Ḥajjāj seized him and had him crucified.

His son was al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd, who governed Iṣṭakhr on behalf of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

His son al-Ḥakam ibn al-Mundhir was the chief of ʿAbd al-Qays. The Liar al-Ḥarmāzī said of him:

[Rajaz]

O Ḥakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd,

The pavilion of glory is spread above you.

You are the generous son of the praised generous man;

You grew in generosity, in a house of generosity—

For a branch may grow from the root of a branch.

He was also called Abū Ghaylān. He died in al-Ḥajjāj’s prison, known as al-Dīmās.

Ṣuḥār ibn al-ʿAbbās al-ʿAbdī

He came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ—and became a Muslim. He was one of the most eloquent and articulate of men. He was ruddy-complexioned and blue-eyed.

One day Muʿāwiya said to him, “O blue-eyed one.” He replied, “The falcon is blue.” Muʿāwiya said, “O red one.” He replied, “Gold is red.”

He was an ʿUthmānī, while ʿAbd al-Qays were Shiʿites, so he differed from them.

He was the grandfather of Jaʿfar ibn Zayd, who was virtuous, excellent, devout in worship, and diligent in religious practice.

Ṣuḥār transmitted two or three reports from the Prophet ﷺ.

Khuraym ibn Fātik al-Asadī

He was from Banū Asad. He accompanied the Prophet ﷺ—and transmitted reports from him.

His son was Ayman ibn Khuraym, the poet.

He was a leper. He used to keep company with the Marwānids, conversing and dining with them.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad told me: al-Aṣmaʿī told us: Zakariyyā al-Ḥabaṭī told us, from his father, who said:

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān said to Ayman ibn Khuraym al-Asadī, “Your father and your uncle both accompanied the Prophet. Take this money and go fight Ibn al-Zubayr.” He refused and said:

[Wāfir]

I am not one to kill a man who prays,

For the authority of another Qurashī.

He has his authority; I would bear the burden—

God forbid folly and rashness!

Shall I kill a believer and live on,

Though my life would profit me nothing?

The Companions Whose Deaths Occurred Late ﵃

Abū Muḥammad said: al-Wāqidī said:

The last of the Companions to die in Kūfa was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā. He died in the year eighty-six.

The last of the Companions to die in Medina was Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī, in the year ninety-one. It is said that he was one hundred years old.

The last of the Companions to die in Basra was Anas ibn Mālik, in the year ninety-one. It is also said: in the year ninety-three.

The last of the Companions to die in Syria was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, in the year eighty-eight.

Among those whose deaths occurred late was Wāʾila ibn al-Asqaʿ. He died in Syria in the year eighty-five, at the age of ninety-eight. He was from Banū Layth ibn Kināna.

Abū al-Ṭufayl al-Kinānī ﵁

He was Abū al-Ṭufayl ʿĀmir ibn Wāthila. He saw the Prophet ﷺ.

He was the last person to die among those who had seen him.

He died after the year one hundred. He fought alongside ʿAlī in all the engagements, and was the standard-bearer of al-Mukhtār. He believed in the Return. He is the one who said: [Ṭawīl]

I remained a single arrow in the quiver,

To be shot, or for the arrow’s breaker to break it.

He is the one who said: [Ṭawīl]

Do they call me an old man, though I have lived an age,

While the women among the wives turn away from me?

My head did not turn gray from years passing one after another;

Rather, the events have turned it gray.

Names of Those Whose Hearts Were Reconciled

Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and his son Muʿāwiya; then their Islam became sound. Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām; then his Islam became sound. Al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, the brother of Abū Jahl ibn Hishām; then his Islam became sound. [Ṣafwān ibn Umayya; then his Islam became sound. Suhayl ibn ʿAmr; then his Islam became sound. [Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā; then his Islam became sound.] Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Ḥāritha al-Thaqafī; ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr; al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis; Mālik ibn ʿAwf al-Naṣrī; and al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī; then his Islam became sound. Qays ibn Makhrama; then his Islam became sound. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim; then his Islam became sound.

Names of the Hypocrites

Those who intended to cast the Messenger of God ﷺ—from the mountain pass during the expedition to Tabūk were: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy; Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ—he was the father of the one who used to write for the Messenger of God ﷺ—and write “Mighty, Wise” in place of “Forgiving, Merciful”; Abū Ḥāḍir al-Aʿrābī; al-Jallās ibn Suwayd ibn Ṣāmit; Mujammiʿ ibn Ḥāritha; Mulayḥ al-Taymī—he was the one who stole the perfume of the Kaʿba and apostatized from Islam, then went away, and it is not known where he went; Ḥuṣayn ibn Numayr—he was the one who raided the alms-dates and stole them; Ṭuʿayma ibn Ubayriq; and Murra ibn Rabīʿ.

Abū ʿĀmir was their leader. They built the Mosque of Harm, and he was the father of Ḥanẓala, the one washed by the angels.

Names of the Three Who Were Left Behind, and About Whom the Qurʾān Was Revealed

Kaʿb ibn Mālik, Murāra ibn al-Rabīʿ, and Hilāl ibn Umayya.

175/ Names of the Caliphs

Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān

Abū Sufyān’s name was Ṣakhr ibn Ḥarb ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murra ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna.

Abū Sufyān had become a Muslim shortly before the conquest of Mecca. The Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed him to collect the alms of al-Ṭāʾif. He lost one of his eyes while with the Prophet ﷺ—on one of the military expeditions. He lived on into the caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁—and became blind before he died.

He died in Medina in the year thirty-two, at the age of eighty-eight.

Abū Sufyān’s mother was Ṣafiyya bt. al-Ḥārith, from Qays ʿAylān.

Muʿāwiya’s mother was Hind bt. ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.

It is said that one of his eyes was lost on the Day of al-Ṭāʾif, and the other on the Day of al-Yarmūk.

Abū Sufyān’s children included Umm Ḥabība—the wife of the Prophet ﷺ—whose name was Ramla; Āmina; ʿAmr; Hind; Ṣakhra; Muʿāwiya; ʿUtba; Juwayriyya; and Umm al-Ḥakam—these four were by Hind bt. ʿUtba—as well as Ḥanẓala, ʿUtba, Muḥammad, Ziyād, Yazīd, Ramla the Younger, and Maymūna.

As for ʿAmr ibn Abī Sufyān, he was taken captive on the Day of Badr, but Abū Sufyān did not pay his ransom. Abū Sufyān captured a Muslim man, and the Prophet ﷺ—released ʿAmr, while Abū Sufyān released the Muslim.

ʿAmr ibn Abī Sufyān left no descendants.

As for Ḥanẓala ibn Abī Sufyān, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib killed him on the Day of Badr. He left no descendants.

As for Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, he was called Yazīd the Good. Abū Bakr appointed him over Syria, and ʿUmar retained him after Abū Bakr. Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb fought under the standard of his son Yazīd on the Day of al-Yarmūk. Yazīd died in Syria while serving as ʿUmar’s governor, during the plague of ʿAmwās, in the year eighteen.

ʿUmar appointed his brother Muʿāwiya to the office Yazīd had held.

Yazīd left no descendants.

As for ʿAnbasa ibn Abī Sufyān, Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Asīd flogged him for drinking wine in al-Ṭāʾif.

He had children, but none left descendants except ʿUthmān ibn ʿAnbasa.

As for Muḥammad ibn Abī Sufyān, he fathered ʿUthmān, who served as governor in Medina for Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. The people of Medina regarded him as an ill omen, and the Battle of al-Ḥarra occurred because of him.

As for ʿUtba ibn Abī Sufyān, he was considered weak. He took part in the Battle of the Camel with ʿĀʾisha ﵂—and Muʿāwiya appointed him governor of Egypt.

He had children, including Muʿāwiya ibn ʿUtba, whom Muʿāwiya appointed governor of Medina.

Another was ʿAmr ibn ʿUtba, who went out with Ibn al-Ashʿath and was killed. ʿUtba had many descendants.

Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān

As for Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān, he was called Abū al-Mughīra. His mother was Asmāʾ bt. al-Aʿwar, from Banū ʿAbd Shams ibn Saʿd.

This is the account of Abū al-Yaqẓān.

Someone else said that his mother was Sumayya bt. Abī Bakra.

We have related her story in the account of Abū Bakra.

Ziyād was born in al-Ṭāʾif in the year of the Conquest. He was a scribe for al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, then wrote for Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, then for Ibn ʿAbbās. Ziyād was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁—and ʿAlī appointed him over Fārs. Muʿāwiya wrote to him, threatening him. Ziyād wrote back: “You threaten me, while ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib stands between you and me? By God, if you reach me, you will find me a redoubtable man, striking with the sword.” Then Muʿāwiya appointed him over Basra and its districts. When al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba died, Muʿāwiya placed both Iraqs under him; he was the first to be given both. He governed for eight years, five of them over Basra and its districts. He died in Kūfa in the year fifty-three.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad told me: al-Aṣmaʿī told us: Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim told us, from al-Zubayr ibn al-Kharīt, from Abū Lubayd, who said:

Ziyād passed by us when he was governor of Basra. With him was one man—or two men—on a mule, with the rope wrapped around its neck beneath the bridle.

Ziyād’s children were ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, al-Mughīra, Muḥammad, Abū Sufyān, ʿUbayd Allāh, and ʿAbd Allāh—their mother was Marjāna—as well as Salm, ʿUthmān, ʿAbbād, al-Rabīʿ, Abū ʿUbayda, Yazīd, ʿAnbasa, Umm Muʿāwiya, ʿAmr, al-Ghuṣn, ʿUtba, Abān, Jaʿfar, Ibrāhīm, Saʿīd, and twenty-three daughters.

As for ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, he was called Abū Ḥafṣ. He was speckled and handsome.

Ziyād married his mother, Marjāna, to Shīrūya al-Uswārī, and entrusted ʿUbayd Allāh to her. He grew up among the Asāwira, and so acquired a lisp. Muʿāwiya appointed him over Khurāsān, then, after his father, over both Iraqs for eight years: five over Basra alone, and three over both Iraqs. When Yazīd died, the people of Basra rose against him and drove him from his residence. He sought protection with Masʿūd ibn ʿAmr al-Azdī. When Masʿūd was killed, he set out for Syria and joined Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. At the Battle of al-Marj, he commanded one of Marwān’s two wings.

When Marwān won, he sent him back to Iraq. As he neared Kūfa, al-Mukhtār dispatched Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ashtar al-Nakhaʿī against him. They met near the Zāb, and ʿUbayd Allāh was killed.

He left no descendants. He was killed on the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ in the year sixty-seven.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ziyād, he was called Abū Khālid. Muʿāwiya appointed him over Khurāsān. He had descendants in Basra.

Al-Mughīra ibn Ziyād left no descendants, and Muḥammad ibn Ziyād likewise left no descendants.

Abū Sufyān ibn Ziyād fled the devastating plague to the desert. He contracted the plague there and died there. He had descendants in Basra.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ziyād had many descendants in Basra.

As for Salm ibn Ziyād, he was called Abū Ḥarb, and was the most generous of the Banū Ziyād.

Yazīd appointed him over Khurāsān. Ibn ʿArāda said of him: [Ṭawīl]

I reproached Salm, but when I shunned him

And kept company with others, I wept for Salm.

He died in Basra. He had descendants.

As for ʿAbbād ibn Ziyād, he was called Abū Ḥarb. Muʿāwiya appointed him over Sijistān for nine years. Ibn Mufarrigh said of him: “ʿAbbād got there first, and his beard followed.”

He had descendants in Syria and Basra.

As for al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād, he was lame. He had a few descendants in Basra.

Salm ibn Ziyād appointed Abū ʿUbayda ibn Ziyād over Kābul. He was captured, and Salm ransomed him for seven hundred thousand dirhams. He had descendants.

Salm ibn Ziyād also appointed Yazīd ibn Ziyād over Sijistān, where the enemy killed him.

He left no descendants.

ʿAnbasa ibn Ziyād died on the road to Mecca during the devastating plague. He left no descendants.

ʿUtba ibn Ziyād had many descendants in Basra.

ʿAmr, al-Ghuṣn, Abān, Jaʿfar, Ibrāhīm, and Saʿīd left no descendants.

Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān ﵁

As for Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān, he was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest and wrote for the Prophet ﷺ. He governed Syria for ʿUmar and ʿUthmān for twenty years, and became caliph in the year forty, when he was sixty-two years old.

He received word that the people of al-Kūfah had pledged allegiance to al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, so he set out intending to go to al-Kūfah.

Al-Ḥasan set out to meet him. They met at Maskin, in the territory of al-Kūfah. Al-Ḥasan made peace with Muʿāwiyah and pledged allegiance to him, then entered al-Kūfah with him. Afterward, Muʿāwiyah returned to Syria. He appointed al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah over al-Kūfah and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir over al-Baṣrah, then combined the two governorships for Ziyād. He was the first to have both combined for him.

Muʿāwiyah held the caliphate for twenty years less one month. He died in Damascus in the year sixty, aged eighty-two.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

He died aged seventy-eight. His illness was al-nāqibāt—that is, al-dubaylah.

No child was born to him during his caliphate. This was because al-Burayk al-Ṣuraymī struck him on the buttock, after which he could no longer have children. Muʿāwiyah had the following children: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiyah, by a slave woman; Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah, whose mother was Maysūn bt. Baḥdal al-Kalbīyah; ʿAbd Allāh, Hind, Ramlah, and Ṣafīyah.

As for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, he left no descendants.

As for ʿAbd Allāh, he was weak, and his nickname was Munqib. He had no male descendants.

He had a daughter called ʿĀtikah, whom Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik married.

About her it was said: [kāmil]

O house of ʿĀtikah, from which I keep away

Fearing the foes, while my heart is bound to it.

Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah

As for Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah, he was known by the kunya Abū Khālid. He became caliph. Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ﵄—set out for al-Kūfah, over which ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād governed on behalf of Yazīd. ʿUbayd Allāh sent ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ against him, and he fought him and killed al-Ḥusayn—may God’s mercy and good pleasure be upon him. The revolt of Ibn al-Zubayr then erupted, and he expelled the Umayyads who were in Medina. Yazīd sent Muslim ibn ʿUqbah al-Murrī with a large army to fight Ibn al-Zubayr. He marched with them until he reached Medina, fought its people and defeated them, and gave the city over to pillage for three days. This was the battle of al-Ḥarrah.

Then Muslim ibn ʿUqbah marched to Mecca, but died on the way before reaching it, and was buried at Qudayd.

Command of the army was given to al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Numayr al-Sakūnī. He proceeded with the army, and they besieged ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr. The Kaʿbah was set on fire until its walls collapsed and its roof fell. Then news reached them of Yazīd’s death, and they turned back toward Syria.

Yazīd’s reign lasted three years and some months. He died at Ḥuwwārīn, in the district of Damascus, in the year sixty-four, aged thirty-eight.

Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah had the following children: Khālid, ʿAbd Allāh the elder, Abū Sufyān, ʿAbd Allāh the younger, ʿUmar, ʿĀtikah, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿAbd Allāh—who was nicknamed Aṣghar al-Aṣāghir (“the smallest of the smallest”)—ʿUthmān, ʿUtbah the one-eyed, Yazīd, Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, Umm Yazīd, Umm ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and Ramlah.

As for Khālid ibn Yazīd, he was known by the kunya Abū Hāshim. He was among the most learned of Quraysh in the various fields of knowledge, and he composed poetry. He had many descendants in Syria.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd, he was among the finest and most devout people of his time.

As for Muʿāwiyah ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah, he held the caliphate after Yazīd—he was seventeen years old—for forty days.

Ibn Isḥāq said:

He held it for twenty days.

Then he died. He was known by the kunya Abū Laylā. The poet said of him: [basīṭ]

I see a turmoil whose cauldrons boil;

After Abū Laylā, kingship belongs to whoever prevails.

Muʿāwiyah ibn Yazīd left no descendants. Yazīd had many descendants through his other children.

Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam

When Muʿāwiyah ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah died, the people of Syria pledged allegiance to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayyah ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Quṣayy ibn Kilāb ibn Murrah ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah.

Marwān was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Malik. His father, al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, had been banished by the Messenger of God ﷺ—and embraced Islam on the day Mecca was conquered. He died during the caliphate of ʿUthmān. The reason the Messenger of God ﷺ—banished him was that:

He used to disclose his secrets, so the Prophet cursed him and exiled him to Baṭn Wajj. He remained in exile throughout the Prophet’s life, the caliphate of Abū Bakr, and that of ʿUmar. Then ʿUthmān brought him back and gave him one hundred thousand dirhams.

Al-Ḥakam had twenty-one sons and eight daughters.

Marwān was born two years after the Hijrah. When the Messenger of God ﷺ—died, he was eight years old.

He governed a district of Ardashīr Khurrah for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir. Then he governed al-Baḥrayn for Muʿāwiyah, and later governed Medina for him twice; after that, allegiance was pledged to him as caliph.

Muʿāwiyah had appointed al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Fihrī—of Kinānah—over al-Kūfah after Ziyād. When Marwān became caliph, al-Ḍaḥḥāk joined Ibn al-Zubayr. He fought Marwān on the day of Marj Rāhiṭ, and Marwān killed him.

Marwān’s reign lasted ten months. He died in Syria in the year sixty-five, aged sixty-three.

It is said that he said to Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah: “Son of the soft one!”—his mother was his wife. When she heard of it, she sat on his face and killed him; thus he is counted among those killed by women.

Marwān had the following children: ʿAbd al-Malik; Muʿāwiyah; Umm ʿAmr; ʿUbayd Allāh; Abān; Dāwūd; ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān; Umm ʿUthmān; ʿAmr; Umm ʿAmr; Bishr; and Muḥammad.

As for Muʿāwiyah ibn Marwān, he was feeble-minded. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Mughīrah.

He had the following children: ʿAbd al-Malik, al-Mughīrah, and Bishr.

Muʿāwiyah was the one who said to his wife’s father: “You have married your daughter to a clan the like of which she has never seen!” He replied: “Had you been a eunuch, we would not have married her to you.”

He came upon a miller whose donkey had a bell around its neck. He asked him, “Why did you put a bell around its neck?” The miller replied, “Sometimes I doze off and it stops. If I don’t hear the bell, I call out to it.” He said, “What if it gets up and shakes its head? How will you know?” The miller said:

“Who could have the like of the prince’s intelligence?”

As for Abān ibn Marwān, he governed Palestine for his brother ʿAbd al-Malik, and al-Ḥajjāj was in charge of his security.

Abān had a son, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abān.

As for ʿAmr ibn Marwān, I know of no descendants of his.

As for Muḥammad ibn Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, he was the most forceful of the Marwānids. He killed Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ashtar and Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr at the monastery of al-Jāthlīq, between Syria and al-Kūfah. He governed al-Jazīrah, and his son Marwān ibn Muḥammad was the last of the Umayyads to hold the caliphate.

As for Dāwūd ibn Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, he was known by the kunya Abū Sulaymān and was one-eyed. It was said of him:

“A one-eyed man has taken the place of the dark-eyed beauty”.15

As for Bishr ibn Marwān, he was known by the kunya Abū Marwān. He governed al-Kūfah, then al-Baṣrah was added to his governorship. He went there and drank al-adhriṭūs, and died there. He was the first governor to die in al-Baṣrah. He had descendants.

As for ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān, he was known by the kunya Abū al-Aṣbagh. He was heir apparent after ʿAbd al-Malik, and Kathīr composed panegyrics about him. He was the father of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. We shall mention him with his brothers in the section on his caliphate, God willing.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān

As for ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, he was known by the kunya Abū al-Walīd and nicknamed Rashḥ al-Ḥajar (“Stone Sweat”) for his stinginess. He was also known by the kunya Abū Dhubbān (“Father of Flies”) because of his foul breath.

Muʿāwiyah had appointed him in place of Zayd ibn Thābit over the register of Medina when he was sixteen years old. His father Marwān then appointed him governor of Hajar. Afterward, he made him his successor as caliph. He became caliph after his father in the year sixty-five.

Ibn al-Zubayr was pledged allegiance as caliph in the year sixty-five. He rebuilt the Kaʿbah, and the people of al-Baṣrah and al-Kūfah pledged allegiance to him.

Al-Mukhtār ibn ʿUbayd rose up in al-Kūfah in the year sixty-six, during the rule of Ibn al-Zubayr, and expelled from al-Kūfah ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṭīʿ, the governor appointed by Ibn al-Zubayr.

Then the people of al-Kūfah revolted against al-Mukhtār. They fought one another at Jubbānat al-Sabīʿ, and al-Mukhtār defeated them. Al-Mukhtār also sent al-Aḥmar ibn Shumayṭ to al-Baṣrah to fight Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, but Muṣʿab killed him at al-Madār. Muṣʿab then advanced and besieged al-Mukhtār in his palace in al-Kūfah, then killed him in the year sixty-nine. ʿAbd al-Malik marched to fight Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr. They met in the territory of Maskin; Muṣʿab was killed, and ʿAbd al-Malik entered al-Kūfah, whose people pledged allegiance to him.

He sent al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf against ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibn al-Zubayr was killed in the year seventy-three, aged ninety-three. The revolt of Ibn al-Zubayr, from the death of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah until his own death, had lasted nine years, three months, and some days.

That year al-Ḥajjāj led the pilgrimage. He demolished Ibn al-Zubayr’s construction of the Kaʿbah and rebuilt it on its original foundations. Then, when he had finished rebuilding the Kaʿbah, he returned to Medina.

Then ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to al-Ḥajjāj, appointing him governor of Iraq. He set out for it in the year seventy-five. Dinars and dirhams bearing Arabic inscriptions were struck for him in the year seventy-six. The Juhāf flood, which carried off the pilgrims at Mecca, occurred in the year eighty. It is said that al-Juḥfah was called al-Ḥajfah that year because the flood there swept away many pilgrims, their possessions, and their mounts. Its name had been Muhīʿah. This happened on a Monday. Abū al-Sanābil said: [rajaz]

My eye has never seen a Monday like that Monday,

More sorrowful, and more tear-provoking to the eye.

The veiled women came out, running,

Out in the open, climbing two mountains.

The flood swept away the people of the two garrison towns.

The revolt of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ashʿath erupted in the year eighty-two. The battle of al-Zāwiyah took place at al-Baṣrah in the year eighty-three, and the battle of Dayr al-Jamājim took place that same year.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

Ibn al-Ashʿath had four battles: one in al-Ahwāz, one at al-Zāwiyah, one at Dayr al-Jamājim, and one at Dujayl.

He said: Abū ʿUbaydah said:

It was called Dayr al-Jamājim because drinking cups were made there from wood.

Al-Ḥajjāj built Wāsiṭ in the year eighty-three.

ʿAbd al-Malik died in Damascus in the year eighty-six, aged sixty-two. He had his teeth bound with gold.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān had the following children: Marwān the elder, al-Walīd, Sulaymān, ʿĀʾishah, Yazīd, Marwān the younger, Hishām, Abū Bakr, Fāṭimah, Maslamah, ʿAbd Allāh, Saʿīd, al-Ḥajjāj, Muḥammad, al-Mundhir, ʿAnbasah, and Qubayṣah.

Al-Mundhir and Qubayṣah left no descendants. ʿAnbasah had no child except al-Fayḍ ibn ʿAnbasah.

As for al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, he had a son, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who was the one charged with killing al-Walīd ibn Yazīd; he had been responsible for besieging him at al-Bukhrāʾ. As for Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, he was nicknamed Saʿīd al-Khayr (“Saʿīd the Good”) and resided at a place called Nahr Saʿīd. He had descendants. Nahr Saʿīd is named after him. It had been a thicket inhabited by wild beasts; he was granted it as a fief and cultivated it.

As for ʿĀʾishah, she was married to Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah.

Fāṭimah was married to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, he governed Egypt for al-Walīd. He had descendants.

As for Maslamah, he was known by the kunya Abū Saʿīd and nicknamed al-Jarādah al-Ṣafrāʾ (“the Yellow Locust”), because a yellow cast used to appear on him. He was brave and made many conquests in the territory of the Byzantines, among them Ṭuwānah.

He governed Iraq for several months. He had many descendants.

As for Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, his name was Bakkār. He was foolish, and he was the one who said, about a falcon he owned that had flown away: “Shut the gates of the city, lest the falcon get out”. He had descendants.

al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik

As for al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, he was known by the kunya Abū al-ʿAbbās. He assumed the caliphate after his father. His rule was wicked. He assumed power in the year eighty-six. In the year eighty-eight, al-Ṭawāna, in the lands of the Byzantines, was conquered by his brother Maslama. In that year he built the mosque of Damascus. al-Walīd appointed ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz governor of Medina for seven years and five months.

al-Ḥajjāj died during his caliphate at Wāsiṭ, in the month of Ramaḍān in the year ninety-five. He had reached the age of fifty-three.

He appointed his son ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Ḥajjāj to lead the prayer, and Yazīd ibn AbīMuslim over the land tax. When news of al-Ḥajjāj’s death reached al-Walīd, he sent Yazīd ibn Abī Kabsha to lead the prayer.

al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik died at Damascus in the year ninety-six, having reached the age of forty-eight. His rule lasted nine years and eight months.

al-Walīd had fourteen sons, among them Yazīd ibn al-Walīd—who assumed the caliphate, and whom we shall mention in his place—and ʿUmar ibn al-Walīd, who was called the Stallion of the Banū Marwān. Sixty men of his own lineage would ride with him. His descendants were numerous. Among them were:

Bishr ibn al-Walīd, the learned man of the Banū al-Walīd;

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Walīd. His brother Yazīd ibn al-Walīd appointed him as his successor. When Marwān ibn Muḥammad marched against him, he renounced the caliphate and handed it over to Marwān;

al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd, the horseman of the Banū Marwān. His mother was a Christian.

Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik

Then, after al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, allegiance was given to his brother Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

He was known by the kunya Abū Ayyūb.

He was fair-skinned, curly-haired, and eloquent. He grew up in the desert among his maternal uncles, the Banū ʿAbs. His rule began in the year ninety-six. It began well and ended well, for he restored wrongfully seized property to its owners, brought back those who had been deported, released the prisoners who were in Baṣra, appointed ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz as his successor, and sent his brother Maslama on the summer campaign. Maslama reached Constantinople and remained there until Sulaymān died. The poet said of him: [rajaz]

O caliph, rightly guided,

a caliph named for the Prophet,

so that the ally may take the ally,

and he demolished al-Dīmās and al-Mansī,

and made both the eastern and western regions secure.

al-Farazdaq said of him: [sarīʿ]

Indeed, we hope that he will restore for us

the ways of the caliphs of the Banū Fihr.

When he assumed power, he had pledged allegiance to his son Ayyūb ibn Sulaymān. He dismissed Yazīd ibn Abī Kabsha and Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim. He appointed Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab to command the forces in Iraq, and Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Tamīmī over its land tax.

Sulaymān died at Dābiq in the year ninety-eight, at the age of forty-five.

Sulaymān had fourteen sons, among them Ayyūb. He was chaste and cultivated. His father had pledged allegiance to him and made him his designated successor, but he died during his father’s lifetime in Syria. He left no descendants.

184/ ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had ten children: ʿUmar, Abū Bakr, Muḥammad, ʿĀṣim—their mother was Umm ʿĀṣim, daughter of ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—al-Aṣbagh, Sahl, Suhayl, Umm al-Ḥakam, Zabbān, and Umm al-Banīn.

As for ʿĀṣim, he had a son named Sufyān. Sufyān married Āmina, daughter of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and she bore him al-Aṣbagh, who was effeminate.

As for al-Aṣbagh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he was learned in knowledge of what would come to pass. He died in Egypt before his father. He left descendants. Among them was Diḥya, daughter of Muṣʿab ibn al-Aṣbagh, who was knowledgeable about what would come to pass.

As for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he was known by the kunya Abū Ḥafṣ. He was the most conspicuous in physical appearance of the Banū Umayya: an animal struck him in the face. When his brother al-Aṣbagh saw the mark, he said, “God is greatest! This is the conspicuously marked man of the Banū Marwān who will rule.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—used to say, “Among my descendants there will be a man with a mark on his face who will fill the earth with justice.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“It is in the Book of Daniel: al-Dardūq the conspicuously marked one.”

ʿUmar assumed power after Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who had designated him as his successor. He dismissed Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab and Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Iraq, and appointed over Kūfa— ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and over Baṣra ʿAdī ibn Arṭāh al-Fazārī.

He died at Dayr Samʿān, in the territory of Ḥimṣ, in the year one hundred and one, at the age of thirty-nine.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz had fourteen sons, among them ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He was among the most devout of men and died before his father, at the age of nineteen and a half.

Among them was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. He was brave and generous. He governed the two Iraqs for Yazīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik for six months. When Yazīd died, the people of Iraq wanted to pledge allegiance to him as caliph. He was the one who dug the canal of Ibn ʿUmar at Baṣra.

He left descendants.

Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik

After ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, allegiance was given to Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He was known by the kunya Abū Khālid.

He was a man of amusement and pleasures, and was devoted to Ḥabāba and Sallāma. During his rule, Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab rose in revolt at Baṣra. He seized ʿAdī ibn Arṭāh and bound him, then left Baṣra heading for Kūfa. Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik sent against him his brother Maslama and his nephew al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd. They met at al-ʿAqr, in the land of Bābil. Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab was killed in the year one hundred and two, then Maslama returned to Syria. Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik appointed ʿUmar ibn Hubayra over the two Iraqs.

Yazīd died in the territory of Ḥawrān, in Shaʿbān of the year one hundred and five. His rule lasted four years and one month. He had reached the age of twenty-nine.

Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik had eight sons, among them ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. His ancestry included seven caliphs: his father Yazīd, his grandfather ʿAbd al-Malik, and ʿAbd al-Malik’s father Marwān. His father’s mother was ʿĀtika, daughter of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. The mother of ʿAbd Allāh was Umm Saʿīd, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. The mother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān was a daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁.

Among his descendants was al-Walīd ibn Yazīd. He was known by the kunya Abū al-ʿAbbās. He was immoral and foolish, assumed the caliphate, and was killed.

Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik

After Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, allegiance was given to Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Walīd. He was cross-eyed and the most resolute of them. He dismissed ʿUmar ibn Hubayra and appointed Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī over Iraq in the year one hundred and six. Then, in the year one hundred and twenty, he appointed Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar over Iraq.

During his rule, Zayd ibn ʿAlī—may God’s mercy be upon him and his pure forefathers—was killed. Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar killed him at Kūfa in the year one hundred and twenty-one.

During his rule, Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik fought Khāqān, king of the Turks, killed him, and built al-Bāb in the year one hundred and thirteen. Hishām died at al-Ruṣāfa, in the territory of Qinnasrīn, in Rabīʿ al-Ākhir of the year one hundred and twenty-five. He had reached the age of fifty-six. His rule lasted twenty years less some months.

Hishām had ten sons, among them Muʿāwiya ibn Hishām. His son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Hishām took control of al-Andalus and died there. His descendants there are numerous.

Among them was Sulaymān ibn Hishām. He met Abū al-ʿAbbās, who gave him a guarantee of safety, and he came to him; Abū al-ʿAbbās seated him beside himself. Sadīf, the poet and client of Abū al-ʿAbbās, said: [khafīf]

Do not let what you see of men deceive you:

beneath their ribs lies a grievous disease.

So draw the sword and raise the whip

until you see no Umayyad upon its back.

Abū al-ʿAbbās killed him.

Among them was Saʿīd ibn Hishām, whose mother was a Christian.

186/ al-Walīd ibn Yazīd

After Hishām, allegiance was given to al-Walīd ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He was known by the kunya Abū al-ʿAbbās. He was immoral and foolish, drank wine, spent his days in amusement and love poetry, and composed melodies for the songs of singers. Yazīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik marched against him and killed him. The person who carried this out was ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

He was killed at al-Bakhrāʾ. His rule lasted one year, two months, and a little more than twenty nights. He had reached the age of forty-two.

al-Walīd had the sons al-Ḥakam and ʿUthmān. The two were called “the twin lambs.” He had pledged allegiance to them, but they were killed with their father.

Yazīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik

Yazīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik entered Damascus in the year one hundred and twenty-six, and allegiance was given to him. His conduct was praiseworthy and approved. He was known by the kunya Abū Khālid, and his epithet was “the Deficient One,” because he reduced the soldiers’ stipends.

He appointed Manṣūr ibn Jumhūr al-Kalbī over Iraq. When Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar learned of this, he fled to Syria.

Yazīd ibn al-Walīd died in Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year one hundred and six, having reached the age of forty-two. His rule, from the killing of al-Walīd, lasted five months. He left many descendants. When Marwān assumed power, he exhumed his grave, took his body out, and crucified it. It is said that he is mentioned in the earlier books for his good conduct and justice. In one of them is this: “O scatterer of treasures, O one who keeps vigil in prayer before dawn, your rule was a mercy, and your death a tribulation. They seized you and crucified you.”

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Walīd

Allegiance was given to Ibrāhīm ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and after him to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Marwān ibn Muḥammad ibn Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam did not pledge allegiance to him and sought the caliphate for himself. The reason was that al-Ḥakam ibn al-Walīd ibn Yazīd—who had been his father’s designated successor—said, while imprisoned in the prison of Yazīd ibn al-Walīd, before he was killed:

[Wāfir]

Would that Kalb had never given birth to us,

and that we had been born of others!

Will ʿĀmir take my blood and my kingdom,

while I have gained neither lean nor fat?

If I die, and my designated successor dies,

then Marwān is commander of the believers.

His brother was his designated successor. For this reason Marwān sought the caliphate for himself. He set out with the people of al-Jazīra, Qinnasrīn, and Ḥimṣ. Ibrāhīm ibn al-Walīd sent Sulaymān ibn Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik with the people of Syria. They met in the territory of al-Ghūṭa. Sulaymān was defeated and fled until he reached Ibrāhīm. Marwān marched until he encamped in the territory of al-Ghūṭa, where allegiance was given to him. Ibrāhīm renounced the caliphate, entered into obedience to Marwān, and pledged allegiance to him. All of this took place in two and a half months.

When ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAbd al-Malik saw that the people were dispersing from them, he sent Yazīd ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī to the prison. Yazīd killed Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar, who had tortured his father Khālid until he died.

Yazīd also killed ʿUthmān and al-Ḥakam, the sons of al-Walīd ibn Yazīd.

Marwān ibn Muḥammad ibn Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam

Marwān assumed the caliphate in the year 127. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Malik.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Shārī rose against him from Shahrizūr, along with those of the Khārijites who had pledged allegiance to him, and advanced against him. Marwān set out to confront him. They met at Kafartūthā in the year 128, in Ṣafar, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk was killed. Al-Khaybarī took his place, and they fought. Marwān was defeated, then returned. The Khārijites appointed Shaybān, who returned with his companions to al-Mawṣil. Marwān followed him, camping wherever he camped, and fought him for a month. Then Shaybān was defeated. Marwān sent ʿĀmir ibn Ḍubārah al-Murrī after him, and appointed Yazīd ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayrah al-Fazārī over al-ʿIrāq. Yazīd advanced until he arrived at Wāsiṭ, where ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was in opposition to Marwān. Yazīd seized him, put him in chains, and sent him to Marwān. He remained imprisoned with one of his sons until he died in prison. Marwān continued to face division in his affairs and turmoil on every side, yet he continued to lead the people on the pilgrimage until the year 130. That was the last time the Umayyads led the people on pilgrimage, and the Umayyad dynasty came to an end.

The Account of Abū Muslim

Abū Muslim ʿAbd al-Raḥmān emerged in Khurāsān, calling people to the Hāshimids. Naṣr ibn Sayyār was there as governor for the Umayyads. Abū Muslim met him with his forces, and Naṣr fled until he died in the land of Sāwah, in Hamadhān.

When Abū Muslim had secured Khurāsān, he sent Qahṭabah ibn Shabīb al-Ṭāʾī with a large force ahead of the people of al-ʿIrāq. A group of Marwān’s supporters there were with Yazīd ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayrah al-Fazārī. The first of their forces whom he encountered was Nubātah ibn Ḥanẓalah al-Kilābī. Qahṭabah killed him and his son, routed their forces, and entered Jurjān, where he killed some of its people, in Dhū al-Ḥijjah of the year 130.

After Nubātah’s death, he marched on until he met ʿĀmir ibn Ḍubārah at Jābalaq, in the land of Iṣfahān. They met in Rajab of the year 131. Qahṭabah killed him and routed his forces.

Qahṭabah then marched until he encamped at Nahāwand, where Marwān had assembled a force of people from al-Shām and Khurāsān—those who had left Khurāsān when Abū Muslim emerged—as well as others from among the people of al-ʿIrāq. He besieged them for two months, then took the city at the sighting of the crescent of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, on condition that he guarantee the safety of the people of al-Shām and al-ʿIrāq there, except for a group whose number was specified, and that they leave him alone with the people of Khurāsān. He killed the people of Khurāsān who were there.

He then advanced until he met Yazīd ibn ʿUmar at the mouth of the Zāb, in the land of Upper al-Fallūjah, in Muḥarram of the year 132. They fought for a while, then Yazīd ibn ʿUmar was defeated. He advanced until he entered Wāsiṭ, where they fortified themselves. That night Qahṭabah was killed—it is said that he drowned—and his death went unrecognized. The people then appointed his son al-Ḥasan ibn Qahṭabah in his place. He marched with them until he entered al-Kūfah, then handed authority over to Abū Salamah Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān, the client of al-Subayʿ—a clan of Hamdān. Abū Salamah took charge of the people’s affairs and sent the armies against Ibn Hubayrah at Wāsiṭ, with al-Ḥasan ibn Qahṭabah in command, accompanied by Khāzim ibn Khuzaymah and Muqātil ibn Ḥakīm, along with many commanders. They besieged him there.

Bassām ibn Ibrāhīm was sent against ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayrah, who was governor of al-Ahwāz for his brother. Bassām fought him until he routed his force, and ʿAbd al-Wāḥid joined Sal[m] ibn Qutaybah, who at that time was governor of al-Baṣrah for his brother Yazīd ibn ʿUmar.

Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Saffāḥ

Abū al-ʿAbbās ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās was pledged allegiance on Friday, when thirteen nights of Rabīʿ al-Awwal had passed, in the year 132.

Abū Salamah came to him and pledged allegiance, then carried him until he led the people in the Friday prayer in the Great Mosque of al-Kūfah.

His mother was Rayṭah al-Ḥārithiyyah.

When Abū al-ʿAbbās assumed power, he appointed his uncle Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī over al-Kūfah and sent a group of his family to the commanders from Khurāsān to obtain their pledge of allegiance to him. He appointed his brother Abū Jaʿfar over the people at Wāsiṭ, together with al-Ḥasan ibn Qahṭabah. Abū Jaʿfar continued to besiege Yazīd ibn ʿUmar until he took the city by treaty in Shawwāl of the year 132. The siege had lasted nine months. Abū Jaʿfar then killed Yazīd ibn ʿUmar and his son Dāwūd ibn Yazīd. Abū al-ʿAbbās wrote to his uncle ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī, ordering him to march against Marwān. Marwān advanced against him with the men he had, and they fought. Marwān was defeated and his force routed. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī pursued him until he encamped at the river of Abī Fuṭrus in the land of Palestine. When he encamped by the river, the Umayyads gathered to him, and some eighty of them were killed. After their deaths, Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās set out in pursuit of Marwān and caught up with him in a village among the villages of al-Fayyūm, in the land of Egypt, called Būṣīr. The man who killed him was a commander in Ṣāliḥ’s vanguard named ʿĀmir ibn Ismāʿīl, from Khurāsān. This took place in Dhū al-Ḥijjah of the year 132.

Marwān had reached the age of fifty-nine. He had two sons: ʿAbd Allāh and ʿUbayd Allāh.

ʿUbayd Allāh left no descendants.

As for ʿAbd Allāh, his father had designated him as his successor. Abū Jaʿfar seized him, and he died in Baghdād. He left descendants.

Abū al-ʿAbbās then moved from al-Ḥīrah to al-Anbār in the year 134, and died there in Dhū al-Ḥijjah of the year 136.

It is said that he assumed the caliphate at the age of twenty-four. It is also said: twenty-eight. His rule lasted four years and eight months from the date he was pledged allegiance.

He had a son named Muḥammad, who died in Baghdād without leaving descendants, and a daughter named Rayṭah, who was married to al-Mahdī.

The Paternal Uncles of Abū al-ʿAbbās

Dāwūd, ʿĪsā, Sulaymān, Ṣāliḥ, Ismāʿīl, ʿAbd al-Ṣamad, Yaʿqūb, ʿAbd Allāh, and ʿUbayd Allāh: all of these were sons of ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

As for Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī, he was an eloquent orator, handsome, and known by the teknonym Abū Sulaymān. He governed Mecca and Medina for Abū al-ʿAbbās. He lived through eight months of their dynasty and died in the year 133. He left descendants.

As for ʿĪsā, his teknonym was Abū al-ʿAbbās. His son was Isḥāq ibn ʿĪsā, known by the teknonym Abū al-Ḥasan. Isḥāq governed Medina and al-Baṣrah. ʿĪsā died during the caliphate of al-Mahdī.

As for Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAlī, he governed Fāris and al-Baṣrah for Abū Jaʿfar.

His son Aḥmad ibn Ismāʿīl governed Fāris, Medina, Mecca, and Egypt for Hārūn. He left descendants.

As for ʿAbd al-Ṣamad, he was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He governed al-Jazīrah for Abū Jaʿfar, as well as Palestine, Mecca, Medina, and al-Baṣrah. He was the most senior of the Hāshimids in his time. In genealogical seniority, he was on a par with ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah. He died in Baghdād. He left descendants.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī, he governed al-Shām for Abū al-ʿAbbās, then rebelled. Abū Jaʿfar sent Abū Muslim against him, and Abū Muslim defeated him. Abū Jaʿfar then imprisoned him, and he died in prison in Baghdād. He left descendants.

His mother was a Berber woman named Hannādah.

Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAlī left no descendants.

Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī governed al-Shām for Abū Jaʿfar and died there.

Among his descendants were ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ṣāliḥ, al-Faḍl, ʿAbd Allāh, and Ibrāhīm.

Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was a contemporary of Abū Jaʿfar; they were both born in the same year.

Sulaymān ibn ʿAlī governed al-Baṣrah, ʿUmān, and al-Baḥrayn for Abū Jaʿfar. He died in al-Baṣrah in the year 142.

Sulaymān’s children were Jaʿfar, Muḥammad, ʿĀʾishah, Zaynab, Asmāʾ, Fāṭimah, Umm ʿAlī, and Umm al-Ḥasan—their mother was Umm al-Ḥasan daughter of Jaʿfar ibn Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; Ibrāhīm, whose mother was a concubine; Hārūn and Mūsā, whose mother was a concubine; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Rayṭah, and ʿAbd al-Raḥīm—their mother was ʿĀʾishah daughter of Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq; Umm Sulaymān, ʿAbd Allāh, and ʿAbd al-Salām, whose mother was a concubine; ʿAlī, whose mother was descended from ʿĀmir, “the Slayer of Lances,” who was Abū al-Barāʾ; and Saʿdā, Lubābah, and al-ʿĀliyah, whose mothers were concubines.

As for Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān, he was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He died in al-Baṣrah, leaving forty-three sons and thirty-five daughters of his own.

Among them was Isḥāq ibn Sulaymān. He held governorships, but was weak. He once passed by a reciter who was saying, “He will gulp it down, and can scarcely swallow it” (Qurʾān 14:17), and said, “O God, make us among those who gulp it down and can swallow it.”

All of Sulaymān’s children left descendants except ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sulaymān.

Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān governed al-Baṣrah and al-Kūfah.

The Brothers of Abū al-ʿAbbās

Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿAbd Allāh al-Manṣūr—their mothers were various concubines; Yaḥyā, whose mother was the daughter of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; and al-ʿAbbās, whose mother was a concubine.

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī died in al-Shām. Ibrāhīm’s sons were ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and Muḥammad.

ʿAbd al-Wahhāb governed al-Shām and died there. He left descendants.

Muḥammad governed Mecca, Medina, Yemen, and al-Jazīrah, and died in Baghdād. He left descendants.

Mūsā ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī had a son, ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā. ʿĪsā governed al-Ahwāz and al-Kūfah. He was known by the teknonym Abū Mūsā and died in al-Kūfah.

ʿĪsā’s sons were Mūsā, al-ʿAbbās, Ismāʿīl, ʿUbayd Allāh, and others.

They held governorships.

Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī governed al-Mawṣil and Fāris for Abū Jaʿfar.

Yaḥyā’s son was Ibrāhīm, who led the people on pilgrimage in the year Abū Jaʿfar died.

He left no descendants.

Some of the Hāshimids stated that Yaḥyā had descendants.

As for al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, he governed al-Jazīrah for Abū Jaʿfar and was known by the teknonym Abū al-Faḍl. He died in Baghdād.

He had sons named ʿAbd Allāh, al-Faḍl, and others.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, he was Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr. He assumed the caliphate at the age of forty-two. His mother was a Berber woman named Salāmah. He was born in al-Sharāt in Dhū al-Ḥijjah of the year 95. Sulaymān ibn Ḥabīb had whipped him for some reason.

He was pledged allegiance as caliph on the day his brother Abū al-ʿAbbās died at al-Anbār. His uncle ʿĪsā ibn ʿAlī was appointed to carry out the matter and send word of it to the people in the various regions. The pledge of allegiance to Abū Jaʿfar reached him while he was on the road. Abū Jaʿfar continued on until he arrived at al-Kūfah and led the people in prayer.

He delivered a sermon to them and set out until he arrived at al-Anbār. Abū Muslim came to him, and he killed him at Rūmiyyat al-Madāʾin in Shaʿbān of the year 137. Abū Jaʿfar set out on pilgrimage in the year 140. He entered the state of consecration at al-Ḥīrah. Before his departure, in the year 139, he had ordered the Mosque of the Kaʿbah to be enlarged. That year was called “the Year of Abundance.” Al-Mahdī later enlarged it and the Mosque of Medina in the year 160.

When Abū Jaʿfar had completed his pilgrimage, he returned to Medina and stayed there as long as God willed. Then he set out for al-Shām until he prayed at Bayt al-Maqdis. He then returned to al-Raqqah, took the route along the Euphrates, and finally encamped in the city of al-Hāshimiyyah at al-Kūfah. He then set out from al-Hāshimiyyah for Nahāwand. From there he returned and attended the pilgrimage season in the year 144. Then he moved to Baghdād in the year 145. He had been there only a short while when Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan revolted in Medina. When news of his revolt reached him, he hurried down to al-Kūfah.

He sent armies to Medina with ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā, with Ḥumayd ibn Qahṭabah at their head. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh was killed in Ramaḍān of the year 145. His brother Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd Allāh had revolted in al-Baṣrah on the first day of Ramaḍān. When news reached him that his brother had been killed, he set out toward al-Kūfah. ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā advanced against him, and they met at Bājimīrā in the land of al-Kūfah. Ibrāhīm and his companions were killed in the year 145. Abū Jaʿfar went out to al-Zawrāʾ—that is, Baghdād—and completed its construction, making it his residence in the year 146. He set out intending to lead the people on pilgrimage in the year 158, but died on the sixth day of Dhū al-Ḥijjah at Biʾr Maymūn. He had reached the age of sixty-three years and some months. His rule lasted twenty-two years. Ibrāhīm ibn Yaḥyā ibn ʿAlī performed the funeral prayer over him.

Al-Haytham said:

ʿĪsā ibn Mūsā ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī performed the funeral prayer over him.

Abū Jaʿfar’s children were al-Mahdī—whose name was Muḥammad—and Jaʿfar—their mother was Umm Mūsā daughter of Manṣūr al-Ḥīriyyah; and Ṣāliḥ—his mother was a bondwoman said to have been the daughter of a king. al-Ṣughd, Sulaymān, ʿĪsā, and Yaʿqūb—their mother was Fāṭima daughter of Muḥammad, a descendant of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh—and al-ʿĀliya—her mother was a descendant of Khālid ibn Asīd—and Jaʿfar, al-Qāsim, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and al-ʿAbbās.

As for Jaʿfar ibn Abī Jaʿfar, he governed al-Mawṣil for his father and died in Baghdād.

Jaʿfar’s children were Ibrāhīm, Zubayda—who was surnamed Umm Jaʿfar—their mother was Salsabīl, a concubine; Jaʿfar ibn Jaʿfar, ʿĪsā ibn Jaʿfar, ʿAbd Allāh, Ṣāliḥ, and Lubāba.

As for Ibrāhīm, he had no descendants.

As for Zubayda, Hārūn al-Rashīd married her.

As for Lubāba, she was married to Mūsā ibn al-Mahdī.

As for ʿĪsā ibn Jaʿfar, he governed al-Baṣra and its districts, Fāris, al-Ahwāz, al-Yamāma, and al-Sind. He died at a monastery between Baghdād and Ḥulwān. He was surnamed Abū Mūsā.

He has descendants who remain.

The other descendants of Abū Jaʿfar had offspring. They held governorships and led the people in prayer during the pilgrimage seasons.

al-Mahdī Muḥammad ibn Abī Jaʿfar

When Abū Jaʿfar died, the people pledged allegiance to his son Muḥammad al-Mahdī in Mecca. His client, Manāra al-Barbarī, brought him the pledge.

Al-Mahdī was surnamed Abū ʿAbd Allāh. His mother was Umm Mūsā, daughter of Manṣūr al-Ḥimyarī. He became caliph at the age of thirty-eight. He ruled for ten years and one month. He died in a village called al-Radhdh, in Mā-sabadhān, in Muḥarram of the year 169. He had reached the age of forty-eight. He was buried there.

Al-Mahdī’s children were Hārūn, Mūsā, and al-Bānūqa—their mother was al-Khayzurān, a concubine—ʿAlī and ʿUbayd Allāh—their mother was Rayṭa, daughter of Abū al-ʿAbbās—al-ʿAbbāsa, by a concubine; al-ʿĀliya, Manṣūr, and Sulayma—their mother was al-Baḥtariyya, daughter of the Iṣbahbadh—Yaʿqūb and Isḥāq, by a concubine; and Ibrāhīm, by a concubine.

As for al-Bānūqa, she died when she was young.

As for al-ʿAbbāsa, Hārūn married her to Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān. When he died, Ibrāhīm ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī married her.

As for ʿAlī ibn al-Mahdī, he led the people on the pilgrimage more than once and died in Baghdād. He had children. As for ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Mahdī, he governed al-Jazīra.

As for Manṣūr ibn al-Mahdī, he governed Filasṭīn and other places, as well as al-Baṣra, and he led the people on the pilgrimage.

Mūsā al-Hādī

As for Mūsā ibn al-Mahdī, he succeeded his father as caliph. His brother Hārūn arranged the pledge of allegiance for him in Baghdād, while Mūsā was in Jurjān. Naṣīr, al-Mahdī’s client, came to him there with the pledge. Then al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥusaynī rose up in Medina and took control of it. Then he set out, intending to go to Mecca, but he was killed at Fakhkh, a parasang from Mecca, on the Day of Tarwiya. Those who undertook his killing were Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān, Mūsā ibn ʿĪsā, and al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad.

Mūsā’s reign lasted one year and one month. He was surnamed Abū Muḥammad. His mother was al-Khayzurān.

He died in Baghdād on Friday, with fourteen nights remaining in Rabīʿ al-Awwal of the year 170. He had reached the age of twenty-five. He had many children.

Hārūn al-Rashīd

He was Hārūn ibn al-Mahdī. The caliphate came to him in the year 170. He was given the pledge of allegiance in Baghdād on the day Mūsā died. His son ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn was born to him on that same day.

He was surnamed Abū Jaʿfar. His mother was al-Khayzurān. He resided at al-Khuld in western Baghdād.

Yaḥyā ibn Khālid was his vizier, and Yaḥyā’s two sons, al-Faḍl and Jaʿfar, resided in the courtyard of al-Khuld. Jaʿfar later built his palace at al-Dūr, but did not reside there before he was killed.

Hārūn led the people on the pilgrimage six times, the last being in the year 186.

That year his two sons and designated heirs, Muḥammad al-Amīn and ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn, accompanied him on the pilgrimage. He wrote a document for each of them concerning the other, and hung it inside the Kaʿba.

When he returned, he stopped at al-Anbār. Then he led the people on the pilgrimage in the year 188.

Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā was killed at al-ʿUmr—a place near al-Anbār—in the year 187, on the last day of Muḥarram. His body was sent to Baghdād.

Yaḥyā and his son al-Faḍl remained imprisoned until they died in al-Raqqa.

During Hārūn’s caliphate, al-Walīd ibn Ṭarīf al-Shārī rebelled and defeated more than one army. Hārūn sent Yazīd ibn Mazīd against him, and Yazīd overcame and killed him.

After him, Khurāsha al-Shārī also rebelled.

Hārūn killed Anas ibn Abī Shaykh, the nephew of the traditionist Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ.

Anas was a friend of Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā. Hārūn had him crucified in al-Raqqa. He was accused of heresy, as were the Barmakids—except those whom God Almighty protected.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said of them: [shortened mutaqārib]

When polytheism is mentioned in a gathering,the faces of the sons of Barmak shine.

When a verse is recited in their presence,they bring forth traditions from Mazdak.

In the year 190, Hārūn raided the Byzantines, captured Hiraqlah, and seized the daughter of its commander, taking her for himself. When he returned, Rāfiʿ ibn Layth ibn Naṣr ibn Sayyār rebelled in Ṭukhāristān against ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā. Hārūn sent Harthama to fight him and to bring ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā before him. When ʿAlī arrived, Hārūn ordered him imprisoned and his property, and that of his son, confiscated.

In the year 192, Hārūn set out—with al-Maʾmūn—with the intention of going to Khurāsān. He reached Ṭūs, fell ill there, and died. He was buried there.

He died on Saturday night, with three nights of Jumādā al-Ākhira having passed, in the year 193. He had reached the age of forty-seven. His reign lasted twenty-three years, two months, and seventeen days.

Among the children of Hārūn were Muḥammad—his mother was Zubayda, daughter of Jaʿfar ibn Abī Jaʿfar—and ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn—his mother was a concubine named Marājil—as well as al-Qāsim al-Muʾtaman, Ṣāliḥ, Abū ʿĪsā, Abū Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim, Abū Yaʿqūb, Ḥamdūna, and others.

Muḥammad al-Amīn

Al-Amīn Muḥammad ibn Hārūn was given the pledge of allegiance in Ṭūs. Ṣāliḥ ibn Hārūn took charge of arranging the pledge, and the eunuch Rajāʾ came to him there on the fifteenth of Jumādā al-Ākhira. He addressed the people.

He was given the pledge of allegiance in Baghdād. Those whom his father had imprisoned were released: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ṣāliḥ, al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim, Sallām ibn Sālim al-Bajalī, and al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī.

Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya, who had been in charge of the administration of grievances for Muḥammad, died in Dhū al-Qaʿda of the year 193. Muḥammad appointed Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī—a descendant of Anas ibn Mālik—to administer grievances and to serve as judge in Baghdād.

He sent for Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ and brought him to Baghdād, intending to entrust him with one of his affairs. Wakīʿ refused to take part in anything, and set out for Mecca in Dhū al-Qaʿda of the year 193. He died on the way.

He appointed al-Faḍl ibn al-Rabīʿ as vizier, made Ismāʿīl ibn Ṣabīḥ his secretary, and made al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl ibn al-Rabīʿ his chamberlain.

Al-Faḍl fomented discord between Muḥammad and al-Maʾmūn. Muḥammad therefore nominated his son Mūsā ibn Muḥammad as heir after him, obtained the pledge of allegiance for him, and gave him the title al-Nāṭiq bi-l-Ḥaqq (“He Who Speaks the Truth”), in the year 194. He placed him in the care of ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā and ordered ʿAlī to go to Khurāsān to fight al-Maʾmūn in the year 195. So he sent al-Maʾmūn sent Harthama from Marw, with Ṭāhir ibn al-Ḥusayn at the head of his vanguard. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā and Ṭāhir met at al-Rayy and fought. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā and a group of his sons were killed in Ramaḍān of the year 195. Ṭāhir seized all the money, equipment, and cavalry that ʿAlī had with him. Muḥammad then sent ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jabala al-Anbārī. He and Ṭāhir met at Hamadhān and Ṭāhir killed him, then entered Hamadhān. Ṭāhir and Harthama joined forces. Ṭāhir took the route through al-Ahwāz, while Harthama took the highway by way of Ḥulwān. Al-Faḍl ibn Sahl sent Zuhayr ibn al-Musayyib along the route through Kirmān. He took Kirmān, then entered al-Baṣra.

When Ṭāhir reached al-Ahwāz, he found there a governor from the Muhallabids, appointed by Muḥammad. Ṭāhir killed him and took control of al-Ahwāz, then marched to Wāsiṭ. Harthama marched to Ḥulwān. Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā rose up with a group in Baghdād, entered upon Muḥammad while he was at al-Khuld, seized him, and imprisoned him in one of the towers of the city of Abū Jaʿfar. Muḥammad’s troops then disbanded on every side. Al-Faḍl ibn al-Rabīʿ disappeared that day, and no trace of him was seen. When al-Maʾmūn entered Baghdād, he sent al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī to Harthama and Ṭāhir, urging them to enter Baghdād. Asad al-Ḥarbī and a group rose up, brought Muḥammad and his son out, and apologized to him. They seized al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and brought him to Muḥammad. After al-Ḥusayn acknowledged his wrongdoing and repented of it, Muḥammad pardoned him. Al-Ḥusayn admitted that he had been deceived and deluded, so Muḥammad released him. When he left Muḥammad and crossed the bridge, he called out, “O Maʾmūn! O Manṣūr!” and headed toward Harthama. They set out in pursuit of him and caught him near the river of Tīr, then killed him and brought his head to Muḥammad. Harthama went to al-Nahrawān, then advanced to the river of Tīrī. Ṭāhir encamped at the gate of al-Anbār. Zuhayr ibn al-Musayyib was at Kalwādhā. They continued fighting. Ṭāhir corresponded with al-Qāsim al-Muʾtaman ibn Hārūn, who was staying in Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā’s palace at al-Dūz. Ṭāhir asked him to come out to him. He did so and handed the palace over to him.

Muḥammad’s position remained unstable. Finally, he took refuge in the city of Abū Jaʿfar and sent word to Harthama: “I will come out to you tonight.” When Muḥammad came out, he fell into the hands of Ṭāhir’s men. They brought him to Ṭāhir, who killed him that night. In the morning, his head was displayed on the New Gate. Then it was taken down and sent to Khurāsān with his cousin Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Muṣʿab. His body was buried in Būstān Muʾnisa in the year 198.

ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn

The rule passed securely to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hārūn al-Maʾmūn in the year 198.

His mother was a concubine named Marājil. His father had punished him in connection with one of his slave girls. Al-Raqāshī said, praising his brother Muḥammad and making an insinuation about al-Maʾmūn: [shortened ramal]

No slave girl did she bear who was knownto the merchants in the market;

neither at a frontier post nor in a khān,nor was she a racer among racehorses.

Abū al-Sarāyā was among Harthama’s companions. They withheld his stipends from him, and he became angry.

He set out and reached al-Anbār, where he killed its governor. Then he went on, with no one knowing where he was headed or what he sought.

Then ʿAlī ibn Abī Saʿīd arrived on behalf of al-Faḍl ibn Sahl and dismissed Harthama and Ṭāhir. They appointed Ṭāhir over al-Jazīra to fight Naṣr ibn Shabath. Al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl came from Khurāsān to al-ʿIrāq with Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd and a large number of commanders. When he drew near to Baghdād, Ṭāhir left for al-Raqqa.

Harthama set out for Khurāsān. Al-Ḥasan arrived and encamped at al-Shammāsiyya. Ibn Ṭabāṭabā al-ʿAlawī appeared in al-Kūfa, and Abū al-Sarāyā joined him. He took control of al-Kūfa, and the ʿAlawids rose up in Mecca, Medina, and Yemen, taking control of them. Ṭāhir sent Zuhayr ibn al-Musayyib against the people of al-Kūfa. He fought them, but the people of al-Kūfa defeated him, plundered his camp, and drove him back to Baghdād. Ṭāhir marched to al-Raqqa, where he and Naṣr ibn Shabath met. Naṣr fought him and inflicted heavy losses on his men, and the war between them continued until al-Maʾmūn arrived in Baghdād and Ṭāhir came to him.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl sent ʿAbdūs ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Khālid against Abū al-Sarāyā. They met, and ʿAbdūs and his men were killed. The people of al-Kūfa then advanced as far as the river Ṣarṣar; they took Wāsiṭ and al-Baṣra. Al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl sent al-Sindī ibn Shāhik to Harthama, who was at Ḥulwān. He turned Harthama back and sent him on. Harthama marched to the river Ṣarṣar, routed them, and pursued them. He caught up with them near the palace of Ibn Hubayra and engaged them, killing many. They fled until they entered al-Kūfa. Ibn Ṭabāṭabā died, and Abū al-Sarāyā installed in his place a young ʿAlawid called Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad. Harthama continued fighting them, though they had inflicted heavy losses on his men, until his forces weakened. They then corresponded with him. Abū al-Sarāyā fled with the ʿAlawid. Harthama entered the city and stayed there for several days, then appointed a deputy over it. He returned to Baghdād and went on to Khurāsān, where he captured Abū al-Sarāyā and the ʿAlawid. He killed Abū al-Sarāyā, then took the ʿAlawid to Khurāsān.

The people of Baghdād fought al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl. Their leader was Muḥammad ibn Abī Khālid al-Marwazī, whose sons were ʿĪsā, Hārūn, and Abū Zanbīl. Al-Ḥasan was at al-Madāʾin. The people were in disarray, with no commander over them. So Sahl ibn Salāma and the volunteers for holy war rose up. Al-Maʾmūn sent for ʿAlī ibn Mūsā—known as al-Riḍā—and brought him to Khurāsān. He pledged allegiance to him as heir after him, and ordered the people to wear green. The people of Baghdād went to Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī and gave him the pledge of the caliphate. He went out to al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl and joined him. to Wāsiṭ, while Ibrāhīm remained at al-Madāʾin. Then al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl sent ʿAlī ibn Hishām and Ḥumayd al-Ṭūsī, and they fought. Ḥumayd routed them, and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā took the place of Sahl ibn Salāma and enjoined him to do what was right. ʿAlī contrived to turn those with him against him, gained the upper hand over him, and handed him over to Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī, who kept him concealed in his custody. Nothing was known of his fate until al-Maʾmūn approached Baghdad. Al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl sent Hārūn ibn al-Musayyab to the Ḥijāz to fight the ʿAlids. They fought, and Hārūn ibn al-Musayyab routed them and captured Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar. He took him to al-Maʾmūn with several members of his family, none of whom returned. Al-Riḍā died in Khurāsān. When Harthama reached Khurāsān, words passed between him and al-Faḍl ibn Sahl in al-Maʾmūn’s presence. Al-Maʾmūn ordered him imprisoned, and he was confined in a dome in al-Maʾmūn’s residence. After remaining there for several days, he was brought out dead, wrapped in a sackcloth, and buried in a trench used by the prisoners at Marw. When Ḥātim ibn Harthama, who was in Armenia, learned what had been done to his father, he corresponded with the Aḥrār there and with the kings, and called them to revolt. While he was thus occupied, death came to him. It is said that this was the cause of Bābak’s revolt. Bābak remained in revolt for more than twenty years.

Abū Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim was with al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl. He fled to Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī. He had been fighting alongside al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl and his companions. Then he and Mahdī al-Shārī met in the year 203, and Abū Isḥāq fled to Baghdad.

War continued between the people of Baghdad and al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl until he gained the upper hand over them Al-Ḥasan captured many of them and took them, along with Aḥmad ibn Abī Khālid, to Khurāsān. He arrived in Khurāsān after al-Faḍl ibn Sahl had been killed at Sarakhs in the year 203. Al-Maʾmūn appointed him vizier in al-Faḍl’s place and appointed Ghassān ibn ʿAbbād as his deputy in Khurāsān. Al-Maʾmūn then set out for Baghdad. When he drew near, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī brought out Sahl ibn Salāma and said to him:

“Call the people to fight al-Maʾmūn.” He did so. Then Ibrāhīm went into hiding. Al-Maʾmūn entered Baghdad on Saturday, four nights into Ṣafar, in the year 204, wearing green. He governed well, looked after the people’s affairs, and sat to hear them. Then famine struck the people. He sent Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh against Bābak, and Shabīb al-Balkhī against Naṣr ibn Shabath. Yaḥyā and Shabīb were routed. He sent Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Mazyad to Egypt to fight ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Sarī. ʿUbayd defeated him and took him prisoner, but pardoned him and those of his companions who had been captured, and released them. Then al-Maʾmūn sent ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir to fight Naṣr ibn Shabath and the Zawāqīl in the year 207.

In that year his father Ṭāhir died, and Naṣr sought safe conduct. ʿAbd Allāh granted it to him. Then ʿAbd Allāh went to Egypt, where Ibn al-Sarī sought safe conduct from him. He granted it and sent him to Baghdad. (199)

In the year 210, al-Maʾmūn gained the upper hand over Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī, granted him safe conduct, and made him his drinking companion.

In this year he married Būrān. Al-Maʾmūn sent for Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Mūsā, the son of al-Riḍā, and brought him to him. He married him to his daughter and permitted him to take her to Medina, which he did. He sent Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd to fight Bābak. They met, and Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd was killed in the year 214. Al-Maʾmūn appointed ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir over the Jibāl and to wage war against the Khurramiyya. He ordered his brother Abū Isḥāq to recruit Turks and bring them in. He wrote to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir, who was at al-Dīnawar in the land of al-Jabal, ordering him to go to Khurāsān. He sent ʿAlī ibn Hishām to fight Bābak. Then, in Muḥarram of the year 215, al-Maʾmūn set out for Tarsus and raided the Byzantines. He took the fortresses of Qurra, Kharshana, and Ṣamālū. Then he returned to Damascus, went on to Egypt, and then came back to Damascus. In the year 217 he set out again against the Byzantines. In that year ʿUjayf brought ʿAlī ibn Hishām to him, and he killed ʿAlī and his brother. In that year ʿAmr ibn Masʿada died at Adana, and Luʾluʾa was conquered. He ordered the building of Ṭuwāna. Then al-Maʾmūn returned and went to al-Raqqa. He then went back to the Byzantine lands and died at the river al-Badhindūn, with thirteen nights remaining in Rajab of the year 218. He was carried to Tarsus and buried there.

His caliphate, from the time Muḥammad was killed, lasted twenty years. He had many descendants.

Muḥammad al-Muʿtaṣim

He was Muḥammad ibn Hārūn. His kunya was Abū Isḥāq. His mother was Mārida, a slave woman.

Abū Isḥāq was with his brother when he died in the Byzantine lands, as was al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Maʾmūn. The people wished to pledge allegiance to al-ʿAbbās, but he refused and handed authority over to Abū Isḥāq. Abū Isḥāq hurried toward Baghdad, fearing for his life because a group of commanders had intended to harm him. He arrived there at the beginning of Ramaḍān in the year 218. He stayed there for two years, then, after the Feast of Breaking the Fast in the year 220, went to Sāmarrāʾ with his Turks. He built there, made it his residence and military encampment, and the Byzantines invaded Zibatra. Abū Isḥāq set out on campaign in Jumādā I of the year 223 and conquered ʿAmmūriyya in Ramaḍān of that year. Then he turned back and attacked al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Maʾmūn and ʿUjayf on the way. He arrived at Sāmarrāʾ in Dhū al-Ḥijja of that year.

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī died at Sāmarrāʾ in Ramaḍān of the year 224. Al-Afshīn was crucified in the year 226.

Abū Isḥāq died with eleven nights remaining in Rabīʿ I of the year 227. His caliphate lasted eight years and eight months. In that same month the ascetic Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith died.

Hārūn al-Wāthiq bi-Allāh, son of Abū Isḥāq

Allegiance was pledged to Hārūn al-Wāthiq bi-Allāh on the day his father died. His mother was Qarāṭīs, a slave woman.

She died at al-Ḥīra while on her way to Mecca.

Aḥmad ibn Naṣr was killed during the inquisition, with two nights remaining in Shaʿbān of the year 231.

Hārūn died on Wednesday, with six nights remaining in Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year 232. His caliphate lasted five years, nine months, and several days.

Jaʿfar al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, son of Abū Isḥāq

Allegiance was pledged to Jaʿfar on the day al-Wāthiq died. His mother was a slave woman named Shujāʿ.

He took the oath of allegiance for his three sons—Muḥammad al-Muntaṣir, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Muʿtazz, and Ibrāhīm al-Muʾayyad—in Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year 235. He was killed in the year 247, three days after the Feast of Breaking the Fast.

Muḥammad al-Muntaṣir

Allegiance was pledged to his son al-Muntaṣir, Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar. He died six months later.

Aḥmad al-Mustaʿīn bi-Allāh

Then allegiance was pledged after him to Aḥmad al-Mustaʿīn bi-Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim. He was deposed at the end of the year 251 and killed in the year 252.

Al-Muʿtazz bi-Allāh

He was al-Zubayr ibn Jaʿfar. Allegiance to al-Muʿtazz was taken in the year 252. He was killed in Rajab of the year 255.

Muḥammad al-Muhtadī

Then Muḥammad ibn Hārūn al-Wāthiq, al-Muhtadī, succeeded him in the caliphate in the year 255. He was killed in Rajab of the year 256.

Al-Muʿtamid ʿalā Allāh Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar al-Mutawakkil

Then Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar al-Muʿtamid ʿalā Allāh succeeded him. His kunya was Abū al-ʿAbbās.

His mother was an umm walad named Futayyān. Allegiance was pledged to him on Tuesday, with fourteen nights remaining in Rajab of the year 256. It is said that he became caliph when he was twenty-five years old.

Notable members of the nobility, the sultan’s companions, and those who rebelled against them

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṭīʿ ibn al-Aswad

He belonged to Banū ʿUwayj ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb, the clan of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. His father, Muṭīʿ ibn al-Aswad, had been called al-ʿĀṣī, but the Prophet ﷺ—renamed him Muṭīʿ. ʿAbd Allāh was in command of Quraysh on the Day of al-Ḥarra. He fled, then went with Ibn al-Zubayr to Mecca and fought, saying: [rajaz]

I am the one who fled on the Day of al-Ḥarra;

today I repay that flight with a charge.

Does an old man flee more than once?

He continued to fight until Ibn al-Zubayr was killed. He himself was wounded and died of his wounds in Mecca. Al-Ḥajjāj prayed over him and said: “O God, this is Your enemy, Ibn Muṭīʿ. He was loyal to Your enemies and opposed Your allies. Fill his grave with fire.”

Al-Shaʿbī was the secretary of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṭīʿ.

Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī

He was al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf ibn al-Ḥakam ibn Abī ʿAqīl ibn Masʿūd ibn ʿĀmir ibn Muʿattib ibn Mālik ibn Kaʿb, of the Aḥlāf, al-Thaqafī.

His grandfather al-Ḥakam had the following sons: Yūsuf, Yaḥyā, Ayyūb, Muḥammad, and Sulaymān.

As for Yūsuf, ʿAbd al-Malik appointed him to some governorships, and he commanded some detachments when he fought al-Ḥantaf ibn al-Sajf and Ḥubaysh ibn Dalja. He was routed, and Yūsuf ibn Tawsʿa al-ʿAbdī said:

[Wāfir]

Yūsuf al-Thaqafī escaped at a gallop—

that was after the standard had fallen.

Had they caught up with him, we would have met our end;

against it, every error has its safeguard.

Yūsuf died while al-Ḥajjāj was in Medina, and al-Ḥajjāj announced his death from the pulpit.

Yūsuf had the following children: al-Ḥajjāj, Muḥammad, and Zaynab.

As for Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf, ʿAbd al-Malik appointed him governor of Yemen, and he remained governor until he died there. Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf had the following children: Yūsuf ibn Muḥammad, Muṣʿab ibn Muḥammad, ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad, and Umm al-Ḥajjāj.

As for Yūsuf ibn Muḥammad, al-Walīd ibn Yazīd appointed him as his deputy.

As for ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad, he was eccentric and arrogant. Al-Walīd said to Ashʿab:

“If you make him laugh, my robe is yours.” Ashʿab kept talking to him until he made him laugh, and took al-Walīd’s robe.

As for Umm al-Ḥajjāj, she was the mother of al-Walīd ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

The descendants of Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf were in Syria.

As for al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, his kunya was Abū Muḥammad. He was narrow-eyed and had a thin voice. The first governorship he held was Tabāla. When he saw it, he thought little of it and left. Hence the proverb: “More insignificant than Tabāla was to al-Ḥajjāj.” On some occasion, he was in charge of the police under Abān ibn Marwān?16 When Ibn al-Zubayr revolted and fighting continued for some time, al-Ḥajjāj said to ʿAbd al-Malik: “I saw in a dream that I was flaying ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr. Send me to him.”

17 [?] with a thousand men. He ordered him to camp at al-Ṭāʾif until he received further instructions. Then he wrote to him, ordering him to fight. He reinforced him, and he besieged Ibn al-Zubayr until he killed him. Then he brought him out and crucified him. This took place in the year 73. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed al-Ḥajjāj governor of the Ḥijāz for three years, and each year he led the prayers during the pilgrimage season. Then he appointed him governor of Iraq when he was thirty-three years old. Al-Ḥajjāj governed it for twenty years, set it in order, and subdued its people.

Abū al-Yamān related from Ḥurayz ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Maysara, from Abū ʿAdhba al-Ḥaḍramī, who said:

I came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—as one of four men from Syria, and we were pilgrims. While we were with him, news came from Iraq that its people had pelted their imam with stones. He went out to the prayer, then said: “Who from Syria is here?” I stood up, along with my companions. He said: “People of Syria, prepare yourselves for the people of Iraq, for Satan has laid eggs and hatched young among them.” Then he said: “O God, they have confused matters for me, so confuse matters for them. O God, hasten for them the Thaqafī youth, who will rule them by the rule of the Age of Ignorance: he will accept no good deed from their virtuous and overlook no misdeed of their wrongdoers.”

When death came upon him, he said to the astrologer: “Do you foresee a king who will die?” He replied: “Yes.”
