“But it is not I, is it?” “I see a king dying whose name is Kulayb.” He said: “By God, I am Kulayb; that is what my mother named me.” He appointed Yazīd ibn Abī Muslim over the land tax and Yazīd ibn Abī Kabsha over the army, and ordered his son ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Ḥajjāj to lead the people in prayer.

He died at Wāsiṭ and was buried there. His grave was obliterated, and water was made to flow over it.

He died in the year 95, in the month of Ramaḍān.

Al-Ḥajjāj had the following children: Muḥammad, Abān, ʿAbd al-Malik, al-Walīd, and a daughter.

Muḥammad died during his father’s lifetime. His descendants were in Damascus. ʿAbd al-Malik’s descendants were in Basra. Abān and al-Walīd left no descendants.

Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar

He was Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥakam ibn Abī ʿAqīl ibn Masʿūd, the paternal cousin of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf. They shared al-Ḥakam ibn Abī ʿAqīl as an ancestor. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Hishām appointed him governor of Yemen, then appointed him governor of Iraq and charged him with auditing Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī and his officials. He tortured them. Khālid died under torture, as did Bilāl ibn Abī Burda. When al-Walīd was killed, Yūsuf fled and reached Syria. He was seized there and imprisoned, then killed in prison. Yazīd ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh was among those who killed him in revenge for his father. Yūsuf’s descendants were in Syria.

Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī

He was Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī ibn Yazīd ibn Asad ibn Kurz al-Bajalī, then al-Qasrī. His grandfather was Yazīd ibn Asad, who came as a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ—embraced Islam, and settled in Syria. When Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh became governor of Iraq, he bought plots of land in Kūfa and built there. He had many descendants and a large family there. His mother was Christian.

His grandfather used to transmit a report from the Messenger of God ﷺ—which Khālid transmitted.

Hushaym related from Sayyār Abū al-Ḥakam (1), who said: I heard Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī say: My father told me, from my grandfather, who said:

The Messenger of God ﷺ—said: “O Yazīd ibn Asad, love for people what you love for yourself.”

Al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra

He is al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra. Abū Ṣufra was Ẓālim ibn Sarrāq, of the Azd al-ʿAtīk—the Azd of Dabā. Dabā lies between ʿUmān and al-Baḥrayn.

Al-Wāqidī said:

The people of Dabā had embraced Islam in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ—but after his death they apostatized and withheld the alms. Abū Bakr therefore sent ʿIkrima ibn Abī Jahl against them. He fought them, defeated them, and inflicted heavy slaughter on them. The remnants took refuge in one of their forts, and the Muslims besieged them. Then they surrendered on ʿIkrima’s terms. He killed one hundred of their notables, took their children captive, and sent them to Abū Bakr. Among them was Abū Ṣufra, a boy who had not yet reached maturity. ʿUmar ﵁—freed them and said, “Go wherever you wish.” They dispersed, and Abū Ṣufra was among those who settled in al-Baṣra.

Al-Muhallab was known by the kunya Abū Saʿīd. He was one of the bravest of men, and he defended al-Baṣra against the Khārijites after its people had fled, except for those strong enough to remain. It was therefore called “al-Muhallab’s Baṣra.” His only fault was said to be lying. Of him it was said: “Rāḥ lying.”

He governed Khurāsān and administered it for five years. He died at Marw al-Rūdh (1) in the year eighty-three, and his son Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab succeeded him. Yazīd was thirty years old. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān deposed him on al-Ḥajjāj’s advice and counsel, and appointed Qutayba ibn Muslim. Yazīd fell into al-Ḥajjāj’s hands, and al-Ḥajjāj tortured him. He escaped from his prison to Syria, intending to go to Sulaymān. He came to him, and Sulaymān interceded for him with al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Al-Walīd granted him security and left him alone. Then, when the caliphate passed to Sulaymān, he appointed Yazīd over Khurāsān. Yazīd conquered Jurjān and Dahistān and set out for al-ʿIrāq. But news of Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik’s death reached him on the way, so he went to al-Baṣra. ʿAdī ibn Arṭāʾa seized him, bound him, and sent him to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. ʿUmar imprisoned him, but he escaped and went to al-Baṣra. When ʿUmar died, Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik rebelled. He sent Maslama against him, and Maslama killed him. The remnants of the family of al-Muhallab fled to the region of Kirmān and Qandābīl (2).

His son Mukhlad ibn Yazīd was a noble and distinguished man despite his youth, and he was given precedence over his father.

It is said that three hundred children issued from al-Muhallab’s loins.

Al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd

He is al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd ibn Masʿūd ibn ʿAmr al-Thaqafī, of the Aḥlāf.

It is said that his grandfather Masʿūd was the “great man of the two townships” (3). Masʿūd had two sons: Saʿd and Abū ʿUbayd. Saʿd was the governor of al-Madāʾin under ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him.

He had descendants in al-Kūfa. As for Abū ʿUbayd, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—appointed him commander of an army that included men among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. At Quss al-Nāṭif (1), near al-Kūfa, he encountered Kharrādhād the chamberlain, who was riding an elephant. Abū ʿUbayd struck the elephant; the elephant fell upon him and killed him.

Abū ʿUbayd’s children were al-Mukhtār, Ṣafiyya, Jabr, and Usayd.

As for Jabr, he was killed with his father on the Day of the Elephant. He left no descendants.

Ṣafiyya was married to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁.

Al-Mukhtār seized control of al-Kūfa during the time of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr. He claimed that Gabriel came to him. He hunted down those who had killed al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ﵁.

He killed ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and his son Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar. He also killed Shamir ibn Dhī al-Jawshan al-Ḍabbābī. He dispatched Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ashtar, who killed ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād and others. A group of people from al-Kūfa left and came to al-Baṣra, seeking their aid and asking them to support them against al-Mukhtār. The people of al-Baṣra set out with Muṣʿab and fought him at al-Kūfa. Al-Mukhtār killed ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁—without recognizing him, in Muṣʿab’s army, as well as Muḥammad ibn al-Ashʿath ibn Qays. Then al-Mukhtār was defeated and killed; Ḍirrār ibn Yazīd al-Ḥanafī killed him. Samura ibn Jundub’s daughter was married to al-Mukhtār. He had two sons by her, Isḥāq and Muḥammad, and other sons by another woman. His descendants in al-Kūfa are numerous.

The Banū Ṣawḥān

They are Zayd ibn Ṣawḥān, Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Ṣawḥān, and Sayḥān ibn Ṣawḥān, of the Banū ʿAbd al-Qays.

As for Zayd, he was among the best of men. A report in the ḥadīth relates that the Prophet ﷺ—said: “Zayd al-Khayr, the maimed one; and Jundub—what of Jundub?” It was said:

“O Messenger of God, are you referring to two men?” He said, “As for one of them, his hand preceded him to Paradise by thirty years; as for the other, he will strike a blow by which he will distinguish truth from falsehood.” One of the two men was Zayd ibn Ṣawḥān. He was present at the battle of Jalūlāʾ (1), where his hand was cut off. He was present with ʿAlī at the Battle of the Camel, and said, “Commander of the Faithful, I think I am to be killed.” He said:

“What makes you think that, Abū Salmān?” Zayd replied, “I saw my hand descending from heaven, beckoning me.” ʿAmr ibn Yathribī killed him, and he killed Zayd’s brother Sayḥān on the day of the Battle of the Camel.

The other was Jundub ibn Zuhayr al-Ghāmidī, who struck and killed a sorcerer performing before al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba.

Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Ṣawḥān was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁—at the Battle of the Camel, and was one of the most eloquent speakers.

Miqṣala ibn Hubayra

He was of the Banū Shaybān. He was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God honor his face—but then fled to Muʿāwiya, and ʿAlī demolished his house. Miqṣala said this when he parted from him:

[Ṭawīl]

ʿAlī had attained his desire from her, and soHis rule among us became tales told by a rider.

Then Miqṣala sent a Christian man to bring his family from al-Kūfa. ʿAlī seized the man and cut off his hand. Muʿāwiya appointed Miqṣala over Ṭabaristān, where he died. Hence the proverb:

“Until Miqṣala returns from Ṭabaristān.” He had descendants in al-Kūfa and a house in al-Baṣra.

Miqṣala ibn Raqaba

He was of ʿAbd al-Qays. His mother was a Jarmāqāniyya. He was one of the most eloquent speakers in the time of al-Ḥajjāj and afterward. Miqṣala’s sons were Kurz ibn Miqṣala and Raqaba ibn Miqṣala.

[They were both orators. Kurz had a sermon known as “The Old Woman.”]

Khālid ibn Ṣafwān

He is Khālid ibn Ṣafwān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ahtam. His name was Sinān ibn Sumayy ibn Sinān ibn Khālid ibn Munqir ibn ʿUbayd ibn Tamīm. Sinān was called al-Ahtam because Qays ibn ʿĀṣim al-Munqirī struck him with his bow, splitting his mouth. Ṣafwān, Khālid’s father, held the leadership of the Banū Tamīm in the days of Masʿūd, and was an orator. Al-Ḥasan witnessed his bequest. He bequeathed one hundred and twenty thousand dirhams, saying, “I prepared them for the bite of hard times and the harshness…” al-Sulṭān (the ruler), rivalry among the clans.” al-Ḥasan said, “You have left it to one who will not praise you, and you are going to one who will not excuse you.” He died in al-Baṣra. His son Khālid lived until he met Abū al-ʿAbbās. He was eloquent, plain-spoken, an orator, miserly, and given to divorcing his wives. He used to say: “There are four things in which no one may hope to prevail upon me: a loan, an obligation, al-ʿarḍ, and that I should pursue someone’s need.”

He was asked, “And what will you do for yourself after these, Abū Ṣafwān?” He replied, “Cold water, and conversation that does not awaken a child.”

He used to say: “No night is dearer to me than a night on which I have divorced my wives, so that I return and find the curtains taken down and the household goods moved. Then one of my daughters sends me a basket containing my food, and the other sends me a bed on which to sleep.”

Among his kinsmen was the orator Shabīb ibn Shayba.

Ibn al-Qirriyya

He was Ayyūb ibn Zayd ibn Qays. Al-Qirriyya was his mother. He belonged to Banū Hilāl ibn Rabīʿa ibn Zayd Manāt ibn ʿĀmir. He was eloquent and an orator. He served under al-Ḥajjāj, who killed him over a matter in which he suspected him of sympathy for Ibn al-Ashʿath.

Musaylima the Liar

He was Musaylima ibn Ḥabīb, of Ḥanīfa ibn Lujaym. He was known by the teknonym Abū Thumāma. He practiced feats of magic. He was the first to put an egg inside a bottle, and the first to join the wing of a bird that had been clipped. Many people followed his example in this. One of the poets of Banū Ḥanīfa lamented him:

[maǧzūʾ al-kāmil]

Alas for you, Abū Thumāma, alas for my two pillars of Tihāma! How many a sign you showed them, like the sun rising from its cloud!

He left no descendants.

Sajāḥ

Sajāḥ, who claimed prophethood, belonged to Banū Yar būʿ. She was called Ṣādir. Musaylima married her, and a group of Banū Tamīm followed her. ʿAṭārid ibn Ḥājib ibn Zurāra said:

[basīṭ]

Our prophetess has become a female we circle around, while the prophets of other people have become males.

Her muezzin was Zuhayr ibn ʿAmr, of Banū Sulayṭ ibn Yar būʿ. It is also said that Shabath ibn Ribʿī called the adhān for her as well.

Qutayba ibn Muslim al-Bāhilī

He was known by the teknonym Abū Ḥafṣ. He was Qutayba ibn Muslim ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥuṣayn ibn Asīd ibn Zayd ibn Quḍāʿī, of Banū Hilāl ibn ʿAmr, of Bāhila. Muslim ibn ʿAmr held a high rank with Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. He was known by the teknonym Abū Ṣāliḥ. A poet said of him:

[mutaqārib]

When Quraysh has lost its rule, the caliphate belongs to Bāhila— to the master of the stubborn steed, Abū Ṣāliḥ. That is no just precedent.

Al-Ḥarūn was his horse.

Muslim’s sons were Bashshār, Ziyād, ʿAbd al-Karīm, Qutayba, ʿAbd Allāh, Ṣāliḥ, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Ḥammād, Zurayq, Ḍirār, ʿAmr, Maʿbad, and al-Ḥuṣayn.

As for Bashshār, he was the eldest of them and the man associated with the Nahr Bashshār. He was the chief of Muslim’s sons until Qutayba surpassed him. Bashshār left descendants.

Ziyād ibn Muslim was killed with Qutayba in Khurāsān. He left descendants.

ʿAbd al-Karīm left descendants in al-Baṣra.

As for Qutayba ibn Muslim, he was governor of Khurāsān on behalf of al-Ḥajjāj. Before that, he had governed al-Rayy. Then he revolted and was killed in Farghāna in the year 97, at the age of forty-five. Wakīʿ ibn Abī Sūd al-Tamīmī killed him. He governed Khurāsān for thirteen years, conquering Khwārazm, Samarqand, and Bukhārā; their people had been unbelievers.

Qutayba’s sons were Muslim ibn Qutayba, Qaṭan ibn Qutayba, Kathīr, al-Ḥajjāj, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Salm, Ṣāliḥ, ʿAmr, Yūsuf, and others.

As for Salm, he governed al-Baṣra twice: once for Ibn Hubayra and once for Abū Jaʿfar. He was the chief of his people and died in al-Rayy. His teknonym was Abū Qutayba.

Salm had several sons, among them Saʿīd ibn Salm. He governed Armenia, al-Mawṣil, al-Sind, Ṭabaristān, Sijistān, al-Jazīra. His descendants were numerous.

Ibrāhīm ibn Salm governed Yemen for Mūsā.

ʿAmr ibn Salm governed al-Rayy and Balkh.

Kathīr ibn Salm governed Sijistān.

As for Qaṭan ibn Qutayba ibn Muslim, he governed Samarqand and other districts of Khurāsān. He left descendants there.

All of Qutayba’s sons were nobles, and they left descendants.

As for ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn ʿAmr, he was killed with his brother Qutayba.

Among his descendants was al-Miswar ibn ʿAbd Allāh. He left many descendants. Maʿbad ibn Muslim was also killed. He left many descendants.

Al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Muslim left descendants in al-Baṣra.

As for ʿAmr ibn Muslim, he was brave and held governorships for Qutayba and ʿAdī ibn Arṭāh. His descendants were numerous.

ʿUmar ibn Hubayra al-Fazārī

He was ʿUmar ibn Hubayra ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAdī ibn Fazāra. His maternal grandfather was Kaʿb ibn Ḥassān ibn Shihāb, chief of Banū ʿAdī in his time. It was at his home that al-Ribāb formed an alliance. He governed the two Iraqs for Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik for six years. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Muthannā. Al-Farazdaq said of him to Yazīd:

[wāfir]

You entrusted Iraq and its two rivers to a Fazārī, quick with his hand in the sleeve. Abū al-Muthannā has made his way in Iraq, and taught his people to eat khabīṣ.

Its two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates. By “quick with his hand in the sleeve,” the poet means that he is quick-handed, accusing him of theft.

Ḥabāba was a singing-girl belonging to Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. She had been taken captive during the governorship of the two Iraqs, and she used to call him “father.”

He died in Syria. ʿUmar’s sons were Yazīd ibn ʿUmar, Sufyān, and ʿAbd al-Wāḥid.

As for Yazīd, he governed al-ʿIrāqayn for Marwān ibn Muḥammad for five years. He was a notable, distributing five hundred thousand dirhams each month among his visitors. Every night in Ramaḍān, he provided an evening meal, then granted the people ten requests without their having to sit and wait. He was handsome in appearance and of great stature. His mother was Sindī.

Yazīd had two sons: al-Muthannā and Mukhlid.

As for al-Muthannā, he governed al-Yamāma for his father, and Abū Ḥammād al-Marwazī killed him in the desert.

As for Mukhlid, his sons were notable. They had standing and numbers in Syria.

Yazīd had a son called Dāwūd, who was killed alongside his father Yazīd. Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr besieged Yazīd at Wāsiṭ for months, then gave him a guarantee of safety and took the city by treaty. Yazīd rode out to him with his household, and Abū Jaʿfar would say: “A king such as this cannot be brought low!” Then he killed him.

Naṣr ibn Sayyār

He was Naṣr ibn Sayyār ibn Rāfiʿ, of the Banū Jundaʿ ibn Layth, of Kināna.

They were the clan of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr ibn Qatāda al-Laythī. Sayyār ibn Rāfiʿ had been with Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr when he stole a baggage case. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura cut off his hand, and he came to be called “the One-Handed.”

His son Naṣr was known by the kunya Abū al-Layth. Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik appointed him governor of Khurāsān, and he remained its governor for ten years, until the civil strife broke out. He set out for al-ʿIrāq, but died on the way, in the region of Sāwa. He had numerous descendants.

Mirdās and ʿUrwa, the sons of Adiyya

They were Mirdās and ʿUrwa, the sons of ʿAmr ibn Ḥudayr, of Rabīʿa ibn Ḥanẓala.

Their grandmother Adiyya belonged to Muḥārib, and they were ascribed to her. It is also said that she was their wet nurse.

Mirdās was known by the kunya Abū Bilāl and was the leader of every Ḥarūrī [reading uncertain]. ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād sent ʿAbbād ibn ʿAlqama al-Māzinī against him, and he killed him at Tawwaj. The Khārijite ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān spoke of him in these verses: [basīṭ]

“After you, I no longer recognize those I once knew;After you, Mirdās, people are no longer people.”

As for ʿUrwa, he was the first to act as an arbiter at Ṣiffīn. ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād seized him, killed him, and crucified him in the cemetery of the Banū Ḥiṣn at al-Baṣra. Mirdās had no descendants; the descendants were those of ʿUrwa.

Shabīb the Khārijite

He was Shabīb ibn Yazīd ibn Nuʿaym, of the Banū Shaybān. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Ṣaḥārī.

He had been with Ṣāliḥ ibn Musarriḥ, the leader of the Ṣufriyya. When Ṣāliḥ died at al-Mawṣil, he designated Shabīb as his successor. Ṣāliḥ was buried there, and none of them would go out to his grave without shaving his head there. Shabīb then rose in revolt at al-Mawṣil. al-Ḥajjāj sent five commanders against him, and Shabīb killed them one by one. Among them was Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh. He left al-Mawṣil for al-Kūfa, while al-Ḥajjāj set out from al-Baṣra for al-Kūfa. Shabīb hoped to meet him before he arrived at al-Kūfa. al-Ḥajjāj spurred on his cavalry and entered al-Kūfa before him. Shabīb passed ʿAttāb ibn Warqāʾ, whom Shabīb killed. He passed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ashʿath, who fled from him, and arrived at al-Kūfa, but did not reach al-Ḥajjāj. He then set out for al-Ahwāz, but drowned in the Dijayl, saying: “That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.”

Ghazāla, who pursued al-Ḥajjāj while he was in flight, was his wife. A poet said of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf: [kāmil]

“A lion against me, but in battle a female ostrich,Broad-footed, fleeing the caller’s whistle.Why did you not charge at Ghazāla in the fray?Your heart, it seems, was in a bird’s wings.”

Abū Muḥammad said: Sahl ibn Muḥammad told me, saying: al-Aṣmaʿī told me, saying: al-ʿAbbās ibn Muḥammad al-Hāshimī told me, saying:

“Someone who had seen Shabīb enter the mosque told me: He wore a ṭaylasān cloak, marked with spots from the rain. He was tall, gray-haired, curly-haired, and dark-complexioned, and the mosque seemed to tremble as he entered.”

Qaṭarī ibn al-Fujāʾa the Khārijite

He was of the Banū Ḥarqūṣ ibn Māzin ibn Mālik ibn ʿAmr ibn Tamīm. He was known by the kunya Abū Naʿāma. He rose in revolt during the time of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, and fought for twenty years, while people addressed him as caliph. al-Ḥajjāj sent one army after another against him. The last was Sufyān ibn al-Abrad al-Kalbī, who killed him; the person who carried this out was Sūra ibn Abjar al-Bāriqī.

Qaṭarī had no descendants.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Fihrī

He was al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Muḥārib ibn Fihr. Muʿāwiya appointed him governor of al-Kūfa after Ziyād. He later joined ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr and fought Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam on the day of al-Marj, commanding all of Qays. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam killed him—this was on the day of Marj Rāhiṭ. His son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk served as governor of al-Madīna for Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān al-Kilābī

This was another man. He was one of the Banū Abī Bakr ibn Kilāb. The Messenger of God ﷺ—appointed him over the Banū Sulaym.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays, the Khārijite al-Shaybānī

He was another man who rose in revolt from the region of al-Jazīra with a band of Khārijites. He came to al-Kūfa, where ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was governor, and fought him for it. al-Ḍaḥḥāk defeated him and took al-Kūfa, then marched against Marwān ibn Muḥammad. Marwān advanced against him, and they met at Kafr Ṭūthā in the year 128, in Ṣafar. al-Ḍaḥḥāk was killed, and al-Khaybarī succeeded him. They fought, and Marwān was defeated. Then Marwān returned, and the Khārijites appointed Shaybān as their leader. He returned with his companions to al-Mawṣil, and Marwān pursued them and fought them for a month. Then Shaybān was defeated, and Marwān sent ʿĀmir ibn Ḍubāra al-Murrī in pursuit of him.

al-Musayyab ibn Zuhayr al-Ḍabbī

He was descended from Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr al-Ḍabbī. The Banū Ḍirār were among the leaders of Ḍabba.

He served as chief of Abū Jaʿfar’s police. al-Mahdī appointed him governor of Khurāsān, and he served as chief of police under Mūsā. His son ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Musayyab governed Egypt, Fāris, and al-Jazīra. Muḥammad ibn al-Musayyab served as chief of police under Muḥammad al-Amīn. al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Musayyab served as chief of police under al-Maʾmūn. Zuhayr ibn al-Musayyab governed Kirmān for Hārūn.

al-Musayyab ibn Zuhayr had a brother called ʿAmr ibn Zuhayr, whom Abū Jaʿfar appointed governor of al-Kūfa.

Yazīd ibn Mazīd al-Shaybānī

He was Yazīd ibn Mazīd ibn Zāʾida ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zāʾida ibn Maṭar ibn Sharīk ibn ʿAmr al-Shaybānī. Zāʾida was lame, as was al-Ḥawfazān ibn Sharīk. Maʿn ibn Zāʾida was Yazīd ibn Mazīd’s paternal uncle. Maʿn was the most generous of the Arabs, and it was said: “You may quote from Maʿn without concern.” Mazīd was known by the kunya Abū Dāwūd. His brother Maʿn ibn Zāʾida said of him: [basīṭ]

“Do not ask Abū Dāwūd to leave it behind;Rely on Mazīd for bread and milk.And, when he draws it, excuse him for the wine—For he is bound by his duty to feed his guests.”

He was generous with food, but miserly in other things. Maʿn was known by the kunya Abū al-Walīd.

Yazīd killed Kharāsha the Khārijite and al-Walīd ibn Ṭarīf al-Shārī.

He governed Armenia. His son Muḥammad ibn Yazīd succeeded him, and became a leader at the age of twenty.

Shabīb the Khārijite was of his clan.

ʿAbbād ibn al-Ḥuṣayn al-Ḥabaṭī

He was known by the kunya Abū Jahḍam. He was the cavalryman of the Banū Tamīm and served as chief of police in al-Baṣra during the time of Ibn al-Zubayr. He was with Muṣʿab during the killing of al-Mukhtār, and was with ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar over the Banū Tamīm during the time of Abū Fudayk. On that occasion, he distinguished himself as no one else did. He took part in the conquest of Kābul with ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir. Al-Ḥasan said: “I did not think anyone could match a thousand horsemen until I saw ʿAbbād.”

He lived through the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath as an elderly man, paralyzed on one side. He gave him advice, and al-Ḥajjāj became afraid and fled toward Kābul, where the enemy killed him. His son Jahḍam was with Ibn al-Ashʿath, and al-Ḥajjāj killed him. His son’s son al-Miswar ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbbād was the leader of the Banū Tamīm in his time and their chief during the revolt of Ibn Suhayl. The rajaz poet said of him: [rajaz]

“You are the one for it, O Miswar ibn ʿAbbād,When swords are drawn from their scabbards.”

ʿAttāb ibn Warqāʾ al-Riyāḥī

He was known by the kunya Abū Warqāʾ and was among the most generous of the Arabs. al-Farkhān, the ruler of al-Rayy, renounced Islam, so ʿAttāb was sent against him, killed him, and conquered al-Rayy. During the revolt of Ibn al-Zubayr, he governed Iṣfahān. al-Ḥajjāj appointed him commander of the army of the people of al-Kūfa in the fight against the Azāriqa. al-Muhallab appointed him commander of the army of the people of al-Baṣra in the fight against them. He governed al-Madāʾin and its region. Shabīb attacked him by night, and his army scattered from him, and he was killed.

His son Khālid was generous. Ṭalḥa al-Ṭalḥāt passed by him on his way back from Sijistān, while Khālid was at al-Rayy. He offered him a gift and asked him for honey. Khālid sent him seven hundred thousand dirhams and wrote: “I have sent you the price of the honey. There was no more honey than this in the treasury.” al-Ḥajjāj wrote to him: “You fled from your father on the night of Shabīb.” He wrote back: “Anyone who saw knows that I did not flee. But you and your father fled on the day of al-Rabadhā from al-Ḥuntaf ibn al-Sajf. You were both on a camel with a pack saddle—so, by God, which of you was riding behind the other?” He then went to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, fearing al-Ḥajjāj, and remained with him until he died.

Wakīʿ ibn Ḥassān ibn Qays ibn Abī Sūd

He was known by the kunya Abū Muṭarrif. He was the leader of the Banū Tamīm and was enrolled with Salm ibn Ziyād. He made his headquarters at Sijistān. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir governed Sijistān and became angry with Wakīʿ over something. He seized and imprisoned him. A son of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, accompanied by a wet nurse, passed by Wakīʿ.

He called for him and seized him, then called for a knife and said: “By God, I will slaughter him, or you will set me free.” ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz heard of this and came to him, saying: “Release him, and we will guarantee your safety.” He replied: “No, by God—not until ten men of the Banū Tamīm come and guarantee you to me. Then they themselves must release me.” He did as he asked. Wakīʿ then moved to Khurāsān, where he became a leading figure. al-Ḥajjāj wrote to Qutayba ordering him to kill him. Wakīʿ had distinguished himself in battle alongside Qutayba, especially on the day of the Turks. So Qutayba removed Wakīʿ from command. When al-Walīd came to power and Qutayba rebelled and marched with the people toward Farghāna, the people agreed to depose him and pledged allegiance to Wakīʿ. They killed Qutayba, took his head, and sent it to Sulaymān. Wakīʿ remained in control of Khurāsān for nine months. Then Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab governed Khurāsān.

al-Ḥuntaf ibn al-Sajf ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAwf ibn Zuhayr ibn Mālik

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was devout and distinguished, and held a position of importance with ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād. When the revolt of Ibn al-Zubayr broke out, Ḥubaysh ibn Dilja al-Qaynī of Quḍāʿa marched from al-Madīna to fight Ibn al-Zubayr. al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Makhzūmī, governor of al-Baṣra, gave al-Ḥuntaf a standard. He marched with seven hundred men and Ḥubaysh came out against him from al-Madīna. They met at al-Rabadhā, where al-Ḥuntaf killed Ḥubaysh and ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥakam, the brother of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf and his father fled that day. al-Ḥuntaf then marched toward Syria, and when he reached Wādī al-Qurā, poison was put in his food, and he died there.

Huraym ibn Abī Ṭaḥma al-Tamīmī

The name of Abī Ṭaḥma was Ḥāritha ibn ʿAdī. Huraym was brave and shrewd. He was with al-Muhallab in the fight against the Azāriqa, and with ʿAdī ibn Arṭāʾa in the fight against Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab. On the day of Sūrā, he took up the standard, then charged in with five horsemen, and Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab was routed. Huraym then grew old, so he had his name changed in the pay register to spare himself military expeditions. He was told: “You do not know how to write.” He replied:

“If I cannot write, I can erase the pages.” His son al-Turjumān was governor of al-Ahwāz and of the Banū Ḥanẓala during the revolt of Ibn Suhayl.

Khāzim ibn Khuzayma al-Nahshalī

He was of the Ṣakhr ibn Nahshal and was the son of a concubine. He was known by the kunya Abū Hazīma.

He governed Khurāsān, killed the ʿAnaziyya, governed ʿUmān, and died in Baghdād. Abū Jaʿfar offered condolences for him.

His son Khuzayma ibn Khāzim was known by the kunya Abū al-ʿAbbās and held governorships.

His son Ibrāhīm ibn Khāzim was killed by al-Walīd ibn Ṭarīf al-Shārī.

ʿĀmir ibn Ḍubāra

He was of the Banū Murra. He was a distinguished leader. Yazīd ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayra sent him to Fāris to fight ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. He defeated ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿāwiya, and remained with Marwān in command of his armies and among his troops.

Nabāta ibn Ḥanẓala

He was of the Banū Abī Bakr ibn Kilāb. He was the cavalryman of the people of Syria, and commanded the mangonel on the day of the Kaʿba. Marwān appointed him governor of Jurjān and al-Rayy, where Qaḥṭaba killed him. His son Ḥayya ibn Nabāta was killed with him. He also had a son called Muḥammad, whom Yazīd ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayra executed.

Isḥāq ibn Muslim ibn Rabīʿa al-ʿUqaylī

He was a close and highly regarded associate of Abū Jaʿfar, eminent and of great standing. In the days of Marwān, when he made peace, the Arabs made peace; when he fought, the Arabs fought. He governed Armenia.

His brothers: Bakkār, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥārith, and ʿAbd Allāh, were distinguished leaders.

Their descendants were in al-Jazīra.

214ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khāzim al-Sulamī

He was known by the kunya Abū Ṣāliḥ. His mother was a dark-complexioned woman called ʿAjlī. He was the bravest of people.

He governed Khurāsān for ten years and conquered al-Ṭaysayn. Then the people of Khurāsān revolted against him and fought him, and Wakīʿ ibn al-Dawraqiyya killed him.

Mālik ibn Mismac

He is Mālik ibn Mismac ibn Sayyār, of Bakr ibn Wāʾil, descended from Jaḥdar, who ransomed his hair on the “Day of the Shaven Locks” with the first horseman to appear. Mismac, Mālik’s father, came to the Prophet ﷺ—then apostatized after the Prophet ﷺ—and was killed in al-Baḥrayn. He was called Abū Sayyār, and was the father of the Mismacites. His son Mālik was the most distinguished of men. A man said to ʿAbd al-Malik:

“If Mālik were angry, a hundred thousand would be angry with him, without asking him why he was angry.”

ʿAbd al-Malik said, “By your father, that is true nobility.” Mālik never held any office, and died in the early part of the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, in al-Baṣra. He left many descendants, as did his brothers.

Ṭalḥa of the Ṭalḥas

He is Ṭalḥa ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khalaf, of Khuzāʿa. His father, ʿAbd Allāh, was a secretary to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—for the registers of al-Kūfa and al-Baṣra. Ṭalḥa was in charge of Sijistān, and died there.

Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, who related traditions from Anas, was his client. Zurayq, the grandfather of Ṭāhir ibn al-Ḥusayn, “the Two-Handed,” was a client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khalaf, Ṭalḥa’s father.

Abū Fudayk the Khārijite

He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thawr ibn Salama, of Banū Saʿd ibn Qays, of Bakr ibn Wāʾil.

Abū al-ʿĀj al-Sulamī

He is Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh. He was called Abū al-ʿĀj because of his front teeth. He was an official of Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar in al-Baṣra.

Abū Muslim, the Leader of the Mission

He is ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muslim. They say that he was born in the year one hundred. There is much disagreement about his lineage. Some said he was from Iṣfahān; others said he was from Khurāsān; and it was said that he was an Arab. He claimed that he was the son of Sulayṭ ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās. Abū Dulāma attributed him to the Kurds, saying:[طويل]

Abū Mujrim, God does not change a blessingfor His servant until the servant changes it.

In al-Mahdī’s reign, did you attempt treachery?Know that the fathers of treachery are Kurds.

Abū Mujrim, you frightened me with death, and the tawny lionsturned upon you with what you had frightened me with.

He was brought up in the household of Idrīs ibn ʿĪsā, the grandfather of Abū Dulaf, who lived on the frontier of Iṣfahān. Abū Jaʿfar had him killed at Rūmiyyat al-Madāʾin in the year one hundred and thirty-seven.

Anecdotes in Genealogical Lore

ʿAbd al-Qays took pride in having among its clients Ṣāliḥ al-Murrī, a client of Banū Murra of ʿAbd al-Qays. He was a virtuous man, and inclined toward a certain doctrine of predestination. He died in al-Baṣra, where his descendants remained.

They also took pride in having among their clients Ḥassān ibn Abī Sinān al-Qannād, one of the most devout men of al-Baṣra.

They also took pride in having among their clients Abān ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh, the jurist. He was called Abū Ismāʿīl.

Among their clients was Ghālib al-Qaṭṭān, a devout and virtuous man.

Al-Bajalī said:

“He is a client of the family of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz, and is Ghālib ibn Khaṭṭāf.”

Among their clients was ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād, known as al-Thaqafī, although he was not Thaqafī; he was a client of ʿAbd al-Qays.

Among them was Riʾāb ibn al-Barāʾ, one of their own, who followed the religion of Jesus son of Mary ﵇—in the pre-Islamic period.

Among their own was Haram ibn Ḥayyān.

When al-Hurmuzān became Muslim, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—named him ʿArfaṭa.

Dhū al-Thudayya: his name was Tharmala.

Dhū al-Kilāʿ: his name was Sumayfaʿ ibn Nākūr, one of the Successors.

Jayashān: a group of Quḍāʿa. Among them was Abū Wahb al-Jayshānī, whose name was Daylam ibn al-Hawshaʿ.

Ṣanābiḥ: a group of Ḥimyar. Among them was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAsīla al-Ṣanābiḥī.

Ghāfiq: a group of Ḥimyar. Among them was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zurayr al-Ghāfiqī.

Yazan: a group of Ḥimyar, among them the family of Dhū Yazan. Among them was Abū al-Khayr Marthad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Yazanī.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥublī, of Ḥimyar. His name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd.

Abū ʿAshāna al-Maʿāfirī, of Yemen. His name was Ḥayy ibn Yuʾman.

Al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā, from whom Wakīʿ related traditions, was al-Sīnānī, from a village among the villages of Marw.

Among those with many children was Juzʾ ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, known as “the Patchwork Man.” He used to say to his mother:[وافر]

Perhaps, mother of Juzʾ, you will let me seea man of abundant good, with family and wealth.

He prospered, and his sons numbered forty. They all died in al-Ḥārif, and he said of this:[وافر]

I buried those who warded off oppression from me,on a rise beside the mountain of Sinām.

I have never seen their like all buried together,nor have I seen a year like this year.

Whenever I remember them all, I say,“May I be sacrificed for those shades and spirits.”

They were descended from Rabīʿa ibn Mālik ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm.

Qays ibn Jaḥdar al-Ṭāʾī was the grandfather of the poet al-Ṭirimmāḥ. He came as a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ was the son of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥakam ibn Nufayr ibn Qays ibn Jaḥdar.

The first standard the Messenger of God ﷺ—commissioned was the standard of Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. It is also said that it was the standard of ʿUbayda ibn al-Ḥārith.

The first Muslim to die in Medina was ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, after Badr and before Uḥud. The Messenger of God ﷺ—said, “He has gone before you; bury your dead beside him.” He was buried in al-Baqīʿ.

The Successors and Those after Them

Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

“He is Ṣakhr ibn Qays ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Ḥiṣn ibn ʿAbbād ibn Murra ibn ʿUbayd, of Tamīm. His clan was Banū Murra ibn ʿUbayd, who sent the alms from their property to the Prophet ﷺ—with ʿIkrāsh ibn Dhuʾayb.”

Another said:

“His name was al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays.”

Al-Aḥnaf’s father was called Abū Mālik. Banū Māzin killed him in the pre-Islamic period.

Al-Aḥnaf was called Abū Baḥr. The Messenger of God ﷺ—came to his people calling them to Islam, but they did not answer him. Al-Aḥnaf said, “He is calling you to Islam and to noble qualities of character, and forbidding you their opposites.” So they became Muslims. Al-Aḥnaf became Muslim but did not come as a delegate to the Messenger of God ﷺ. In ʿUmar’s time, he came as a delegate to him. He fought alongside ʿAlī ﵁—at Ṣiffīn, but fought at neither side in the Battle of the Camel.

Another said:

“His mother’s name was Ḥabbī daughter of ʿAmr ibn Thaʿlaba, of Banū Awd, of Bāhila.

“It is also said that she was Ḥubbā daughter of Qurṭ. Her brother al-Akhṭal ibn Qurṭ was one of the brave men.

“Al-Aḥnaf said on the Day of al-Jafra: ‘Who has an uncle like my uncle?’

“Al-Aḥnaf was born with his buttocks fused together, until the space between them was cut open. Al-Aḥnaf was one-eyed.”

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

“Al-Aḥnaf had an uncle called al-Mutashammas ibn Muʿāwiya, who was considered superior to al-Aḥnaf in forbearance.

“It is said that he and al-Aḥnaf went to Musaylima the Liar to hear him. When they came out, al-Aḥnaf said, ‘What do you think of him?’ He said, ‘I think he is a liar.’ Al-Aḥnaf said, ‘What makes you sure I will not go back to him and tell him what you said?’ He replied, ‘Then tell him that you said it, and I will swear an oath with you’—meaning, ‘I will swear and you will swear.’ Al-Mutashammas became Muslim after that, and was a good Muslim.

“His younger uncle, Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Muʿāwiya, was the leader of Banū Tamīm during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya. His horse, al-Ṭurra, cost ninety thousand dirhams.

“Al-Aḥnaf lived until the time of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr. He went with him to al-Kūfa and died there, having grown very old.”

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

“Al-Aḥnaf was buried in al-Kūfa, near the grave of Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān. Ziyād’s grave is at al-Thawiyya.”

Al-Aḥnaf had a son, Baḥr, who was weak-minded. One day he said to Zabrāʾ, his father’s slave-girl, “You shameless woman!” She replied, “If you were as you say, you would have given your father a son like yourself.”

He was asked, “What prevents you from having some of your father’s qualities?” He replied, “Laziness.”

Baḥr had a daughter, who died.

Al-Aḥnaf left no descendants.

It was said: “The man of Banū Tamīm who had the standing of their leader in al-Kūfa was Muḥammad ibn ʿUmayr ibn ʿAṭārid ibn Ḥājib ibn Zurāra.” He left no descendants.

“Their leader in al-Baṣra was al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays.” He left no descendants.

ʿUmar sent him to Khurāsān. The enemy attacked them by night, and al-Aḥnaf was the first to mount, saying:[رجز]

Every chief has a duty:to stain the lance red, or let it be broken.

Then he charged them and killed the drummer. The enemy fled, and they pursued them until they conquered Marw al-Rūdh, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān—may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him.

ʿUbayda al-Salmānī

He is ʿUbayda ibn Qays al-Salmānī, of Murād.

Ibn Sīrīn said: ʿUbayda said:

“I became Muslim two years before the Prophet ﷺ—died. I prayed, but never met the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

He died in the year seventy-two, and al-Aswad performed the funeral prayer over him.

ʿAmr ibn Maymūn

He was of Awd. He lived in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ—and performed sixty pilgrimages, counting both ḥajj and ʿumra. He died in the year seventy-four.

Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī

He is ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mall, of Quḍāʿa. He lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ—but did not see him. He died in al-Baṣra at the beginning of al-Ḥajjāj’s governorship of Iraq.

He had lived in al-Kūfa, but when al-Ḥusayn ﵁—was killed, he moved to al-Baṣra and settled there. He said, “I will not live in a town where the son of the daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—was killed.”

Abū ʿUthmān said:

“I accompanied Salmān for twelve years.”

He also said:

“Thirty years have passed over me, and there is nothing left that I have not found objectionable, except my hope; I find it just as it was.”

He took part in the conquests of al-Qādisiyya, Jalūlāʾ, Tustar, Nihāwand, al-Yarmūk, and Ādharbayjān.

Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī

He is Saʿd ibn Iyās. He used to say, “I remember hearing the Messenger of God ﷺ—while I was tending camels belonging to my family at Kāẓima.” He lived for one hundred and twenty years.

Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh

He was called Abū Maryam. He was the most eloquent in Arabic of men. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd used to ask him about Arabic. He was older than Abū Wāʾil and lived for one hundred and twenty years.

Mālik ibn Aws ibn al-Ḥadathān

He was from an earlier generation, but his conversion to Islam came late. We have no report that he saw the Prophet ﷺ—or related anything from him. He related traditions from ʿUmar and ʿUthmān.

He died in Medina in the year seventy-two.

Suwayd ibn Ghafala al-Madhḥijī

He lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ—and came as a delegate to him, but found that he had died. After that, he accompanied Abū Bakr and fought alongside ʿAlī ﵁—at Ṣiffīn.

He was called Abū Umayya. He died in al-Kūfa in the year eighty-two, at the age of one hundred and twenty-seven. He used to say, “I am the same age as the Messenger of God ﷺ; I was born in the Year of the Elephant.”

Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī

His name was ʿImrān ibn Taym. It is also said: ʿAṭārid ibn Bardhāʾ. It is also said: ʿImrān ibn ʿAbd Allāh.

He was born eleven years before the Hijra. He was descended from ʿAṭārid ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. It is also said that he was their client.

Abū Rajāʾ said:

“When news reached me that the Prophet ﷺ—had begun killing, we fled. We came upon a buried rabbit carcass, dug it up, cut it open, and put some of the plants of the earth over it. I will never forget that meal.”

Al-Riyāshī related to us, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, who said:

“I asked Abū Rajāʾ, ‘What do you remember?’ He said, ‘I remember the killing of Bisṭām ibn Qays at al-Ḥasan’—al-Ḥasan is a sand mountain.”

Abū Muḥammad recited to me:[وافر]

He fell upon the acacia, with no pillow beneath him,as though his brow were a polished sword.

He died in the year one hundred and seventeen, at the age of one hundred and twenty-eight.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Abū al-Ashhab al-ʿUṭāridī related to us:

A woman came to Abū Rajāʾ in the middle of the night and said, “Abū Rajāʾ, a night visitor has a right, and the sons of so-and-so have gone to Safwān, leaving behind some of their belongings.”

He put on his sandals, took the books, and delivered them. Then he led us in the dawn prayer. The journey was a night’s travel by camel.

Al-Miswar ibn Makhrama

He is al-Miswar ibn Makhrama ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra. His mother was the sister of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf. He was regarded as equal to the Companions, though he was not one of them.

Some people have reported from him that he heard the Prophet ﷺ—say: “If the Banū Hāshim ibn al-Mughīra were to ask my permission to marry their daughter to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, I would not give permission; then again, I would not give permission.” Al-Miswar had said, “Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya drinks wine.” This reached Yazīd, and he wrote to the governor of Medina, who flogged al-Miswar with the prescribed penalty. Al-Miswar said: [long metre]

Does Abū Khālid drink it neat, breaking its seal,while al-Miswar is flogged with the prescribed penalty?

The Prophet ﷺ—died when al-Miswar was eight years old. Al-Miswar died in the year 64. He was with Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca when a stone struck him and he died.

Al-Miswar’s son was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Miswar. His mother was the daughter of Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasana, from a clan of Yemen that had joined Zuhra during Islam. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Miswar. He died in the year 90.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s son was Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He was a poet, and he is the one who said: [khafīf metre]

While we were at Balākith in the plain,racing, as the camels sped swiftly, A thought of your remembrance crossed my heart, and here I was, unable to go on.

I said, “At your service,” when longing called me to you,and to the two camel drivers: “Turn the mounts back!”

Makhrama ibn Nawfal was al-Miswar’s father. He lived to the age of one hundred and fifteen years, and lost his sight before he died.

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār

He is Kaʿb ibn Mātiʿ. His kunya was Abū Isḥāq. He was from Ḥimyar, from the house of Dhū Ruʿayn. He had followed the Jewish religion and lived in Yemen, where he became Muslim. Then he came to Medina during the caliphate of ʿUmar ﵁—and afterwards went to Syria. He lived in Ḥimṣ until he died there, in the year 32, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁. Nawf al-Bakkālī was the son of Kaʿb’s wife, and Tabīʿ was also her son.

His kunya was Abū ʿUbayd—though it is also said: Abū ʿĀmir.

Kaʿb ibn Sūr

He was from al-Azd. ʿUmar ﵁—appointed him judge over the people of Baṣra after he approved of his judgment between a woman and her husband: he ruled that she was entitled to one night in every four. He went out with ʿĀʾisha on the Day of the Camel, carrying a copy of the Qurʾān aloft and walking between the two lines of battle. A stray arrow struck and killed him. He was known for his piety. He has no hadith.

220ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad

He is ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, after whom al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth was named. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was among the best of the Muslims, regarded as equal to the Companions, though he was not one of them. His father, al-Aswad, was one of those who mocked the Prophet.

Al-Haytham reported from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda:

Something concerning al-Aswad was reported to Abū Bakr, as related by al-Aswad’s son. Abū Bakr said, “What was the severest form of mutilation among the Arabs?” They answered, “Burning with fire.” So Abū Bakr killed him and then burned him. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān said to one of his sons, alluding to him: [long metre]

The Veracious never burned my grandfather—nor, by my father!—when a man is distracted by obscenity from his noble concerns.

Abū Muḥammad said:

It is said that he was sexually passive.

Al-Jushamī Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, companion of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd

He is ʿAwf ibn Mālik ibn Naḍla, from Jusham ibn Muʿāwiya. He was killed by the Khārijites, the followers of Qaṭarī ibn al-Fujāʾa. His father, Mālik, reported from the Prophet ﷺ.

ʿAlqama, companion of ʿAbd Allāh

He is ʿAlqama ibn Qays, from al-Nakhaʿ, the clan of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī. His kunya was Abū Shibl. He never had a child. His brother was Yazīd ibn Qays, father of Abū al-Aswad ibn Yazīd, the companion of ʿAbd Allāh. ʿAlqama died in the year 62.

Al-Shaʿbī said:

Al-Aswad was given to fasting and prayer, while ʿAlqama was slow-paced, yet he outstripped the swift.

Al-Aswad, companion of ʿAbd Allāh

He is al-Aswad ibn Yazīd ibn Qays, from al-Nakhaʿ. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

He died in the year 74. It is also said: in the year 75.

His son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad was one of the best men. He performed the funeral prayer over Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī. When reciting the talbiya, he used to say: “At your service; I am the pilgrim, son of the pilgrim.” His father had performed pilgrimage eighty times, between ḥajj and ʿumra.

Al-Aswad ibn Yazīd had a brother called ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, who was one of the best men. His son Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd was known by the kunya Abū Jaʿfar. He was called al-Kayyis, “the discerning,” for his skill in worship.

Al-Maʿrūr ibn Suwayd

He was from the Banū Asad. He lived to the age of one hundred and twenty years and never turned gray.

Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ

He is Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ, from Hamdān. His kunya was Abū ʿĀʾisha.

He died in the year 63.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said:

His father, al-Ajdaʿ ibn Mālik, was a poet, and he is the one who described horses: [ramal metre]

As though their fallen riders were dice of gamblers,thrown upon a slope, they lie scattered.

Salmān ibn Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī

He was the first judge appointed by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁—in Iraq, and the first to distinguish between thoroughbreds and crossbred horses. He took part in the Battle of al-Qādisiyya and served as judge there; then he served as judge at al-Madāʾin. Salmān was killed at Balanjar, in the land of the Turks, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ﵁. It is also said that Balanjar is in Armenia.

It is said that his bones are kept by the people of Balanjar in a coffin. When rain is withheld from them, they bring it out and pray for rain by means of it, and rain comes to them. Ibn Jumāna al-Bāhilī said: [long metre]

We have two graves: a grave at Balanjar,and a grave in Upper China—what a grave that is!

The one in China, his conquests spread far and wide;the one among the Turks brings down the rain.

By the grave in China he meant the grave of Qutayba ibn Muslim.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

Qutayba’s grave is in Farghāna; the poet made it part of China.

Shurayḥ the Judge

He is Shurayḥ ibn al-Ḥārith al-Kindī. ʿUmar appointed him judge over Kūfa. He remained a judge for seventy-five years thereafter, with only three years away from office: during the turmoil of Ibn al-Zubayr, when Shurayḥ asked al-Ḥajjāj to excuse him from judging, and al-Ḥajjāj did so. He did not judge between people again until he died, in the year 79. It is also said: in the year 80. His kunya was Abū Umayya. He lived to the age of one hundred and twenty years.

He was a witty man. Two men came before him in a dispute over something. One admitted what the other had claimed against him, without realizing it, and Shurayḥ ruled against him. The man said, “Are you ruling against me without evidence?” He replied, “A trustworthy witness testified before me.” The man asked, “Who is he?” Shurayḥ replied, “Your maternal aunt’s sister’s son.”

Another man said to him, “Where are you, may God set you right?” He replied, “Between you and the wall.” The man said, “I am a man from Syria.” He replied, “A faraway place.” The man said, “I have married a woman.” He replied, “May you live together in harmony and have sons.” The man said, “She has borne a boy.” He replied, “May the horseman bring you joy.” The man said, “I stipulated a house for her.” He replied, “The stipulation has the stronger claim.” The man said, “Judge between us.” He replied, “I have done so.” The man asked, “How?” He replied, “Tell a woman two stories; if she refuses, then four.”

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī

He is ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr ibn Qatāda, from Kināna, from the Banū Jundaʿ ibn Layth.

He was the judge of the people of Mecca. He died around the time of Ibn ʿAbbās, in the year 68. His son ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr died in the year 113.

Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī

He is Ẓālim ibn ʿAmr ibn Jandal ibn Sufyān ibn Kināna. His mother was from the Banū ʿAbd al-Dār ibn Quṣayy. He was intelligent, resolute, and miserly. He was the first to establish Arabic grammar, and he was an accomplished poet. He fought at Ṣiffīn with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁. He governed Baṣra for Ibn ʿAbbās, suffered paralysis in Baṣra, and died there, having reached old age.

His sons were ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Ḥarb. ʿAṭāʾ and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar al-ʿAdwānī further developed Arabic grammar after Abū al-Aswad. ʿAṭāʾ left no descendants.

As for Abū Ḥarb ibn Abī al-Aswad, he was intelligent and a poet. Al-Ḥajjāj appointed him over Jūkha, and he remained there until al-Ḥajjāj died.

Hadiths were related from Abū Ḥarb. He had numerous descendants in Baṣra. He used to say to his children: “Do not compete with God in generosity, for He is more generous and more glorious. Had He wished to provide abundantly for all people, so that none would be in need, He would have done so. Do not exhaust yourselves in giving generously, or you will perish.”

In jest18

He heard a man say, “Who will feed a hungry person?” So he fed him. Then the beggar went to leave, and Abū Ḥarb said, “Not so fast! You must not harm the Muslims tonight.” Then he put his foot in the stocks.

Harm ibn Ḥayyān

He was from ʿAbd al-Qays and was among the best of people. He held governorships in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁. He was in charge of ʿAbd al-Qays at Tawwaj on the day Shahrak was killed, in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁.

Ḥumrān, client of ʿUthmān

He is Ḥumrān ibn Abān ibn ʿAbd ʿAmr. His kunya was Abū Zayd. Al-Musayyib ibn Najaba al-Fazārī captured him at ʿAyn al-Tamr during the time of Abū Bakr ﵁. The commander of the army was Khālid ibn al-Walīd. They found that he was circumcised. He was a Jew, and his name was Ṭuwaydā. He was purchased for ʿUthmān. Then ʿUthmān freed him, and he became a scribe in his service. Later ʿUthmān became angry with him and sent him to Baṣra, where he served as governor. He was the one who wrote to ʿUthmān concerning ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd al-Qays when ʿĀmir was exiled. When Muṣʿab was killed, Ḥumrān rose up and seized Baṣra. He remained in that position until Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh arrived and deposed him. When al-Ḥajjāj arrived in Baṣra, he mistreated Ḥumrān and took one hundred thousand dirhams from him. Ḥumrān wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān to complain, and ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to al-Ḥajjāj: “Ḥumrān is the brother of those who have passed away and the uncle of those who remain. Treat him well as a neighbor and return his property to him.”

Ḥumrān married a woman from the Banū Saʿd. His children married among the Arabs.

Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh

He is Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr, from the Banū al-Ḥuraysh ibn Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿa.

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. His father had been a Companion. He lived at a watering place called al-Shikhkhīr, three nights’ journey from Baṣra, and would come to Baṣra on Friday. It is said that a light used to shine for him in his whip.

ʿUmar ﵁—died when Muṭarrif was twenty years old, so it was as though Muṭarrif had been born during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

He had descendants in Baṣra and in a district of Nīshāpūr called Khwāf.

He died during the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, after the year 87.

His brother, Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr, Abū al-ʿAlāʾ, died in the year 111.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib

He is Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib ibn Ḥazn ibn Abī Wahb, from the Banū ʿImrān ibn Makhzūm.

His mother was Sulaymiyya. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad. His grandfather, Ḥazn, came to the Messenger of God ﷺ—and the Prophet said to him, “Are you Sahl?” He replied, “No, I am Ḥazn”—three times. The Prophet said, “Then you are Ḥazn.” Saʿīd said, “And we have continued to know that harshness among ourselves.”

His father, al-Musayyib, traded in oil. Saʿīd remained estranged from his father and did not speak to him until he died.

Saʿīd was the most learned in jurisprudence among the people of the Ḥijāz and the most skilled of people at interpreting dreams. A man said to him:

“I saw in a dream that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān urinated in the direction of the qibla of the Prophet’s Mosque four times.”

He replied, “If your dream is true, four caliphs will arise from his loins.”

Another man said to him, “I saw in a dream that I seized ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, laid him on the ground, then turned him onto his belly and drove four stakes into his back.”

He replied, “You did not see it; Ibn al-Zubayr saw it. If his dream is true, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān will kill him, and four men will come from ʿAbd al-Malik’s loins, all of them caliphs.”

Another man said to him, “I saw myself urinating into my hand.” He replied, “A close female relative is beneath you.” He looked, and it turned out that his wife and he had shared a wet nurse.

Abū Hurayra’s daughter was married to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib. Jābir ibn al-Aswad was governor of Medina and summoned Saʿīd to swear allegiance to Ibn al-Zubayr, but he refused. Jābir flogged him sixty lashes. Hishām ibn Ismāʿīl also flogged him sixty lashes and paraded him through Medina, wearing a haircloth undergarment, because he had summoned him to swear allegiance to al-Walīd and Sulaymān as the designated successors, but Saʿīd refused.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib was born two years after the beginning of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s caliphate. He died in Medina in the year 94.

Saʿīd’s son was Muḥammad, who was a genealogist. He disavowed some people of the Makhzūm clan, and the matter was reported to al-Walīd, who had him flogged with the prescribed penalty. Those whom he disavowed were the Āl ʿAnkatha.

Saʿīd also had other children. He has descendants still living in Medina.

Bard was his client. Saʿīd said to him, “Bard, beware of lying about me, as ʿIkrima lies about Ibn ʿAbbās.”

He also said, “Every hadith reported to you by Bard alone, which you find objectionable, is a lie.”

ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAnbarī

He is ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Qays, descended from Kaʿb ibn Jundub, of the Banū al-ʿAnbar. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was a virtuous and excellent man.

One day ʿUthmān saw him in his vestibule. He saw an old man with sparse hair and a protruding lower lip, wearing a cloak. ʿUthmān took exception to his presence and did not recognize him. He said, “Bedouin, where is your Lord?” ʿĀmir replied, “He is lying in wait.”

At ʿUthmān’s order, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir exiled him to Syria, where ʿĀmir died.

He left no descendants, and his clan too is small.

The reason he was sent away was that Ḥumrān ibn Abān wrote about him that he did not eat meat, consort with women, or accept appointments—implying that he was a Kharijite. ʿUthmān wrote to Ibn ʿĀmir: “Summon ʿĀmir. If these traits are indeed found in him, send him away.”

He questioned him, and ʿĀmir said: “As for meat, I once passed a butcher slaughtering an animal without pronouncing God’s name. So when I desire meat, I buy a sheep and slaughter it myself. As for women, I have enough to occupy me without them. As for appointments, how many others can you find besides me?” Ḥumrān said to him: “May God not increase our number with men like you.” ʿĀmir replied: “Rather, may God increase our number with men like you: street sweepers and cuppers.”

Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī

He was from the people of Syria. His name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thawb. He was the one who entered upon Muʿāwiya and said to him, “Peace be upon you, Commander,” then spoke to him about the subjects.

He died during the caliphate of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.

Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī told me: al-Aṣmaʿī told me: ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr told me, on the authority of a man from Syria, who said:

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār asked a group of people from Syria: “What is your opinion of Abū Muslim?”

They replied: “We think very well of him, and we have learned from him.” He said: “The people most indifferent to a learned man are his own people. The case is like that of a garden among a people: strangers long for it, while those near at hand have no desire for it. Then, while matters stood thus, its water dried up, and these people had taken its produce, while those others remained lamenting”—that is, regretting it.

al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī

He was al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan. His father’s name was Yasār, a client of the Anṣār.

His mother’s name was Khayra, a client of Umm Salama, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

They say that his mother Khayra would sometimes be away, and he would cry. Umm Salama would then give him her breast to soothe him until his mother returned; her breast would produce milk, and he would drink it. They consider that his wisdom and eloquence came from the blessing of this.

Al-Ḥasan grew up in Wādī al-Qurā.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Riyāshī told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, on the authority of Ḥammād ibn Zayd and Ḥammād ibn Salama, on the authority of ʿAlī ibn Zayd ibn Judʿān, who said:

Al-Ḥasan was born into slavery.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, on the authority of Qurra, on the authority of Qatāda:

Al-Ḥasan’s mother was a client of Umm Salama.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

The father of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and the father of Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn were among the captives of Maysān. Al-Mughīra had conquered it in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, when he appointed him governor of al-Baṣra.

Others say: Yasār was from the people of Nahr al-Marʾa.

Al-Ḥasan was among the handsomest people of al-Baṣra until he fell from his mount, and his nose was injured as it was.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, on the authority of his father, who said:

I never saw anyone with a broader forearm than al-Ḥasan’s: its breadth was a span. He had spoken about predestination, then recanted.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār was a preacher and held the doctrine of predestination. He had a lisp. He and Maʿbad al-Juhanī used to come to al-Ḥasan and ask him: “Abū Saʿīd, these rulers shed the blood of Muslims, seize property, and do this and that, and then say: ‘Our actions occur only according to God’s predestination.’” He replied: “The enemies of God lie.” They seized upon this and similar remarks against him.

He was likened to Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj for the eloquence of his speech and his command of Arabic. He was born two years before the end of ʿUmar’s caliphate and died in the year 110. In that same year Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn died, a hundred days after him. Ibn Sīrīn did not attend his funeral because of something that had passed between them.

Al-Ḥasan was the secretary of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād al-Ḥārithī in Khurāsān. Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd was asked: “Do you know anyone who acts as al-Ḥasan did?” He replied: “By God, I know no one who speaks as he did, so how could anyone act as he did?”

Then he described him, saying: “When he came forward, it was as though he had just come from burying a close relative. When he sat down, it was as though he had been ordered to have his neck struck. When the Fire was mentioned, it was as though it had been created for him alone.”

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn

They say:

Sīrīn, the father of Muḥammad, was a slave of Anas ibn Mālik. Anas contracted to free him for twenty thousand, and he paid the sum of the contract. He was among the captives of Maysān, which al-Mughīra had conquered.

It is also said that he was among the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr. His mother Ṣafiyya was a client of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁. Three of the Prophet’s wives ﷺ—prepared her with perfume and prayed for her. Eighteen veterans of Badr attended her wedding, among them Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who prayed, while they said “Amen.”

Sīrīn was called Abū ʿAmra. He had twenty-three children, born to various slave-mothers.

Sīrīn had land at Jarjarāyā, which came into the possession of Muḥammad and his brother—whose name was Yaḥyā.

Among his children were Maʿbad ibn Sīrīn—older than Muḥammad and Yaḥyā, and who died at Jarjarāyā—and Anas ibn Sīrīn. He also had sisters, among them ʿAmra, Ḥafṣa, and Sawda, the daughters of Sīrīn.

Muḥammad was a cloth merchant and was called Abū Bakr. He was imprisoned for a debt he owed, and he was deaf.

He had thirty children with one woman, whom he had married as an Arab woman. None of them survived except ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad. He was born two years before the end of ʿUthmān’s caliphate.

Anas ibn Sīrīn said this. He said: “I was born in the year before the end of his caliphate.”

He died in the year 110, a hundred days after al-Ḥasan. He was seventy-seven years old.

His son ʿAbd Allāh paid off thirty thousand dirhams on his behalf. By the time ʿAbd Allāh died, his property had been valued at seventy thousand dirhams.

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn was the secretary of Anas ibn Mālik in Fārs.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Al-Ḥasan is a generous master. If the deaf man”—meaning Ibn Sīrīn—“tells you something, hold fast to it; and Qatāda is a night-gatherer of firewood.”

Abū Saʿīd al-Maqburī

His name was Kaysān. He was a slave of a man from Banū Jundaʿ. His master contracted to free him for forty thousand and a sheep for every ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā, and he paid this. His home was by the graves, so he was called al-Maqburī.

He transmitted from ʿUmar. He died in the year 100, during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

It is also said that he died in Medina during the caliphate of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yazīd al-Laythī

He was called Abū Muḥammad. He was of the very people of Kināna. Al-Zuhrī transmitted from him. He died in the year 107, aged eighty-two.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ

He was ʿAṭāʾ ibn Aslam, one of the descendants of al-Jund. His mother was a Black woman named Baraka.

He grew up in Mecca and learned the Qurʾān there. He was a client of Banū Fihr. He was called Abū Muḥammad.

He was Black, one-eyed, flat-nosed, lame in one arm, and lame in one leg; later, he became blind.

He died in the year 115, aged eighty-eight.

His son was Yaʿqūb ibn ʿAṭāʾ. [He had performed the pilgrimage seventy times and entered upon ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. ʿAbd al-Malik seated him before him and said: “What do you need, Abū Muḥammad?”

He replied: “The sanctuary of God and the sanctuary of the Messenger of God ﷺ—so take care of them.” He said: “Yes.” Then ʿAṭāʾ said: “And fear God with regard to the children of the Emigrants and the Anṣār, for through them you attained this station. Do not cut off the stipends of those who are at your door or those who are far from your door; you are answerable for them.” He said: “I will.” Then ʿAṭāʾ rose without asking anything for himself. ʿAbd al-Malik said: “By your father, this is nobility and lordship.”]

Mujāhid ibn Jabr

He was Mujāhid ibn Jabr. He was a client of Qays ibn al-Sāʾib al-Makhzūmī.

Mujāhid said: “It was revealed concerning my client Qays ibn al-Sāʾib: ‘And for those who can bear it, there is a ransom: feeding a poor person.’” He therefore broke the fast and fed a poor person each day.

Mujāhid was called Abū al-Ḥajjāj. He died in Mecca while prostrating, in the year 103, aged eighty-three.

[Al-Aʿmash said: “If only you had seen Mujāhid at Tawj, when his donkey had gone astray!”

He said: “Whenever you saw him, you would see him grief-stricken, with his head bowed.” He was asked about this.

He replied: “ʿAbd Allāh took [me]”—then he said—“The Messenger of God ﷺ—took me by the hand and said to me: ‘ʿAbd Allāh, be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler passing through.’”]

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

He was a client of Banū Wāliba, of Banū Asad. He was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was Black and served as a scribe for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba ibn Masʿūd, then for Abū Burda.

He was in charge of the judiciary and the treasury. He joined Ibn al-Ashʿath’s revolt. When Ibn al-Ashʿath’s companions were defeated at Dayr al-Jamājim, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr fled to Mecca. Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī, the governor of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik over Mecca, captured him and sent him to al-Ḥajjāj. Al-Ḥajjāj ordered that his head be struck off. It fell to the ground and rolled, while he said, “There is no god but God.” He continued in this state until al-Ḥajjāj ordered someone to put his foot on his mouth, whereupon he fell silent.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb told me: Abū Dāwūd told us, on the authority of ʿUmāra ibn Zādhān, who said:

Abū al-Ṣahbāʾ told us, who said:

Al-Ḥajjāj said to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: “Choose whichever manner of death you wish.” He replied: “Rather, choose for yourself, for retribution awaits you.” He said to him: “You wretch, son of Kusayr, when I first came to al-Kūfa, was an Arab the only one leading the prayer there? Did I not make you the prayer leader?” He replied: “Yes.” He said:

“Did I not appoint you to the judiciary, when the people of al-Kūfa made an uproar and said that only an Arab was fit to judge? Did I not appoint Abū Burda as judge and order him not to decide anything without you?” He replied: “Yes.” He said:

“Did I not include you among my intimates?” He replied: “Yes.” He said: “Did I not give you such-and-such money to distribute among the needy, and then never ask you about any of it?” He replied: “Yes.” He said:

“Then what made you rise against me?” He replied: “I had an oath of allegiance to Ibn al-Ashʿath binding on me.” Al-Ḥajjāj grew angry and said: “But the oath of allegiance to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd al-Malik, was binding on you before that. By God, I shall kill you.”

Al-Ḥajjāj killed him in the year 94. He was forty-nine years old. He had two sons, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Saʿīd, who transmitted from him.

Abū Qilāba

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd al-Jarmī. His administrative register was in Syria. He died at Dāriyā in the year 104 or 105.

Abū Ḥātim told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, on the authority of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, on the authority of Ayyūb, who said:

Abū Qilāba instructed that his books be given to me. They were brought from Syria and handed over to me, and I mixed up some of what I had heard from him.

Abū Ḥātim told me, on the authority of al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Ayyūb’s companions told me, on the authority of Ayyūb, who said:

Abū Qilāba used to urge me to earn my living, saying: “Wealth is part of well-being.”

Bishr ibn Saʿīd

He was a client of the Ḥaḍramīs. He was devout and lived in seclusion. He transmitted from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Zayd ibn Thābit, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and others.

He traveled with al-Farazdaq. They rode together in a litter, to the astonishment of the people. Bishr used to say: “I have never seen a better traveling companion than al-Farazdaq”; al-Farazdaq said the same of him.

He died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, in the year 100, and left no shroud.

Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb

He was from Khuzāʿa. He was called Abū Isḥāq. He was in charge of the signet ring of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. Al-Zuhrī transmitted from him. It was he who brought al-Zuhrī before ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, who provided for him and assigned him a stipend.

Qabīṣa died in Syria in the year 86 or 87. I know of no descendants of his.

Yazīd ibn Shajara

He was Yazīd ibn Shajara al-Ruhāwī. He and his companions were killed at sea in the year 58.

Shahr ibn Ḥawshab

He was from the Ashʿarīs and was weak in hadith.

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh told us, on the authority of al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl, who said:

Shahr was mentioned before Ibn ʿAwn, who said: “They abandoned Shahr”.

He died in the year 98. It is also said: in the year 112. He entered the treasury and took a purse. Someone then said: [al-ṭawīl]

Shahr sold his religion for a purse; Who, Shahr, can trust the Qurʾān reciters after you?

al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab

As for al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab, he was from Shaybān. He was called Abū ʿĪsā.

He died in the year 148.

Maymūn ibn Mihrān

Maymūn was a contracted slave of Banū Naṣr ibn Muʿāwiya, and he was freed. His son ʿAmr ibn Maymūn was a slave of a woman from al-Azd, of Thumāla, called Umm Nimr. She freed him. He remained in al-Kūfa until the uprising at Dayr al-Jamājim, then moved to the Jazīra. Maymūn was governor of the land tax for ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz over al-Jazīra, and his son ʿAmr ibn Maymūn was in charge of the bureau. Maymūn was a cloth merchant, and would sit in his shop while administering the land tax. He died in the year 117.

His son ʿAmr died in the year 145.

Abū Wāʾil

He was Shaqīq ibn Salama al-Asadī. His mother was a Christian. He had a reed enclosure where he and his horse would stay. Whenever he went on a campaign, he dismantled it; when he returned, he put it back up.

Ḥammād ibn Zayd related from ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, who said:

“I came upon people who used to take this night as a mount. They would drink jar wine—that is, wine kept in jars—and wear safflower-dyed garments, seeing no harm in it. Among them were Abū Wāʾil and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh.”

Abū Wāʾil died during the time of al-Ḥajjāj, after the Battle of al-Jamājim.

Abū Muḥammad said:

“Al-jarr means wine.”

Abū Naḍra

His name was al-Mundhir ibn Mālik. He was from al-ʿAwqa, a branch of ʿAbd al-Qays. He died during the governorship of ʿUmar ibn Hubayra, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī led his funeral prayer.

Al-Shaʿbī

He was ʿĀmir ibn Sharāḥīl ibn ʿAbd al-Shaʿbī. He was from Ḥimyar, though counted among Hamdān. He was named after a mountain in Yemen, which Ḥassān ibn ʿAmr al-Ḥimyarī settled with his son and where he was buried. Those of his descendants who lived in Kūfa were called Shaʿbīs; those who lived in Egypt and the Maghrib were called al-Ashʿabūn; those among them who lived in Syria were called Shaʿbānīs; and those who lived in Yemen were called the descendants of Dhū Shaʿbayn.

Al-Shaʿbī’s kunya was Abū ʿAmr. He was thin and slight.

He was asked, “Why do we see you so thin?” He replied, “I was crowded in the womb”—for he and a brother had been born in the same womb.

Abū Isḥāq was asked, “Are you older, or al-Shaʿbī?” He replied, “He is two years older than I am.”

Al-Riyāshī related to us from al-Aṣmaʿī:

“Al-Shaʿbī’s mother was among the captives of Jalūlāʾ.” He said, “It is a village in the region of Fārs.”

He was born six years into the caliphate of ʿUthmān. He served as secretary to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muṭīʿ al-ʿAdawī and to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Khaṭmī, and as governor of Kūfa for Ibn al-Zubayr. He was fond of joking.

Abū Marzūq related to me from Zājir ibn al-Ṣalt al-Ṭalḥī, from Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān:

“Al-Shaʿbī said to a tailor he passed: ‘We have a broken jar. Can you sew it?’ The tailor said, ‘Yes, if you have threads made of wind.’”

Abū Muḥammad said: He also related this to me through the same chain:

“A man came in to see him while there was a woman in the house with him. The man asked, ‘Which of you is al-Shaʿbī?’ He replied, ‘This one.’”

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He died in the year 105, aged seventy-seven. It is also said that he died in the year 104.”

It has also been related from him that he said, “I was born in the year of Jalūlāʾ.” If this is true, he died aged eighty-six, since Jalūlāʾ took place in the year 19, during the caliphate of ʿUmar ﵁.

Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī

He was Sulaymān ibn Abī Sulaymān, a client of theirs. He died in the year 129. He used to say, “If this report were good, it would have been shortened.”

Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī

He was ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from a branch of Hamdān called al-Sabīʿ.

Sharīk said: “Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī was born with three years remaining in ʿUthmān’s reign. He died in the year 127, aged ninety-five.”

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me from his uncle, from Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, who said:

“My father lifted me up until I saw ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib preaching from the pulpit, with his head white and his beard.” His son Yūnus ibn Abī Isḥāq died in the year 159.

His son ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus, whose kunya was Abū ʿAmr, moved from Kūfa to the frontier region and settled at al-Ḥadath. He died there in the year 191.

Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd

He was a client of Ashjaʿ. He had brothers who also related hadith: ʿUbayd, ʿImrān, Ziyād, and Muslim, the sons of Abī al-Jaʿd.

They said: Abī al-Jaʿd had six sons. Two of them were Shīʿīs, two were Murjiʾites, and two held the views of the Khārijites. Their father used to say to them, “My sons, God has made you differ from one another.”

Sālim died in the year 100 or 101. Mughīra did not consider the hadith of Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, the hadith of Khilās, or the scroll of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar to be reliable. He said, “He had a scroll he called ‘The Truthful One.’ I would not care to have it even for two fils.”

Makhūl al-Shāmī

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He was from Kābul, a client of a woman from Hudhayl.”

Ibn ʿĀʾisha said: “Makhūl al-Shāmī was a client of a woman from Qays. He was a Sindi and did not speak clearly.”

Nūḥ ibn Qays said:

“One of the governors asked him about predestination. He replied, ‘Am I a magician?’—meaning, ‘a sorcerer.’ He held the doctrine of predestination.”

Maʿqil ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā al-Qurashī said:

“I heard him say to a man, ‘What happened to that hāja?’—meaning, ‘need.’”

He died in the year 113.

Makhūl al-Azdī

Sahl related to me from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Makhūl and Abū al-ʿĀliya were both ḥamīlayn. This Makhūl was eloquent and related traditions from Ibn ʿUmar.”

Jābir ibn Zayd

Al-Wāqidī said:

“He was from al-Azd, and his kunya was Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ.”

Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ was from Jawf in Yemen, and he was one-eyed. He died in the year 103.”

Abū Baṣīr

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

“He was from Banū Yashkur ibn Wāʾil. When they brought him to Musaylima as a boy, Musaylima wiped his face, and he became blind. He was given the kunya Abū Baṣīr—‘Father of Sight’—by way of inversion, just as the crow was called ‘one-eyed’ because of its sharp sight.

“He used to relate traditions from him, and lived to the time of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī.”

Abū al-ʿĀliya

Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī related to me:

“Abū al-ʿĀliya was a client of Banū Riyāḥ. A woman from among them emancipated him. His name was Rufayʿ. His son Ḥarb ibn Abī al-ʿĀliya performed the pilgrimage sixty times.”

Abū al-ʿĀliya died in the year 90.

Abū Ḥātim related to me from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Abū al-ʿĀliya and Makhūl—that is, Makhūl al-Azdī—were both ḥamīlayn. Abū al-ʿĀliya was fond of joking.”

Aḥmad ibn al-Khalīl related to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related to us from Abū Khilda, who said:

“I asked Abū al-ʿĀliya about killing ants. He gathered up a great many of them and said, ‘Poor things—how clever they are!’ Then he killed them and laughed.”

Ṭāwūs

He said:

“He was Ṭāwūs ibn Kaysān, a client of Buḥayr al-Ḥimyarī.”

Sahl related to me from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Ṭāwūs was a client of the people of Yemen, and his mother was a client of Ḥimyar. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He died in Mecca in the year 106, one day before the Day of Tarwiya. Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik led his funeral prayer.”

His son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāwūs used to relate hadith from him. He died during the caliphate of Abū al-ʿAbbās.

ʿIkrima, the Client of Ibn ʿAbbās

He was a slave belonging to Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās died while ʿIkrima was still a slave, and ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās sold him to Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya for four thousand dinars. ʿIkrima came to ʿAlī and said to him, “What good has this done you? You have sold your father’s knowledge for four thousand dinars!” ʿAlī asked to have the sale rescinded. The buyer agreed, and ʿAlī emancipated him.

His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

Jarīr related from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, who said:

“I went in to see ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, with ʿIkrima bound at the door of a privy. I said, ‘Do you do this to your client?’ He replied, ‘This man lies about my father.’”

Ibn al-Khallāl related to me, saying: I heard Yazīd ibn Hārūn say:

“ʿIkrima came to Baṣra. Ayyūb, Sulaymān al-Taymī, and Yūnus came to him. While he was relating traditions to them, he heard the sound of singing. ʿIkrima said, ‘Be quiet, so we can listen.’ Then he said—may God fight him—‘He sang well!’ Or he said, ‘How well he sang!’ As for Sulaymān and Yūnus, they did not go back to him; Ayyūb did.”

Yazīd said:

“Ayyūb did well.”

Al-Riyāshī related to me from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Nāfiʿ al-Madanī, who said:

“The poet Kathīr and ʿIkrima died on the same day.”

Al-Riyāshī said: Ibn Sallām also related to me:

“The people went to Kathīr’s funeral.”

ʿIkrima held the views of the Khārijites. When one of the governors sought him, he went into hiding with Dāwūd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn, and remained with him until he died. ʿIkrima died in the year 105, having reached the age of eighty.

Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī

He was from Muzayna of Muḍar. Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s mother was wealthy and had a husband with much money. Bakr dressed very well.

ʿAffān related from Muʿtamir, from his father:

“Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s clothing was valued at four thousand dirhams.”

Someone else said:

“Bakr bought a ṭaylasān for four hundred dirhams. When the tailor was about to cut it, he went to sprinkle dust on it to mark where it should be cut. Bakr said to him, ‘Do not hurry,’ and ordered that camphor be ground, then sprinkled over it.”

He died in the year 108. Al-Ḥasan attended his funeral. Bakr’s grandfather had been a Companion, and Bakr left no surviving descendants.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim

He was from Banū ʿAbd Manāf ibn Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, the clan of Zaynab, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

His kunya was Abū al-Qāsim. He was born after two years, and had cut his second teeth. He was a teacher. He went to Khurāsān and settled there. He died in the year 102.

Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz

He was Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz ibn Ziyād, from Ghassān of Tamīm. The Ghassān of Tamīm have died out.

Ṣafwān was one of the companions of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. He died in Baṣra in the year 74, during the governorship of Bishr ibn Marwān. He left no descendants. He was the one who said:

“If I enter my house, eat my loaf, and drink water with it, then let the world be destroyed.”

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī

His kunya was Abū Ḥamza.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muʿtab related from Abū Burda, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:
