“I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ—say: ‘A man will emerge from the two soothsayer tribes who will study the Qurʾān with a thoroughness unmatched by anyone after him.’ It was said that this meant Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb. The two soothsayer tribes are Qurayẓa and Naḍīr.”

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb wrote out his lineage and said, ‘Al-Quraẓī.’ He was asked, ‘Or al-Anṣārī?’”

He replied, “I would dislike claiming credit before God for something I did not do.” He used to preach, and his mosque collapsed upon him and his companions, killing them. It is said that he died in the year 108. It is also said: in the year 117 or 118.

Wahb ibn Munabbih

He was descended from the Persians whom Kisrā sent to Yemen.

He was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He said, “I have read seventy-two books of the Books of God.”

He had brothers, among them Hammām ibn Munabbih, who was older than Wahb. He related from Abū Hurayra and died before Wahb.

Among them, too, were Maʿqil ibn Munabbih and ʿUmar ibn Munabbih, from both of whom he also related.

Wahb died in Ṣanʿāʾ in the year 110; it is also said that he died in the year 114.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

Yasār was the client of Maymūna al-Hilāliyya, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

Yasār’s sons were ʿAṭāʾ, Sulaymān, Muslim, and ʿAbd al-Malik, the sons of Yasār; all of them were jurists.

Someone else said:

ʿAṭāʾ was a preacher and held the doctrine of predestination.

He was called Abū Muḥammad. He died in the year 103, aged eighty-four.

Sulaymān died in the year 107, aged seventy-three. He was called Abū Ayyūb. ʿAbd al-Malik died in the year 110.

Miqsam, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās

He was the client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

He was called the client of Ibn ʿAbbās because he kept close to him, devoted himself to him, and related from him.

He was called Abū al-Qāsim. He also related from Umm Salama, having heard from her herself—may God, exalted is He, be pleased with her.

Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾama

He was Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾama. Abū Ṣāliḥ’s name was Nabḥān. Al-Tawʾama was the daughter of Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumaḥī. She and a sister were born in the same birth, so one was given a name and this one was called al-Tawʾama, “the twin.”

She freed Abū Ṣāliḥ. This Abū Ṣāliḥ was a man of old age. He related from Abū Hurayra and lived until he died in Medina in the year 125. He had only a few hadiths, and his hadiths are considered weak.

Nāfiʿ, the client of Ibn ʿUmar

He was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was from Abarshahr, and ʿAbd Allāh captured him on one of his campaigns. He died in the year 117.

His children were ʿUmar ibn Nāfiʿ, Abū Bakr ibn Nāfiʿ, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nāfiʿ.

All of them related from him.

Sahl related to me, saying: al-Aṣmaʿī related to us, saying: al-ʿUmarī related to us, from Nāfiʿ, who said:

“I went with Ibn ʿUmar to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. He offered him twelve thousand dirhams for me, but he refused to sell me. He set me free—may God, exalted is He, set him free.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir

He was Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir ibn Hudayr, of Banū Taym of Quraysh, the kin-group of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq—may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him.

Al-Munkadir had a brother named Rabīʿa ibn Hudayr, one of the jurists of the Ḥijāz.

He was asked, “Which deeds are best?” He replied, “Bringing joy to a believer.”

He was asked, “What of this world do you love most?” He replied, “Generosity toward one’s brothers.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir died in the year 130—or 131—and left descendants in Medina. Muḥammad had two brothers who were jurists and devout worshippers: Abū Bakr ibn al-Munkadir and ʿUmar ibn al-Munkadir.

Among the clients of the family of al-Munkadir was al-Mājishūn.

Al-Mājishūn, the client of the family of al-Munkadir

He was al-Mājishūn ibn Abī Salama. His name was Yaʿqūb. His descendants and his cousins were affiliated with him, and they were called the Banū al-Mājishūn.

Yaʿqūb al-Mājishūn was a jurist, as was his son Yūsuf ibn Yaʿqūb. Al-Mājishūn had a brother named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Salama. His son ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He died in Baghdad during the caliphate of al-Mahdī. Al-Mahdī performed the funeral prayer over him and buried him in the cemetery of Quraysh. This was in the year 164.

He was among the clients of the family of al-Munkadir.

Rabīʿa al-Raʾy

He was Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. We shall mention him among those who held opinions and gave legal opinions.

Qatāda

He was Qatāda ibn Diʿāma, of the tribe of Sadūs. His father was born in al-Diʿāmiyya, an Arab of the desert, and his mother was a concubine born among the Arabs of the desert. The poet said: [basīṭ]

“The waterholes of al-Diʿāmiyya have become desolate,

though Umm Kulthūm may yet be there.”

Qatāda was called Abū al-Khaṭṭāb. He died in the year 117.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Shuʿba, who said:

“When Qatāda related a good hadith and then went off to bring another one, I would run after him, so that he would not forget the first. He used to memorize and not write.”

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī

He was Ibrāhīm ibn Yazīd, of al-Nakhaʿ, in Yemen, the kin-group of ʿAlqama and al-Aswad.

Abū Sufyān ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said:

“We differed about Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī in the presence of Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān. He sent someone to ask about him, and they said, ‘He is a client of al-Nakhaʿ.’”

Abū ʿUbayda related from Yūnus:

“He was born among the Arabs. He was called Abū ʿImrān. He acquired knowledge from him when he was eighteen years old. He died at the age of forty-six.”

He was a joker. He was told, “Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says such-and-such.” He replied, “Tell him:

‘He is taking the path through the valley of fools.’”

Saʿīd was told, “Ibrāhīm says such-and-such.” He replied, “Tell him: ‘He should sit in cold water.’”

Al-Aʿmash said:

“Ibrāhīm came to visit me when I was ill. He saw my house and said, ‘You can tell from your house that you are not the son of one of the two great towns.’”

He died at the age of forty-six.

Sahl related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī:

“Ibrāhīm died in the year 96, during the governorship of Ibn Abī Muslim.”

He said: Abū ʿAwn said, “I was at Ibrāhīm’s funeral, and there were only seven people there. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad ibn Yazīd performed the funeral prayer over him; he was his maternal cousin.”

Al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtayba

He was a client of Kinda. He was called Abū ʿAbd Allāh—and it is also said, Abū Muḥammad. He and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī were born in the same year. He died in Kūfa in the year 115.

Ibn Idrīs said: “I was born in the year al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtayba died.” He had brothers.

Sahl related to us, saying: al-Aṣmaʿī related to us, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said:

Al-Nakhaʿī said to me, “Do not keep company with the Banū ʿUtayba, for they are liars”—meaning the brothers of al-Ḥakam.

Abū al-Zinād

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dhakwān, the client of Ramla bt. Shayba ibn Rabīʿa. Ramla was married to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁.

Abū al-Zinād was called Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, but Abū al-Zinād became the name by which he was known.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Abū al-Zinād, that he said:

“Our origin is from Hamdān.”

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz appointed him to collect the land tax of Iraq, together with ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

Abū al-Zinād died suddenly in his bathhouse, in the month of Ramaḍān in the year 130, aged sixty-six.

236/ ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Zinād

His son was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-Zinād. He was called Abū Muḥammad. He administered the land tax of Medina, came to Baghdad, and died there in the year 174, aged seventy-four.

His brother Abū al-Qāsim ibn Abī al-Zinād related from him. His son Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was seventeen years younger than his father and survived him by twenty-one years. He had met his father’s teachers, but did not relate from them until his father died. He too died in Baghdad, and he and his father were buried in Baghdad, in the cemetery of Bāb al-Tabbān.

Al-Aʿraj, the companion of Abū Hurayra

He was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz. He was called Abū Dāwūd and was the client of Muḥammad ibn Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. He went to Alexandria and stayed there until he died. His death was in the year 117.

Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm

He was one of the Anṣār. His name was his kunya. He died in Medina in the year 120.

He was eighty-four years old.

ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda ibn al-Nuʿmān

He was an authority on campaigns and military expeditions. He died in the year 120, and his line died out, with none of them left. His grandfather Qatāda ibn al-Nuʿmān was one of the Companions and one of the renowned archers. The last surviving members of his line were ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb, the sons of ʿUmar ibn Qatāda. They died without leaving descendants.

Abū Mijlaz

He was Lāḥiq ibn Ḥumayd ibn Sadūs ibn Shaybān. He lived in Khurāsān, and his descendants were there. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz sent for him and had him brought in order to ask him about it.

Qurra ibn Khālid said:

“Abū Mijlaz was in charge of the treasury and of minting coin.”

He died during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, before al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī died.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas

He was from Baṣra, of Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil. He met Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir, and Anas ibn Mālik. He fled from al-Ḥajjāj and went to Marw, where he settled in one of its villages. Later, when the call of the descendants of al-ʿAbbās appeared, he was sought in Khurāsān and went into hiding. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak found his way to him while he was in hiding and heard forty hadiths from him.

ʿAbd Allāh used to say, “I would not trade them for such-and-such”—naming something. He died during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

237/ Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya

He was Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra ibn Iyās, of Muzayna of Muḍar, the kin-group of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaf­fal. He was called Abū Wāʾila. Iyās, his great-grandfather, had been a Companion.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz appointed him judge of Baṣra. He was accurate in his judgment and discerning in affairs. He had a concubine who bore him a child. His home was by al-Sayy, and he died there in the year 122. He left descendants in Baṣra and elsewhere.

Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra was asked, “What is your son like to you?” He replied, “An excellent son: he took care of my worldly affairs and freed me for my hereafter.”

Abū al-Aʿwar al-Sulamī

He was ʿUmar ibn Sulaymān, of Dhakwān Sulaym. His mother was a Qurashī woman, of Banū Sahm.

Abū Ḥabra

He was Shayḥa ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays, of Ḍubayʿa ibn Rabīʿa ibn Nizār. He was one of the companions of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁. He died in Baṣra at an advanced age.

He left no descendants.

Abū Jamra, the companion of Ibn ʿAbbās

He was Naṣr ibn ʿImrān ibn Wāsiʿ, of Ḍubayʿa ibn Rabīʿa ibn Nizār.

He died in Baṣra and had descendants there.

Abū al-Tayyāḥ

He was Yazīd ibn Ḥumayd, of Banū Bahtha. He was one of the jurists of Baṣra. He died there and left no descendants.

Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb

He was of ʿAnaza. He was imprisoned by al-Ḥajjāj, then released after al-Ḥajjāj’s death.

He was one of the leading Murjiʾites. He died in Wāsiṭ and left no descendants.

Khārija ibn Muṣʿab

He was of Banū Shajna, of Ḍubayʿa. He was among the most learned people of Khurāsān, and the most esteemed among them. His father, Muṣʿab ibn Khārija, was with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁. His descendants were in Khurāsān.

ʿAmr ibn Dīnār

He was the client of Ibn Bādhān, one of the Persians of Yemen. He was called Abū Muḥammad. He died in the year 125.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Najīḥ

He was a client of Banū Makhzūm and was known by the teknonym Abū Yasār. He held the doctrine of free will.

Al-Bajalī related to us:

The name of Abū Najīḥ was Yasār. He was a client of Thaqīf. Abū Najīḥ died in the year 109. His son ʿAbd Allāh died in the year 132.

Abū al-Malīḥ al-Hudhalī

He was ʿĀmir ibn Usāmah. Ayyūb related from him. He died in the year 112. As for Abū al-Malīḥ al-Fazārī, he was al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmar, a client of ʿUmar ibn Hubayrah. He was born in al-Raqqah and died in the year 181.

238/ Abū al-Jawzāʾ al-Rabaʿī

He was Aws ibn Khālid.

He said:

“I lived as a neighbor of Ibn ʿAbbās in his house for twelve years. There was no verse in the Qurʾān about which I had not asked him.”

He went out with Ibn al-Ashʿath and was killed at Dayr al-Jamājim in the year 83.

Muʾarriq al-ʿIjlī

He was Muʾarriq ibn Mishmarij. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Muʿtamir. He was among the devout, and he used to comb lice from his mother’s head.

A man said to him, “Is all your affair sound?” He replied, “I wish a tenth of it were sound.”

A man said to him, “I complain to you of myself: I cannot manage to pray or fast.”

He replied, “How badly you have praised yourself! Since you are too weak for good, then be too weak for evil. For I rejoice in the sleep that I get.”

Sometimes he would visit one of his brothers and put some dirhams down with them, saying:

“Keep these until I come back to you.” Then, when he left, he would say, “You are released from any claim to them.”

Muʾarriq died during the governorship of ʿUmar ibn Hubayrah over Iraq.

Mālik ibn Dīnār

He was a client of Banū Sāmah ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fihr ibn Mālik. He was known by the teknonym Abū Yaḥyā. He used to copy out Qurʾāns for payment. He died shortly before the plague, which occurred in the year 131.

Ibn Shubrumah

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shubrumah, of Ḍabbah, descended from al-Mundhir ibn Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr. He was known by the teknonym Abū Shubrumah. He was judge for Abū Jaʿfar over the Sawād of Kūfah.

He was a poet, well-mannered, and generous. Sometimes he would clothe people until he was left with hardly any clothes.

He had two nephews, called ʿUmārah and Yazīd, sons of al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Shubrumah; he related traditions from them.

Ibn Shubrumah used to say to his son, “My son, do not make yourself available to people, for the boldest people toward wild beasts are those who have had the most dealings with them.”

Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī

He was Ayyūb ibn Abī Tamīmah. The name of Abū Tamīmah was Kaysān. Ayyūb was known by the teknonym Abū Bakr. He was a client of Banū ʿAmmār ibn Shaddād. ʿAmmār was a client of ʿAnazah, so Ayyūb was a client of a client. He used to shave his hair once a year, and when it grew long he would part it.

Ḥammād ibn Zayd said:

“Ayyūb’s shirt was of fine Herati cloth and reached the ground. His hair hung down, his moustache was full, and he had a fine Kurdish cloak and a Turkic cap. If he had asked you for a drink of water in a state of ritual devotion, you would not have given it to him.”

He had seen Anas ibn Mālik. He died in Basrah during the plague, in the year 131. On the day he died, he was sixty-three years old. He had descendants.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Ṣuhayb

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was enslaved, and both his parents were enslaved. Iyās ibn Muʿāwiyah accepted the testimony of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz alone.

Al-Zuhrī

He was Muḥammad ibn Muslim ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shihāb ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilāb.

His great-grandfather ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shihāb fought with the polytheists at Badr. He was one of the men who made a pact on the day of Uḥud that, if they saw the Messenger of God ﷺ—they would kill him, or die defending him. They were ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shihāb, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Ibn Qamīʾah, and ʿUtbah ibn Abī Waqqāṣ.

His father, Muslim ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, was with Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zuhrī remained with ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, then with Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik had appointed him judge.

He died in the month of Ramaḍān, in the year 124, and was buried on his estate beside the road, so that passersby might pray for him. The place where he was buried marked the end of the district of al-Ḥijāz and the beginning of the district of Palestine; his farm was there.

Al-Zuhrī’s brother, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim, was older than al-Zuhrī and was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He had met Ibn ʿUmar ﵁—and related traditions from him and others. He died before al-Zuhrī.

Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah

He was of Kindah. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Miqdām—and it is also said that he was known by the teknonym Abū Naṣr.

Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim said:

“I saw Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah: his head was red and his beard was white.”

He died in the year 112.

Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥibbān

He related many traditions and was trustworthy. He died in Madinah in the year 121, during the caliphate of Hishām, at the age of seventy-four.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr

He was of Lakhm. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAmr and was nicknamed al-Qibṭī. He was appointed judge over Kūfah after al-Shaʿbī. A year later, he asked al-Ḥajjāj to relieve him, and al-Ḥajjāj did so; al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was appointed judge in his place.

ʿAbd al-Malik lived to the age of one hundred and three. He died in the year 136.

Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī said:

“I was among those following behind his bier in the funeral procession.”

He was very ugly. He wrote poetry, and the effeminate men nicknamed him “Repeller of Ghouls.”

240/ Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān

He transmitted the teachings of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī. He was known by the teknonym Abū Ismāʿīl. He was a client of Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

His father’s name was Muslim. He was among those whom Muʿāwiyah sent to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī when the latter was at Dūmat al-Jandal.

Ḥammād was a Murjiʾī. He died in the year 120.

Al-Mughīrah, transmitter from Ibrāhīm

He was al-Mughīrah ibn Miqsam. He was known by the teknonym Abū Hishām and was a client of Ḍabbah. He was blind.

He died in the year 136. In that same year, ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib al-Thaqafī—known by the teknonym Abū Zayd—also died. Al-Mughīrah had no descendants. He had suffered confusion in his final years.

Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir al-Sulamī

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAttāb.

Ibn ʿUyaynah said: “He had become bleary-eyed from weeping. He fasted for sixty years and kept vigil at night for sixty years.”

Someone else said:

“He was from Abyssinia. Yazīd ibn ʿUmar appointed him judge, and he sat to hear the people, who came before him. He kept saying, ‘I do not know how,’ until he was dismissed.”

He died in the year 132.

Ibn Abī Mulaykah

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Mulaykah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān al-Taymī, of Quraysh, from the clan of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁.

The name of Abū Mulaykah was Zuhayr.

Abū al-Yaqẓān mentioned:

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān was childless, so he claimed a man as his son, named him Zuhayr, and gave him the teknonym Abū Mulaykah. All his descendants were then ascribed to Abū Mulaykah. Abū Mulaykah disappeared and did not return.

“He had made a dish of porridge, then went out on an errand and did not return. Hence the proverb: ‘I will not do such-and-such until Abū Mulaykah returns to his porridge.’”

He had a brother called Abū Bakr ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, who related traditions from him.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Mulaykah died in the year 117.

His cousin ʿAlī ibn Zayd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Mulaykah was among the jurists of Basrah.

He died in a place called Sīālah, in the lands of Ḍabbah. He had no descendants.

Sulaymān al-Taymī

He was Sulaymān ibn Ṭarḥān. He was among the clients of ʿAmr ibn Murrah ibn ʿAbbād, of Ḍabīʿah.

He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Muʿtamir. He was ascribed to Banū Taym because his home and mosque were among them.

The daughter of al-Faḍl ibn ʿĪsā al-Raqāshī, the judge, was his wife, and she bore him al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān, who was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. This is the account of Abū al-Yaqẓān.

Al-Bajalī informed me:

“He was Sulaymān ibn Ṭarkhān.”

He said:

“Ṭarkhān was a mukātab for Banū Murrah, and Ṭarkhān’s wife was a mukātabah for Banū Sulaym. She was manumitted before Ṭarkhān, and she gave birth to Sulaymān when she was free. Thus Sulaymān became a client of Banū Sulaym.”

Sulaymān died in Basrah in the year 143. Al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān was born in the year 106 and died in Basrah in the year 187.

Sahl related to me; he said: I heard al-Aṣmaʿī say:

“The most devout of the four was Sulaymān, the most learned in jurisprudence was Ayyūb, the most exacting about money was Yūnus, and the most careful with his tongue was Ibn ʿAwn.”

Thābit al-Bunānī

He was Thābit ibn Aslam. Bunānah was of Quraysh; they were the descendants of Saʿd ibn Luʾayy.

Bunānah was their mother, and they were ascribed to her. Some of them were from among her own people. He was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He died during the governorship of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh over Iraq.

Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ ibn Jābir

He was of al-Azd. He served in the army of Qutaybah ibn Muslim in Khurāsān. In his time, no one surpassed him in asceticism and devotion. He died in the year 120.

One of his sons had wronged a man, and his father said to him, “Would you wrong him while I am your father? I bought your mother for one hundred dirhams.”

He was asked, “Will you not sit reclining?” He replied, “That is how the secure sit.”

Jaʿfar said:

“Whenever I sensed hardness in my heart, I would go to Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ and look at him. Whenever I saw him, I thought his face was that of a bereaved woman.”

He was told, “You are content with little.” He replied, “The one content with little is the one content with this world.”

Layth ibn Abī Sulaym

He was a client of ʿAnbasah ibn Abī Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and was known by the teknonym Abū Bakr. His father, Abū Sulaym, was one of those who devoted themselves to worship in the congregational mosque of Kūfah. When Shabīb the Kharijite entered Kūfah, he came to the mosque, attacked its occupants by night, and killed them, including Abū Sulaym. From that time on, people stopped keeping vigil in the mosque.

Layth was a righteous, devout man, though his traditions were considered weak. He died at the beginning of the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq mentioned, from Maʿmar, who said:

Ayyūb was asked, “Why do you not write down traditions from Ṭāwūs?” He replied, “He was surrounded by two burdensome men: ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Abī Umayyah and Layth ibn Abī Sulaym. I could not bring myself to sit with him.”

Abū al-Ashhab al-ʿAṭāridī

He was Jaʿfar ibn Ḥayyān.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

Abū al-Ashhab said to me, “I was born in the year of al-Jafrah”, that is, the year 70.

He said:

He died in Basrah in the year 165.

242/ Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān

His name was Dhakwān. He was also called al-Zayyāt. He was a client of Juwayriyah, a woman of Qays. He had two sons, ʿAbbād ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ and Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, who related traditions from him. ʿAbbād was the older of the two. Suhayl related traditions from his brother ʿAbbād. Suhayl died during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

Abū Ṣāliḥ, the Exegete

He was Abū Ṣāliḥ, the client of Umm Hāniʾ bt. Abī Ṭālib, the sister of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib. His name was Bādhām—or, it is said, Bādhān—and he was not good at reading the Qurʾān.

Abū Ḥātim related to us, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from his father, who said:

Al-Shaʿbī would see him, seat him, and say to him: “You interpret the Qurʾān, yet you cannot read it by looking at the text!”

Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Ḥanafī

His name was Māhān al-Ḥanafī. Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid related from him.

Abū Ḥāzim of Medina

He was Salama b. Dīnār, the client of the Banū Layth b. Bakr b. ʿAbd Manāt.

He was lame and used to preach in the mosque of Medina. He had a donkey that he rode to the mosque.

He died during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar, after the year 140.

His son ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Abī Ḥāzim was known by the kunya Abū Tammām. He died suddenly in Medina in the year 184.

Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Anṣārī

He was known by the kunya Abū Saʿīd. He came to Abū Jaʿfar in Kūfa, while Abū Jaʿfar was at al-Hāshimiyya, and appointed him judge at al-Hāshimiyya. He died there in the year 143.

His brother ʿAbd Rabbihi b. Saʿīd died in the year 139.

His brother Saʿīd b. Saʿīd died in the year 141.

Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid

He was the client of the Banū Aḥmas of Bajīla, and was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was two years younger than Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, and had seen six people who had seen the Prophet ﷺ—including Anas b. Mālik and ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth.

He died in Kūfa in the year 146.

Jābir al-Juʿfī

He was Jābir b. Yazīd. His ḥadīth was weak. He belonged to the extremist Rāfiḍīs, who believed in the Return. He was given to doubts and conjuring tricks. Al-Thawrī and Shuʿba related from him.

He died in the year 128.

Yūnus b. ʿUbayd

He belonged to ʿAbd al-Qays. It is said that he was their client. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He died in the year 138. It is also said: in the year 140.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

Abū al-ʿAbbās gave money to some people of Baṣra. Yūnus received a thousand dirhams from it, and said: “I consider nothing of my property more lawful than this.”

Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl

He was Ḥumayd b. Ṭarkhān, the client of Ṭalḥa al-Ṭalaḥāt al-Khuzāʿī. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿUbayda. He died in the year 142.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

Iyās b. Muʿāwiya used to say: “Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl is a date that benefits the common people, while al-Ḥajjāj al-Aswad is a skin of honey.”

Misʿar b. Kidām

He belonged to the Banū ʿAbd Manāf b. Hilāl b. ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. He was known by the kunya Abū Salama.

He died in Kūfa in the year 152. He used to say: “May God make whoever hates me a traditionist!”

Dāwūd b. Abī Hind

He was the client of the Banū Qushayr, and was known by the kunya Abū Bakr. Abū Hind’s name was Dīnār.

He was from Sarakhs, where his descendants remained.

He died on the road to Mecca in the year 139.

Al-Jarīrī

He was Saʿīd b. Iyās, of the Banū Jarīr. He was known by the kunya Abū Masʿūd. His memory became confused toward the end of his life.

He died in the year 144.

Bahz b. Ḥakīm

He belonged to Qushayr b. Kaʿb and was among the best of people.

ʿAbbād b. Manṣūr al-Nājī

He belonged to the Banū Sāma. He served as judge of Baṣra during the time of Abū Jaʿfar.

His ḥadīth is considered weak.

ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd

He was ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd b. Bāb, the client of the family of ʿArāda b. Yarbuʿ b. Mālik.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿUthmān.

His father, ʿUbayd, used to frequent the associates of evil in Baṣra. When people saw ʿAmr with his father, they would say: “The best of men, the son of the worst of men!” ʿUbayd would reply: “You speak truly: this is Ibrāhīm, and I am Āzar.”

He held the doctrine of free will and called others to it. He and some of his companions separated from al-Ḥasan, and they were called the Muʿtazila.

Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm b. Ḥabīb b. al-Shahīd related to me, from ʿAmr b. al-Naḍr, who said:

I passed by ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd, and he mentioned something about free will. I said, “That is what our companions say.” He asked, “And who are your companions?” I said, “Ayyūb, Ibn ʿAwn, Yūnus, and al-Taymī.”

He replied, “Those are filthy, foul people, dead and not living.”

ʿAmr died on the road to Mecca and was buried at Marrān, two nights’ journey from Mecca, on the road to Baṣra. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī led the funeral prayer for him, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr elegized him in these verses: [Kāmil]

May God’s blessings be upon you, you who lie beneatha grave I passed at Marrān,

a grave containing a believer, one devoted to pure faith,who affirmed God’s truth and followed the Criterion.

If this age had preserved a worthy man,it would have preserved for us a living Abū ʿUthmān.

Ghaylān al-Dimashqī

He was a Copt and a proponent of free will. No one before him had spoken about free will and called others to it, except Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

Ghaylān was known by the kunya Abū Marwān. Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik seized him and crucified him at the gate of Damascus. People believed that this had come about through the imprecation of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz against him.

Mihyār al-Rāwī related to me, saying: I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. Yazīd al-Dimashqī say: I heard al-Awzāʿī say:

“The first to speak about free will was Maʿbad al-Juhanī, then Ghaylān after him.”

ʿUmāra b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣayyād

He was known by the kunya Abū Ayyūb. His father was an ally of the Banū al-Najjār. It is not known to whom he belonged.

Mālik b. Anas would not prefer anyone over him in merit, and he related from him.

ʿUmāra related from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib.

His father, ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣayyād, was the one said to be the Antichrist, because of things he used to do.

ʿAbd Allāh became Muslim, [and his Islam was good]. He made the pilgrimage and campaigned with the Muslims, and settled in Medina.

His son ʿUmāra died during the caliphate of Marwān b. Muḥammad.

Muslim the Dyer

He was Muslim b. Abī Muslim. He related from Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayra.

He lived until Sufyān b. ʿUyayna met him. He resided in Medina, in Dār al-ʿAṭṭārīn.

ʿĪsā b. Abī ʿĪsā al-Khayyāṭ

He was the client of Quraysh and was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad. His father’s name was Maysara. He used to say: “I am a tailor, a grain dealer, and a baker; I have worked at all of them.”

He heard from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib. He came to Kūfa on a business trip and met al-Shaʿbī, from whom he heard.

He died during the caliphate of al-Manṣūr.

Ibn Abī Dhiʾb

He was Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Dhiʾb. Abū Dhiʾb’s name was Hishām b. Shuʿba.

Abū Dhiʾb had gone to Caesar and was denounced to him. Caesar imprisoned him, and he died in prison.

He belonged to the Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy themselves.

245 / ### Ashʿath, the Companion of al-Ḥasan

He was Ashʿath b. ʿAbd al-Malik, the client of Ḥumrān b. Abān. He was known by the kunya Abū Hānī.

He died in the year 146, before ʿAwf. In that same year, Hishām b. Ḥassān al-Firdawsī, of al-Azd, died.

Ashʿath b. Sawwār

He belonged to Thaqīf as their client, and worked with wood.

He died at the beginning of the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

Ṣāliḥ b. Kaysān

He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad. His clientage was through a woman who was the client of the family of Muʿayqīb b. Abī Fāṭima al-Dawsī; thus he was the client of a client.

He died after the year 140.

Ṣāliḥ b. Ḥassān

He related from Muḥammad b. Kaʿb al-Quraẓī and others. He was a man of distinction who filled the gathering when he spoke. He kept singing slave girls, and they were the ones who brought him into disrepute among people.

He came to Kūfa, and the Kūfans heard from him. He lived into the time of al-Mahdī.

Al-Haytham said: I heard him say: “The most learned of people is Waḍḍāḥ al-Yaman” in his saying: [Ṭawīl]

When I said, “Come, give me,” “Give me a kiss,” she smiledand said, “God forbid that I do what He has forbidden!”

She gave me nothing until I pleaded with her,and told her what God has permitted concerning minor sins.

Sulaymān b. Qatta

He was named after his mother, Qatta. He was the client of Taym Quraysh.

Alongside his transmission of ḥadīth, he was a poet. He was the one who said: [Ṭawīl]

God may withhold from a young man though he is intelligent,and give wealth to a young man who has no sense.

Ibn ʿAwn

He was ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAwn b. Arṭabān. Arṭabān was the client of Ibn Barza al-Muzanī; it is also said that he was the client of ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughfal al-Muzanī—Muzayna of Muḍar. ʿAbd Allāh was known by the kunya Abū ʿAwn. ʿAbd Allāh married an Arab woman, and Bilāl b. Abī Burda flogged him.

ʿAṭāʾ b. Farrūkh was the son of Arṭabān’s brother, and Farrūkh was the son of his sister.

ʿAwn’s mother was from Khurāsān.

Sahl b. Muḥammad related to me, saying: al-Aṣmaʿī related to us, saying:

A man who used to visit Ibn ʿAwn related to me that he said: “My father received the news of my birth at Hāṭarī, in al-Madhār, when Muṣʿab set out to fight al-Mukhtār. Muṣʿab was at Hāṭarī in the year 66.”

Ḥammād b. Zayd said:

Ibn ʿAwn was born three years before al-Jārif.

He died in the year 151, and had seen Anas b. Mālik.

246 / ### Ibn Jurayj

He was ʿAbd al-Malik b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Jurayj, and was known by the kunya Abū al-Walīd. Jurayj had been a slave belonging to Umm Ḥabīb bt. Jubayr, who was married to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd; thus Ibn Jurayj was affiliated through clientage.

He was born in the year 80, the year of al-Juḥāf. Al-Juḥāf was a torrent at Mecca.

He died in the year 150.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Abū Hilāl, who said:

Ibn Jurayj used red dye on his hair.

Al-Wāqidī related, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī al-Zinād related to us, saying:

I was present when Ibn Jurayj came to Hishām b. ʿUrwa and said: “Abū al-Mundhir, is the document you gave so-and-so your ḥadīth?” He replied: “Yes.”

Al-Wāqidī said:

After that, I heard Ibn Jurayj say repeatedly, “Hishām b. ʿUrwa related to us,” with ḥadīths too numerous for me to count.

He said:

I asked him about reading a ḥadīth aloud to the traditionist. He said: “Someone like you asks about this? People only disagreed over the case of someone who takes a written sheet and says, ‘I will transmit what is in it,’ without having read it. But if he has read it, that is the same as hearing it.”

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Sabra

He used to give legal opinions in Medina. Then he was summoned in writing, so he came to Baghdad and was appointed judge by Mūsā al-Hādī ibn al-Mahdī, who was heir apparent.

He died in Baghdad in the year 162, during the caliphate of al-Mahdī. When he died, Abū Yūsuf was appointed judge in his place.

Al-Wāqidī said: Abū Bakr said:

Ibn Jurayj said to me: “Write down for me some good ḥadīths of yours.” I wrote a thousand ḥadīths for him and gave them to him. He did not read them aloud to me, nor did I read them aloud to him.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Then I saw that Ibn Jurayj had included many ḥadīths from him in his books, saying:

“Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh told me”—meaning Ibn Abī Sabra.

Al-Aʿmash

He was Sulaymān ibn Mihrān. He was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He was a client of Banū Kāhil, of Banū Asad.

They related that his father witnessed the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ﵄—and that al-Aʿmash was born on the day al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī was killed, which was the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ in the year 61.

His father was a ḥamīl. When his father died, Masrūq inherited him from him.19

Al-Aʿmash died in the year 148.

Wakīʿ said:

Al-Aʿmash went off to Friday prayer with a fur cloak turned inside out, its leather against his skin and its wool on the outside. On his shoulders he had the cloth used to cover a dining tray in place of a cloak.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said: “I heard al-Aʿmash say, ‘By God, they never come to anyone without making him lie. By God, I know of no people worse than they are.’ I objected to this, and he said, ‘They are never satisfied.’”

Abū Bakr mentioned tadlīs.

247 / Muḥārib ibn Dithār

He was of Banū Sadūs ibn Shaybān. He was known by the teknonym Abū Muṭarrif.

He was appointed judge of Kūfa by Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī. He died in Kūfa during Khālid’s governorship.

Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān

He was a client of al-Ḥurqa, of Juhayna. He lived to an advanced age and survived into the beginning of the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

Mālik said: Al-ʿAlāʾ had a written sheet from which he transmitted. If a man wanted to copy part of it, he would say to him, “Either take all of it or leave all of it.” His written sheet is well known in Medina.

Abū Ḥazra

He was Yaʿqūb ibn Mujāhid. He was known by the teknonym Abū Yūsuf. I think he was a client of Banū Makhzūm.

He was a preacher. He died in Alexandria in the year 149—or 150.

Abū Wajza al-Saʿdī

His name was Yazīd ibn ʿUbayd. He was of Banū Saʿd Bakr ibn Hawāzin, wet nurses of the Prophet ﷺ.

He was an accomplished poet, prolific in verse; among those from whom ḥadīth was transmitted, no one is known to have matched him in poetry.

He died in Medina in the year 130.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq

He was Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Yasār, a client of Qays ibn Makhrama ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manāf. They relate that Yasār was among the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr, whom Khālid ibn al-Walīd sent to Abū Bakr in Medina.

He had two brothers from whom he transmitted: Mūsā ibn Yasār and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yasār.

Muḥammad had gone to Abū Jaʿfar in Ḥīra, where he wrote down the accounts of the military campaigns for him. For this reason, the people of Kūfa heard from him.

He transmitted from Fāṭima bt. al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr, who was the wife of Hishām ibn ʿUrwa. When this reached Hishām, he disapproved and said, “Did he used to enter upon my wife?”

Abū Ḥātim related to us, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from al-Muʿtamir, who said: My father said to me:

“Do not take anything from Ibn Isḥāq, for he is a liar.”

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

ʿUrwa ibn Udhayna

Mālik ibn Anas used to transmit jurisprudence from him.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“ʿUrwa ibn Udhayna was trustworthy and reliable.”

Qalūṣ said:

ʿUrwa is the one who said: [mīdīd]

O dwellings of the people in al-Ajuma,

Your home has not been made clear by Kalima.

The poem is his, and he composed its melody. He is also the one who said: [basīṭ]

She said, while I disclosed to her my longing and made it plain:

“I thought you once loved concealment, so conceal yourself.”

“Do you not see those around me?” I said to her.

“Your love has clouded my sight, and what I suffer has covered my eyes.”

A woman came upon him and said: “Are you the one called a righteous man, and yet you say: [basīṭ]

When I feel the burning of love in my liver,

I make for the people’s water-skin, to cool myself.

Suppose I cool the outside with the water’s coolness—

Who will quench the fire blazing in my innermost parts?”

“By God, no righteous man ever said this!”

The Partisans of Legal Opinion

Ibn Abī Laylā

He was Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā. Abū Laylā’s name was Yasār.

He was descended from Uḥayḥa ibn al-Jallāḥ. The judge Ibn Shubruma and others disputed this lineage. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shubruma said: [mutaqārib]

How can you be expected to decide disputes

when you have not reached sound judgment within yourself?

You claim to be of the line of Ibn al-Jallāḥ—

How far your claim is from your true stock!

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān served as judge for the Umayyads, then served as judge for the Abbasids. He was a jurist who gave legal opinions according to personal reasoning.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān transmitted from ʿUmar, ʿAlī, ʿAbd Allāh, and Ubayy.

He went out with Ibn al-Ashʿath and was killed at Dujayl.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said:

“I remember nothing about my father, except that I know he had two wives and two green jugs, and that he would brew in one woman’s house one day and in the other’s the next.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā died in the year 148 while serving as judge. Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr appointed his brother’s son in his place.

Abū Ḥanīfa, the Partisan of Legal Opinion

He was al-Nuʿmān ibn Thābit, one of the clients of Taym Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba. He was a silk merchant in Kūfa. Ibn Hubayra summoned him to serve as judge, but he refused, so Ibn Hubayra had him beaten for several days, ten lashes each day.

It is said that Abū Ḥanīfa was from the Rabīʿa and a client of Banū Qufl.

He died in Baghdad in Rajab of the year 150, then seventy years old, and was buried in the cemeteries of al-Khayzurān.

Abū Ḥanīfa’s son was Ḥammād ibn Abū Ḥanīfa, who was known by the teknonym Abū Ismāʿīl. He died in Kūfa.

Among the descendants of Ḥammād were Abū Ḥayyān, Ismāʿīl, ʿUthmān, and ʿUmar.

Ismāʿīl ibn Ḥammād served as judge of Baṣra for al-Maʾmūn. Musāwir praised him, saying: [wāfir]

When one day people challenge us

with an ingenious, novel legal opinion,

we bring them a sound measure,

an ancient inheritance in Abū Ḥanīfa’s style.

When the jurist hears it, he takes it in

and records it with ink on a page.

A respondent among the Partisans of Ḥadīth answered him: [wāfir]

When the man of opinion argues by analogy

and brings a foolish, vile innovation,

we bring them God’s own ruling on it,

and noble, distinguished reports.

How many a chaste, virtuous woman

has Abū Ḥanīfa made lawful to violate!

Rabīʿa, the Partisan of Legal Opinion

He was Rabīʿa ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s name was Farrūkh. He was a client of the family of al-Mundhir, of the Taymīs. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿUthmān.

He died in the year 136 at Anbār, in the city of Abū al-ʿAbbās.

He had appointed him to the judgeship.

He talked a great deal and used to say, “The silent person is between the sleeper and the mute.”

One day he was speaking, with a Bedouin present, and asked, “What is incapacity of speech?” The Bedouin replied, “What you have been doing all day.”

Zufar, the Partisan of Legal Opinion

He was Zufar ibn al-Hudhayl ibn Qays, of Banū al-ʿAnbar. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Hudhayl.

He had heard ḥadīth, but legal opinion came to predominate in his work. He died in Baṣra.

Abū al-Hudhayl was in charge of Iṣfahān.

Al-Awzāʿī

Al-Bajalī related to me:

His name was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAmr. He was from al-Awzāʿ, a branch of Hamdān.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He lived in Beirut, and his writing office was in Yamāma; for that reason he heard from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr.

He died in Beirut in the year 157, then seventy-two years old.

Sufyān al-Thawrī

He was Sufyān ibn Saʿīd ibn Masrūq. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. His lineage was traced to:

Thawr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Add ibn Ṭābikha ibn al-Yās ibn Muḍar. Thawr is also called Thawr Aṭḥal; it is a mountain.

Among Thawr’s descendants was al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym. It is said that among Banū Thawr there were thirty men, none of them inferior to al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym. They were in Kūfa; there was not one of them in Baṣra.

Sufyān died in Baṣra, in hiding from the authorities, and was buried at night. The poet said: [ṭawīl]

Sufyān took precautions and fled with his faith,

while Sharīk spent the evening lying in wait for dirhams.

Al-Wāqidī said:

He died in the year 161, aged sixty-four. He told me that he was born in the year 97.

Wakīʿ said:

When Sufyān died, he had merchandise worth one hundred and fifty dinars. He entrusted ʿUmāra ibn Yūsuf with his books, and ʿUmāra erased and burned them.

Sufyān left no descendants. He had a son, but the son died before him. He bequeathed everything he owned to his sister and her children, and left nothing to his brother al-Mubārak ibn Saʿīd.

His brother al-Mubārak died in Kūfa in the year 180.

Mālik ibn Anas

He was Mālik ibn Anas ibn Mālik ibn Abī ʿĀmir, of Ḥimyar. He was reckoned among Banū Taym ibn Murra, of Quraysh.

Mālik’s paternal uncle, al-Rabīʿ ibn Mālik, transmitted ḥadīth. His father, Mālik ibn Abī ʿĀmir, transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, and Abū Hurayra; he was trustworthy.

Mālik was carried in the womb for three years. He was very fair, tending toward blond; tall, with a large head, and bald. He wore fine Yemeni garments. He disliked shaving the moustache and denounced it, considering it mutilation. He did not dye his gray hair.

Al-Wāqidī said:

Mālik used to go to the mosque, attend the prayers, Friday prayer, and funerals, visit the sick, attend to people’s needs, and sit in the mosque, where his companions would gather around him. Then he stopped sitting in the mosque: he would pray and then return home, and he stopped attending funerals, He used to visit his companions to console them, then he abandoned all of that. He no longer attended the prayers in the mosque or the Friday prayer, visited anyone to console him, or fulfilled anyone’s claim against him. People put up with this from him until he died in that state. When he was sometimes spoken to about it, he would say, “Not everyone is able to speak in his own defense.”

He was denounced to Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān, and they said, “He considers the oaths of allegiance you have taken to be worthless.” Jaʿfar grew angry, summoned him, stripped him, and flogged him. His hand was stretched until his shoulder was dislocated, and a terrible thing was done to him. Yet after that beating, he remained in high standing and esteem, as though those lashes had been ornaments with which he had been adorned.

He died in the year 179, at the age of eighty-five, and was buried in al-Baqīʿ.

Abū Yūsuf the Judge

He was Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ḥabīb ibn Saʿd ibn Ḥabta, of Bajīla. Saʿd ibn Ḥabta had been considered too young to fight on the day of Uḥud.

He settled in al-Kūfa and died there. Zayd ibn Arqam led the funeral prayer over him and pronounced five takbīrs over him.

Abū Yūsuf related traditions from al-Aʿmash, Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, and others. He was a traditionist and a memorizer, but then he attached himself to Abū Ḥanīfa, and legal opinion came to dominate him. He was appointed judge of Baghdad and remained its judge until he died in the year 182, during the caliphate of Hārūn.

His son Yūsuf also served as judge of the western quarter during his father’s lifetime. He died in the year 192.

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan the Jurist

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was a client of Shaybān.

His father came to Wāsiṭ, where Muḥammad was born. He grew up in al-Kūfa, sought out traditions, and heard them from Misʿar, Mālik ibn Mighwal, ʿUmar ibn Dharr, al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, and their like. He kept company with Abū Ḥanīfa and heard traditions from him. He studied legal opinion, which came to dominate him, and became known for it. He came to Baghdad and settled there, where traditions and legal opinion were heard from him. He went to al-Raqqa, and Hārūn appointed him judge of al-Raqqa, then dismissed him. He returned to Baghdad, and when Hārūn set out on his first expedition to al-Rayy, he ordered him to accompany him. He died in al-Rayy in the year 189, aged fifty-eight.

Hadith Scholars

Shuʿba

He was Shuʿba ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn al-Ward, a freed client of al-Ashāqir. He was known by the kunya Abū Bisṭām. He was ten years older than al-Thawrī.

He died in al-Baṣra in the year 160, aged seventy-five.

He used to say, “By God, I am safer in poetry than I am in hadith. Had I sought God, I would not have come out to you; had you sought God, you would not have come to me. But we love praise and dislike blame.”

He had a speech impediment.

Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ

He was Khālid ibn Mihrān, known by the kunya Abū al-Mubārak. He was a client of Quraysh, belonging to the family of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz.

He was not a shoemaker, but used to sit with shoemakers.

Fahd ibn Ḥayyān said:

“Khālid never made shoes at all. He would only say, ‘Take this hadith from me,’ and so he was nicknamed al-Ḥadhdhāʾ.”

He died in the year 141.

Abū al-Muhazzim

He was Yazīd ibn Sufyān.

Shuʿba considered him weak.

Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm related, on the authority of Shuʿba, that he said:

“I saw Abū al-Muhazzim lying prostrate in the mosque of Thābit al-Bunānī. If a man gave him two fals, he would relate seventy traditions to him.”

Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim

He was Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim ibn Zayd al-Jahḍamī, of al-Azd. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Naḍr.

He was born in the year 85.

He died in the year 170.

His son Wahb ibn Jarīr, known by the kunya Abū al-ʿAbbās, was criticized by ʿAffān. He died at al-Munjashāniyya, six miles from al-Baṣra, while returning from the pilgrimage. His body was carried to and buried in al-Baṣra.

His brother Yazīd ibn Ḥāzim, known by the kunya Abū Bakr, died in the year 147.

Among their clients was Ḥammād ibn Zayd.

Ḥammād ibn Zayd

He was Ḥammād ibn Zayd ibn Dirham. He was known by the kunya Abū Ismāʿīl and was an ʿUthmānī.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb said:

“Ḥāzim, the father of Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim, died, and Zayd, the father of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, was his slave. Yazīd and Jarīr, the sons of Ḥāzim, freed him.”

He died on a Friday in the month of Ramaḍān, in the year 179—the year in which Mālik and al-Aḥwaṣ died. Isḥāq ibn Sulaymān al-Hāshimī, then governor of al-Baṣra on behalf of Hārūn, led his funeral prayer.

His brother Saʿīd ibn Zayd had related traditions from him and died before Ḥammād ibn Zayd.

Ḥammād ibn Salama

He was Ḥammād ibn Salama ibn Dīnār, a client of Rabīʿat al-Jūʿ ibn Mālik ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. He was the son of the sister of Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl. Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl was a client of Ṭalḥa al-Ṭalaḥāt al-Khuzāʿī, and his mother was a client of Khuzāʿa.

He died in al-Baṣra in the year 167. In that same year, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Muslim died.

It is also said that he died in the year 164.

It is said that Ḥammād ibn Salama was learned in grammar and Arabic, and that the grammarian Sībawayh took dictation from him.

Abū ʿAwāna

His name was al-Waḍḍāḥ. He was a client of Yazīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Bazzār, whom people considered weak in his hadith.

Ibn ʿĀʾisha said:

“Abū ʿAwāna belonged to a man from among the people of Wāsiṭ, a cloth merchant named Yazīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ. One day a beggar came to him asking for alms, and he gave him two or three dirhams. The beggar said to him, ‘Abū ʿAwāna, I shall surely benefit you.’ When the day of ʿArafa came, the beggar stood among the people and said, ‘Pray for Yazīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ the cloth merchant, for on this day he has drawn near to God through Abū ʿAwāna by setting him free.’”

When the people departed, they passed by his door and began praying for him and thanking him; they did so in great numbers.

He said, “Who can turn these people away? He is free, for the sake of God.”

Abū ʿAwāna was in Wāsiṭ; he moved to al-Baṣra and died there in the year 170.

253/ Hishām ibn Saʿd

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbbād and was a client of the family of Abū Lahab. He was a camel-litter proprietor20 and was a Shīʿī partisan of the family of Abū Ṭālib.

He died in al-Madīna at the beginning of al-Mahdī’s caliphate.

Abū Maʿshar

He was Najīḥ. He was under a contract of manumission with a woman of Banū Makhzūm; he paid it off and was freed.

Umm Mūsā, daughter of Manṣūr al-Ḥimyarī, purchased his clientage.

He died in Baghdad in the year 170.

Another Abū Maʿshar

He was Ziyād ibn Kulayb, of Banū Mālik ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm.

Some say his name was Zayd ibn Kulayb.

He died during the governorship of Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar over Iraq.

Thawr ibn Yazīd al-Kilāʿī

He was known by the kunya Abū Khālid and was from among the people of Ḥimṣ.

He was a Qadarite, reliable in his hadith. His grandfather had fought at Ṣiffīn alongside Muʿāwiya and was killed. Whenever Thawr mentioned ʿAlī, he would say, “I do not like a man who killed my grandfather.”

He died in Bayt al-Maqdis in the year 153.

[It is also said: in the year 155.]

Ibn Lahīʿa

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Lahīʿa ibn ʿUqba ibn Lahīʿa al-Ḥaḍramī, one of their own.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He was weak in hadith, and those who heard from him early on were in better condition than those who heard from him later. Things that were not among his traditions would be read to him and he would remain silent. When he was questioned about this, he said, “What fault is that of mine? They bring a book, read it, and leave. If they asked me, I would tell them it was not among my traditions.”

He died in Egypt in the year 174.

al-Layth ibn Saʿd

He was a client of Qays and was known by the kunya Abū al-Ḥārith. He was reliable, noble, and generous. It is said:

His income was five thousand dinars each year, and he would distribute it during prayers and in other ways.

Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār said:

“I went to al-Layth, and he gave me one thousand dinars. He said, ‘Who is this, with the wisdom God has bestowed upon you?’”

He died in the year 175.

Maʿmar, the Companion of ʿAbd al-Razzāq

He was Maʿmar ibn Rāshid, a client of al-Azd. He was from among the people of al-Baṣra, then moved from there to Yemen.

He died in the year 153.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿUrwa.

Hushaym

He was Hushaym ibn Bashīr. He was known by the kunya Abū Muʿāwiya and was a client of Banū Sulaym.

He was born in the year 105. He died in Baghdad in the year 183.

254/ Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna

He was Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna ibn Abī ʿImrān, a client of a group descended from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, the clan of Maymūna, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad.

His grandfather Abū ʿImrān had been one of the officials of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī. When Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh was removed from office in Iraq and Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar appointed in his place, Yūsuf sought out Khālid’s officials. Abū ʿImrān fled from him to Mecca and settled there.

Sufyān was born in the year 107. He died in the year 198.

In that same year, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd died.

He was the most concise of men. He was asked about what Ṭāwūs said concerning the ritual slaughter of fish and locusts. He replied, “Their ritual slaughter is their capture.”

Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya

He was named after his mother. He was among the best of people.

His father was Ibrāhīm, who held the office of handling grievances in Baghdad.

He died in the year 193.

Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ

He was of Banū Ruʾās ibn Kilāb ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿĀmir. He was known by the kunya Abū Sufyān.

His father al-Jarrāḥ was in charge of al-Mahdī’s treasury, in partnership with Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Muqaddam.

He died on the road to Mecca, at Fayd, in the year 197.

Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūba

The name of Abū ʿArūba was Mihrān. He was one of the clients of Banū ʿAdī ibn Yashkur.

He was known by the kunya Abū al-Naṣr. He was a Qadarite.

He died in the year 156—or 157. He left no descendants. It is said that he never touched a woman at all. His mind became confused toward the end of his life.

Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ

He was Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ ibn Yazīd ibn al-Tawʾam. He was known by the kunya Abū Muʿāwiya.

He died in al-Baṣra in the year 182.

His father Zurayʿ held the deputyship of the chief of police in al-Baṣra. He had descendants.

ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal

He was ʿĀṣim ibn Sulaymān. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh and was a client of Banū Tamīm.

He was inspector of weights and measures in al-Kūfa. Then Abū Jaʿfar appointed him judge over al-Madāʾin. He died in the year 141—or 142.

Sharīk

He was Sharīk ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sharīk, of al-Nakhaʿ. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was born in Bukhārā, in the land of Khurasān.

His grandfather had witnessed [the battle of] al-Qādisiyya.

Sharīk died at Kūfa in the year 177 AH.

He was judge over Kūfa. ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Minhāl said of him: [wāfir]

Would that Abū Sharīk were alive,

so that Sharīk might judge when he saw him,

and leave those whom he scatters among us,

when we say to him, “This is your father.”

al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy al-Kūfī

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He was a Shiʿite. He married his daughter to ʿĪsā ibn Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and hid with him in one place until ʿĪsā ibn Zayd died. al-Mahdī was looking for them but could not find them.

al-Ḥasan died six months after ʿĪsā.

Abū al-Aḥwaṣ

He was Sallām ibn Sulaym, a client of Banū Ḥanīfa.

He died at Kūfa in the year 179 AH.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh

He was a client of Wāṣil ibn Ḥayyān al-Aḥdab.

He died at Kūfa in the year 193 AH, in the same month in which Hārūn died at Ṭūs.

Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl

He was Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl ibn Ghazwān. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. His grandfather, Ghazwān, was a Roman slave belonging to a man of Banū Ḍabba. He witnessed [the battle of] al-Qādisiyya with his master, who then freed him.

Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl died at Kūfa in the year 195 AH.

Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth ibn Ṭalq

He was of al-Nakhaʿ, from Madhḥij. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAmr. Hārūn appointed him judge in eastern Baghdad, then appointed him judge of Kūfa, where he died in the year 194 AH. His son ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ died at Kūfa in the year 222 AH.

Abū Muʿāwiya al-Ḍarīr

He was Muḥammad ibn Ḥāzim, a client of Tamīm.

He died at Kūfa in the year 195 AH. He was a Murjiʾite. One day he came out to his companions reciting: [maẓūʾ al-ramal]

When the stomach boils,

hurl a mangonel at it:

three [measures] of nabīdh,

neither sweet nor delicate.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs ibn Yazīd was of Madhḥij. He was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad. He was our patient.

He died at Kūfa in the year 192 AH. al-Zanjī ibn Khālid

He was Muslim ibn Khālid, from Syria, a client of Makhzūm. He was fair-skinned with a ruddy complexion. “al-Zanjī” was a nickname [that clung to him because of his whiteness, just as an Ethiopian was called Abū al-Bayḍāʾ.

He was devout and diligent in worship. He died in the year 180 AH.

256/ Dāwūd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿAṭṭār

His father, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, was a Christian from Syria and practiced medicine. He came to Mecca and settled there, where sons were born to him; they became Muslims.

Dāwūd was born in the year 100 AH. He died in the year 174 AH.

al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAlī, and was of Tamīm. He was born at Abīward, in Khurāsān.

He came to Kūfa as an older man and heard traditions from Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir and others. Then he devoted himself to worship and moved to Mecca, where he settled until he died in the year 187 AH.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and was from Marw. He was born in the year 118 AH.

He died at Hīt while returning from a military expedition, in the year 181 AH.

Abū Hilāl al-Rāsibī

He was Muḥammad ibn Sulaym. He was blind.

He died in the year 165 AH.

Hishām al-Dastawāʾī

He was Hishām ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh. The name of Abū ʿAbd Allāh was Sanbar. He was a client of Banū Sadūs and was accused of Qadarism.

He died after the year 153 AH.

ʿAbd al-Wārith ibn Saʿīd

He was known as al-Tannūrī and by the teknonym Abū ʿUbayda. He was a client of Banū al-ʿAnbar, from Banū Tamīm.

He died at Baṣra in Muḥarram of the year 180 AH.

ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbbād

He was ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbbād ibn Ḥabīb ibn al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra. He was known by the teknonym Abū Muʿāwiya.

He died in the year 181 AH.

Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh

He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Muthannā and was of Banū al-ʿAnbar.

He held the judgeship of Baṣra for Hārūn, then was dismissed.

He died at Baṣra in the year 196 AH.

Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal

He was known by the teknonym Abū Ismāʿīl and was a client of Banū Riqqāsh.

He died in the year 186 AH.

Azhar al-Sammān

He was Azhar ibn Saʿd, a client of Bāhila. He was known by the teknonym Abū Bakr. Ibn ʿAwn appointed him as his executor.

He died at Baṣra at the age of ninety-four.

Ghundar, the companion of Shuʿba

He was Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, a client of Hudhayl. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He died at Baṣra in the year 194 AH.

257/ ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād al-Thaqafī

He was a client of ʿAbd al-Qays. He was known as al-Thaqafī.

He died in the year 177 AH.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī

He was known by the teknonym Abū Saʿīd.

He died at Baṣra in the year 198 AH, at the age of sixty-three.

ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAbd al-Majīd al-Thaqafī

He was known by the teknonym Abū Muḥammad.

He was born in the year 108 AH. He died at Baṣra in the year 194 AH.

Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān

He was known by the teknonym Abū Saʿīd. He died at Baṣra in the year 198 AH.

Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd

He was Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd ibn Abān ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ al-Umawī, from Kūfa. He came to Baghdad and settled there.

He transmitted from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, al-Aʿmash, and Hishām ibn ʿUrwa.

He died at Baghdad in the year 194 AH, having reached the age of eighty.

Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī, author of the accounts of military campaigns

He was Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Asmāʾ ibn Khārija. He was virtuous and excellent, but made many mistakes in his traditions.

He died at al-Maṣṣīṣa in the year 188 AH.

Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī

He was Dāwūd ibn Nuṣayr. He was known by the teknonym Abū Sulaymān and was of Ṭayyiʾ, from among their own people.

He had heard traditions, studied jurisprudence, and learned grammar and the accounts of historical events. Then he devoted himself to worship and did not speak about any of those subjects.

Al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn said:

“When I saw Dāwūd, I saw a man who did not resemble the Qurʾān reciters. He wore a tall black cap of the kind merchants wear. He sat in his house for twenty years or so. When he died, I attended his funeral, and I had never seen such a crowd. He died in the year 165 AH.”

al-Darāwardī

He was ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Muḥammad, a client of Quḍāʿa. His origin was in Darāward, a village in Khurāsān.

Some say:

“He is ascribed to Darābjird, in Fārs, by an irregular form. The regular form is ‘Darābjirdī’.” But he was born in Medina and grew up there.

He died in the year 187 AH.

Yazīd ibn Hārūn

He was known by the teknonym Abū Khālid and was a client of Banū Sulaym.

He was born in the year 118 AH and died at Wāsiṭ in the year 206 AH,

during the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn.

258/ ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim

He was ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Ṣuhayb, a client of Banū Tamīm. He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Ḥasan.

He made mistakes in his traditions, so his traditions were abandoned.

He was born in the year 109 AH. He died at Wāsiṭ in the year 201 AH.

[During the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn.

His son ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAlī transmitted from him. He died at Wāsiṭ in the year 221 AH.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bakr al-Sahmī

He is ascribed to a branch of Bāhila called Banū Sahm. He was from Baṣra.

He died at Baghdad in the year 208 AH.

Abū al-Bakhtarī

He was Wahb ibn Wahb ibn Wahb ibn Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zumʿa ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy.

He came to Baghdad, and Hārūn appointed him judge at the Camp of al-Mahdī. Then he dismissed him and appointed him over the City of the Prophet ﷺ—after Bakkār ibn ʿAbd Allāh. He entrusted him with its military affairs as well as the judgeship. Then he was dismissed, and came to Baghdad. He died there in the year 200 AH.

He was weak in hadith.

Yaḥyā ibn Ādam ibn Sulaymān

He was a client of Khālid ibn ʿAmāra ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ.

He died at the Mouth of al-Ṣulḥ. al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl led the funeral prayer over him in the year 103 AH.

Abū Usāma

He was Ḥammād ibn Usāma, a client of al-Ḥasan ibn Saʿd, who was a client of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵃. Thus, he was a client of a client.

He died at Kūfa in the year 201 AH, at the age of eighty.

Yaʿlā and Muḥammad, the two sons of ʿUbayd al-Ṭanafisī

He was Yaʿlā ibn ʿUbayd ibn Umayya. He was known by the teknonym Abū Yūsuf and was a client of Iyād.

He died at Kūfa in the year 209 AH. His brother Muḥammad died before him at Kūfa in the year 204 AH.

Jaʿfar ibn ʿAwn

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAwn and was of Makhzūm.

He died at Kūfa in the year 207 AH.

Zayd ibn al-Ḥubāb al-ʿUklī

He was known by the teknonym Abū al-Khayr.

He died at Kūfa in the year 203 AH.

Abū Aḥmad al-Zubayrī

He was Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, a client of Banū Asad.

He died at al-Ahwāz in the year 203 AH. al-Wāqidī

He was Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Wāqid, a client of Banū Sahm, from Aslam. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He moved from Medina and settled in Baghdad, where he held the judgeship for al-Maʾmūn at the Camp of al-Mahdī for four years.

He died while still holding the judgeship, in the year 207 AH. Muḥammad ibn Samāʿa al-Tamīmī, who at that time held the judgeship in western Baghdad, led the funeral prayer over him.

al-Wāqidī was born at the beginning of the year 130 AH.

The judge al-ʿAwfī

He was al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn Saʿd. He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He held the judgeship of the eastern district after Jaʿfar ibn Ghiyāth, then was transferred to the Camp of al-Mahdī during the caliphate of Hārūn, then [was dismissed.

He died in the year 201 or 202 AH.

He was a client of Banū ʿAwf ibn Saʿd, of Qays ʿAylān.

ʿAṭiyya ibn Saʿd was a jurist in the time of al-Ḥajjāj and was a Shiʿite.

Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmr al-Azdī

He was known by the teknonym Abū ʿAmr. He was a companion of Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī and Zāʾida.

He died at Baghdad in the year 214 or 215 AH.

Hawdha

He is Hawdha ibn Khalīfa ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakra. His mother, too, was descended from Abū Bakra. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Ashhab.

He was born in the year 125. His books were lost, and only a little remained with him.

He studied with ʿAwf, Ibn ʿAwn, Ibn Jurayj, Ashʿath, and al-Taymī.

He died in Baghdad in the year 210.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā al-ʿAbsī

He was from ʿAbs. He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad. He studied with ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy. He used to recite the Qurʾān in his mosque and was a Shiʿite. He transmitted objectionable reports about this, and for that reason many people regarded him as weak.

He died in the year 213.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muqriʾ

He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd, from among the people of Basra. He moved to Mecca.

He died there in the year 213.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq

He is ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn Hammām ibn Nāfiʿ, a client of Ḥimyar. He was known by the kunya Abū Bakr.

His father, Hammām, used to transmit from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh and others.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq died in Yemen in the year 211.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī

He was descended from Anas ibn Mālik. He held the judgeship of Basra after Muʿādh ibn Muʿādh, then was transferred to Baghdad and held the judgeship of the Mahdī’s Camp after al-ʿAwfī, in the final years of Hārūn’s caliphate. When Muḥammad came to power, he dismissed him from the judgeship and appointed ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Masʿūdī in his place. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh then held the jurisdiction over grievances after Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya. He was subsequently appointed judge of Basra again, then dismissed, with Yaḥyā ibn Aktham appointed in his place. Al-Anṣārī remained in Basra, transmitting traditions there, until he died in the year 215.

260/ ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dāwūd al-Khuraybī

He was from the people of Hamdān themselves. He moved from Kufa to Basra and settled in al-Khurayba (1).

He died in the year 213.

Abū ʿĀṣim al-Nabīl

He is al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Makhlad, from Shaybān.

He died in the year 212.

Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī

He is Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd.

He died in Basra in the year 203, at the age of seventy-two. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā, the cousin of al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl, who was then governor of Basra, led the funeral prayer over him.

Abū ʿĀmir al-ʿAqdī

He is ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAmr, a client of Banū Qays.

He died in Basra in the year 204.

Abū al-Walīd al-Ṭayālisī

He is Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

He died in Basra in the year 227, at the age of ninety-four.

Ḥabbān ibn Hilāl

He was known by the kunya Abū Ḥabīb. He was from Bāhila. He had stopped transmitting traditions before his death.

He died in Basra in the year 216.

Bishr ibn ʿUmar al-Zahrānī

He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad. He was a transmitter of Mālik ibn Anas.

He died in Basra in the year 209, and Yaḥyā ibn Aktham led the funeral prayer over him.

Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh, transmitter of Mālik ibn Anas

He was hard of hearing.

He died in Medina in the year 220. al-Ḥajjāj al-Anmāṭī

He is al-Ḥajjāj ibn al-Minhāl. He was known by the kunya Abū Muḥammad.

He died in Basra in the year 217.

Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm

He is Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm, a client of al-Azd, and was known as al-Shaḥḥām. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAmr.

He died in Basra in the year 222.

Mūsā ibn Masʿūd al-Nahdī

He was known by the kunya Abū Ḥudhayfa. They report that Sufyān al-Thawrī married his mother when he came to Basra.

He died in the year 220.

ʿĀrim

He is ʿĀrim ibn al-Faḍl al-Sadūsī. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Nuʿmān. His name was Muḥammad.

“ʿĀrim” was his sobriquet.

He died in Basra in the year 224. In that same year, ʿAmr ibn Marzūq al-Bāhilī died.

261/ Abū Salama

He is Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl al-Nabūdhakī.

He died in Basra in the year 223.

Al-Muʿallā ibn Asad al-ʿAmmī

He was known by the kunya Abū al-Haytham. He was a schoolteacher.

He died in Basra in the year 218.

Abū ʿAmr al-Ḥawḍī

He is Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar.

He died in Basra in the year 225.

Ibn ʿĀʾisha

He is ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ al-Taymī, of Taym Quraysh. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

His son, too, was called Ibn ʿĀʾisha.

He died in Basra in the year 228. al-Qaʿnabī

He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maslama ibn Qaʿnab al-Ḥārithī. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

I heard Abū Mūsā al-Laythī say:

“Al-Qaʿnabī died in Mecca on Thursday, six nights into Muḥarram, in the year 221.”

Ādam al-ʿAsqalānī

He is Ādam ibn Abī Iyās, from the people of Marw al-Rūdh.

He sought traditions in Baghdad and heard a great deal directly from Shuʿba. Then he moved and settled in ʿAsqalān, where he died in the year 220. He was a bookseller and was short.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ, scribe of al-Layth

He was from Juhayna.

He died in Egypt in the year 223.

ʿAffān ibn Muslim al-Ṣaffār

He is ʿAffān ibn Muslim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, a client of ʿUrwa ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī.

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿUthmān.

He died in Baghdad in the year 220. ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim led the funeral prayer over him.

Khālid ibn Khidāsh ibn ʿAjlān

He was known by the kunya Abū al-Haytham. He was a client of al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra.

He died in the year 223.

Bishr al-Ḥāfī (1)

He was known by the kunya Abū Naṣr. He was descended from people of Khurāsān and was from the people of Marw.

He had sought traditions and heard a great deal directly from Ḥammād ibn Zayd, Sharīk, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Hushaym, and others. Then he withdrew and did not transmit traditions until he died in Baghdad in the year 227.

ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd

He was a client of Umm Salama al-Makhzūmiyya, the wife of Abū al-ʿAbbās, Commander of the Faithful.

He was born in the year 136. He died in Baghdad in the year 230.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir died in that same year.

ʿAbd al-Munʿim

He is ʿAbd al-Munʿim ibn Idrīs ibn Sinān, the son of the daughter of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

He died in the year 228, having reached or nearly reached the age of one hundred. He had become blind.

262/ Abū Nuʿaym

He is al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn ibn Ḥammād, a client of the family of Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Taymī.

He died in Kufa in the year 219.

Qabīṣa ibn ʿUqba

He was known by the kunya Abū ʿĀmir. He was from Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa.

He died in Kufa in the year 215.

Al-Ḥumaydī, companion of Ibn ʿUyayna

He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr al-Makkī.

He died in Mecca in the year 219.

Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb al-Wāshiḥī

He was from the people of al-Azd themselves. He was known by the kunya Abū Ayyūb. He held the judgeship of Mecca, then was dismissed and returned to Basra.

He died there in the year 224, at the age of eighty-four.

Musaddad

He is Musaddad ibn Musarhad ibn Musarbāl ibn Sharīk al-Asadī. He was known by the kunya Abū al-Ḥasan.

He died in Basra in the year 228. In that same year, al-Ḥammānī and al-ʿĀʾishī died.

Abū al-Rabīʿ al-Zahrānī

He is Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd.

He died in the year 234. In that same year, in Basra, Sulaymān al-Shādhakūnī died. In that same year, ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Najīḥ al-Madanī died in Surra Man Raʾā.

Shabāba ibn Sawwār al-Fazārī

He was a client of Fazāra. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAmr. He was a Murjiʾī. He was from the people of Baghdad, descended from people of Khurāsān. He moved to al-Madāʾin and settled there, and withdrew from public life. Then he went to Mecca and stayed there until he died.

He was severe toward the Rāfiḍa and frequently spoke of them.

Marḥūm al-ʿAṭṭār

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told me, from his uncle, who said:

“I asked Marḥūm al-ʿAṭṭār, ‘How did your father come to be in Syria?’ He replied, ‘Muslim ibn ʿAmr presented him, among a group of young servants, to Muʿāwiya.’”

He said: “He told me, from his father, from the custodian of the Sanctuary of Jerusalem, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said to the muezzin:

‘When you give the call to prayer, draw it out; and when you commence the prayer, be brisk.’”

Authorities in Qurʾanic Readings

Abū Jaʿfar al-Madanī

He is Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, a client by manumission of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī.

He transmitted from Abū Hurayra, Ibn ʿUmar, and others.

He died during the caliphate of Marwān ibn Muḥammad.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī al-Kūfī

He is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥabīb, one of the companions of ʿAlī.

He was a Qurʾān reciter, and jurisprudence was learned from him.

263/ Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ

He is Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ al-Madanī ibn Sarjis ibn Yaʿqūb, a client of Umm Salama.

We know of no one who transmitted from Niṣāḥ except his son, Shayba.

In his time, Shayba was the leading authority on Qurʾānic recitation among the people of Medina.

Nāfiʿ al-Madanī

He is Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nuʿaym. He had studied with Abū Maymūna, a client of Umm Salama, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

Sahl told me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Nāfiʿ the reciter, that he said:

“My origin is in Isfahan.”

Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif

He was from Hamdān. He was known by the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

He was the reciter of the people of Kūfah. When he saw that many people were gathering around him, he disliked it and went to al-Aʿmash to read to him. The people then turned to al-Aʿmash and away from Ṭalḥah.

He died in the year 112.

Al-Aʿmash of Kūfah

We have mentioned him among the traditionists, because ḥadīth was more prominent in his work than recitation.

He died in the year 148.

Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb of Kūfah

He was a client of Banū Kāhil, of Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah.

He died in Kūfah in the year 103.

They report that he read to ʿUbayd ibn Naḍlah, a companion of ʿAbd Allāh.

Ḥamzah al-Zayyāt

He was Ḥamzah ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿUmārah. His kunya was Abū ʿUmārah. He was a client of the family of ʿIkrimah ibn Rabīʿ al-Taymī. He used to transport oil from Kūfah to Ḥulwān, and cheese and walnuts from Ḥulwān to Kūfah.

Ḥamzah died in Ḥulwān in the year 156, during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar.

ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd

He was ʿĀṣim ibn Bahdalah, a client of Banū Judhaymah ibn Mālik ibn Naṣr ibn Quʿayn ibn Asad.

His kunya was Abū Bakr.

Those who transmitted recitation from him were Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh and Abū ʿUmar al-Bazzār. They differed greatly over many readings.

ʿĀṣim had read to Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh.

Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj

He was Ḥumayd ibn Qays, a client of the family of al-Zubayr.

He was the reciter of the people of Kūfah. He knew many traditions, the rules of inheritance, and arithmetic. He read to Mujāhid. His brother was ʿUmar ibn Qays. (1)

264/ Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith al-Dhimārī

He was ascribed to Dhimār, and Dhimār is a district among the districts of Yemen.

Yaḥyā was learned in recitation, and people read to him. He had read to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir al-Yaḥṣubī.

He transmitted few traditions.

He died in the year 145.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ

He was one of the people of recitation, except that rare vocabulary and poetry were more prominent in his work, so we mentioned him among the specialists in rare vocabulary.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar

He was one of the people of recitation, except that rare vocabulary and poetry were more prominent in his work, so we mentioned him with them.

al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥaraqī

He was from al-Ḥaraqah. He taught people to recite, but ḥadīth was more prominent in his work, so we mentioned him among the traditionists.

Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār

He heard many traditions from Sharīk, Abū ʿAwānah, and Ḥammād ibn Zayd, though he was better known for recitation. He read to Sulaym, the companion of Ḥamzah, and differed from Ḥamzah on many points. He died in Baghdād in the year 229. He was from Famm al-Ṣulḥ.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muqriʾ

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd. He was renowned for ḥadīth and recitation, so we mentioned him in both places.

He was from Baṣrah, then moved to Makkah. He died there in the year 213.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā al-ʿAbsī

He read to ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and to ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy. He used to recite the Qurʾān in his mosque. Ḥadīth was more prominent in his work, so we mentioned him among the traditionists.

Ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Muqriʾ

He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq. He was a client of the Ḥaḍramīs.

Among his descendants was Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, the reciter of Baṣrah.

ʿAbd Allāh had learned his recitation from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim.

Hārūn al-Aʿwar

He was Hārūn ibn Mūsā. Hārūn had been Jewish, then became Muslim.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

Hārūn said to me: “I used to read Īdhām in Hebrew”—meaning Ādam.

Sallām al-Qāriʾ

He was Sallām ibn Sulaymān. His kunya was Abū al-Mundhir.

265/ Reciters of Melodies

The first to recite with melodies was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Bakrah. His recitation was mournful (1), and was not in any of the melodies of singing or camel-driving chants. His grandson, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, inherited this from him; it is he whose recitation is called “the recitation of Ibn ʿUmar.”

The Ibāḍī learned this from him. Saʿīd al-ʿAllāf and his brother learned the recitation of Ibn ʿUmar from the Ibāḍī.

Hārūn al-Rashīd admired Saʿīd al-ʿAllāf’s recitation. He would favor and reward him, and Saʿīd was known as the reciter of the Commander of the Faithful.

All the reciters—al-Haytham, Abān, Ibn Aʿyan, and others—would incorporate into their recitation melodies from singing, camel-driving chants, and monastic chants. Some would slip in a little of this subtly; others would make it so overt that it stripped the recitation of its character. An example is al-Haytham’s recitation:

“As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who worked at sea”—he stripped it from a singing tune resembling this [Basīṭ]:

“As for the partridge, I shall describe it, with a description that fits some of its qualities.”

Ibn Aʿyan used to incorporate such things discreetly. Then there was Muḥammad ibn Saʿd al-Tirmidhī, who recited to newly composed songs, stripping them out in his recitation just as they were.

Genealogists and Historians

Daghfal the Genealogist

He was Daghfal ibn Ḥanẓalah al-Sadūsī. He lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ—but heard nothing from him. He visited Muʿāwiyah. Qudāmah ibn Jarād al-Qurayʿī came to him, and Daghfal traced his genealogy until he reached the father who had begotten him. He said: “Jarād had two sons: one was a foolish poet, and the other an ascetic. Which of the two are you?” He replied: “I am the foolish poet. You have got my lineage and everything else right. Tell me, I beg you, when will I die?”

He said: “As for that, I do not know.”

The Azāriqah killed him.

ʿUbayd ibn Sharyah al-Jurhumī

He lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ—but heard nothing from him. He visited Muʿāwiyah, who asked him about ancient reports, the kings of Yemen, the reason languages became confused, and people’s dispersion across lands. He lived to a very old age.

Among the genealogists:

The Bakrī Genealogist

He is the one from whom Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj transmitted the statement: “Knowledge has a blemish, a hardship, and an affliction.”

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

He was a Christian.

Among the genealogists:

Ibn Lisān al-Ḥamrah the Genealogist

He was Warqāʾ (1) ibn al-Ashʿar, and his kunya was Abū Kilāb. He was the most skilled genealogist among the Arabs,

and the keenest-sighted of them.

Among them:

ʿUmayr ibn Ḍamḍam (2), Ṣāliḥ al-Ḥanafī, and Ibn al-Kayyis al-Namirī.

Among them:

Ibn al-Kawwāʾ the Genealogist—he was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, of Banū Yashkur. He was a genealogist, a great scholar, and Maskīn al-Dārimī says of him [Wāfir]:

Come to the sons of al-Kawwāʾ, and let them decide by their judgment the lineages of men.

His father was called al-Kawwāʾ because he cauterized in the pre-Islamic period.

Among them:

Shubayl ibn ʿUrwah al-Ḍubaʿī was a transmitter, a genealogist, learned in rare vocabulary, and a poet. For seventy years he was a Rāfiḍī, then afterward became a Khārijite. His kunya was Abū ʿAmr.

He died in Baṣrah. He has descendants there.

Among them: al-Kalbī, the author of the commentary

He was Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib ibn Bishr al-Kalbī. His kunya was Abū al-Naḍr. His grandfather was Bishr ibn ʿAmr.

His sons al-Sāʾib, ʿUbayd, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān fought at the Battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn alongside ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵁.
