Al-Sāʾib was killed alongside Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr. Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī fought at al-Jamājim alongside Ibn al-Ashʿath. He was a genealogist and learned in Qurʾānic exegesis.

He died in Kūfah in the year 146.

Ibn al-Kalbī, Hishām ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib

He was the most learned of people in genealogies.

Ibn al-Kalbī related from his father, who said:

I went in to see Ḍirār ibn ʿUṭārid, a descendant of Ḥājib ibn Zurārah, in Kūfah. There was a man with him, looking like a rat rolling about in brocade. Ḍirār nudged me and said, “Ask him who he is descended from.” So I asked him, “Who are you descended from?” He said, “If you are a genealogist, trace my lineage. I am from Banū Tamīm.” I began tracing the lineage of Tamīm until I reached Ghālib, his father. I said, “Ghālib had a son, Hammām.” He sat upright and said, “By God, my parents gave me that name for no more than a single part of the day.” I said, “By God, I even know the day your father named you al-Farazdaq.” He said, “What day was it?” I replied, “He sent you on an errand, so you went out walking, wearing your mustaqa (1).” He said, “By God, you are like al-Farazdaq, the Persian village headman”—he named a village in al-Jabal. Then he said, “You have spoken truly, by God!” He asked me, “Do you know any of my poetry by heart?” I said, “No, but I know a hundred poems by Jarīr.” He said, “You know the poetry of Ibn al-Marāghah, but not mine?

“By God, I shall satirize a dog for a year, unless you learn as much of my poetry as you know of Jarīr’s.”

I kept going to him and reading the invectives back and forth, for fear of him, though I had no need of any of them.

Among them: Mujālid ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿUmayr

He was from Hamdān. His kunya was Abū ʿUmayr.

Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī used to transmit from him and did so frequently. Mujālid transmitted from al-Shaʿbī and Masrūq, and he was a genealogist. The chief part of his work was transmitting historical reports, and his ḥadīth was considered weak.

He died in the year 144.

Mujālid’s grandfather, ʿUmayr, was the man called Dhū Marān al-Hamdānī. The Prophet ﷺ—wrote to him, and he became Muslim.

He had a son called Yazīd ibn ʿUmayr. Al-Mukhtār killed him on the day of Jābiyat al-Sabīʿ.

Mujālid used to say: “The letter of the Messenger of God ﷺ—to my grandfather is in our possession.”

Among them: Abū Mikhnaf al-Azdī

He was Lūṭ ibn Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd ibn Mikhnaf ibn Sulaym. He was a historian and genealogist, though historical reports were more prominent in his work.

His grandfather, Mikhnaf ibn Sulaym, had accompanied the Prophet ﷺ—and transmitted from him.

Among them: Ibn Diʾb

He was ʿĪsā ibn Yazīd ibn Bakr ibn Diʾb. He was from Kinānah, of Banū al-Shaddākh.

His kunya was Abū al-Walīd. He has descendants in Baṣrah.

His brother was Yaḥyā ibn Yazīd. Their father Yazīd was also learned in the reports and poetry of the Arabs.

He was also a poet, though historical reports were more prominent among the family of Diʾb.

Among them: al-ʿUtbī

He was Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, a descendant of ʿUtbah ibn Abī Sufyān ibn Ḥarb. Historical reports were more prominent in his work; most of his reports concern the Banū Umayyah and their battles (1), which he transmitted from Saʿd al-Qaṣīr. Saʿd al-Qaṣīr was their client.

Ibn al-Zubayr killed him in Makkah.

Al-ʿUtbī was a poet. He lost some of his sons and elegized them. He was addicted to drink, and he composed poetry about ʿUtbah.

He died in the year 228.

Among them: al-Madāʾinī

His kunya was Abū al-Ḥasan. He was ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sayf. The chief part of his work was transmitting historical reports.

Among them: al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī

He was from Ṭayyiʾ and held the views of the Khawārij. He has descendants in Baghdād.

He was born before the year 130.

He said:

“I was riding behind him in the funeral procession of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr.” ʿAbd al-Malik died in the year 136. Al-Haytham died in the year 209.

Among them was Ibn ʿAyyāsh,

from whom al-Haytham transmitted. He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAyyāsh. He was known as al-Muntūf, “the plucked,” because he used to pluck his beard, it was said. He was a close associate of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr.

Among them was al-Sharqī ibn Quṭāmī.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad told me: al-Aṣmaʿī told me: one of the transmitters told me:

I said to al-Sharqī ibn Quṭāmī, “What did the Arabs say in their prayers over their dead?” He said, “I do not know.” I pressed him, and said, “They used to say:

[Ṭawīl]

I was no wakkāk, nor [one who] bazūnuk;Take it slowly, until the One who raises creation raises it.”21

Then I found him on Friday reciting it in the enclosed prayer area.

Transmitters of poetry and authorities on rare vocabulary and grammar

Ibn al-ʿAlāʾ

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAmmār ibn al-ʿAryān. His brother was Abū Sufyān ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAmmār.

Their names were their kunyas. They were from Khuzāʿī ibn Māzin ibn Mālik ibn ʿAmr ibn Tamīm.

Al-Farazdaq said of Abū ʿAmr: [Basīṭ]

“I kept opening doors and closing them,until I came to Abū ʿAmr ibn ʿAmmār.”

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ died in the year 154. He died on the road to Syria, having set out there to solicit a gift from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Ibrāhīm.

He and his brother Abū Sufyān had descendants in Baṣra.

Among them was ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar.

He was affected in his speech, using rare vocabulary in it and in his recitation.

Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayra had him flogged—on some pretext—and he said:

“By God, they were only little garments in little sacks, taken by your tax collectors.”

He died in the year 149, five—or six—years before Abū ʿAmr.

Among them was Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb,

a client of Banū Ḍabba. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Grammar was his predominant field.

He died in the year 182, aged eighty-eight.

One day he entered the mosque, walking unsteadily between two people because of his advanced age. A man who suspected him of being fond of him said, “You have reached the state I see!” He replied, “That is what you see; may I never reach it.”

Among them was Ḥammād al-Rāwiya.

He was Ḥammād ibn Hurmuz. Hurmuz had been among the captives taken by Maknaf ibn Zayd al-Khayl, and was a Daylamī. His kunya was Abū Laylā.

Abū Ḥātim told me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“I kept company with Ḥammād al-Rāwiya, but did not take three hundred words from him, and I did not approve of his transmission. He was a reciter.”

Abū al-Bilād al-Kūfī

He was among the most accomplished transmitters in Kūfa and the most learned of them. He was blind and eloquent. He was a client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghaṭafān. He lived in the time of Jarīr and al-Farazdaq.

ʿAbbād ibn Kusayb

He was from Banū ʿAmr ibn Jundub, of Banū al-ʿAnbar. His kunya was Abū al-Khansāʾ.

He was a transmitter of poetry and learned in the reports of the Arabs. He had descendants.

Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad

He was the authority on prosody. He was affiliated with Yaḥmad, of al-Azd, from a branch called al-Farāhīd. He was intelligent, refined, perceptive, and a poet.

Ibn Hāniʾ, the associate of al-Akhfash, recited to us. He said: al-Akhfash recited to me his own verse: [Basīṭ]

“Act according to my knowledge, and do not look at my deeds;My knowledge will benefit you, and my shortcomings will not harm you.”

He also recited to us this verse of his: [Mutaqārib]

“His two hands were not created for generosity,Nor was their stinginess an innovation.

One hand is withheld from doing good,Just as a hundred was reduced by seven.

And three thousand were withheld,And nine hundred were its allotted share.”22

Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl al-Marwazī

He was from Banū Māzin and was originally from Baṣra. He moved to Marw. He was an authority on rare vocabulary, poetry, grammar, and ḥadīth, and was knowledgeable about the annals of peoples and jurisprudence.

He died in Khurāsān in the year 203.

Muʾarrij

He was Muʾarrij ibn ʿAmr, a Sadūsī. His kunya was Abū Fayd.

He died in the year 195.

Ibn Kināsa al-Kūfī

He was Abū Yaḥyā Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn Kināsa al-Asadī, of their own people.

He was the nephew of the ascetic Ibrāhīm ibn Adham. He was known for poetry, rare vocabulary, and ḥadīth, and for his knowledge of the stars according to the Arabs’ system—on which he composed a book—as well as his knowledge of the annals of peoples.

He died in Kūfa in the year 207.

Abū ʿUbayda

He was Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā, a client of Taym Quraysh. Rare vocabulary, and the reports and annals of the Arabs, were his predominant fields. Despite his learning, he would sometimes fail to keep a verse intact when reciting it, breaking its meter; and when reading the Qurʾān from a written copy, he would make mistakes. He disliked the Arabs and wrote a book on their faults. He held the doctrine of the Khārijites.

He died in the year 210, or 211, having nearly reached the age of one hundred.

Al-Aṣmaʿī

He was ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Qurayb, from Bāhila, a descendant of al-Aṣmaʿ.

His father had seen al-Ḥasan and kept his company. Transmission and lexical meanings were his predominant fields. He was extremely cautious about interpreting the Qurʾān and the ḥadīth of the Prophet ﷺ.

We do not know that he ever transmitted a Prophetic ḥadīth as marfūʿ except for a few. In his other ḥadīth transmissions he was truthful, and he was a follower of the Sunna. His kunya was Abū Saʿīd. He was born in the year 123. He lived for more than ninety years. He had descendants.

Khalaf al-Aḥmar

He was a transmitter, learned in rare vocabulary, and a poet who composed much excellent poetry. None among his peers could compose poetry like his.

Abū Ḥātim told me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Khalaf al-Aḥmar was a client of Abū Burda ibn Abī Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. He emancipated him and his parents, who were both from Farghāna.”

Al-Yazīdī

He was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Mubārak. For a long time he was a teacher across from the house of Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ. He had descendants.

He was called Yazīdī because he tutored the son of Yazīd ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥimyarī.

Sībawayh

He was ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān. Grammar was his predominant field. He had come to Baghdād, where he met with the grammarians and was humiliated. He returned and went to one of the cities of Fārs, where he died while still a young man.

Abū Ḥātim told me: Abū Zayd told me:

“Sībawayh was a boy who used to come to my gathering, and he had two braids.” He said, “When you hear him say, ‘Someone whose command of Arabic I trust told me,’ he means me.”

Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī

He was Saʿīd ibn Aws ibn Thābit, from the Anṣār. Languages and rare usages within rare vocabulary were his predominant fields. He held the doctrine of predestination. He lived a very long life, nearly reaching one hundred.

Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī, the transmitter

He was al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Muḥammad, a descendant of Sālim ibn Abī al-Ḍabbī. He was a Kūfan.

Al-Kisāʾī

He was ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza. His kunya was Abū al-Ḥasan. He accompanied al-Rashīd on his first journey to al-Rayy, and died there in the same year as the jurist Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, who died in al-Rayy in the year 189.

Al-Farrāʾ

He was Yaḥyā ibn Ziyād. His kunya was Abū Zakariyyāʾ.

He died in the year 207 on the road to Mecca.

Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī

He was Isḥāq ibn Marrār, from al-Rammāda in Kūfa. He lived as a neighbor to a man of Shaybān, and so was affiliated with Shaybān.

Al-Akhfash al-Aṣghar, the grammarian

He was Saʿīd ibn Masʿada. Grammar was his predominant field. He was ajlaʿ—and an ajlaʿ is someone whose upper lip is deficient and who cannot bring it together with the lower lip.

Al-Riyāshī told us: I heard al-Akhfash say:

“When Sībawayh had written something in his book, he would show it to me, thinking that I knew more than he did. He knew more than I did, but today I know more than he did.”

Ibn al-Aʿrābī

He was Muḥammad ibn Ziyād. His kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He used to say that he was the stepson of al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī, and that his mother was married to him.

Abū Mahdiyya al-Aʿrābī

He was a Bedouin, an authority on rare vocabulary, from whom the Baṣrans transmitted.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

“Once a fit seized him, and we used to give him a flask of vinegar to drink each day. One day Khalaf al-Aḥmar came with some young men from Quraysh, wearing fine clothes. He said, ‘Bring your vinegar, Redhead!’ He drank it, then held the rest of the flask in his mouth and spat it out, covering their clothes. He said, ‘The grammarians looked into my mouth, and there were strings of saliva in it; I looked into the Fire and saw that the poets had squeaking [voices]. I hope God will forgive Jarīr for the kindness he showed in raising the reputation of the women of Qays—and of me. Thus [was it] from your mother, Satan!’”23

The teachers

Abū Ṣāliḥ, the associate of al-Kalbī, used to teach boys; and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, who was blind; and Maʿbad al-Juhanī, the Qadarī.

Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said:

“Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith used to teach and took no payment.”

Among them were:

Qays ibn Saʿd;

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ;

Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb;

ʿAbd al-Karīm Abū Umayya;

Ḥusayn the teacher—he was Ḥusayn ibn Dhakwān;

and al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymira al-Hamdānī.

Among them was:

the poet al-Kumayt ibn Zayd.

Abū Ḥātim told me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from Khalaf al-Aḥmar, who said:

“I saw al-Kumayt teaching boys in the mosque of Kūfa.”

Among them was:

Ḥabīb the teacher, a client of Maʿqil ibn Yasār.

Among them was:

ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, the secretary of the Umayyads;

Abū al-Baydāʾ;

and Abū ʿAbd Allāh, the letters secretary.

Among them was:

al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, who used to teach in al-Ṭāʾif. His name was Kulayb.

His father, Yūsuf, was also a teacher.

Mālik ibn al-Rayb said of al-Ḥajjāj: [Ṭawīl]

“What can al-Ḥajjāj accomplish, for all his efforts,once we have passed Ḥufayr of Ziyād?

Were it not for the Marwānids, Ibn Yūsufwould be as he was: a slave among the slaves of Iyād.

A time when the slave acknowledged his abasement,going to and fro among the village boys.”

Another said of him: [Mutaqārib]

“Does Kulayb forget the time of hunger,and teaching Sūrat al-Kawthar?

A loaf for him, shaped like a spindle,and another like the bright full moon.”

He means that a teacher’s bread varied in size.

And among the teachers:

ʿAlqama ibn Abī ʿAlqama, a client of ʿĀʾisha. Mālik ibn Anas used to transmit from him. He had a school where he taught Arabic, grammar, and prosody. He died during the caliphate of al-Manṣūr.

And among the teachers:

Abū Muʿāwiya the grammarian, whose name was Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. He was a client of Banū Tamīm.

He tutored the son of Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī and was a traditionist.

And among them:

Abū Saʿīd the tutor, whose name was Muḥammad ibn Muslim ibn Abī al-Waḍḍāḥ, of Quḍāʿa. Al-Manṣūr attached him to al-Mahdī, and afterward attached Sufyān ibn Ḥusayn to him. Abū Saʿīd transmitted from Sālim al-Afṭas, Khuṣayf, ʿAlī ibn Budhayma, Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, and al-Aʿmash.

And among the teachers:

Abū Ismāʿīl the tutor—Ibrāhīm ibn Sulaymān. He was also a traditionist.

And among them:

Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, a client of al-Azd and one of the sons of the people of Khurāsān. He was a tutor. He held the judgeship of Ṭarsūs in the days of Thābit ibn Naṣr ibn Mālik, and remained with him and his son. After arriving in Baghdad, and after composing the books he composed, he went on pilgrimage.

He died in Mecca in the year 224.

Those who severed relations

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ:

He was estranged from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir until they both died. Saʿd said to him: “We used to count you among the foremost of Muḥammad’s Companions ﷺ—until there remained of your life only a donkey’s watering interval, when you cast off the bond of Islam from your neck.” Then he said to him: “Which do you prefer: affection tainted by resentment, or a graceful severance?” He replied: “A graceful severance.” He said: “I vow to God that I shall never speak to you again.”

And ʿĀʾisha:

She was estranged from Ḥafṣa until they both died.

ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān was estranged from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf until they both died.

And Ṭāwūs was estranged from Wahb ibn Munabbih until they both died.

Something happened between al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, and al-Ḥasan died while Ibn Sīrīn did not attend his funeral.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab shunned his father and did not speak to him until he died.

His father was an oil merchant.

Al-Thawrī used to speak against Ibn Abī Laylā. When Ibn Abī Laylā died, al-Thawrī did not attend his funeral.

The Firsts

Zayd ibn Akhzam related to me: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad related to us. He said: Shuʿba related to us. He said: al-Mughīra related to us. He said: I heard Simāk ibn Salama say:

The first to be greeted with the title of emir was al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba.

Zayd ibn Akhzam related to us: Kathīr ibn Hishām related to us, from Furāt, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said:

The first man with whom men walked while he rode was al-Ashʿath ibn Qays.

Ibn al-Yaqẓān and others said:

The first to establish blood money at one hundred camels was Abū Sayyāra al-ʿAdwānī, who led the people away from al-Muzdalifa.

It is said that the first to establish this was ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Quraysh and the Arabs adopted it, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—affirmed it in Islam.

They said:

Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra was the first in the pre-Islamic era to remove his sandals before entering the Kaʿba; people then removed their sandals in Islam.

And he was the first to judge by the oath procedure known as qasāma in the pre-Islamic era; the Messenger of God ﷺ—affirmed it in Islam.

And the first to forbid wine to himself in the pre-Islamic era.

And the first to have a hand cut off for theft in the pre-Islamic era; the Messenger of God ﷺ—then had hands cut off in Islam.

In the pre-Islamic era, they used to say: “By the two garments of al-Walīd, the worn and the new.”

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

Judgment by mutual oath was revealed by God—Exalted is He—to Moses for every slain person found between two villages or two settlements. The Children of Israel continued to judge by it, and the Messenger of God ﷺ—judged by it.

Wahb said:

The first to draw with the pen was Idrīs.

He was also the first to sew clothes and wear them; before him, people wore skins.

Sahl ibn Muḥammad related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī—or someone else—who said:

The first to write in Arabic was Marāmir ibn Murra, from the people of al-Anbār. From al-Anbār, it spread among the people.

He said: Al-Aṣmaʿī also said:

They say that Quraysh were asked, “From whom did you get writing?” They said, “From the people of al-Ḥīra.” The people of al-Ḥīra were asked, “From whom did you get writing?” They said, “From al-Anbār.”

Someone else said:

Bishr ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-ʿIbādī taught writing to Abū Sufyān ibn Umayya and Abū Qays ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra, and they taught the people of Mecca.

They said:

The first to rule concerning a hermaphrodite by observing the urinary passage was ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarb al-ʿAdwānī, and this practice continued in Islam. He is the one who said to his daughter: “If, when judging, you find that I have misunderstood anything, strike the shield with a stick for me.” Al-Mutalammis said:

[Ṭawīl]

For the man of judgment, before this day, the stick is not struck;A human being is taught only so that he may learn.

It is also said that this man of judgment was Ṣayfī, father of Aktham.

And it is said: ʿAmr ibn Ḥamma al-Dawsī, who lived to an advanced age.

They said:

The first of the people of Mecca to dye his hair black was ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim. A man from Ḥimyar had dyed it for him that way in Yemen, and supplied him with wasma. The first to make litters and carry people in them was al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf.

The first to set up a screened enclosure in a mosque was Muʿāwiya. This was because he once saw a dog on his pulpit.

The first to mint coins inscribed in Arabic was ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

The first to date documents and seal clay was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

The first to wear a ṭaylasān in Medina was Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim.

The first in Basra to wear plain leather boots and linen clothes was Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān.

The first among the Arabs to wear silk brocade and round the opening of the ṭārūnī was ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir.

The first to wear black durāʿāt was al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd. People said:

“The emir is wearing a bear’s hide.”

The first to make soap was Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd ﵉ both.

The first to make paper was the Prophet Joseph ﷺ.

The first to make thin, flatbread was Nimrod.

The first to make sandals was Jadhīma al-Abrash ibn Mālik.

He was also the first to set up the mangonel, to travel by night among kings, and to have candles raised for him. He would keep the two stars, al-Farqadān, as drinking companions, taking pride in himself: he would drink a cup and pour a cup on the ground for each star, until Mālik and ʿUqayl kept him company.

The first head to be carried from one town to another was the head of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥamiq al-Khuzāʿī. We have already related his story.

Mujāhid said:

The Prophet ﷺ—saw a party of riders with a camel-driver chanting for them. He asked, “Who are these people?” They replied, “From Muḍar.” He asked, “What is the matter with your camel-driver?” A man among them said, “We are the first to chant for camels.” He asked, “How so?” The man said, “One of us was with his camels during the springtime. He ordered a servant of his to do something, but the servant was slow, so he struck him with a stick. The servant began to recite to the camels, saying, ‘O my hands!’ They said to him, ‘Keep at it, keep at it!’ From then on, people began the camel-driver’s chant.

The first to have a bier made for her was Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. She was a well-built woman. Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays said, “I saw biers for their dead in Abyssinia.” So she made a bier for Zaynab. When ʿUmar saw it, he said, “What a fine shelter for a woman in a howdah!”

People used to hurry at funerals. When ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ died, people walked at his funeral; he was the first at whose funeral they walked.

The first of the Arabs to cross the river of Balkh was Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.

The greatest ransom among the Arabs was paid by Ḥājib ibn Zurāra: he ransomed himself for a thousand camels.

Mālik Dhū al-Ruqayba al-Qushayrī had captured him on the Day of Jabala. He was called Dhū al-Ruqayba because he was short-necked.

After him came al-Rabīʿ ibn Masʿūd al-Kalbī, who ransomed himself for five hundred camels. Al-Ḥārith ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhayma al-ʿAbsī had captured him. One of the people of Yemen, boasting, said:

“Al-Ashʿath ibn Qays paid the greatest ransom of all the Arabs. The Madhḥij captured him, and he ransomed himself for three

thousand camels. The ransom for kings was only one thousand she-camels, so he ransomed himself for the blood-money of three kings.”

ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib said:

[Wāfir]

His ransom was two thousand young she-camels,And a thousand of the choicest, both newly acquired and inherited.

The first to strike the gate of Constantinople with his sword and to call the prayer in the lands of the Romans was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kulayb, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa. He was with Maslama. Caesar wanted to kill him, but he said, “By God, if you kill me, not one church in the lands of Islam will remain unpulled down.”

The first woman whose hand was cut off for theft was the daughter of Sufyān ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, of Banū Makhzūm. The Prophet ﷺ—cut it off, and said, “If it had been Fāṭima, I would have cut off her hand.” Among the men, [the first was] al-Khayyār ibn ʿAdī ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf. He stole, and his hand was cut off. I do not know whether he was the first of them or not.

The Prophet ﷺ—also cut off the hand of ʿAmr ibn Samura, the brother of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura, for theft.

The first to be named Yaḥyā was Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā ﵉ both. The first in Islam to be named ʿAbd al-Malik was ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

Before the Prophet ﷺ—there was no one in the pre-Islamic era named Muḥammad except Muḥammad ibn Uḥayḥa ibn al-Jallāḥ, the maternal half-brother of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; Muḥammad ibn Sufyān ibn Mujāshiʿ ibn Dārim; and Muḥammad ibn Sawʾa ibn Jusham ibn Saʿd.

In the pre-Islamic era, no one had the teknonym Abū ʿAlī except Qays ibn ʿĀṣim and ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl.

Anas ibn Mālik said:

The Prophet ﷺ—sold a saddle blanket and a drinking cup to the highest bidder.

The first to deliver sermons in Mecca was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr ibn Qatāda al-Laythī.

It is said that the first to deliver sermons was al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ al-Tamīmī, one of the Companions. In his sermons about the dead, he used to say:

[Ṭawīl]

If you escape from it, you escape a terrible thing;Otherwise, I do not think you will escape.

Al-Farazdaq stole these lines.

The first to hold the Friday congregational prayer in Islam was Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn ʿAbd al-Dār, the bearer of the Messenger of God’s standard ﷺ. He gathered the Muslims for Friday prayer in Medina. They were twelve men, and on that day he slaughtered a sheep for them.

Abū Hilāl related from Abū Ḥamza, who said:

The first person we saw performing ablution with water in Basra was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Bakra. We said, “Look at this Abyssinian, rubbing his backside”—meaning, washing himself with water after relieving himself.

The first child born in Basra was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakra. On that day, while they were at al-Khurayba, they slaughtered a camel and fed the people of Basra, and they were satisfied. At the time, they numbered about three hundred.

The first child born in Kufa was Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr, of Banū al-Bakkāʾ, of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿa.

The first to bribe in Islam was al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba. He said, “Sometimes the dirham would grow damp in my hand as I raised it to Yarfaʾ, so that he would make it easier for me to gain access to ʿUmar.”

The first to use the jamāzāt and carry them on the jamaz was Umm Jaʿfar.

The first archer in the path of God was Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. He said: [Wāfir]

No archer in battle can count an arrowAs preceding mine, O Messenger of God.

The first judge to give judgments in Medina was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf. He resembled the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Hurayra said, “This is the first judge I saw in Islam.”

The first judge to give judgments in Iraq was Salmān ibn Rabīʿa, in al-Madāʾin.

The first judge to give judgments in Kufa was Abū Qurra al-Kindī. His teknonym was his name. When people laid out the town of Kufa, Abū Qurra was their judge. Then ʿUmar appointed Shurayḥ ibn al-Ḥārith al-Kindī as judge after him. He gave judgments for seventy-five years.

The first judge to give judgments over Basra was Kaʿb ibn Suwwār al-Azdī, whom ʿUmar appointed as judge.

The first village built on earth after the Flood was a village in Qardā called Sūq Thamānīn. Nūḥ ﵇—built it and gave a house to each of the eighty men who had believed with him. To this day, it is called Sūq Thamānīn.

Mosques

The Kaʿba

Wahb ibn Munabbih related:

When God ﵎ sent down Ādam to earth, he grieved and wept bitterly for Paradise. God consoled him with a tent from among the tents of Paradise, which He set up for him at Mecca, in the place of the Kaʿba, before the Kaʿba existed. The tent was a red ruby from the rubies of Paradise. In it were lamps of gold, made from the pure gold of Paradise. The Corner descended with it at that time; it was a white ruby, and served as a chair on which Ādam sat. When the Flood came in the time of Noah ﵇—it was raised up. The earth remained desolate for two thousand years, until God ﵎ commanded Abraham to build His House. The sakīna came, like a cloud containing a speaking head with a face like a human face. It said: “Abraham, take my shadow and build upon it.” He and Ishmael built the House, and gave it no roof. God guarded Ādam and the House with the angels; the Sanctuary was then the angels’ dwelling place. Ādam’s tent ﵇—remained until he died, then God raised it up to Himself. After him, the children of Ādam built a house of clay and stones in its place. Then the Flood swept it away and obliterated its site, until God—exalted is He—sent Abraham ﵇—who dug down to its foundations and built it beneath the shadow of the cloud. It was the first House established for humankind.

The first to cover it with hides and Yemeni brocade was Asʿad Abū Kurayb al-Ḥimyarī, who said:

[Khafīf]

We clothed the House that God made sacredwith a padded cloak and brocade Quraysh built it five years before the Prophet’s mission ﷺ.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr built it after he had been pledged allegiance as caliph.

When Ibn al-Zubayr was killed, al-Ḥajjāj demolished Ibn al-Zubayr’s construction and rebuilt it on the original foundations.

Then Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr enlarged the mosque of the Kaʿba in the year he assumed the caliphate.

Then al-Mahdī added to it in the year 160.

Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, from ʿUmar ibn Qays, who said:

Within the House, the Ḥijr measures seven cubits and some fingers—or, he said, two fingers.

He said: Al-Aṣmaʿī said, Abū Gharāza said:

The Black Stone is level with the walls—that is, the corner of the Kaʿba beside the Multazam.

He related to me from him, from al-Aʿmash, from Mujāhid, who said:

The saʿy is between the house of ʿAbbād and the well of Ibn Muṭʿim, but people have hidden it beneath buildings.

More than one person said:

The Kaʿba measures four hundred and ninety square cubits.

Some people related:

That Ubayy ibn Sālim al-Kalbī arrived in Mecca while Quraysh were building the House. They disputed over who would provide the funds, so he asked them to entrust him with one of its corners. They entrusted him with the quarter containing the Yemeni Corner, and he built it. It was therefore called the Yemeni Corner. Their poet said:

[Ṭawīl]

Ours is the right side of the House you worship,an inheritance from what Ubayy ibn Sālim left behind.

Most people hold that it was called “Yemeni” only because it lies on the side facing Yemen. Its muezzins are descendants of Abū Maḥdhūra.

Bayt al-Maqdis

Wahb related:

Isaac, the prophet son of Abraham ﵉ both—commanded his son Jacob not to marry a woman from among the Canaanites, but to marry one of the daughters of his maternal uncle, Lāyā, daughter of Nāhir ibn Āzar.24 His uncle lived in al-Faddān. Jacob set out to him, and night overtook him along the way. He spent the night with a stone for a pillow. In a dream, he saw a ladder set up to one of the gates of Heaven at his head, with angels descending and ascending upon it. God ﵎ revealed to him:

“I am God; there is no god but Me. I am your God and the God of your fathers Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac. I have granted you this holy land as an inheritance, and your descendants after you. I have blessed you and them, and placed among you the Book, wisdom, and prophethood. I will be with you until I bring you back to this place and make it a House in which you and your descendants will worship Me.”

It is said that this was Bayt al-Maqdis.

David built it, and Solomon completed it ﵉ both. Then Bukht Naṣṣar destroyed it. The prophet Isaiah passed by and saw it and the town in ruins, and said: “How will God bring this to life after its death?”

God caused him to die for one hundred years.

A king of the kings of Persia, called Cyrus, rebuilt it.

The Mosque of Medina

Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān, from Nāfiʿ, that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī informed him:

The mosque—that is, the Mosque of Medina—was, in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ—built of mud bricks, with a roof of palm fronds and supports made of palm trunks. Abū Bakr ﵁—made no additions to it. ʿUmar ﵁—added to it. Then ʿUthmān ﵁—altered it and made a great addition. He built its walls of carved stone and silver, made its supports of carved stone, and roofed it with teak.

Al-Mahdī enlarged it in the year 160.

Al-Maʾmūn added greatly to it and enlarged it.

Its muezzins are descendants of Saʿd al-Qaraẓ, the client of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir.

I read this inscription at the place of al-Maʾmūn’s addition: “ʿAbd Allāh commanded the building of the Mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ—in the year 202, seeking God’s reward, seeking God’s recompense, and seeking God’s favor. For with God is the reward of this world and the Hereafter, and God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.

ʿAbd Allāh commanded ʿAbd Allāh to fear God, to be mindful of Him, to maintain ties of kinship, to act according to the Book of God and the Sunna of His Messenger ﷺ—to honor the rights of God that tyrants have diminished, to revive the justice they have extinguished, to diminish the transgression and oppression they have magnified, to obey God and obey whoever obeys God, and to disobey whoever disobeys God—for there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to God—and to treat them equally in their spoils and allot the fifths to their proper recipients.”

Basra, its Mosque, and its Canals

The first to establish Basra as a garrison city was ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān ibn Yāsir, one of the Companions. He laid it out in the year 14. He passed by the site of al-Mirbad and found there coarse gravel. He said:

“This is al-Baṣra. Settle there in God’s name.” By order of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he built the congregational mosque of reeds.

Then Ibn ʿĀmir built it of mud brick for ʿUthmān.

Then Ziyād built it of baked brick for Muʿāwiya, and built its two sides.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād completed it.

Its muezzins are descendants of al-Mundhir ibn Ḥassān al-ʿAbdī. He had been the muezzin of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, and his descendants continued to give the call to prayer in the mosque.

The Nahr Maʿqil is named after Maʿqil ibn Yasār, one of the Companions.

The bank of ʿUthmān was a grant to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ibn ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī; he brought it to life and developed it.

The Nahr ʿAdī is named after ʿAdī ibn Arṭāʾ.

The Nahr Ibn ʿUmar is named after ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who had it dug.

The Nahr Umm ʿAbd Allāh is named after Umm ʿAbd Allāh bint ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz.

The Nahr Murra is named after Murra ibn Abī ʿUthmān, the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq. ʿĀʾisha had written to Ziyād recommending him, so Ziyād granted him that canal.

Yazīd al-Rishk said: “I measured Basra during the governorship of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī, and found it to be two farsakhs long and two farsakhs wide, less one dāniq.”

Kufa and its Mosque

When the Muslims settled in al-Madāʾin and stayed there for a long time, the dust and flies troubled them. ʿUmar wrote to Saʿd, instructing him to send out scouts to seek a place that was both inland and near the sea, for the Arabs thrive only in lands suited to sheep and camels. Saʿd asked those around him about such a place. Men of standing among the Arabs who knew Iraq pointed to the elevated ground called al-Lisān, which is the upland behind Kufa. The Arabs used to say, “The open country has thrust out its tongue into the cultivated land.” The part of it that lay beside the Euphrates was al-Milṭāṭ; the part that lay beside the marshy ground was al-Najaf. ʿUmar wrote to Saʿd ordering him to settle there. They settled in Kufa in the year 17.

Basra is three years older than Kufa. Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān was the builder of the Mosque of Kufa.

It is related in some report that the oven burst forth from the site of its mosque.

The Mosque of Damascus

Al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik built the Mosque of Damascus in the year 88.

The Arabian Peninsula

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

Its length extends from the farthest part of ʿAdan Abyan to the cultivated land of Iraq. Its breadth extends from Jeddah and the neighboring coast of the sea to the outskirts of Syria.

This is how Abū ʿUbayda related it from him.

Al-Riyāshī related to us from him that he said:

The Arabian Peninsula extends between Najrān and al-ʿUdhayb. Abū ʿUbayda said:

The Arabian Peninsula extends lengthwise from the wells of Abū Mūsā to the farthest part of Yemen, and breadthwise from the sands of Yabrīn to al-Samāwa.

The Sawād

There are two Sawāds: the Sawād of Basra and the Sawād of Kufa.

The Sawād of Basra comprises al-Ahwāz, Dasht Maysān, and Fārs.

The Sawād of Kufa extends from Kaskar to the Zāb, and from Ḥulwān to al-Qādisiyya.

The Jazīra

The Jazīra lies between the Tigris, the Euphrates, and Mosul.

Najd, Tihāma, and the Ḥijāz

Al-Riyāshī related to us from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

When you leave the Ḥijāz heading upward, you have entered Najd. You remain in Najd until you descend through the passes of Dhāt ʿIrq. When you do that, you have entered Tihāma, toward the sea.

When you encounter the rocky lava fields as you descend, that is the Ḥijāz.

When you descend through the passes of al-ʿArj and face the arāk and marakh trees, you have entered Tihāma.

It was called the Ḥijāz because it forms a barrier between Najd and Tihāma.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Asadī said:

The first boundary of the Ḥijāz is Baṭn Nakhl, upper Ramma, and the high ground of Ḥarrat Laylā.

The second boundary, toward Syria, is Shaghb and Badāʾ.

The third boundary, toward Tihāma, is Badr, al-Suqyā, Rahāṭ, and ʿUkāẓ.

The fourth boundary is Sāya and Waddān; it then descends to the first boundary, Baṭn Nakhl.

The Conquests: Khurasan

Khurasan was conquered by treaty during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, by ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz. The farthest places conquered there during ʿUthmān’s caliphate were:

Marw and Marw al-Rūdh.

As for the lands beyond them, they were conquered after ʿUthmān, by treaty for Muʿāwiya, at the hands of Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān: Samarqand, Kashsh, Nasaf, and Bukhara.

After that, at the hands of al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra and Qutayba ibn Muslim:

Ṭabaristān, Jurjān, and Rayy

As for Rayy, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī conquered it by treaty during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.

As for Ṭabaristān, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ conquered it by treaty during ʿUthmān’s governorship. Then ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ conquered it, along with Ṭāliqān and Dunbāwand, in the year 157.

Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab conquered Jurjān during the caliphate of Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, in the year 98.

Kirmān and Sijistān

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz conquered Kirmān and Sijistān by treaty during ʿUthmān’s caliphate.

Al-Jabal

As for al-Jabal, it was all conquered by force in the battles of Jalūlāʾ and Nihāwand, at the hands of Saʿd and al-Nuʿmān ibn Muqarrin.

Al-Ahwāz, Fārs, and Iṣfahān

As for al-Ahwāz, Fārs, and Iṣfahān, they were conquered by force for ʿUmar, at the hands of Abū Mūsā, ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān. Iṣfahān in particular was conquered at the hands of Abū Mūsā.

Al-Sawād

As for al-Sawād, it was all conquered by force at the hands of Saʿd during the caliphate of ʿUmar.

Al-Jazīra

As for al-Jazīra, it was conquered by treaty at the hands of ʿIyāḍ ibn Ghanm.

Syria

As for Syria, Ajnādayn was conquered by treaty during the caliphate of Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar ibnal-Khaṭṭāb conquered Jerusalem. All the cities of Syria were conquered by treaty, but their lands were conquered by force, for ʿUmar, at the hands of Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān, Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasana, Abū ʿUbayda, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd.

Egypt

As for Egypt, it was conquered by treaty at the hands of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.

The Maghrib

Part of the Maghrib was conquered by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ for ʿUthmān: namely, Ifrīqiya, which he conquered by force. The frontier regions and Caesarea were conquered by Muʿāwiya by force for ʿUmar.

Al-Andalus

It was conquered by Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād, the client of Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr al-Lakhmī, in the year ninety-two.

Hajar, al-Yamāma, and Bahrain

As for Hajar and Bahrain, they paid the poll tax to the Messenger of God ﷺ. Likewise, Dūmat al-Jandal and Adhruḥ.

As for al-Yamāma, Abū Bakr conquered it [by force.

India

As for the land of India, it was conquered by al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad al-Thaqafī in the year ninety-three.

A List of Those Who Governed Both Iraqs

The first to be given both cities—al-Kūfa and al-Baṣra—was Ziyād, then his son ʿUbayd Allāh, Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, Bishr ibn Marwān, al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab, Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, ʿUmar ibn Hubayra al-Fazārī, Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī, Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Yazīd ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayra.

After these men, the two Iraqs were never united under anyone.

The Distinction Between the First Emigrants and the Later Ones

Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd related to me, from Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī (1), from Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zāʾida, from al-Shaʿbī, who said:

“The first emigrants are those who were present at the Pledge of Riḍwān.”

Qatāda and Abū Hilāl asked Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib about the distinction between the first emigrants and the later ones. He said: “Whoever prayed facing both qiblas is one of the first emigrants.”

Identifying the Mukhaḍramūn

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

“Some people embraced Islam while on camels and cut off their ears. Thus, everyone who lived through both Islam and the Jāhiliyya was called a mukhaḍram. A man is a mukhaḍram only if he reached adulthood while Islam had already come, but did not embrace Islam until after the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

The Reason the Alms Levy Was Doubled for the Christians of Taghlib

They said:

“The alms levy was doubled for the Christians of Banū Taghlib because ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb wanted to take the poll tax from them, so they fled. Zurʿa ibn al-Nuʿmān—or al-Nuʿmān ibn Zurʿa al-Taghlibī—said to him: ‘I adjure you by God concerning them. They are Arabs who disdain the poll tax, and they are a people capable of striking back, so do not aid your enemy against yourself.’ So he doubled the alms levy for them and stipulated that they not make their children Christians.”

The Trades of the Notables

Abū Ṭālib sold perfume, and sometimes sold wheat.

Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq was a cloth merchant.

ʿUthmān was a cloth merchant.

Ṭalḥa was a cloth merchant.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf was a cloth merchant.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ fashioned arrow shafts.

Al-ʿAwwām, Abū al-Zubayr’s father, was a tailor.

Al-Zubayr was a butcher.

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ was a butcher.

Al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām, Abū Jahl’s brother, was a blacksmith.

ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz was a butcher.

Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra was a blacksmith.

ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ was a wine seller.

ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥa, to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ—handed the key to the House, was a tailor.

Qays ibn Makhrama was a tailor.

Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb sold oil and hides.

ʿUtba ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Saʿd’s brother, was a carpenter.

Umayya ibn Khalaf sold stone cooking pots.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān had a slave-trading business, with slave girls who solicited customers (1), and he sold their children.

Al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ’s father, worked with horses and camels.

Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada sang to the lute.

Al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam’s father, did likewise.

So too did Ḥurayth ibn ʿAmr, Abū ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth’s father.

So too did Qays al-Fihrī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays’s father.

So too did Maʿmar ibn ʿUthmān, the grandfather of ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar.

So too did Sīrīn, Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn’s father.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī said:

“Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab had a garden built in his house in Khurāsān. When Qutayba ibn Muslim became governor, he made it a place for his camels. Marzubān Marwān (1) said to him: ‘This used to be a garden, and you have made it a place for your camels.’ Qutayba said: ‘My father was an ishtar-bān—that is, a camel driver—and Abū Zayd was a bustān-bān—that is, a gardener.’”

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn was a cloth merchant.

Mujammaʿ al-Zāhid was a weaver.

Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī sold sakhtiyān leather, and was named for it.

Al-Musayyab, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab’s father, was an oil merchant.

Maymūn ibn Mihrān was a cloth merchant.

Mālik ibn Dīnār was a copyist who wrote Qurʾāns.

Abū Ḥanīfa, the master of legal opinion, was a silk merchant.

People with Physical Afflictions

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ was dark-skinned, one-eyed, with a withered limb, flat-nosed, and lame; later, he became blind.

Abān ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān was deaf—profoundly deaf. He was a leper, and dyed the leprous patches on his hand but did not dye them on his face. He was paralyzed. In Medina, people would say, “May God strike you with Abān’s palsy”—because of its severity. He was also cross-eyed.

Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ was hunchbacked and had a withered limb from a wound he had received on the day of al-Qādisiyya; he was also paralyzed.

Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays was one-eyed. It is said that he lost his eye at Samarqand; it is also said that he lost it to smallpox.

His feet turned inward, so that he walked on their outer edges (1); his teeth overlapped, his head was small, his chin slanted, and his side whiskers were sparse.

Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī was lame, paralyzed, and foul-breathed.

ʿAmr ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAdas, of Banū Dārim, was their horseman. He was a leper and foul-mouthed, so his descendants were called:

“The mouths of dogs.”

Al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis was lame and bald, and for that reason was called al-Aqraʿ.

ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī was deaf and one-eyed.

Leprosy

Anas ibn Mālik had leprosy on his face.

Some people reported that ʿAlī ﵁—asked him about the words of the Messenger of God ﷺ—“O God, befriend whoever befriends him, and be hostile to whoever is hostile to him.” He replied, “I have grown old and forgotten.” ʿAlī ﵁—said to him, “If you are lying, may God afflict you with a white patch that your turban cannot conceal.”

Abū Muḥammad said:

This has no basis.

Balʿāʾ ibn Qays was a leper, and he used to say, “The sword of God has polished it.”

Jadhīmah al-Abrash—“al-Abrash” was used euphemistically for a leper.

Yarbuʿ ibn Ḥanẓalah ibn Mālik was a leper, and his descendants were called Banū al-Abraṣ.

The poet said: [rajaz]

The sons of al-Abraṣ were its horsemen;

they caught up with the later and the earlier.

Al-Saffāḥ al-Taghlibī was a leper. He stood to deliver a sermon during the war between Bakr ibn Wāʾil and Taghlib, and broke wind. He said, “Every piebald horse breaks wind.”

The poet al-Mughīrah ibn Ḥabnāʾ was a leper. He is the one who said: [basīṭ]

I am a man of Ḥanẓalah when you trace my lineageto Lām of al-ʿAtīk; my maternal uncles are not al-ʿAwq.

Do not reckon whiteness in me a defect:the noble steeds among their fellows have piebald markings.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād al-ʿAbsī was a leper. Labīd said of him: [rajaz]

Gently, may you live long, O king; do not eat with him:his buttocks are mottled with leprosy.

Qushayr ibn Kaʿb was a leper, and for that reason he was called Qushayr.

Saʿd ibn Ḥārithah ibn Lām al-Ṭāʾī was a leper.

Ḍamrah ibn Ḍamrah ibn Jābir was a leper. He was called “Shiqqah ibn Ḍamrah,” but al-Nuʿmān renamed him Ḍamrah.

Al-Abyaḍ ibn Mujāshiʿ ibn Dārim was a leper.

The poet al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah was a leper.

Shimr ibn Dhī al-Jawshan al-Ḍibbābī, one of the killers of al-Ḥusayn ﵁ and may He curse his killer—was a leper.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qushayrī, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s governor over Khurāsān, was a leper.

Ayman ibn Khuraym was with ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān, and was a leper.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Qaḥṭabah was a leper.

ʿAbd al-Wārith ibn Saʿīd, the traditionist,

was a leper.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dāwūd, the traditionist,

was a leper.

Lameness

Abū Ṭālib, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Muʿādh ibn Jabal.

Al-Ḥawfazan ibn Shurayk.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān al-Laythī.

ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ.

Ziyād ibn Khaṣafah.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Masʿūd al-Kalbī.

ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

ʿAlqamah ibn Qays, companion of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.

Al-Shaʿbī said:

ʿAlqamah fought at Ṣiffīn until he became lame.

Rashīd al-Hajrī.

Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah.

Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh.

Abū Ḥāzim al-Madanī.

Al-Ghamr ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rajāʾ, the traditionist, who lived in Mecca.

Mujālid ibn Masʿūd, one of the Companions.

The Deaf

ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī.

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd ibn Hurmuz, client of the Dawsīs, was profoundly deaf.

The poet al-Kumayt was deaf and completely unable to hear anything.

Those with severed ears or noses

ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir: his hand was cut off on the Day of al-Yamāmah.

Al-Muraqqish the Elder: his nose was severed; a lion ate his nose.

286 / Those afflicted with leprosy

Abū Qilābah was afflicted with leprosy.

And Muʿayqīb, who was in charge of the signet ring of the Messenger of God ﷺ—was afflicted with leprosy.

Those who were cross-eyed

Abū Jahl ibn Hishām.

Abū Lahab, the paternal uncle of the Prophet ﷺ.

Abū Ḥudhayfah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah.

Samurah ibn Jundub.

ʿUrwah ibn al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Mūsā al-Ashʿarī.

Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

Ziyād ibn Abī Sufyān; one of his eyes was split.

ʿAdī ibn Zayd, the poet.

Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, the traditionist.

The Blue-Eyed

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was blue-eyed.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAyyāsh ibn Ṣaḥḥār was blue-eyed and ruddy.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

In some accounts: al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām was blue-eyed.

Baldness

ʿUtbah ibn Abī Sufyān.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵃—[and] Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam; no caliph after him was bald.

Those with short arms

Shurayḥ the judge.

Qays ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿAmārah.

Prognathism

Yazīd ibn Yazīd ibn Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

Foul breath

ʿAmr ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAdas, of Banū Dārim, had foul breath. [It is said of his descendants:]

“The mouths of dogs”.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān had foul breath, and was called Abū Dhubbān, on account of the severity of his foul breath. The implication is that flies would fall when they came near his mouth, because of the strength of its odor.

Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī.

One-eyed

Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb lost his eye on the Day of al-Ṭāʾif.

Al-Ashʿath ibn Qays lost his eye on the Day of al-Yarmūk.

Al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah lost his eye on the Day of al-Yarmūk.

Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī lost his eye at Hamadhān, where he was governor for ʿUthmān.

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim lost his eye on the Day of the Camel.

ʿUtbah ibn Abī Sufyān lost his eye on the Day of the Camel.

Qabīṣah ibn Dhuʾayb lost his eye on the Day of al-Ḥarrah.

Al-Ashtar al-Nakhaʿī lost his eye on the Day of al-Yarmūk.

Al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād struck him in the face with a whip, and he lost his eye.

Mālik ibn Mسمع lost his eye at al-Jafrah. (1) Qays ibn Makshūḥ al-Murādī lost his eye on the Day of al-Yarmūk.

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

Al-Ḥantaف ibn al-Sajf.

ʿAlī ibn al-Haytham al-Sadūsī.

Ibn Aḥmar, the poet.

Ibn Muqbil, the poet.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī, brother of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr, lost his eye on the Day of Jūr (2), and his father’s leg was cut off on the Day of Ḥunayn. ʿAbd Allāh was called “the master of the Qurʾān reciters.”

Al-Aswad ibn Yazīd lost one of his eyes from fasting.

Al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar, companion of ʿAlī.

Abū Mukhallad al-Sadūsī.

Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit was tall and one-eyed.

Jābir ibn Zayd, Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ.

The Blind

Abū Quḥāfah, father of Abū Bakr.

Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith.

Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib.

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī.

Kaʿb ibn Mālik al-Anṣārī.

Ḥassān ibn Thābit.

Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb.

ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib.

Abū Usayd al-Sāʿidī.

Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān.

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī.

Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah.

Al-Mughīrah ibn Miqsam, transmitter of Ibrāhīm’s reports.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām.

Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr lost his sight at the end of his life.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah ibn Masʿūd.

Abū al-ʿUbaydayn, one of Ibn Masʿūd’s companions; his name was Muʿāwiyah ibn Sabrah.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ lost his sight at the end of his life.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā lost his sight.

ʿAlī ibn Zayd, a descendant of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān, was born blind.

Abū Hilāl al-Rāsibī.

Maḥall ibn Muḥriz al-Ḍabbī, Abū Yaḥyā.

Three blind men in succession

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās.

His father: al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

His father: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim.

He said:

For that reason, Muʿāwiya said to Ibn ʿAbbās: “You, sons of Hāshim, are afflicted in your eyesight.”

Ibn ʿAbbās replied: “And you, sons of Umayya, are afflicted in your insight.”

Six men killed in succession

We know of no six men among the Arabs killed in succession except among the family of al-Zubayr:

ʿUmāra was killed on the day of Qudayd.

His father, Ḥamza, was also killed that day.

His father, Muṣʿab, was killed in the war between him and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

His father, al-Zubayr, was killed at Wādī al-Sibāʿ.

His father, al-ʿAwwām, was killed on the Day of al-Fijār.

His father, Khuwaylid, was killed in the pre-Islamic period.

Three judges in succession

Bilāl ibn Abī Burda was judge in Basra.

His father, Abū Burda ibn Abī Mūsā, was judge in Kufa.

His father, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, was a judge for ʿUmar.

Likewise, Sawwār ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qudāma ibn ʿAnaza ibn Kaʿb, of Banū al-ʿAnbar, served as judge for Abū Jaʿfar in Basra for seventeen years. He led the prayers in Basra twice and died while serving as its governor.

His son: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sawwār.

His son: Sawwār ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sawwār.

Three names in succession

Abū al-Bukhtarī the judge, namely Wahb ibn Wahb ibn Wahb.

Among the kings of Persia: Bahrām ibn Bahrām ibn Bahrām.

Among the Ṭālibids: Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan ibn Ḥasan.

Among the kings of Ghassān: al-Ḥārith the Younger ibn al-Ḥārith the Lame ibn al-Ḥārith the Elder.

Five clients in succession

Dāwūd ibn Khālid ibn Dīnār.

His two brothers: Sahl and Yaḥyā, sons of Khālid.

All of them are people from whom ḥadīth was transmitted. They were clients of the family of Ḥunayn, among whom was Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥunayn. Al-Zuhrī transmitted from him.

The family of Ḥunayn were clients of Mithqab; Mithqab was a client of Masḥal; Masḥal was a client of Shammās; and Shammās was a client of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Four men who saw the Messenger of God ﷺ in succession

Abū Quḥāfa.

His son: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁.

His son: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr.

His son: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Four brothers who witnessed Badr

They were ʿĀqil, Iyās, Khālid, and ʿĀmir, the sons of al-Bukayr, of the Layth tribe. Muʿāwiya used to boast of them to the Anṣār, saying: “No four brothers other than these witnessed Badr with the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

Three leaders in succession

Al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra.

His son: Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab.

His son, Mukhallad ibn Yazīd, became a leader while still a boy. Ḥamza ibn Bayḍ said of him: [mutaqārib]

You reached, with seven years of your life behind you,what the gray-haired leader reaches;

your concerns already are weighty matters,while your peers’ concern is to play.

Likewise, Khārija ibn Ḥiṣn. He became leader of the people of Kufa.

His father, Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfa, became leader of Asad and Ghaṭafān.

His father, Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, was called “Lord of Maʿadd.”

Among them was al-Ḥakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd, of ʿAbd al-Qays, who became a leader.

His father and grandfather [were leaders].

288/ Two brothers with a great difference in age

Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda, from whom ḥadīth is transmitted: his brother ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayda was sixty years older than he was, and Mūsā transmitted from his brother.

A father and son close in age

There were twelve years between ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and his son ʿAbd Allāh.

The tall

Ḥabīb ibn Maslama al-Fihrī was so tall that he seemed to loom over his mount.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was so tall that he seemed to be riding while people walked.

Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, when walking among the crowds, seemed like a camel litter atop a she-camel, with everyone else below him.

Because of his height, Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī could spit onto the camel’s hump, and his sandal was a cubit long.

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim was tall; when he rode a horse, his foot almost dragged on the ground.

Qays ibn Saʿd was tall and massive. The king of the Byzantines wrote to Muʿāwiya: “Send me the trousers of the tallest, largest man you have.” Muʿāwiya said:

“I know of no one but Qays ibn Saʿd.” He said to Qays: “When you return, send me your trousers.” Qays took them off and threw them to him. Muʿāwiya said, “Why didn’t you send them from your house?” Qays replied:

[ṭawīl]

I wanted people to know that these areQays’s trousers, with the delegations as witnesses;

and so people would not say, on mere guesswork,that they are the trousers of ʿĀdī, whose line descended from Thamūd.

ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād was tall; anyone who saw him walking would think he was riding, because of his height.

ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAbbās was tall and handsome. Some people marveled at his height.

A man said, “Glory be to God! How people have shrunk! I remember seeing al-ʿAbbās circumambulate this House, looking like a white tent.” This was related to ʿAlī, who said: “I came up to my father’s shoulder, and my father came up to my grandfather’s shoulder.”

Jabala ibn al-Ayham, the last of the kings of Ghassān, was twelve spans tall. When he rode, his foot brushed the ground. He accepted Islam during ʿUmar’s caliphate, then later became a Christian and went to the lands of the Byzantines.

ʿUmāra ibn ʿUqba al-Ḥanafī, the Kharijite, was tall. Al-Ḥajjāj granted him safe-conduct; he died in Basra. When he died, they could find no bier large enough to carry him, so they added planks to the bier.

The short

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd was extremely short; people sitting down could almost conceal him because of his height.

Ibrāhīm ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf was short. He married Sukayna bint al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ﵄—but she was not satisfied with him and obtained a separation from him. He was the father of Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm.

Abū Zayd the grammarian related, from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, from al-Ḥasan, that he said:

“Pharaoh was no more than a cubit tall.”

Al-Ḥuṭayʾa, the poet, was extremely short, which is why he was nicknamed al-Ḥuṭayʾa. So too were Dhū al-Rumma, the poet, and al-Marrār, the poet. He is the one who said: [ṭawīl]

And one waiting for ṣatman25 said, “I saw him … thin;indeed, the ṣatam man is disgraced …”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān, client of Fāṭima bint al-Walīd ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, was carried for more than three years. When he was born, his teeth had already come in.

Mālik ibn Anas was carried for more than two years.

Al-Wāqidī said: “I heard women of the family of al-Jaḥḥāf, descendants of Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, say: ‘No woman among us has carried a child for less than thirty months.’”

Harm ibn Ḥayyān was carried for four years, which is why he was named Harm.

Those whose gestation was shorter than its term

The Messiah, Jesus ﵇—was born after eight months; for that reason, no child born after eight months survives.

Al-Shaʿbī was born after seven months, as one of twins.

Jarīr, the poet, was born after seven months.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Marwān was born after six months.

Those attributed to tribes and fathers other than their own

Al-Zanjī ibn Khālid was fair-skinned with a reddish tinge. “Al-Zanjī” was only a nickname for him, just as a fair-skinned man was called Abū al-Jawn, and a Ḥabashī man Abū al-Bayḍāʾ.

Ibrāhīm ibn Yazīd al-Khūzī, one of those from whom ḥadīth was transmitted, was a client of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He was not from Khūz; he was given this name because he settled in the ravine of Khūz in Mecca.

He died in the year 151.

Miqsam, the client of Ibn ʿAbbās, was not a client of Ibn ʿAbbās. Rather, he was a client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. He was attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās only because he kept his company, attached himself to him, and transmitted from him.

Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ was not a cobbler; he used to sit with cobblers, and so was attributed to them.

Sulaymān al-Taymī was not from Taym, nor was he their client. Rather, he lived among Taym, and his mosque was among them, so he was attributed to them. He was a client of Banū Murra ibn ʿAbbād ibn Ḍubayʿa.

Abū Saʿīd al-Maqburī lived near the graves, and so he was called al-Maqburī.

ʿUthmān al-Battī was ʿUthmān ibn Sulaymān ibn Jarmūz. He was from the people of Kufa, then moved to Basra. He was a client of Banū Zuhra and used to sell coarse cloth, so he was named after it.

Al-Suddī used to sell wine at a covered arcade in Medina, and so was named after it. His name was Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim al-Makkī, the traditionist, was not from Mecca. Rather, he lived in Mecca for a time, but was a Basran. When he returned to Basra, he was called al-Makkī.

Al-Qāsim ibn al-Faḍl al-Ḥadānī, Abū al-Mughīra, was not from Ḥadān. Rather, he lived among Banū Ḥadān and was attributed to them; he was from the Azd.

ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād al-Thaqafī was not from Thaqīf; he was a client of ʿAbd al-Qays, but was attributed to Thaqīf.

The Yazīdī, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mubārak, used to tutor the children of Yazīd ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥimyarī, and so he was called “Yazīdī.”

Ibn Umm Maktūm was attributed to his mother. His father was Qays. His name was ʿAbd Allāh.

It is also said: ʿAmr.

Sharḥabīl ibn Ḥasana was attributed to his mother. His father was ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muṭāʿ.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Buḥayna was attributed to his mother. His father was Mālik.

Khafāf ibn Nadba was attributed to his mother. His father was ʿUmayr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Sulamī.

Abū Lubāba was given a kunya after a daughter of his called Lubāba. His name was Bashīr.

Muʿādh and Muʿawwidh, the sons of ʿAfrāʾ, were attributed to their mother. Their father was al-Ḥārith ibn Rifāʿa. Muʿādh had descendants; Muʿawwidh had none.

Fayrūz al-Ḥimyarī, the slayer of al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī, was a non-Arab, from Daylam.

It was said that he was called Ḥimyarī because he settled among Ḥimyar.

Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya was attributed to his mother. His father was Ibrāhīm ibn Miqsam.

[ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿĀʾisha was attributed to a grandmother of his. His father too was known as “Ibn ʿĀʾisha.” He was ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ al-Tamīmī.

Mirdās ibn Adiya was attributed to a grandmother of his, or to a wet nurse.

Ibn al-Qirriyya was attributed to his mother. He was Ayyūb ibn Yazīd.

Ibn al-Iṭnāba, the poet, was attributed to his mother. He was ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir.

Ibn al-Dumayna and Ibn Mayyāda were attributed to their mother.

Sulaymān ibn Qatta was attributed to his mother. He was a poet from whom ḥadīth was transmitted, and he was a client of Taym Quraysh.

Al-ʿUmānī, the poet, was not from Oman. Rather, he had a yellowish face and a large belly. The rajaz poet Dukayn saw him drawing water and said, “Who is this ʿUmānī?” For the people of Oman have yellow faces and large bellies.

Those Known by Their Patronymics

Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, one of the Anṣār.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh. His name was his patronymic. It is also said that his name was Shuʿba.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Sabra.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, and his brother, Abū Sufyān ibn al-ʿAlāʾ: the names of both were their patronymics.

Abū Qurra al-Kindī, the first judge to give judgments in Kūfa. His name was his patronymic.

Abū Hubayra ibn al-Ḥārith, one of the Anṣār. His name was his patronymic.

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām al-Makhzūmī. His name was his patronymic.

He was called the Monk of Quraysh.

Abū Bakr ibn Abī Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. His name was his patronymic.

Abū Umayya and Abū al-Ḥaḍramī, of Taym al-Ribāb. Their names were their patronymics.

Those Given Two or Three Patronymics

ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ﵁—was known by the patronymics Abū ʿAbd Allāh, Abū ʿAmr, and Abū Laylā.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr was known by the patronymics Abū Bakr, Abū Ḥabīb, and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

Qaṭarī ibn al-Fujāʾa was known by the patronymics Abū Muḥammad, Abū Naʿāma, and Abū Ḥanẓala.

ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was known by the patronymics Abū Lahab and Abū ʿUtba.

ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl was known by the patronymics Abū ʿAlī and Abū ʿAqīl.

Qays ibn Makshūḥ was known by the patronymics Abū Asad and Abū Ḥassān.

Ḥassān ibn Thābit was known by the patronymics Abū al-Walīd and Abū al-Ḥusām.

Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was known by the patronymics Abū Yaʿlā and Abū ʿUmāra.

Ṣakhr ibn Ḥarb was known by the patronymics Abū Sufyān and Abū Ḥanẓala.

Accounts of Plagues and Their Dates

Abū Muḥammad said: Abū Ḥātim related to me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

The first plague in Islam was the plague of ʿAmwās in Syria. Muʿādh ibn Jabal, his two wives and his son, and Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ died in it.

And the plague of Shīrawayh ibn Kisrā in Iraq occurred at the same time. Both were in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. A long interval separated the plague of Shīrawayh from the plague of ʿAmwās.

Then came the plague of al-Jārif in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr, in the year sixty-nine. At that time, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maʿmar was in charge of Baṣra.

Then came the plague of the Maidens, so called because it began among unmarried girls and young women in Baṣra, Wāsiṭ, Syria, and Kūfa. At that time al-Ḥajjāj was in Wāsiṭ, during the governorship of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān died in it, or shortly afterward. Also dying in it were Umayya ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Asīd, ʿAlī ibn Aṣmaʿ, and Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Ḥiṣn. It was called the Plague of the Notables.

Then came the plague of ʿAdī ibn Arṭāʾ in the year one hundred.

Then came the plague of Gh urāb in the year one hundred and twenty-seven.26 Ghurāb was a man of al-Ribāb, and he was the first to die in it. This was during the governorship of al-Walīd ibn Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

Then came the plague of Salm ibn Qutayba in the year one hundred and thirty-one, in Shaʿbān and Ramaḍān. It abated in Shawwāl, and Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī died in it.

He said: Al-Aṣmaʿī also said on another occasion:

The plague of Salm broke out in Iraq on the day of the departure—that is, the day of the feast—in the year one hundred and thirty-one. In Syria it broke out in the year one hundred and thirty-five. When it began, its victim would be terrified of it.

The poet says of the Plague of the Notables:

[Long]

The plague left no kinsman behindto whom one might return when homeward came the time.

No plague ever broke out in Medina or Mecca.

Accounts of Famous Days in the Jāhiliyya

The Day of Dhū Qār:

Its cause was this: when al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir fled from Abrūwīz, he entrusted his family and a hundred coats of mail to Hāniʾ ibn Masʿūd ibn ʿĀmir al-Shaybānī. Abrūwīz sent to him demanding the coats of mail and al-Nuʿmān’s two sons, but he refused to hand them over. Abrūwīz sent an army against him, and they fought at Dhū Qār. The Banū Shaybān were victorious. It was the first day on which the Arabs prevailed over the Persians.

The First Fijār:

The first Fijār was between Quraysh and those with them from Kināna, on the one side, and Qays ʿAylān on the other. The cause was that a man of Banū Kināna owed a debt to a man of Banū Naṣr ibn Muʿāwiya. The Kinanī became insolvent over it. The Naṣrī came to the market of ʿUkāẓ with a monkey, stood with it in the marketplace, and said: “Who will buy this, with my claim against so-and-so, the Kinanī, as its price?”

A man of Kināna passed by and struck the monkey with his sword, killing it. The Naṣrī cried out to Qays, and the Kinanī cried out to Kināna. The people rallied until they nearly came to blows; then they made peace. There was no fighting between them. The fighting took place only in the Second Fijār.

The Second Fijār:

Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr ibn ʿAmr led all of Asad and Ghaṭafān. His son ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn was one of those whose hearts had been reconciled. ʿUyayna came to the market of— ʿUkāẓ and saw people buying and selling. He said: “I see these people gathered here without covenant or agreement. If I live until next year, they will know what is what.” The following year he raided them and attacked them. This was the cause of the Second Fijār. The war was between Kināna and Qays, and victory fell to Qays ʿAylān.

The Pact of al-Fuḍūl:

Its cause was that Quraysh were wronging one another in the Sacred Precinct. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān and al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stood up and called their people to swear an alliance to support one another and secure the rights of the wronged against the wrongdoer. They accepted their invitation and swore the pact in the house of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān.

The Pact of the Perfumed Ones:

The Perfumed Ones were ʿAbd Manāf, Zuhra, Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, Taym, and al-Ḥārith ibn Fihr. The cause was that the Banū Quṣayy wished to take away from the Banū ʿAbd al-Dār some of what they held: the provision for pilgrims, the standard, the council house, and the custodianship of the Kaʿba. The Banū ʿAbd al-Dār had only the provision of water. They formed an alliance to fight them and prepared for battle, but then abandoned the plan and left in their hands what they had held. The provision for pilgrims was something Quṣayy had imposed on Quraysh each year to provide food for the pilgrims.

The Day of al-Waqīṭ:

A day in the Islamic period, between Banū Tamīm and Bakr ibn Wāʾil.

The Day of Shuwayḥiṭ:

A day in the Jāhiliyya between Yemen and Muḍar. At that time, the people were led by Zurāra ibn ʿAdas.

The War of Bakr and Taghlib, the two sons of Wāʾil ibn Rabīʿa

The cause was that Kulayb ibn Rabīʿa was of Taghlib. In his time, he had fortified Rabīʿa—hence the saying “more powerful than Kulayb of Wāʾil.” A herd of camels belonging to Jassās ibn Murra ibn Dhuhl ibn Shaybān ibn Thaʿlaba passed by him. He shot one of them with an arrow, piercing its udder. The she-camel belonged to Basūs, Jassās’s maternal aunt. Jassās rode out with ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Dhuhl to Kulayb. They stabbed Kulayb and cut off his head. War then raged between them for forty years. They had six famous battle-days, with Muhalhil, Kulayb’s brother, directing the fighting:

The Day of ʿUnayza:

On this day they fought to a draw.

The Day of Wāridāt:

Taghlib had the advantage over Bakr.

The Day of al-Ḥanw:

Bakr had the advantage over Taghlib.

The Day of al-Quṣaybāt:

Taghlib had the advantage over Bakr. They slew many of Bakr, and on this day Hammām ibn Murra, Jassās’s brother, was killed.

The Day of Qiḍḍa: It is the Day of al-Faṣīl.

The Day of the Shaving of the Forelocks:

On this day Jaḥdar was killed. The women killed him because he had not shaved his hair, and they did not recognize him.

After this there was no further day that was recorded. Instead, they raided and skirmished against one another, and Jassās was not killed before their conflict came to an end.

The War of Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ:

This was a war between ʿAbs ibn Bughayḍ ibn Rayth ibn Ghaṭafān ibn Saʿd ibn Qays ʿAylān and Dubyān ibn Bughayḍ ibn Rayth ibn Ghaṭafān ibn [sic] Saʿd ibn Qays ʿAylān.27

Its cause was that Qays ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhayma al-ʿAbsī and Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr al-Dhubyānī wagered twenty camels: whichever man’s horses won would take them from the other. They set the finish line at a hundred bowshots’ distance, the training period at forty nights, and the course from Dhāt al-Iṣād. Qays entered Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ in the race, and Ḥudhayfa entered Qurzul—also said to have been al-Khaṭṭār and al-Ḥanfāʾ. The Banū Fazāra, Ḥudhayfa’s clan, set an ambush along the route. They turned al-Ghabrāʾ back and struck her, though she had been in the lead. Qays said, “She won.” They denied him his claim, and conflict broke out between them. Qays said, “Give us one camel to slaughter for the people at the watering place.” Ḥudhayfa said:

“We are not going to concede to you that you won the race.” When Qays saw this, he left them, parting from them. Some time later, Qays raided them and encountered ʿAwf ibn Badr, Ḥudhayfa’s brother, and killed him. He paid blood compensation of a hundred pregnant she-camels. Mālik ibn Zuhayr set out in a certain direction, and Ḥaml ibn Badr encountered and killed him. Qays sent word to Ḥudhayfa: “Return our camels to us, for you killed Mālik ibn Zuhayr in exchange for ʿAwf ibn Badr.” The camels had produced offspring while with Ḥudhayfa, and he returned them without their young. The Banū ʿAbs would accept nothing less than their camels and their young, and war raged between them until al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf al-Murrī brought an end to the bloodshed between them.

Stories of People Whose Names Became Proverbs

Ḥājib’s Bow:

He was Ḥājib ibn Zurāra. During a drought that had befallen his people because of the Messenger of God’s supplication against them ﷺ—he went to Kisrā and asked him to permit him and his people to settle in one of the districts of his realm, so that they might prosper. Kisrā said to him: “You Arabs are a treacherous and grasping people. If I permit you, you will ruin the land, raid the subjects, and harm them.”

Ḥājib said: “I guarantee to the king that they will not do so.” He said, “Who will guarantee that you will keep your word?” Ḥājib said:

“I pledge my bow to you.” The people around him laughed. Kisrā said, “He would never surrender it.” But he accepted the bow from him and permitted them to enter the cultivated lands. The people prospered through the Messenger of God’s supplication for them ﷺ. Ḥājib had died, and ʿAṭārid ibn Ḥājib went to Kisrā seeking his father’s bow. Kisrā returned it to him and gave him a robe. When ʿAṭārid came in a delegation to the Messenger of God ﷺ among the Banū Tamīm, and became Muslim, he offered the robe to the Messenger of God ﷺ—but the Messenger would not accept it. ʿAṭārid sold it for four thousand dirhams to a Jewish man.

Abū al-Yaqẓān said:

The bow today is with the descendants of Jaʿfar ibn ʿUmayr ibn ʿAṭārid ibn Ḥājib, because they are his eldest descendants.

Bāqil:

The man whose slowness of speech became proverbial.

He was from the Banū Qays ibn Thaʿlaba. He had bought a she-goat for eleven dirhams. They asked him, “How much did you pay for the she-goat?” He opened both hands, spread his fingers, and stuck out his tongue—meaning eleven. When they mocked him for this, he said:

[Mutāqārib]

They reproach Bāqil for his foolishness,as though folly had never been created.

So do not reproach him excessively for his dullness:for dullness suits the fool best.

The sticking out of the tongue and spreading of the fingersare dearer to us than eloquence.

Maryah’s earring

It is said: “She was Maryah daughter of Ẓālim ibn Wahb ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Kindī.”

Her sister was Hind al-Hunūd, the wife of Ḥujr Ākil al-Murār al-Kindī. Her son was al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj, whom al-Nābighah mentions in the words: [Rajaz]

And al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj is the best of mankind.

It was her that Ḥassān ibn Thābit meant when he said: [Basīṭ]

The sons of Jafna around their father’s grave—the grave of Maryah’s son, noble and distinguished.

Khuraim al-Nāʿim

He was Khuraim ibn ʿAmr, of Banū Murrah ibn ʿAwf ibn Saʿd ibn Dhubyān. His son was ʿAdī ibn Khuraim, and ʿAdī’s two sons were ʿUthmān and Abū al-Hind, the mother of the sons of ʿUmārah.

He was called al-Nāʿim because he wore old clothes in summer and new clothes in winter.

Umm Khārijah

She was Umm Khārijah daughter of Qirād, of Bajīlah. They would ask her, “A betrothal?” and she would reply, “A marriage.” [Hence the saying: “Quicker than Umm Khārijah’s marriage.”] She bore to Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāh: al-Layth, al-Duʾl, and ʿUrayj. She was also the mother of al-ʿAnbar, al-Hujaym, and Usayyid.

She also bore among Banū al-Qayn of Yemen a people called Banū al-Ḥurrah.

She bore among Bahraʾ.

Khārijah was her son, though it is not known who his father was.

The barber of Sābāṭ

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

The Sābāṭ of Kisrā is called in Persian Balāshābādh. Balāsh is a man’s name. They made it proverbial for emptiness because armies used to pass by it, and he would shave them on credit, because business was slack, until they returned.

The anemones of al-Nuʿmān

Abū Muḥammad said:

The anemones are attributed to al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir. He went out to the open country, where the plants had grown thick, in shades of red, green, and yellow. There he saw many of these anemones and said, “How beautiful they are! Protect them.” So they protected them, and they were named the anemones of al-Nuʿmān.

The tale of Khurāfah

Abū Sufyān al-Ghanawī told me: Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Sulamī told us: ʿAlī ibn Abī Sārah told us, from Thābit, from Anas ibn Mālik:

The Prophet ﷺ—said to ʿĀʾishah: “The truest of stories is the tale of Khurāfah.” He was a man of Banū ʿUdhrah whom the jinn had taken captive. He lived among them, and when they eavesdropped on heaven, they told him what they had heard. He would then tell the people of the earth, and they found it just as he had said.

Barjān the thief

He was Faḍl ibn Barjān, a client of Banū Imriʾ al-Qays. He had two companions, named Sahm and Sihām, whom Mālik ibn al-Mundhir killed. Khalaf ibn Khalīfah said: [Basīṭ]

If you have not asked about Sahm and his companion,ask Faḍl ibn Barjān about Mālik.

He will tell you of him, he who climbed to a high place,until he towered over houses and buildings.

Saḥbān Wāʾil

He is affiliated with Wāʾil Bāhilah: Wāʾil ibn Maʿn ibn Aʿṣur. He was an orator, and so he became proverbial. The poet said of a guest who had come to stay with him: [Ṭawīl]

Saḥbān Wāʾil came to us, and we had none to match himin eloquence or in knowledge of what he would say.

He kept eating morsels until he seemedlike Bāqil, from his dullness, once he began to speak.

His son was ʿAjlān ibn Saḥbān, who said of Ṭalḥah al-Ṭalaḥāt: [Majzūʾ al-Kāmil]

From you comes the gift, so give to me;and in public, I shall praise you.

Ṭufayl, after whom the Ṭufayliyyūn are named

He was Ṭufayl, from Kūfah, descended from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghaṭafān ibn Saʿd. He was called Ṭufayl al-ʿArāʾis, because he would enter wedding feasts and follow them about.

The treasure of al-Naṭf

The Arabs say: “If so-and-so had the treasure of al-Naṭf, he would not have gone beyond it.” He was a man of Banū Yarbuʿ who was poor and carried water on his back, which would drip—yanṭufu. He had raided property that Bādhān had sent from Yemen to Kisrā. One day he gave from it until the sun had set, and the Arabs made him proverbial.

The regret of al-Kasʿī

He was a man who shot and hit his target, but thought he had missed and broke his bow. When he learned the truth, he regretted breaking the bow. He became proverbial for any matter that ended in regret.

ʿUrqūb’s promises

Yaʿqūb was a man of the ʿAmālīq. His brother came to him asking for something, and ʿUrqūb said to him, “When my palm trees bear fruit.” When they did, his brother came to him, and he said, “When they have formed their dates.” When they had, his brother came to him, and he said, “When they turn yellow.” When they had, his brother came to him, and he said, “When they ripen.” When they had, his brother came to him, and he said, “When they become dates.” When they had become dates, he took them during the night and gave his brother nothing. The Arabs made him proverbial for breaking promises. The poet said:

[Ṭawīl]

You promised, though breaking promises is your nature:ʿUrqūb’s promises to his brother at Yathrib.

This is how I read it in the book of Sībawayh, with tāʾ and a fatḥah over the rāʾ.

Ḥunayn’s two sandals

Ḥunayn was a cobbler from al-Ḥīrah. A Bedouin bargained with him over a pair of sandals, and they disagreed until Ḥunayn became angry. Wanting to vex the Bedouin, Ḥunayn took one sandal after he had set off and threw it down; then he threw the other farther along the road. When the Bedouin passed the first, he said, “How like this is to one of Ḥunayn’s sandals! If the other were with it, I would take them.” He went on, but when he reached the other sandal, he regretted leaving the first. He made his mount kneel, took the sandal, and went back for the first.
