Ḥunayn had been lying in wait for him, and seized his mount and everything it carried. The Bedouin came back with nothing but the two sandals. His people asked him, “What have you brought back?” He said, “Ḥunayn’s two sandals.” The Arabs made this proverbial for someone who returns empty-handed.

The perfume of Manshim

They have disagreed about Manshim. The best account I have heard is that she was a woman who sold embalming spices in the pre-Islamic period. It was said to people when they went to war, “Grind Manshim’s perfume among them,” meaning: the perfume of the dead.

The bathhouse of Minjāb

It is attributed to Minjāb ibn Rāshid al-Ḍabbī. People became fond of mentioning it because of the saying of a poet: [Basīṭ]

How often a woman, weary from walking, has asked:“Which way is the bathhouse of Minjāb?”

Khalīf

The man after whom Khalīfī falūdhaj is named was Khalīf ibn ʿUqbah, of Banū Rabīʿ ibn al-Ḥārith—who are al-Maqāʿis—of Banū Tamīm. His kunyah was Abū Bakr.

Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, who was one of his companions, gave him this kunyah. He was one of the wittiest people of Baṣrah, and he has descendants there.

Sulaym

The man after whom Aṣfar Sulaym is named belonged to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakrah, who had three stewards called Sulaym al-Nāṣiḥ, Sulaym al-Ghāshsh, and Sulaym al-Sāḥir. This was the one who made Aṣfar Sulaym.

Saʿīd

The man after whom Saʿīdī garments are named was Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Saʿīd.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God ennoble his face—had killed his father at Badr, while his son Saʿīd was still a boy. The Messenger of God ﷺ—clothed him in a robe. It was after this robe that Saʿīdī garments were named.

Saʿīd was the first to mark camels on the bone. He had about twenty sons and twenty daughters.

Among his descendants was ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Ashdaq, whom ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān killed.

Ibn Raghbān

The man after whom the mosque in Baghdād is named was a client of Ḥabīb ibn Maslamah, of Quraysh, of Muḥārib ibn Fihr. Ḥabīb was of great stature and held governorships in the time of ʿUthmān and Muʿāwiyah. He is counted among those famous for their height.

The archers of the eye

They have disagreed about them. Some said they were from Ṭayyiʾ. Others said:

They are the Nūbah. They shoot arrows with Arab bows, and the Arabs call them “archers of the eye.” They own camels, sheep, cattle, and horses, fine-bred like the Arabs.

The gifts

The origin of the practice of giving a jāʾizah or jawāʾiz is this: Qaṭan ibn ʿAbd ʿAwf ibn Aṣram, of Banū Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah, governed Fārs for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir. Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays passed by him with his army, on campaign to Khurāsān. Qaṭan stood at the bridge of al-Karr and would ask each man about his lineage, then give him according to his rank. He would give them a hundred each, but when their numbers grew large, he said, “Send them on with gifts,” and they were given gifts. He was the first to establish the practice of gifts.

The poet said: [Wāfir]

May my paternal uncle and maternal uncle be ransomedfor the noblest of men, the sons of Hilāl, despite their faults.

They established the giving of gifts among Maʿadd,and the nights made it another custom.

The Aḥābīsh, Quraysh’s allies

They were Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, al-Ḥayyu ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAmr, and Banū al-Hawn ibn Khuzaymah. They assembled at the foot of Ḥabashī—a mountain below Makkah—and swore an oath by God: “We are a single hand against all others as long as night covers us, day shines, and Ḥabashī remains fixed in its place.”

They were thus called Aḥābīsh, after the mountain.

Ḥammād al-Rāwiyah said:

They were called Aḥābīsh because they gathered together. In the language of the Arabs, gathering together is taḥabbush.

The Ḥums

They were Quraysh and those of Kinānah who followed their religion. Taḥammus means strictness in religion. During the days of Minā, they did not seek shade, nor did they make ghee spoil; they did not enter houses through their doors [and they were forbidden], and they would stand at al-Mashʿar but not go to ʿArafah, nor would they pick up al-jillah.

The two al-Qāriẓs

The Arabs say, “I will not do such-and-such until the two al-Qāriẓs return.” The first is al-Qāriẓ al-ʿAnazī, namely Yadhkur ibn ʿAnazah. Khuzaymah ibn Nahḍ ibn Zayd was in love with his daughter Fāṭimah. He said of her: [Wāfir]

When al-Jawzāʾ follows close behind al-Thurayyā,I imagine all sorts of things about Fāṭimah’s family.

Her father went out in search of qaraẓ. Khuzaymah met him and killed him. He did not return, and the circumstances of his death remained unknown, until Khuzaymah said: [Mutāqārib]

A maiden whose breath, like ambergris,is perfumed in her mouth with ginger—

I killed her father out of love for her;so she may be sparing, if she is sparing, or may give.

When he had recited these two verses, they went to war.

The other al-Qāriẓ was Abū Rahm, a man of ʿAnazah. He fell in love with his cousin. They met while gathering qaraẓ, and he carried her off on his camel until he came among Banū Ḍābiʾ of Hamdān. They are now called Banū Qāriẓ.

Abū Dhuʾayb said of the two of them: [Ṭawīl]

Until both al-Qāriẓs returnand Kulayb ibn Wāʾil is raised among the slain.

ʿAmr

He is the man referred to in the saying, “ʿAmr has grown beyond the collar.” He was ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī ibn Naṣr, the sister’s son of Jadhīmah al-Abraš. When the warriors were picking dates in front of his maternal uncle, he was a boy and used to say: [Rajaz]

This is my picking, and the best of it is here;every picker’s hand goes to his mouth.

The jinn carried him off for a time. Later, Mālik and ʿUqayl found him. He gave them his lineage, and they brought him to Jadhīmah, who rejoiced greatly and let them decide his fate. They decreed that he should be his drinking companion.

So they became Jadhīmah’s drinking companions. Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah al-Taymī said, lamenting his brother: [Ṭawīl]

We lived for a time like the two drinking companions of Jadhīmah,until it was said that they would never be parted.

Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī said: [Ṭawīl]

Do you not know that before us there were partedtwo friends of pure affection, Mālik and ʿUqayl?

His mother washed him, dressed him in the garments of kings, put a collar around his neck, and ordered him to visit his maternal uncle.

When his uncle saw his beard and the collar around his neck, he said, “ʿAmr has grown beyond the collar.” Al-Zabbāʾ had killed his maternal uncle, and ʿAmr and Quṣayr avenged him by killing her.

The Kurds

The Persians claim that the Kurds were the surplus of Bayūrāsf’s food. He would order two men to be slaughtered for him each day and make his food from their flesh. He had a vizier called Armāʾīl, who would slaughter one man and spare the other, sending him to the mountains of Fārs. They reproduced in the mountains and grew numerous.

The Khūz

Al-Aṣmaʿī said:

The Khūz are the laborers who built the tower for Pharaoh. Their name is derived from the word for pig; in Persian they are called khūk.

304/ The Jews

They were called Jews because, out of fear of something, they traced their lineage to one of the kings, to Yahūd son of Jacob.

The Christians

They were named Christians after the village in which the Messiah settled. It is Nāṣira, in the land of al-Khalīl.

Their saying:

“At the hands of ʿAdl”

He was ʿAdl son of So-and-so, of Saʿd al-ʿAshīra. He was in charge of Ṭubbaʿ’s police force. Whenever Ṭubbaʿ was angry with a man, he handed him over to ʿAdl. So people would say of anything whose destruction they feared, “It is at the hands of ʿAdl.”

It is also said that “al-ʿAdl” means the arbiter between two people who have wagered on a pledge. When something is in his hands, its owner stands on the brink of either loss or gain.

Similar to this is their saying, “He is at risk.” Al-khaṭar is what two gamblers stake between them for the winner.

More impious than a donkey

He was a man from the remnants of ʿĀd. He had protected a place in the land of ʿĀd called al-Jawf, and settled there. It had trees and water, and he had ten sons. They all died, so he grew angry and became exceedingly impious, killing every Muslim he found. A fire came from beneath al-Jawf amid a violent wind, until it burned all of al-Jawf, burning him and those with him. By morning, al-Jawf was as though it were night; its water had sunk away, and it had become a playground for the jinn. Everyone who traveled through it feared it. The Arabs made it proverbial, saying, “A valley like the donkey’s hollow,” and, “A valley like the ass’s hollow.” They also said, “More impious than a donkey.”

More foolish than Dagha

He said:

Her name was Māriya daughter of Rabīʿa, of ʿIjl. She was married to Jundub ibn al-ʿAnbar and bore him ʿAdī ibn Jundub. She was foolish and beautiful, and there are stories about her foolishness.

The Sikīnan tress

It is attributed to Sukayna daughter of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib ﵄.

The Religions of the Arabs in the Jāhiliyya

Christianity was found among Rabīʿa, Ghassān, and some of Quḍāʿa.

Judaism was found among Ḥimyar, Banū Kināna, Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, and Kinda.

Zoroastrianism was found among Tamīm.

Among them were Zarāra ibn ʿAdas al-Tamīmī and his son Ḥājib ibn Zarāra—who married his daughter and then regretted it.

Among them were al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis—who was a Zoroastrian—and Abū Sūd, the grandfather of Wakīʿ ibn Ḥassān, who was a Zoroastrian.

Irreligion was found among Quraysh; they took it from al-Ḥīra.

In the Jāhiliyya, the Banū Ḥanīfa made a god out of ḥays (a dish of dates, clarified butter, and dried cheese), worshipped it for a long time, then famine struck them and they ate it. A man of Banū Tamīm said: [Khafīf]

“Ḥanīfa ate its lord, driven by hunger, A hunger long familiar to them, and want.”

Another said: [Majzūʾ al-kāmil]

“Ḥanīfa ate its lord In the time of hardship and famine.

They did not fear from their lord Evil consequences and retribution.”

The Sects

The Ibāḍiyya:

They are among the Khārijites. They are affiliated with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibāḍ, who was of Banū Murra ibn ʿUbayd, of Banū Tamīm—the clan of al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays.

300The Azāriqa:

They are among the Khārijites. They are affiliated with Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, who was of al-Dawl ibn Ḥanīfa. He left no descendants. After him, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Māḥūz rose among the Khārijites.

Al-Muhallab killed him near al-Ahwāz.

The Bayhasiyya:

They are among the Khārijites. They are affiliated with Abū Bayhas, of Banū Saʿd ibn Ḍubayʿa ibn Qays. His name was Hayḍam ibn Jābir. ʿUthmān ibn Ḥayyān, governor of Medina, cut off his hands and feet.

The Khashabiyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ashtar encountered ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, and most of Ibrāhīm’s companions had wooden clubs with them; so they were called the Khashabiyya.

The Kaysāniyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. They are the followers of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd, and it is reported that his epithet was Kaysān.

The Sabaʾiyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. They are affiliated with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sabaʾ. He was the first of the Rāfiḍīs to profess unbelief, and he said that ʿAlī was the Lord of the worlds. ʿAlī and his companions burned him in the fire.

The Mughīriyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs, affiliated with al-Mughīra ibn Saʿīd, the client of Bajīla. He was a Sabaʾī, and used to say: “Had ʿAlī wished, he could have brought ʿĀd and Thamūd back to life, along with the generations between them.”

He rebelled against Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who killed and crucified him at Wāsiṭ, by the Bridge of al-ʿĀshir.

The Manṣūriyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. They are affiliated with Abū Manṣūr al-Kasf, who was called Kasf because he said to his followers: “It was concerning me that God Almighty revealed: ‘And if they see a fragment falling from the sky’” (Qurʾān 52:44).

Among them are the stranglers.

The Khaṭṭābiyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. They are affiliated with Abū al-Khaṭṭāb. I do not know who he was, except that he used to order his followers to bear false witness against those who opposed them concerning property, blood, and sexual relations. He said: “Their blood and their women are lawful to you.”

The Ghurābiyya:

They are among the Rāfiḍīs. These people were not affiliated with a man; rather, they were called Ghurābiyya because they claimed that ʿAlī resembled the Prophet ﷺ—as closely as one raven resembles another. Gabriel made a mistake when he was sent to ʿAlī, because of his resemblance to the Prophet ﷺ.

The Zaydiyya:

They are affiliated with the slain Zayd ibn ʿAlī. They are the least extreme among the Rāfiḍīs, though they hold that one should join in revolt with anyone who revolts.

301/ Names of the Ghulāt

Among the Rāfiḍīs

Abū al-Ṭufayl:

The standard-bearer of al-Mukhtār, and the last person to have seen the Messenger of God alive.

And al-Mukhtār, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Jadalī, Zarāra ibn Aʿyan, and Jābir al-Juʿfī.

The Shīʿa

Al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar, Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Ṣawḥān, al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubāta, ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, Ṭāwūs, Sulaymān al-Aʿmash, Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī, Abū Ṣādiq, Salama ibn Kuhayl, al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtayba, Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Ḥabba ibn Juwayn, Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Shuʿba ibn al-Ḥajjāj, Fiṭr ibn Khalīfa, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Ḥayy, Sharīk, Abū Isrāʾīl al-Mulāʾī, Muḥammad ibn Fuḍayl, Wakīʿ ibn al-Jarrāḥ, Ḥumayd al-Ruʾāsī, Zayd ibn al-Ḥubāb, al-Faḍl ibn Dukayn, al-Masʿūdī the younger, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā, Jarīr ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dāwūd, Hushaym, Sulaymān al-Taymī, ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī, Jaʿfar al-Ḍubaʿī, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān, Ibn Lahīʿa, Hishām ibn ʿAmmār, al-Mughīra, the companion of Ibrāhīm, Maʿrūf ibn Kharrabūdh, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Maʿmar, and ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd.

The Murjiʾa

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, ʿAmr ibn Murra, Dharr al-Hamadānī, Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Abū Ḥanīfa, the proponent of personal opinion, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Dāwūd and his son ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, Khārija ibn Muṣʿab, ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Māṣir, Abū Muʿāwiya al-Ḍarīr, Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zāʾida, Abū Yūsuf, the proponent of personal opinion, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib, and Misʿar ibn Kidām.

The Qadariyya

Maʿbad al-Juhanī, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yāsir, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Ghaylān al-Qibṭī, al-Faḍl al-Raqāshī, ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid, Wahb ibn Munabbih—who later recanted—Qatāda, Hishām al-Dastawāʾī, Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūba, Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, ʿAwf ibn Abī Jamīla, Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim al-Makkī, ʿUthmān ibn Miqsam al-Barī, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Abī Najīḥ, Khālid al-ʿAbdī, Hammām ibn Yaḥyā, Makḥūl al-Shāmī, Saʿīd ibn Ibrāhīm, Nūḥ ibn Qays al-Ṭāḥī—who was also a Rāfiḍī—Ghunder, Thawr ibn Zayd, ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd al-Wārith al-Tannūrī, Ṣāliḥ al-Murrī, Kahmas, ʿAbbād ibn Ṣuhayb, Khālid ibn Maʿdān, and Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq.

The Book of Kings

The Kings of Yemen

Abū Muḥammad said:

Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān traveled to Yemen with his descendants and settled there. He was the first of the descendants of Adam to speak Arabic, and the first whose descendants greeted him with the greeting of kings: “May you never be cursed, and may you greet the morning in good health.”

All Yemen is descended from him. Yaʿrub’s son was Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub, and Yashjub’s son was Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub. Kingship was among his descendants. It is said that he was named Sabaʾ because he was the first among the descendants of Qaḥṭān to take captives.

The first king among his descendants was Ḥimyar ibn Sabaʾ, who ruled until he died of old age.

Kingship remained among the descendants of Ḥimyar. Their rule did not extend beyond Yemen, and none of them went on campaign, until generations had passed and kingship came to al-Ḥārith al-Rāʾish.

Al-Ḥārith al-Rāʾish:

Al-Ḥārith was the first among them to go on campaign, seize spoils, and bring them into Yemen. It is said that fifteen forefathers stood between al-Rāʾish and Ḥimyar. He was called al-Rāʾish because he brought spoils, wealth, and captives into Yemen, enriching its people.

In his time, Luqmān, master of the vultures, died. Luqmān was the man whom ʿĀd had sent with its delegation to the Sanctuary to pray for rain. He was offered a choice: the lifespan of seven brown cows among the gazelles, or of gazelles on a rugged mountain that the rain could not reach, or the lifespan of seven vultures, each of which, when it died, would be succeeded by another vulture. He chose the lifespans of the vultures, and the last of his vultures was Labad. The poets have mentioned him. Al-Nābigha said: [Basīṭ]

“She became desolate, and her people departed; what befell Labad has also laid her low.”

Labīd ibn Rabīʿa al-ʿĀmirī said: [Basīṭ]

“When Labad saw the vultures taking flight, he raised his pinions, like a beggar bereft of clothing.”

The poets attribute him to ʿĀd. It is said that he lived for two thousand four hundred and fifty-odd years. The furthest extent of al-Rāʾish’s first campaign was India; after that he campaigned against the Turks in Azerbaijan and the regions around it, took their children captive, and then returned.

Al-Rāʾish mentioned our Prophet ﷺ—in a poem in which he foretold who would rule among them and others. He said: [Wāfir]

“After them a great man shall rule, a prophet who does not permit what is forbidden.

He shall be called Aḥmad. Would that I might live a year beyond his coming forth.”

His reign lasted one hundred and twenty-five years.

Abraha ibn al-Rāʾish:

His son Abraha ibn al-Rāʾish succeeded him. He was called Dhū al-Manār because he was the first to set up beacons along the route of his campaigns, so that he could find the way when returning. His reign lasted one hundred and eighty-three years.

306Ifrīqīs ibn Abraha:

His son Ifrīqīs ibn Abraha ibn al-Rāʾish succeeded him. He campaigned toward the West, into the land of the Berbers, until he reached Tangier and transferred the Berbers from the land of Palestine, and Egypt and the coast to their present-day settlements. The Berbers were the remnants of those whom Joshua son of Nun had killed.

Ifrīqīs was the one who built Ifrīqiya, which was named after him. His reign lasted one hundred and sixty-four years.

Al-ʿAbd ibn Abraha:

His brother al-ʿAbd ibn Abraha succeeded him. He was Dhū al-Adhʿār. He was given this name because he campaigned against the land of the Nasnās, killed a great many of them, and returned to Yemen with some of their captives, a people whose faces were on their chests. The people were terrified of them, and so he was called Dhū al-Adhʿār.

This happened during his father’s lifetime. When he became king, he suffered a stroke, and one side of his body was paralyzed before his campaign. His reign lasted twenty-five years.

Haddād ibn Sharḥabīl:

Haddād ibn Sharḥabīl ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Rāʾish succeeded him. He was the father of Bilqīs, the consort of Solomon ﵇. It is said that he married a woman of the jinn, who bore him Bilqīs. He lived only a short while before dying; when he was near death, he appointed her to succeed him.

Bilqīs:

Bilqīs ruled. She was among the finest and most intelligent and resolute people of her time. What transpired between her and Solomon ﵇—is what God Almighty has related to us in His Book. It is said that Solomon married her, and she bore him Dāwūd ibn Sulaymān, who died during his father’s lifetime.

It is also said that a man of the maqāwil married her and sent her back to her kingdom, and that he would come to her land every month.

It is said that Sulaymān’s reign lasted forty years. It is also said:

Twenty-four years.

Bilqīs died a short while after him.

Yāsir ibn ʿAmr

After her, Yāsir ibn ʿAmr ibn Yaʿfur ibn ʿAmr ibn Sharāḥbīl became king. He was known as Yāsir al-Naʿam, because of his generosity toward people. After Sulaymān ﵇—the kingship was restored to them.

He was a powerful ruler, strong in his command. He set out on a campaign toward the Maghrib, until he reached the flowing Valley of Sand. He sent an army into the sands, and they perished there; not one of them returned. He ordered a statue of copper to be made and had an inscription written on it in musnad: “There is no passage beyond me.” Then he turned back.

His reign lasted eighty-five years.

Shammar ibn Ifrīqīs

After him, Shammar ibn Ifrīqīs ibn Abraha ibn al-Rāʾish became king. He is the one called Shammar Yarʿash, because he suffered from a tremor. He set out with a great army and entered the land of Iraq. Then he headed toward China, taking the route through Persia, Sijistān, and Khurāsān. He conquered the cities and fortresses, killed and took captives, and entered the city of al-Ṣughd, which he demolished—so it was called Shammar-kand, that is, “Shammar ruined it.” People Arabized the name and said Samarqand. Then he returned. His reign lasted one hundred and thirty-seven years.

Al-Aqran ibn Shammar

After him, his son al-Aqran ibn Shammar Yarʿash became king. He campaigned against the lands of the Byzantines, whose people at that time worshipped idols. He penetrated deep into their territory, until he reached the Valley of Rubies, but died before entering it, and was buried there. His reign lasted fifty-three years.

Tubbaʿ ibn al-Aqran

After him, his son Tubbaʿ ibn al-Aqran ibn Shammar Yarʿash became king. He was Tubbaʿ the Elder and the first of the Tubbaʿs. For twenty years he remained without campaigning. Then news came to him from the Turks that displeased him, so he marched against them by way of the two mountains of Ṭayyiʾ, then al-Anbār—the route taken by al-Rāʾish. He met them on the border of Azerbaijan, defeated them, took captives from them, and returned.

Then he campaigned against China. When he returned, he left a great army stationed at al-Tibet. Their descendants in al-Tibet still know of this.

This Tubbaʿ is the one who said: [kāmil]

The sun’s turning and its risingFrom where it sets no more forbid abiding;

Its rising, white and clear,Its setting, yellow as wars dye;

It runs across the sky’s centerAs the dove of death runs through the soul.

Today we know what it brings;Yesterday passed with its judgment settled.

Some transmitters say that these verses belong to the bishop of Najrān. His reign lasted one hundred and sixty-three years.

Kulaykarib ibn Tubbaʿ the Elder

After him, Kulaykarib ibn Tubbaʿ the Elder became king. He was weak and small in ambition, and undertook no campaigns before he died. His reign lasted thirty-five years.

Tubbaʿ ibn Kulaykarib

After him, his son Tubbaʿ ibn Kulaykarib became king. He was Asʿad Abū Karib, and was Tubbaʿ the Middle. He campaigned extensively, and left no route taken by his forefathers untaken himself. He campaigned by the stars, traveling by them and conducting his affairs according to their indications. His reign grew long and his rule grew harsh. The people of Ḥimyar grew weary of him, and the burden he imposed on them through campaigning became too much. They asked his son Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ to help them kill him and make him king, but he refused. So they killed Tubbaʿ, then regretted his murder. They disagreed over whom to make king next, until circumstances compelled them to make his son Ḥassān king. They did so, taking from him a pledge that he would not hold them to account for what they had done to his father.

It is said that this Tubbaʿ was the one who believed in the Messenger of God ﷺ—and said: [mut aqārib]

I bear witness concerning Aḥmad:He is a messenger from God, who fashioned all living beings.

If my life were extended to his lifetime,I would be his minister and cousin.

It is also said that he clothed the House with al-aqṭāʿ.

It is also said that it was Tubbaʿ the Later [who did this].

The reign of Tubbaʿ the Middle lasted three hundred and twenty years.

Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ

After him, his son Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ became king. He was the one who sent an expedition against Jadīs in al-Yamāma and annihilated them. Ṭasm and Jadīs lived in al-Yamāma, and Ṭasm had a king whose conduct had become wicked. They would not marry a woman of Jadīs without sending her to him on the night she was presented to her husband, so that he would deflower her before her husband. Jadīs rose against Ṭasm while they were off their guard, killed a great many of them, and killed that king. A man of Ṭasm went to Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ to call for his aid. Ḥassān sent an army to al-Yamāma, whose name at that time was Jaww. There was a woman there called al-Yamāma, who could see a caravan from a distance of three days’ journey. Jaww was named Jaww al-Yamāma after her. When the people feared that she would see them, they cut down trees, and each man carried a tree in front of him. Al-Yamāma looked out and said, “People of Jadīs, the trees are moving toward you, and Ḥimyar is coming!” They said, “What do you mean?” She said, “I see a man among the trees carrying a shoulder blade and eating from it, or a sandal and patching it.” They disbelieved her. Ḥimyar fell upon them at daybreak and dealt them a blow that wiped them out, with only a few survivors.

The poets have told the story of the woman. Al-Aʿshā said: [basīṭ]

No sharp-lashed woman ever sawAs she saw that day, nor did the wolves see as they howled:

“She said, ‘I see a man with a shoulder blade in his hand,Or one patching a sandal—alas, what a sight!’

They disbelieved what she told them, and at daybreakThe kin of Ḥassān came, driving death and arrows toward them.”

They drove the people of Jaww from their dwellingsAnd brought down the lofty buildings, making them fall.

Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ continued to find fault with those who had killed his father. He killed them one by one, forced them to campaign, and dealt harshly with them. They went to his brother ʿAmr ibn Tubbaʿ, who made a pact with them, and they made a pact with him to kill his brother and make him king afterward. One of their nobles, a man called Dhū Raʿayn, was the exception: he forbade ʿAmr and warned him of the evil consequences, telling him that if he did it, he would be deprived of sleep. ʿAmr did not heed him and killed his brother Ḥassān.

ʿAmr ibn Tubbaʿ

ʿAmr ibn Tubbaʿ became king, but sleep deserted him. He complained of this, and was told, “Sleep will not come to you unless you kill the man who killed your brother.” He proclaimed to all the people of his kingdom, “The king wishes to make a declaration tomorrow.” They gathered, and he had men stationed for them. He sat in the royal audience chamber, then ordered them to enter in groups of five and ten. As each group entered, he led them aside and had them killed, until he had killed the greater part of the people. Then Dhū Raʿayn was brought in. When ʿAmr saw him, he remembered what Dhū Raʿayn had said and recited a verse of his poem that went: [wāfir]

“Who will trade wakefulness for sleep?Fortunate is he who lies down with a tranquil eye.

If Ḥimyar has betrayed and acted treacherously,May God’s pardon be granted to Dhū Raʿayn.”

He ordered that Dhū Raʿayn be released, honored him, brought him close, and made him one of his intimates. ʿAmr’s affairs fell into disorder, and he abandoned campaigning. He was called Mūthabān, meaning “the one who sits”: wathāb means a bed, and they meant that he kept to his bed.

During his reign, ʿAmr ibn Ḥujr al-Kindī, the grandfather of the poet Imruʾ al-Qays, married a daughter of Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ. She bore him al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥujr. ʿAmr ibn Ḥujr was the lord of Kindah, and he had served her father, Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ. In his time, ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyāʾ, his children, and those who followed him left the land of Yemen when he sensed the onset of the Flood of the Dam. ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir was the forefather of Khuzāʿah, Aws, and Khazraj. His reign lasted thirty-three years.

ʿAbd Kalāl ibn Mūthab

After him, ʿAbd Kalāl ibn Mūthab became king. He was a believer in the religion of Jesus ﵇—but concealed his faith. His reign lasted seventy-four years.

### Tubbaʿ ibn Ḥassān

After him, Tubbaʿ ibn Ḥassān ibn Tubbaʿ ibn Kulaykarib ibn Tubbaʿ ibn al-Aqran became king. He was Tubbaʿ the Younger, the last of the Tubbaʿs, and was imposing. He sent his sister’s son al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥujr al-Kindī, the grandfather of the poet Imruʾ al-Qays, to Maʿadd and made him king over them. He marched to Syria, whose kings were Ghassān, and they submitted to him. They apologized for having entered Christianity and went to his sister’s son al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, who was at al-Mishqar, in the region of Hajar. Some people came to him who had settled in Yathrib among those who had left with ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyāʾ. They had opposed the Jews in Yathrib. They complained to him about the Jews, spoke of the Jews’ poor treatment of them and their breach of the agreement they had made when the newcomers settled there, and appealed to him on the grounds of kinship. This enraged him so he marched to Yathrib and camped at the foot of Uḥud. He sent for the Jews and had three hundred and fifty of them put to death. He intended to destroy the city, but a Jew who was two hundred and fifty years old stood before him and said, “O king, a man like you does not kill in anger or accept a false report. Your rank is too great for a fit of rashness or a sudden impulse to sway you. And you will not be able to destroy this settlement.” He said, “Why not?” The man replied, “Because it is the place to which a prophet from the descendants of Ismāʿīl will migrate. He will emerge from this structure”—meaning the Sacred House. Tubbaʿ desisted, then set out for Mecca with this Jew and another learned Jew. They were the two rabbis. He came to Mecca, covered the House, and gave food to the people. He was the one who said: [khafīf]

We clothed the House that God has made sacredIn a quilted covering and striped garments.

Some people say that the one who said this was Tubbaʿ the Middle. Then he returned to Yemen with the two rabbis. He had adopted their religion and believed in Moses and what had been revealed in the Torah. The people of Yemen heard of this and disagreed with him, refusing to follow him in his religion. He put the matter to a trial by fire: the two rabbis and some of the people entered the fire. The people were burned, while the two rabbis and the Torah were unharmed. Then they submitted to him and followed him. Thus Judaism entered Yemen.

This Tubbaʿ was the one who made an alliance between Yemen and Rabīʿah.

His reign lasted seventy-eight years.

Murthid ibn ʿAbd Kalāl

After him, Murthid ibn ʿAbd Kalāl became king. He was Tubbaʿ’s maternal brother, a man of judgment, courage, and generosity. After him, the kingship of Ḥimyar broke apart, and their kings no longer ruled Yemen and its people.

His reign lasted forty-one years.

After him, his son Walīʿah ibn Murthid became king. He was intelligent and a good administrator.

His reign lasted thirty-seven years.

Abraha ibn al-Ṣabbāḥ

After him, Abraha ibn al-Ṣabbāḥ became king. He was learned and generous, and knew that kingship would belong to the Banū al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah. He therefore treated Maʿadd with honor.

He ruled for seventy-three years.

Ḥassān ibn ʿAmr ibn Tubbaʿ

Then Ḥassān ibn ʿAmr became king. He was the one to whom Khālid ibn Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb al-ʿĀmirī came with the captives of his people, and he set them free. Khālid praised him.

His reign lasted fifty-seven years.

Dhū Shanāṭir

After him, a man who was not of the royal house became king, but was one of the sons of the maqāwil. He was called Dhū Shanāṭir. He was coarse, harsh, and murderous. Whenever he heard of a boy of royal descent who had come of age, he would send for him and corrupt him. He sent for one of them, a boy called Dhū Nuwās, who had two long locks swaying over his shoulders; from them he took the name Dhū Nuwās. He was brought before Dhū Shanāṭir with a small knife concealed on him. When he approached Dhū Shanāṭir, who sought to force him into sexual intercourse, he slit open his belly and severed his head.

Dhū Shanāṭir ruled for twenty-seven years.

Dhū Nuwās

When Ḥimyar learned what Dhū Nuwās had done, they said, “We can think of no one more deserving of kingship than the man who rid us of him.” So they made Dhū Nuwās king. He was the master of the Ditch, which God Almighty mentions in His Book (1). He followed Judaism. He heard that the people of Najrān had adopted Christianity under a man who had come to them from the Āl Jafna—the kings of Ghassān—and taught them that religion. So he went there himself and brought them before trenches he had dug in the ground and filled with glowing embers. Whoever followed his religion he released; whoever remained Christian he cast into them. Then a woman was brought to him with her seven-month-old child. He said to her, “Woman, go forward in your religion, for there is no fire after this.” He cast the woman and her child into the fire and stopped.

A man from Yemen called Dhū Thaʿlabān went by sea to the king of Abyssinia, who was a Christian, and told him what Dhū Nuwās had done to the people of his religion. The king of Abyssinia wrote to Caesar and informed him of this, asking his permission to march to Yemen. Caesar wrote back, ordering him to go there and telling him that he would prevail over it. He instructed him to appoint Dhū Thaʿlabān to govern his people and to leave in Yemen whoever would remain with him. The king of Abyssinia came with seventy thousand men. Dhū Nuwās assembled his forces and fought them, but they defeated him, killed many of his men, and drove them out. Dhū Nuwās fled, with the enemy in pursuit, until he reached the sea. He plunged into it and drowned, as did the remainder of his companions. That was the last anyone saw of him.

Then Dhū Jadan al-Ḥimyarī took his place. They fought him and defeated him too, until they forced him to the sea. He plunged into it and drowned, along with the companions who followed him.

Dhū Nuwās ruled for sixty-eight years.

Kings of Abyssinia in Yemen

The Abyssinians remained in Yemen with Abraha al-Ashram, the one who intended to demolish the Kaʿbah. He marched against it with the elephant, but God destroyed his army with the birds in flocks. A gangrenous disease broke out on his body, and he was carried to Yemen, where he died.

In that era, the Prophet ﷺ—was born.

Yaksūm ibn Abraha

After him, Yaksūm ibn Abraha became king. The conduct of the Abyssinians in Yemen grew wicked, and they committed grave outrages against its people. Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan set out and went to Kisrā Anūshirwān ibn Qubādh in the last days of his reign—so say the Persians in their histories. I believe he was Hurmuz ibn Anūshirwān, according to what I found in the historical account. Sayf complained to him about the Abyssinians’ oppression and asked him to send an army to fight them. Kisrā sent with him a commander called Wahriz, with seven thousand five hundred men. They sailed toward Yemen. The people of Yemen heard of their approach, and many of them came to join them. They fought the Abyssinians, defeated them, killed them, and drove them out; not one returned to his own land. They took their women and children captive.

There is considerable disagreement about how long the Abyssinians remained in Yemen.

Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan

Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan ruled as a king appointed by Kisrā. He corresponded with him and acted on his counsel in affairs, until he was killed. The reason for his murder was that he had taken some of those Abyssinians as servants. One day they cornered him while he was out hunting and stabbed him with their spears. They killed him, They fled to the mountain peaks, and his companions pursued them and killed them all. Their affair spread throughout Yemen. They did not appoint a single ruler; rather, the people of each district appointed a man of Ḥimyar as their ruler. Thus they were like the kings of the ṭawāʾif, until God brought Islam.

It is said that Yemen remained in the hands of the kings of Persia, and that the Prophet ﷺ—appointed Bādhān, the governor of Abrawīz, over it. With him were two commanders from among Abrawīz’s commanders, named Fīrūz and Dādhūyah; they embraced Islam.

The Kings of Syria

Abū Muḥammad said:

The first of the Arabs to enter Syria were Sulayḥ, who were of Ghassān—it is also said, of Quḍāʿah. They adopted Christianity, and the king of the Romans appointed one of them as their king. His name was al-Nuʿmān ibn ʿAmr ibn Mālik. His son Mālik ruled after him, then his son ʿAmr; no others from among them ruled.

When ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyā left Yemen with his children and kin, and those of al-Azd who followed him, they went to the lands of ʿAkk. Their ruler at that time was Samlaqah. They asked him to let them stay until they could send out people to seek places for them to settle, then return to them. He gave them permission. ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir sent three of his sons—al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, Mālik ibn ʿAmr, and Ḥārithah ibn ʿAmr—and sent others as scouts. ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir died in the land of ʿAkk before his sons and scouts returned to him. He had appointed his son Thaʿlabah ibn ʿAmr as his successor. A man of al-Azd named Judhaʿ ibn Sinān contrived to kill Samlaqah, and war broke out between them. ʿAkk suffered a crushing defeat, and its people fled. This greatly grieved Thaʿlabah ibn ʿAmr, who swore that he would not remain there. He and his followers set out until they reached Mecca. Its people at that time were Jurhum, the custodians of the House. They camped at Baṭn Marr and asked Jurhum to let them stay among them. Jurhum fought them, but al-Azd prevailed, drove them out of Mecca, and Khuzāʿah took charge of the House. They remained its custodians, and their power and dominion grew, until they committed abuses and set up idols.

Then Quṣayy set out for Mecca and fought Khuzāʿah with his followers. Caesar aided him against them, and guardianship of the House passed to him and his descendants. He gathered Quraysh, who had been scattered in the outlying districts and surrounding areas; he was called Majmaʿ (“Gatherer”). Al-Azd remained for a time, but when they saw how hard it was to make a living in Mecca, they departed. Khuzāʿah, for its part, gave up guardianship of the House. Some went to al-Sawād, where they appointed Mālik ibn Fahm, father of Judhaymah ibn Mālik al-Abrash, over themselves, along with his followers.¹ Some went to Yathrib; they were al-Aws and al-Khazraj. Some went to Oman, and some went to Syria; they were the House of Jafnah, the kings of Syria.

Judhaʿ ibn Sinān, who had killed Samlaqah, also went to Syria. Sulayḥ were there, and the king of Sulayḥ wrote to Caesar seeking his permission to settle them there. Caesar granted permission on conditions that he imposed on them. Caesar’s governor came to collect their tribute and demanded it of them, among whom was Judhaʿ. Judhaʿ said to him, “Take this sword as security until we pay you.” The governor said, “Put it in such-and-such place in your mother.” Judhaʿ drew his sword and struck off his head. One of the men said:

“Take from Judhaʿ what he gives you.”

This became a proverb. The governor’s scribe went to Caesar and informed him. Caesar sent a thousand men against them, while Judhaʿ gathered from among al-Azd whoever would follow him. They fought the Romans, defeated them, seized their weapons, and grew stronger thereby. Then they moved to Yathrib, while the Banū Jafnah remained in Syria and became Christians. When Judhaʿ came to Yathrib, where the Jews were living, they entered into an alliance with them and lived among them under certain conditions. When the Jews broke the conditions, they went to the Last Tubbaʿ and complained to him. He marched against the Jews and killed some of them. This has already been mentioned. Ṭayyiʾ left the lands of Yemen a short while after ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir.

They settled in the Two Mountains, Ajāʾ and Salmā. Banū Asad entered into an alliance with them after Ṭayyiʾ had humiliated and subdued them.

The first of the House of Jafnah to rule Syria was:

al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn Muḥarriq

Genealogists differ about his lineage after ʿAmr. He was called Muḥarriq because he was the first to burn Arabs in their own lands; they are therefore called the House of Muḥarriq. He was al-Ḥārith the Elder, and his kunyah was Abū Shamir.

al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir

Then al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir ruled after him. He was al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj ibn al-Ḥārith the Elder. His mother was Māriyah Dhāt al-Qurṭayn (“Māriyah of the Two Earrings”). He was the best of their kings, the most auspicious in fortune, the farthest ranging in his raids, and the most resourceful in stratagem. He raided Khaybar and took captives from among its people, then freed them after he had returned to Syria.

Al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ marched against him with a hundred thousand men. He sent against them a hundred men, including the poet Labīd, who was then a youth. He made it appear that he had sent them only to make peace. They surrounded al-Mundhir’s pavilion and killed him, as well as those with him in the pavilion. They mounted their horses; some escaped and some were killed. The Ghassānid cavalry charged al-Mundhir’s army and routed them. Al-Ḥārith had a daughter named Ḥalīmah. That day, she perfumed the young men and dressed them in shrouds and coats of mail. The proverb “The day of Ḥalīmah is no secret” arose from this.

Among those taken captive that day were men of Banū Asad. The poet al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānī came to him and asked him to release them, so he did. ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbadah also came to him with captives from Banū Tamīm, including his brother Shaʾs ibn ʿAbadah, and he released them. ʿAlqamah said of him:

[Ṭawīl]

To al-Ḥārith, the lavish giver, I drove my she-camel,Her breast and forelegs throbbing as she went.

Among every tribe I have sought a favor,So Shaʾs has a rightful claim to some of your bounty.¹

Al-Ḥārith said, “Yes—and to a second share as well.”

al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith

Then al-Ḥārith the Younger ibn al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj ibn al-Ḥārith the Elder ruled after him. He had brothers, among them al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Ḥārith. It was of him that al-Nābighah said: [Rajaz]

This is a handsome youth,Facing good fortune, swift to maturity;

Son of al-Ḥārith the Elder and al-Ḥārith the Younger,And al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj, best of humankind.

Al-Nābighah also said of him, when he had gone on a raid: [Ṭawīl]

If al-Nuʿmān returns, we shall rejoice and be glad,And Maʿadd shall regain its kingdom and springtime.

Ghassān will regain its kingship and glory—Those are our hopes, if only we could attain them.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Ḥārith had three sons: Ḥujr ibn al-Nuʿmān, after whom he was known; al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Nuʿmān; and ʿAmr ibn al-Nuʿmān. Of them Ḥassān ibn Thābit said: [Madīd]

Who can deceive himself about Time, or trust it,After the deaths of ʿAmr and Ḥujr—

Two kings, from the Mountain of SnowTo both shores of Aylah, ruling slave and free?

Among the descendants of al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj was also ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith. When al-Nābighah parted from al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir, he went to him. Al-Nābighah said of him: [Ṭawīl]

Upon me rests a favor after favor from ʿAmr,And from his father—one free of spite.

ʿAmr was called Abū Shamir the Younger. Among his descendants were al-Mundhir ibn al-Ḥārith and al-Ayham ibn al-Ḥārith. This al-Ayham was the father of Jabalāh ibn al-Ayham. Jabalāh was the last of the kings of Ghassān. He was twelve spans tall, and when he rode, his foot brushed the ground. He lived into the time of Islam and embraced Islam during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, but then apostatized, became a Christian, and joined the Romans. The reason he became a Christian was that he was riding through the market of Damascus when his horse trod on a man. The man sprang up and slapped him. The Ghassānids seized the man and brought him before Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ. They said, “This man slapped our lord.” Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ said, “Let there be proof that this man slapped you.” He said, “What will you do with proof?” He replied, “If he slapped you, I will slap him in return.” He said, “Will he not be killed?” He replied, “No.” He said, “Will his hand not be cut off?” He replied, “No. God has commanded only retaliation; it is a slap for a slap.” Jabalāh left and went to the land of the Romans, where he became a Christian. He remained there until he died.

The Kings of al-Ḥīrah

The First of the Kings of al-Ḥīrah

Mālik ibn Fahm ibn Ghanm ibn Daws

He was of al-Azd. He had left Yemen with ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyā when they sensed the Flood of the Dam. When al-Azd reached Mecca and wrested guardianship of the House from Jurhum, they stayed for a time and then departed, except for Khuzāʿah, which remained in charge of the House. Mālik ibn Fahm went to Iraq and ruled Iraq for twenty years. Then he died, and his son ruled.

Judhaymah ibn Mālik al-Abrash

His son Judhaymah al-Abrash ruled after him. He was called al-Abrash and al-Waḍḍāḥ because he had leprosy. He used to reside at al-Anbār and go to al-Ḥīrah, then return. He would not drink in anyone’s company, out of pride; instead, he would drink with the two Furqad stars. Whenever he drank a cup, he poured a cup for each of them.

He was the first to make a mangonel, the first for whom sandals were made to fit, and the first to have candles raised for him.

He had a sister named Umm ʿAmr.

The most favored and closest of his servants was a young man of Lakhm named ʿAdī ibn Naṣr ibn Rabīʿah al-Lakhmī. It is said that his father, Naṣr, was Naṣr ibn al-Sāṭirūn, king of the Syriac people and lord of the fortress. He was a Jarmqānī from Mosul, from a district called Bājarmā. Al-Maʿārif by Ibn Qutaybah Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim used to say that ʿAdī was of Banū Qanṣ ibn Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnān, and that Judhaymah married his sister Umm ʿAmr to ʿAdī ibn Naṣr while drunk, bringing him to her, and he slept with her. When Judhaymah sobered up, he regretted it and ordered that ʿAdī be beheaded. His sister conceived ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī. Judhaymah loved him and felt tenderness toward him. Then the jinn carried him off, and Judhaymah grieved greatly at his loss, promising to grant whatever authority he asked to whoever brought him back. After some time, Mālik and ʿUqayl returned him to Judhaymah, and they claimed the right to drink in his company. It is said that they drank with him for forty years and told him stories, never repeating any to him. When they brought him back, his mother put a neck-ring on him. When his uncle saw the neck-ring and beard, he said, “ʿAmr has outgrown the neck-ring.” This became a proverb.

Judhaymah proposed marriage to al-Zabbāʾ, daughter of the king of al-Jazīrah, who had become queen after her husband. She accepted him, and he went to her. When he entered her presence, she killed him. His sister’s son ʿAmr and his servant Quṣayr sought vengeance for him. They killed her, left a man behind in her city, and returned with the spoils. This was the first booty from the Romans to be divided among the Arabs. Judhaymah’s reign lasted sixty years.

ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī

ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī, his sister’s son, ruled after him. The kings honored and feared him because of his stratagem in seeking vengeance for his uncle, which he finally achieved.

His reign lasted more than sixty years.

Imruʾ al-Qays

Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī ruled. It is also said that al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAdī ruled instead, and it is said that he was the one called Muḥarriq. Concerning them, al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur said:

[Kāmil]

What can I hope for after the House of Muḥarriq?They left their homes, and so did Iyād—

The land of al-Khawarnaq, al-Sudayr, and Bāriq,And the high-towered palace of Sindād.

al-Nuʿmān ibn Imruʾ al-Qays

Then al-Nuʿmān ibn Imruʾ al-Qays ruled after him. He was one-eyed. He was the one who built al-Khawarnaq. He was al-Nuʿmān the Elder. It is said that Anūshirwān ibn Qubādh was the one who appointed him king. One day he looked out from al-Khawarnaq at what lay around it and said, “Will all that I see come to an end and pass away?” They said, “Yes.” He said, “What good is there in something that passes away? I shall seek a life that does not pass away.” He renounced his kingship, put on sackcloth, and wandered the earth. He is the one ʿAdī ibn Zayd mentioned when he said: [Khafīf]

And the lord of al-Khawarnaq reflected¹As he looked out one day, lost in thought.

His state pleased him,² and the abundance of what he possessed,And the sea before him, and al-Sudayr.¹

Then his heart returned to reason, and he said:“What joy is there in a living soul that must die?”

al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays

Anūshirwān then made al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays, his brother, king after him. Al-Mundhir’s mother was of Banū al-Namir ibn Qāsiṭ. She was called Māʾ al-Samāʾ (“Water of the Sky”) because of her beauty and loveliness; her father was ʿAwf ibn Jashm. As for Māʾ al-Samāʾ of al-Azd, he was ʿĀmir, father of ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir, who left Yemen. ʿĀmir was called Māʾ al-Samāʾ because when rain was scarce, he would sit with his possessions around him, making his wealth stand in place of the rain. Thus he was called Māʾ al-Samāʾ, since his wealth took the rain’s place.

His son ʿAmr was called Muzayqiyā because every day he would tear apart two garments that he had worn, refusing to wear them again and disdaining that anyone else should wear them.

He said:

I have mentioned this here to distinguish between Māʾ al-Samāʾ, who was a woman, and Māʾ al-Samāʾ, who was a man.

Hind, daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr al-Kindī Ākil al-Murār, was married to al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays. It is of her that the poet says:

“If only Hind had borne three…”

Hind gave birth to three sons, one after another: ʿAmr ibn Hind, the stone-splitter; Qābūs, the wedding songstress—for he was gentle by nature—and al-Mundhir ibn al-Mundhir. Al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays remained ruler of al-Ḥīrah until al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir al-Ghassānī, that is, al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj, raided him and killed him at al-Ḥiyār.¹

al-Mundhir ibn al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays

Then his son al-Mundhir ruled after him and went out to avenge his father’s death. Al-Ḥārith also killed him, at ʿAyn Abāgh.² I have also heard some say that his killer was Murrah ibn Kulthūm al-Taghlibī, brother of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm.

ʿAmr ibn Hind

Then ʿAmr ibn Hind, the stone-splitter, ruled. He was given that name because of the force of his tread and his sternness. He was also called Muḥarriq because he burned ninety-eight men of Banū Dārim in a fire, and made up their number to a hundred with one man from al-Barājim and a woman of Nahshal. Hence it was said, “The wretched man is the emissary of al-Barājim.” One of their men had accidentally killed a son of his. He is the one who owned…

Ṭarafa and al-Mutalammis. He had written a letter for the two of them to his governor in al-Baḥrayn, making them think that he had ordered a gift for them in it, but in fact he had written to the governor commanding him to kill them.

As for al-Mutalammis, he handed his letter to a man from al-Ḥīra, who read it. When he learned what it contained, he threw it into a river near al-Ḥīra and turned back. Hence the expression “the letter of al-Mutalammis.”

As for Ṭarafa, he went on with his letter until he delivered it to the governor, who killed him. I have related their story at length and in full in the Book of the Poets.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir:

His successor as king was al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays. He was kunya-named Abū Qābūs. He was the patron of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī and the owner of the two Ghariyyān, two towers that he would stain with the blood of anyone he killed when he rode out on his Day of Misfortune. He had two days: a Day of Misfortune and a Day of Good Fortune.

On his Day of Misfortune he killed the poet ʿUbayd ibn al-Abraṣ, who had come to praise him, unaware that it was his Day of Misfortune.

He was also the killer of the poet ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī. ʿAdī was the interpreter of Abrūwīz and his secretary in Arabic. He described al-Nuʿmān to him and advised him to appoint him; he contrived matters until Abrūwīz appointed him ahead of his brothers. Al-Nuʿmān was the most blameworthy and the ugliest of them. Then al-Nuʿmān became suspicious of him and contrived against him until he had him in his power and imprisoned him. ʿAdī composed poetry in prison, and then al-Nuʿmān killed him. His son Zayd ibn ʿAdī gained access to Abrūwīz until he was given his father’s position. Zayd ibn ʿAdī spoke to Abrūwīz about al-Mundhir’s women, describing them as beautiful and accomplished. Abrūwīz wrote to al-Nuʿmān, asking for his sister or daughter in marriage.

When al-Nuʿmān read the letter, he said: “What would the king do with our women? Why does he not look to the wild cows of al-Sawād?” By “wild cows” he meant cows; that is, “Why does he not look to the women of al-Sawād, who are like wild cows?” The Arabs liken women to wild cows. Zayd distorted his words when reporting them to Abrūwīz, saying: “Why does he not look to cows, whom he cannot marry?” Abrūwīz summoned al-Nuʿmān. Al-Nuʿmān fled from him for a time, but then decided to go to him and came to him at al-Madāʾin. Abrūwīz displayed eight thousand slave girls to him in two rows. When al-Nuʿmān passed between them, they said to him: “Can the king find no use for us, apart from the cows of al-Sawād?” Al-Nuʿmān realized that he would not escape him. Kisrā ordered him imprisoned at Sābāṭ, then had him thrown beneath the feet of elephants, which trampled him until he died. Al-Aʿshā said of Abrūwīz: [ṭawīl]

He brought al-Nuʿmān into a house whose roof wasthe elephants’ breasts, after a house with a curtained canopy.

Iyās ibn Qabīṣa:

Then kingship passed out of the house of al-Mundhir, and Kisrā appointed Iyās ibn Qabīṣa al-Ṭāʾī for eight months. Kisrā’s affairs became unsettled and they were distracted; then God brought Islam. Iyās ibn Qabīṣa died at ʿAyn al-Tamr. Zayd al-Khayl said of him:

[ṭawīl]

If the Lord of ʿAyn has left his place,then every pleasure is bound to pass away.

The Deputyship

He said:

No Arabs raided the kings of al-Ḥīra more than Banū Yarbuʿ of Tamīm. They made peace with them on the condition that they be granted the deputyship and refrain from raiding the people of al-ʿIrāq.

The deputyship consisted in the king sitting with the deputy seated to his right. When the king drank, the deputy drank before the people. When the king went on campaign, the deputy sat in his place and acted as his deputy over the people until he returned. When the king’s cavalry raided, the deputy took the quarter-share! Jarīr, who was of Banū Yarbuʿ, recalled this and said: [ṭawīl]

We held the quarter-share and served as deputies to kings, so they cast their shade over us,and the unmilked camels’ udders yielded freely, their milk unrestrained.

The first of them to serve as deputy was ʿAttāb ibn Hurmī ibn Riyāḥ al-Yarbūʿī, followed by his son ʿAwf ibn ʿAttāb, then his son Yazīd ibn ʿAwf, in the time of al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ.

Al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ sent an army against Banū Yarbuʿ, commanded by his two sons Qābūs and Ḥassān. It is said that Ḥassān, his brother, sought to take the deputyship away from them. Banū Yarbuʿ fought them, and the two sides met at Ṭakhfa. Banū Yarbuʿ defeated al-Mundhir’s army and took his two sons prisoner. Al-Mundhir sent them two thousand camels as ransom for his sons and confirmed the deputyship in their hands. Jarīr said: [ṭawīl]

On the day Qābūs came, we did not grant him his wish,but we split the blades until they were shattered.

The Kings of the Persians

I read in books of the histories of the Persians:

The kings who ruled before the Kings of the Dynasties used to reside: some in Balkh, in Khurāsān; some in Bābil; and some in Fārs.

Among those who resided in Fārs was:

Jamm—whose reign lasted nine hundred and sixty years. In their account, he is the Prophet Solomon ﷺ.

Among them was:

Ṭahmūrath—who reigned for a thousand years.

Among them was:

Bīwarāsf—who reigned for a thousand years. They said: he was al-Ḍaḥḥāk al-Ḥimyarī.

Among those who resided in Khurāsān was:

Kishtāsf—the one to whom Zoroaster brought the book of the Magians. His reign lasted ninety years.

Among them was:

Bahman ibn Isfandiyār.

He lived in the time of Moses ﵇. When he learned that there was a people in the region of al-Maghrib, in the land of Ūrāshlīm, who had introduced a religion, he sent one of his commanders against them, a man called Bukht Narsī, whom they call Bukht Naṣṣar. He ordered him to kill them and take their descendants captive. He did so, expelled them from Bayt al-Maqdis, and scattered them throughout the lands.

Abū Ḥātim related to us, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said:

The people of Marw are descendants of the kings who ruled in Khurāsān before the Persians.

It was said to Kisrā: “Do you not see their beauty and bearing? Move them away from you.” So he settled them in Marw.

Affairs remained in good order until the kingship came to:

Dārā ibn Dārā.

He resided in Bābil. Alexander the Roman marched against him, seized his kingdom, and killed him. Then he entered the land of Fārs, where he carried out much killing, captivity, and destruction. He ordered their religious books burned and their fire temples demolished. In each region he installed as king one of the nobles of Fārs whom he had taken captive. Each man resisted him and defended his own domain. These were the Kings of the Dynasties, and affairs remained thus for four hundred and sixty-five years.

Ardashīr ibn Bābak ibn Sāsān was one of the Kings of the Dynasties in the land of Iṣṭakhr. They descended from the earlier kings, those who had ruled before the Kings of the Dynasties. He considered himself the heir to their kingdom. So he wrote to the Persian kings nearby and to the Kings of the Dynasties farther away, informing them of what he had resolved to undertake: the pursuit of kingship, for the sake of the subjects’ welfare and the establishment of religion and the Sunna. He wrote a letter beginning:

“In the name of God, the Possessor of mercy, the Originator of all things. From Ardashīr, deprived of his rightful due, dispossessed of his inheritance from his forefathers, calling to the establishment of God’s religion and Sunna, and seeking the aid of God, who has promised victory to those who uphold the truth and ordained success for them, to whoever among the governors of the Dynasties receives this letter of mine.

“Peace be upon you, in keeping with the measure of your recognition of the truth and your rejection of falsehood and injustice.”

Some acknowledged his authority; some held back until he came to them; and some disobeyed him, in which case their end was killing and destruction. Thus his rule became firmly established. He was the one who captured the fortress opposite Maskin, where the king of al-Sawād had taken refuge. The Arabs call it al-Sāṭirūn. Abū Duwād said:

I see death lowering from al-Ḥaḍrupon the lord of its people, al-Sāṭirūn.

His daughter had fallen in love with Ardashīr, and she showed him a vulnerable place in the city’s fortress.

He built the city of Jūr in Fārs; the city of Ažd Shabr in Fārs; Bahman Ardashīr—which is the Euphrates of al-Baṣra; and Istārābād, which is:

Karḫ Maysān, which is Kūrat Dijla; the city of the market of al-Ahwāz; the city of al-Ubulla; and other places.

His reign lasted fourteen years and six months.

Shāpūr ibn Ardashīr:

His son Shāpūr ibn Ardashīr succeeded him as king. He followed his father’s conduct and his approach to strictness and resolve. He marched to Naṣībīn, where a great number of Caesar’s troops were stationed, and besieged them until he captured it. Then he advanced deep into Roman territory and captured cities in Syria. Afterward he returned to his kingdom and distributed the captives he had with him among three cities: Jundaysābūr, Shāpūr—which is in Fārs—and Tustar, which is in al-Ahwāz.

When death approached him, he summoned his son Hurmuz, appointed him heir to his kingdom, and charged him with it.

His reign lasted thirty years and one month.

Hurmuz ibn Shāpūr:

His son Hurmuz succeeded him. He was called Hurmuz the Hero. He resembled Ardashīr in appearance, build, and courage, but he did not possess the sound judgment of his forefathers. He ruled according to a good and just policy, and built the city in Daskarat al-Malik.

His reign lasted one year and ten months.

Bahrām ibn Hurmuz:

His son Bahrām succeeded him as king. He governed with the most fitting policy and followed the example of his forefathers.

His reign lasted three years and three months.

Bahrām ibn Bahrām:

His son Bahrām ibn Bahrām succeeded him as king. He ruled well, made peace with the kings neighboring him, and left them undisturbed.

His reign lasted seventeen years.

Bahrām ibn Bahrām ibn Bahrām:

His son Bahrām succeeded him as king. He was called Shāhān Shāh.

His reign lasted four months.

Narsī ibn Bahrām:

Narsī ibn Bahrām succeeded him as king. He ruled well, and was one of the kings most beloved by his people.

His reign lasted nine years.

Hurmuzīn Narsī:

His son Hurmuzīn Narsī succeeded him as king. Before his accession he was harsh and rough, but when he became king he gave that up.

He remained king for seven years and five months.

Shāpūr ibn Hurmuz, the Possessor of the Shoulders:

When Hurmuz died, and they had no son whom they could install in his place, the people were distressed. They then asked about his wives, and were told that one of them was pregnant. They sent her this message: “Woman, a woman who has experienced pregnancy and understands women’s affairs may know the signs of male and female children. Tell us what you think the child in your womb will be.” She sent back this reply:

“From the freshness of my complexion, the movement of the fetus on my right side, and the slightness of the pregnancy and its lightness upon me, I hope that the child will be a boy.”

They rejoiced at this, placed the crown upon the woman’s belly, and continued waiting until she gave birth to a boy, whom they named Shāpūr. He was nicknamed “the Possessor of the Shoulders.” The ministers continued to manage the affairs of the kingdom, dispatch letters to the governors, collect the land tax, and carry out the administration as they had been accustomed to do, while Shāpūr was a child.

The news spread to the far reaches of the earth, and their enemies coveted their lands. The Arabs who lived near them in the regions of ʿAbd al-Qays, Kāẓima, and al-Baḥrayn advanced and seized the territories, palm groves, and trees of Fārs. They spread corruption widely. The Persians grew negligent among themselves and sent no one against them. Their kingdom continued to decline until all their enemies coveted it.

One night, while Shāpūr was asleep—by then he had lost his baby teeth and reached adolescence—he awoke to the people’s voices and commotion. He asked his attendants about it, and they informed him that it was the noise of the people on the bridge, and the shouts of those coming toward those going away, telling them to move aside. He said:

“What makes them endure this hardship, when they could put an end to it with the least effort?”

“Why do they not build two bridges, one for those coming and the other for those going—the ones returning—so that people do not crowd one another?” Those present were delighted by his words and the refinement of his intelligence at so young an age, and they built another bridge.

When he reached the age of sixteen, he ordered them to select a thousand men of proven valor for him. They did so. He provided them with stipends, then marched with them toward the regions of the Arabs who had been ravaging their land. He killed as many as he could reach, cut off their shoulders, and dried up their water sources. He took neither money nor plunder from them.

When he had finished, he said to the soldiers with him: “I want to enter Roman territory in secret, so that I may learn about it, assess the extent of their strength and equipment, and discover the routes through their lands. Once I have learned what I need, I will return to my country and then march against them with the armies.” They warned him against risking himself, but he did not accept their counsel and sent them back. He set out in disguise, entered their territory, and remained among them for a time.

While he was there, he heard that Caesar’s son had held a banquet and ordered that the poor be gathered to eat. Shāpūr went and disguised himself as a beggar. He attended the gathering and joined the meal. A cup from Shāpūr’s tableware, engraved with Shāpūr’s likeness, was brought to Caesar. His attendants used it to serve drinks. When the cup reached one of the nobles, who was skilled in physiognomy, he looked at the image on it. He had previously looked at Shāpūr’s face, and now he held the cup and said: “I see something astonishing.” Caesar said: “What is that?”

He replied: “I see among those seated here the man whose image this is!” And he pointed to Shāpūr. Caesar ordered Shāpūr brought closer to him and questioned him about himself, but Shāpūr offered various excuses. The physiognomist said to them: “Do not believe him.” They kept pressing him until he admitted that he was Shāpūr. Caesar ordered that he be placed inside a hollow cow-shaped effigy made of cowhide, then sealed him inside it.

Caesar marched with his troops to the land of Fārs, taking Shāpūr with him. He killed and laid waste in the land until he reached Jundaysābūr. He set up siege engines against it and breached its wall. One night, the men entrusted with guarding Shāpūr were careless and failed to close the opening through which his food was passed. He came out in the middle of the night, contrived to loosen his bonds, and made his way to the city gate. When the guards saw him, they shouted. He signaled for them to be quiet and told them his name. They opened the city gate for him, and he entered. Their joy grew intense and their resolve strengthened. Shāpūr said to them: “Prepare yourselves. When you hear the first sound of the Romans’ bell, mount your horses. When you hear the second, charge them.”

They did so, killing the Romans in a terrible slaughter and taking Caesar prisoner. They plundered his camp and possessions. Shāpūr said to him: “I will repay you for what you did to me, spare your life as you spared mine, and make you repair what you destroyed.” He did not let Caesar go until he had carried earth from the land of Syria and rebuilt what he had demolished.

Among what he rebuilt was the breached section of Jundaysābūr’s wall, so that part of the wall was made of mud brick and part of baked brick and plaster. For every palm tree he had cut down, he planted an olive tree, though there had been no olives in the land of Fārs. Then he released Caesar. Shāpūr marched into Roman territory, where he killed and took captives.

Then he built a city in al-Sūs and named it Fīrūz Shāpūr. He built Naysābūr, a city in Sind, and another in Sijistān. He also dug rivers, built bridges, and established villages. Old age came upon him early, and his ailments multiplied. He sent to the king of India, asking him to send a physician. The physician treated him until his nerves and skin grew firm, his eyesight improved, he became eager for women, and he was able to ride. Shāpūr treated the physician well and ordered him to choose, from his own land, a town where he might settle. He chose the city of al-Sūs, and remained there until he died. The people of al-Sūs inherited his medical knowledge, and for that reason became the physicians of the people of Persia, as well as because they inherited it from those of the Roman captives who had settled there.

The total duration of Sābūr’s reign was seventy-two years. He was the builder of the īwān at al-Madāʾin.

Ardashīr ibn Hurmuz:

Then his brother Ardashīr ibn Hurmuz ruled after him. His son Sābūr ibn Sābūr was still a boy at that time. Ardashīr continued to govern well and was approved as ruler.

His reign lasted four years.

Sābūr ibn Sābūr:

Then Sābūr ibn Sābūr ibn Hurmuz ruled after him. He governed well and dealt justly with his subjects.

His reign lasted five years and four months.

Bahrām ibn Sābūr:

Then Bahrām ibn Sābūr ruled after him, the one called Kirmān Shāh. He conducted his reign with a moderate course and good intentions, and built the city of Kirmān.

His reign lasted eleven years.

Yazdegerd ibn Bahrām:

Then Yazdegerd ibn Bahrām ruled after him.

He was harsh, severe in disposition, and exceedingly arrogant. He acted tyrannically and recklessly, and did not consult anyone about his affairs. So the people gathered and prayed to God against him, complained to Him of the injustice and oppression they suffered, and asked Him to hasten their relief from him. They related that they saw a horse approach and stop at his gate. People crowded around it, marveling at its beauty. Its owner told him about it, and he went out to look. He admired it and ordered it saddled. When it had been saddled, he stroked its face and forelock and circled around it. It struck him with a kick that pierced his heart and killed him. Then the horse filled its tracks with its droppings and could not be caught.

His reign lasted twenty-one years, five months, and eighteen days.

Bahrām Gūr ibn Yazdegerd:

Then they made his son Bahrām Gūr king after him, though they disliked him and subjected him to many ordeals. He left behind good works that raised up the weak and benefited all. He entered the land of India in disguise and remained there for some time, unrecognized, until he heard that a raging elephant had appeared there, blocking the roads and killing people. He asked them to show him where it was so that he could rid them of it. His case was brought before the king, who sent a guide with him to lead him to it. When he reached the elephant, the guide climbed a tree to watch what Bahrām would do. Bahrām shouted at the elephant, which came out to meet him. He shot it with an arrow that lodged between its eyes, and continued shooting arrows at it until he brought it down. Then he approached it, seized it until it fell, cut off its head, and brought it to the king. The king honored him and asked about his story. Bahrām told him that he was from Persia and had sought refuge with him because of something he had done. The king was angered by this. One of that king’s enemies, from among the surrounding peoples, marched against him, and he was greatly alarmed. Bahrām said to him, “Do not be dismayed by him; with God’s permission, I will deal with him for you.” Bahrām mounted in his armor and said to the Indian cavalrymen, “Guard my rear, then watch what I do before me.” They were a people unskilled in archery, and most of them were on foot. He charged the enemy and routed them, then would go to a man and strike him on the head, cleaving him in two. He would go to an elephant and strike its trunk, making it fall, then seize those riding it and kill them. He charged the horsemen, pulling a man from his horse and slaughtering him on the pommel of his saddle. He seized two men and struck one against the other until he killed them. He shot, and not a single arrow missed. They turned and fled in terror.

Bahrām’s companions charged them and killed many of them, taking their possessions as booty.

The king of India returned, married him to his daughter, and bestowed on him al-Daybul, Makrān, and their rule, along with the lands of Sind adjoining them; he had this formally witnessed.

Bahrām then returned to his kingdom, and the wealth of those lands continued to be brought to him in Persia. Then he met the king of the Turks with a large force. Despite having few soldiers, Bahrām ravaged his camp and appointed his brother Narsī over Khurāsān.

He reigned for twenty-three years.

Yazdegerd ibn Bahrām:

Then they made Yazdegerd ibn Bahrām king after him. He was well regarded. He reigned for eighteen years and five months, less some days.

When Yazdegerd died, his two sons, Fīrūz and Hurmuz, disputed the kingship. War broke out between them, until Hurmuz and three men of his household were killed, and Fīrūz gained control of the kingship.

Fīrūz ibn Yazdegerd:

Fīrūz assumed power. In the first seven years of his reign, the people suffered crop failure and drought, until they were on the brink of destruction. Then God succored them with His mercy. Once his rule was secure, he built two cities at Kaskar named after himself. Then he marched with his armies toward Khurāsān to wage war on Akhūnshuwār, king of the Hephthalites, at Balkh. The king of the Hephthalites outwitted him with a stratagem, until he overcame him while he was off his guard and weak, as were his troops. Fīrūz asked him to release him in return for his pledge never to invade him again. The king of the Hephthalites did so. But when Fīrūz returned to Persia, his pride took hold of him. He gathered troops and invaded the king treacherously. The king of the Hephthalites defeated his army, ravaged it, killed its men, and took some of his sons and relatives captive. Fīrūz perished among those who perished.

A man from Ardashīr named Sūkhra was in charge of Sīstān. He set out with those of his cavalrymen who were with him toward the Hephthalites and gathered Fīrūz’s troops around him. Then he sent word to the king of the Hephthalites, giving him a choice between war and releasing the Persian captives in his hands. The king of the Hephthalites released them. Sūkhra’s standing rose, and he returned to al-Madāʾin.

Fīrūz’s reign lasted twenty-seven years.

Then Fīrūz’s sons, Qubādh and Balāsh, disputed the kingship. Balāsh prevailed and drove Qubādh out. Qubādh fled to Khurāsān to ask the Khāqān, king of the Turks, to help and support him.

Balāsh ibn Fīrūz:

Balāsh ruled and continued to govern well, eager to develop the land. His reign lasted four years, until his death.

When Qubādh set out for Khurāsān, he stopped on the way at the house of one of the cavalrymen. He had become desirous of women, so he asked to marry the householder’s daughter. The man married her to him without knowing who he was. Qubādh spent the night with the woman, and she conceived by him. Then Qubādh went on to the Khāqān, and sought his aid, and the Khāqān kept him waiting for four years. Then he sent an army with him. On his return, Qubādh passed the house where the woman had been and found that she had given birth to a boy. He took her and the boy, who was three years old, with him. When he reached al-Madāʾin, he learned that his brother had died.

Qubādh ibn Fīrūz:

Qubādh became king. Between Persia and al-Ahwāz, he built the city of Arrajān, settling there the captives from Hamadhān. He built the city of Ḥulwān, in the direction of al-Māhābah, and another city called Qubādh-Khurrah. He was weak and ineffectual in his rule. Marduq and his companions rose up and said, “God Most High made the earth equal for His servants, but people have wronged one another, and some have taken more than their share at the expense of others. We will divide things among the people and restore to the poor their rights in the wealth of the rich.” They began entering men’s homes and taking control of their houses, their women, and their property. Some demanded Qubādh’s women, while others demanded his blood, in order to bring him into the open. They induced him to kill Sūkhra. Sūkhra’s son killed Marduq and many of his followers, together with those nobles who supported him, and restored Qubādh to his kingship. Then he plotted against Qubādh and deceived him until Qubādh killed him. Qubādh’s affairs then spread into disorder and declined; there was no stronghold in which a rebel did not rise, and he died in that state.

His reign lasted forty-three years.

Khosrow Anūshirwān ibn Qubādh:

Then Khosrow Anūshirwān ruled after him. He was the son of the woman who had borne Qubādh a child on his way to Khurāsān. He was a stern man. He restored affairs to their proper state, expelled the leaders of the Mazdakites, followed the course of Ardashīr, and conquered Antioch, where the greatest part of Caesar’s army was stationed.

He built a city called Rūmiyya near al-Madāʾin, modeled on Antioch, and settled captives there. He conquered the city of Heraclius and Alexandria, and appointed the house of al-Mundhir to rule the Arabs. He marched against the Hephthalites, enlisting the help of the Khāqān, to whom he was related by marriage, until he avenged Fīrūz. He stationed his troops at Farghāna. When he returned from Khurāsān, Ibn Dhū Yazan came to him, seeking his aid against the Abyssinians. He sent one of his commanders, named Wahriz, with an army of the Daylamites. They conquered Yemen, expelled the Blacks, and settled there.

His reign lasted forty-seven years and seven months.

Hurmuz ibn Khosrow:

Then his son Hurmuz ruled. He acted unjustly and tyrannically. The Khāqān, king of the Turks, marched against him, and Hurmuz sent Bahrām Shūbīna against him with twelve thousand men. Bahrām killed the Khāqān and ravaged his camp. Then Bahrām rebelled against Hurmuz and renounced his obedience, because of what is reported about Hurmuz’s evil conduct. The soldiers of Bahrām who were in Iraq rose up against Hurmuz, put out his eyes, and then killed him.

His reign lasted eleven years and seven months.

Hurmuz had a son named Abrawīz in Ādharbayjān. When word of his father’s fate reached him, he went to the Romans and sought help from Caesar. Caesar received him, married him to his daughter, and sent an army with him. Abrawīz set out, and Bahrām Shūbīna marched against him. They fought, and Shūbīna was defeated and fled to the Turks. He continued plotting against Shūbīna and contriving schemes until Shūbīna was killed there.

Abrawīz ibn Hurmuz—known as Khosrow:

Then Abrawīz ruled. He turned to oppression and reckless rule over his subjects, killed his father’s killers and the Mubadhān-Mubadh, withheld spending, invaded Syria, and reached Egypt. He besieged the king of the Romans at Constantinople. That king carried his treasures to the sea, but a storm blew up and cast them ashore at Alexandria, where Abrawīz’s men seized them. He called them “the Treasures of the Wind.” His reign lasted a long time, until the people grew weary of him and deposed him, after thirty-eight years of his rule.

Shīrūya ibn Abrawīz:

Then they appointed his son Shīrūya in his place. He was the grandson of Caesar through his daughter. He ordered that his father’s eyes be put out and killed eighteen of his brothers. The rest of his household fled. He reduced the burden on the people and lifted the land tax. The plague broke out, and he died among those who perished. His reign lasted five years and some months, counted from the Prophet’s arrival ﷺ—in Medina.

His reign lasted seven months.

Ardashīr ibn Shīrūya:

Then his son Ardashīr ibn Shīrūya ruled. He was seven years old. He was killed, and his reign lasted five months.

Khurrahān:

Then a man who was not of the royal house ruled after him. A woman of the royal house, named Būrān, plotted against him and killed him.

His reign lasted twenty-two days.

Khosrow ibn Qubādh:

Then a man descended from Hurmuz ruled after him, named Khosrow ibn Qubādh. He had been born in the land of the Turks and came when he heard of the discord. The king of Khurāsān rose against him and killed him.

His reign lasted three months.

Būrān:

Then Būrān, daughter of Khosrow, ruled for a year and six months. She did not collect the land tax; she distributed the wealth among the soldiers and nobles. The Prophet ﷺ—heard about her and said, “A people who entrust their affairs to a woman will not prosper.” Then a man from among Khosrow’s cousins ruled after her for two months, and was then killed.

Then Āzarmīdakht, daughter of Khosrow, ruled. She was poisoned and then died. Her reign lasted four months.

Then another man ruled for a month and was killed. When the people of Persia saw the disorder they were in, they sought a grandson of Khosrow named Yazdegerd ibn Shahrīyār and made him their king. He was fifteen years old. He remained amid the disorder at al-Madāʾin for eight years.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ arrived at al-ʿUdhayb and ordered that his wealth and treasuries be sent to China. He remained with only a small number of troops and little wealth at Nihāwand. He left at al-Madāʾin a brother of Rustam, and sent Rustam to fight Saʿd. Rustam encamped at al-Qādisiyya and remained there until he was killed. When Yazdegerd heard of this, he knew that their appointed time had run out. He set out for Fārs, then fled to Marw by way of Sīstān, where he was killed.

His reign lasted twenty years in all.
